title: Our Restaurant TV Menu Never Showed Page 5: A Polling Refresh, a Rotating Carousel and Array Identity in React
description:
We build a point-of-sale and QR menu product for cafes and restaurants. One small feature is a TV menu: a public URL that the restaurant types into the browser of the smart TV hanging in the dining room. It shows the whole menu in large type, product names on the left, prices on the right. No ordering, no clicks. Customers look at it and tell the waiter what they want.

Two requirements shaped the screen. First, the TV must never need a human. If the owner changes a price in the admin panel, the TV has to pick it up on its own, so the page polls the menu endpoint every 60 seconds. Second, the menu must never scroll. A cafe with 20 items gets one screen with big letters. A restaurant with 300 items gets split into pages, and the pages rotate every 15 seconds.

Both requirements worked in testing. Together they produced a bug that only shows up with a long menu: the TV never showed anything after page 4.

The setup

Stripped down, the component looked like this:

const [sections, setSections] = useState<Section[]>([]);
const [page, setPage] = useState(0);

// 1. Poll the menu every 60 s
useEffect(() => {
  const load = async () => {
    const menu = await api.fullMenu(slug);
    setSections(menu.sections);
  };
  load();
  const t = setInterval(load, 60_000);
  return () => clearInterval(t);
}, [slug]);

// 2. Measure rendered heights, split into pages
const pages = useMemo(() => paginate(sections, columns, measurement),
  [sections, columns, measurement]);

// 3. Data or layout changed: go back to the first page
useEffect(() => { setPage(0); }, [sections, columns, measurement]);

// 4. Rotate pages
useEffect(() => {
  if (pages.length < 2) return;
  const t = setInterval(() => setPage(p => (p + 1) % pages.length), 15_000);
  return () => clearInterval(t);
}, [pages.length]);

Effect 3 is reasonable on its own. If the owner deletes a category and the menu shrinks from 9 pages to 6, the current page index might point past the end. Resetting to page 0 when the data changes is the simple, safe answer.

What actually happened

Every 60 seconds, effect 1 called setSections with a freshly parsed array from the API. The content was identical to the previous response, but the array was new. React compares dependencies with Object.is, so to React the sections had changed.

That set off a chain:

  1. sections changed, so the measurement effect re-ran and produced a new measurement object.
  2. sections and measurement changed, so effect 3 ran and set the page back to 0.
  3. pages.length was still 9, so the rotation interval was not restarted. It just kept ticking from wherever it was.

With a 15-second page duration and a 60-second refresh, the timeline looked like this:

Time What the TV shows
0 s page 1
15 s page 2
30 s page 3
45 s page 4
60 s refresh: back to page 1
75 s page 2

A full tour of 9 pages takes 135 seconds. The refresh fired every 60. Pages 5 to 9 were never displayed. Ever. Small menus were fine because they fit on 4 pages or fewer, and so did our test data.

The bug was invisible in development for the same reason. Nobody sits and watches a carousel for two minutes. And when you reload the page to check something, you start at page 1 anyway, which looks correct.

Why the usual checks missed it

There was nothing to catch. No error, no warning, no failed request. The network tab showed a successful request every minute. React DevTools showed the component re-rendering once a minute, which is what polling is supposed to do. Each piece did what it was written to do. The bug lived in the interaction between two timers with different periods and a reset rule that treated "new object" as "new data".

For a restaurant, that means whatever sits at the end of the menu, often desserts and drinks, simply does not exist on the TV.

The fix: only touch state when the content changes

The fix was to stop handing React a new array when nothing had changed. We build a signature from the fields that actually affect what the TV draws and compare it with the last one:

const signatureRef = useRef<string>("");

const load = async () => {
  const menu = await api.fullMenu(slug);
  const next = menu.sections ?? [];
  const signature = JSON.stringify(
    next.map(s => [
      s.id, s.name, s.image,
      s.products.map(p => [
        p.id, p.name, p.price, p.isAvailable, p.soldOut, p.description,
        (p.priceOptions ?? []).map(o => [o.id, o.name, o.price]),
      ]),
    ])
  );
  if (signature !== signatureRef.current) {
    signatureRef.current = signature;
    setSections(next);
  }
};

Now an unchanged response does nothing. No new array, no new measurement, no reset. The carousel keeps rotating through all 9 pages. When the owner changes a price, the signature changes, the menu re-renders with the new price and the reset to page 1 is the correct behaviour, because the layout may have changed.

A few notes on the choice:

  • Why not compare the whole response? The API also returns things the TV ignores, such as timestamps and fields used by the ordering screen. Including them would make the signature change for reasons the customer cannot see. The signature lists exactly what is drawn.
  • Why JSON.stringify and not a deep-equal library? The menu is a few hundred products at most. Stringifying it once a minute costs less than a millisecond on a TV browser, and the code is obvious to the next person who reads it.
  • Why a ref and not state? The signature is bookkeeping. Storing it in state would itself cause a render.

The general lesson

The pattern is common: a polling hook or a WebSocket feed sets state on every message, and somewhere downstream an effect treats "the dependency changed" as "the data changed". In most components this costs an extra render and nobody notices. It becomes a bug when the downstream effect does something visible or stateful: resets a page, clears a form, scrolls to the top, restarts an animation, refetches something else.

What we check now when a component both polls and holds UI state:

  1. Does the fetch set state unconditionally? If so, ask whether an unchanged response should be a no-op. It usually should.
  2. Which effects depend on the polled data, and do any of them reset something? Reset effects are where identity changes turn into user-visible behaviour.
  3. Are there two timers with different periods? A refresh interval and a rotation interval, a refresh and a debounce, a refresh and a toast timeout. Write down the timeline for the longest realistic case, like we did in the table above. Ten seconds with a pencil would have found this bug.
  4. Test with production-sized data. A short test menu fits on a page or two. The bug needed more than four.

Libraries like TanStack Query help here because they keep referential identity for unchanged data through structural sharing. If you write the polling yourself, you get to do that part yourself.

A related design choice

The same screen does not hide sold-out products. They stay in place, dimmed, with a "SOLD OUT" label. Removing them would reflow the whole menu and move items between pages every time stock changed, which is the same kind of surprise from the customer's side: the thing you were reading a moment ago is somewhere else now.

We write about the products behind this, restaurant POS and QR menus among them, at alestaweb.com. The TV screen itself is one URL and a smart TV browser, which is about as low-tech as a feature gets. It still managed to hide more than half of a long menu.

title: Building Reliable Inventory and Booking Workflows for a Multi-Provider Rental Marketplace
description:
Introduction

At first glance, building a vehicle rental marketplace looks like a standard catalog application: let providers upload vehicles, index the attributes, and render search results. In practice, static catalog engineering breaks down the moment two customers try to book the same vehicle for overlapping dates, or when an independent fleet operator updates offline availability mid-session.

In a multi-provider ecosystem like MotoShare Gulf—which connects customers with independent vehicle owners and local rental businesses across the UAE, particularly in Dubai and Abu Dhabi—the core engineering challenge is state synchronization over time. A vehicle appearing in search results simply confirms that a listing exists and matches static filters. It does not guarantee that the physical asset is operationally ready, unencumbered by maintenance, or free of overlapping reservation holds for a specific Friday-to-Monday window.

To operate reliably, a rental marketplace requires more than a vehicle listing database. It demands consistent inventory records, date-aware availability checks, strict reservation conflict prevention, clear provider ownership boundaries, and resilient booking workflows.

Modeling a Multi-Provider Vehicle Inventory

A common early mistake in marketplace design is conflating the physical asset with the public listing. When a single table stores vehicle VINs, daily pricing, marketing descriptions, and active booking flags together, schema rigidity quickly follows. If a provider pauses a listing for seasonal maintenance or lists the same vehicle under different regional delivery terms, mutating a monolithic record risks corrupting historical reservation references.

Separating physical assets, provider ownership, commercial listings, and time-bound reservations creates a clean relational foundation:

CREATE TABLE providers (
    provider_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    business_type VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'fleet_operator' | 'individual_owner'
    verification_status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE locations (
    location_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    emirate VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL, -- e.g., 'Dubai', 'Abu Dhabi'
    zone_name VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    coordinates POINT
);

CREATE TABLE vehicles (
    vehicle_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    provider_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES providers(provider_id),
    category VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'motorcycle' | 'sports_bike' | 'standard_car' | 'luxury_car'
    make VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    model VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    model_year INT NOT NULL,
    vin_hash VARCHAR(128) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    operational_status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL -- 'active' | 'maintenance' | 'retired'
);

CREATE TABLE vehicle_listings (
    listing_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    vehicle_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicles(vehicle_id),
    location_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES locations(location_id),
    listing_status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'published' | 'unlisted' | 'suspended'
    daily_rate_minor_units BIGINT NOT NULL,
    currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AED',
    min_rental_hours INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 24
);

CREATE TABLE reservations (
    reservation_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    vehicle_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicles(vehicle_id),
    listing_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicle_listings(listing_id),
    customer_id UUID NOT NULL,
    start_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    end_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'held' | 'confirmed' | 'cancelled' | 'completed'
    hold_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(128) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT valid_period CHECK (end_at > start_at)
);

Notice that reservations references both listing_id (capturing the commercial terms at booking time) and vehicle_id (anchoring availability to the physical unit). Even if a provider edits pricing or unpublishes a listing later, the underlying physical vehicle identity and provider ownership remain immutable for active and historical bookings.

Designing Date-Based Availability Checks

Availability in a rental system is never a boolean column (is_available = true). Instead, availability is a derived query across multiple state layers:

  1. Listing Visibility: Controls whether customers can discover the listing (published vs. unlisted).
  2. Operational Availability: Reflects whether the physical vehicle is roadworthy or blocked by the provider for servicing, inspection, or offline use.
  3. Temporary Reservation Holds: Short-lived locks created when a customer initiates checkout or awaits provider approval.
  4. Confirmed Reservations: Committed bookings that block the vehicle for the requested interval, plus any mandatory turnaround buffer for cleaning and inspection.
  5. Cancelled or Expired Reservations: Historical records that no longer block calendar intervals once transitioned out of active states.

Two half-open time intervals $[A_{\text{start}}, A_{\text{end}})$ and $[B_{\text{start}}, B_{\text{end}})$ overlap if and only if:

$$A_{\text{start}} < B_{\text{end}} \quad \text{AND} \quad A_{\text{end}} > B_{\text{start}}$$

Using half-open intervals allows back-to-back bookings (e.g., Reservation A ends at 10:00, Reservation B starts at 10:00) without false conflicts, though production systems typically inject an explicit turnaround buffer (such as 2 hours) to end_at before running the check.

interface TimeWindow {
  startAt: Date;
  endAt: Date;
}

interface ExistingBooking {
  id: string;
  startAt: Date;
  endAt: Date;
  status: 'held' | 'confirmed' | 'cancelled' | 'completed';
  holdExpiresAt?: Date;
}

/**
 * Illustrative overlap check.
 * Assumptions: Timestamps are normalized to UTC; turnaround buffers are pre-applied.
 * Limitations: In-memory evaluation only; must be paired with database-level locking
 * to prevent race conditions between read and write operations.
 */
function isVehicleAvailable(
  requested: TimeWindow,
  bookings: ExistingBooking[],
  now: Date = new Date(),
  turnaroundBufferMs: number = 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000
): boolean {
  if (requested.endAt <= requested.startAt) {
    throw new Error('Invalid rental period: endAt must be after startAt');
  }

  for (const booking of bookings) {
    if (booking.status === 'cancelled' || booking.status === 'completed') {
      continue;
    }

    // Ignore expired temporary holds even if a background cleanup worker has not run yet
    if (
      booking.status === 'held' &&
      booking.holdExpiresAt &&
      booking.holdExpiresAt <= now
    ) {
      continue;
    }

    const effectiveEnd = new Date(booking.endAt.getTime() + turnaroundBufferMs);

    const overlaps =
      requested.startAt < effectiveEnd && requested.endAt > booking.startAt;

    if (overlaps) {
      return false;
    }
  }

  return true;
}

Evaluating holdExpiresAt <= now directly inside the availability predicate ensures stale holds release capacity immediately at the exact millisecond of expiration, rather than relying solely on asynchronous cron jobs.

Preventing Double Bookings

When two customers attempt to book the same vehicle for overlapping dates within milliseconds of each other, standard SELECT followed by INSERT application logic fails due to Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race conditions. Both transactions read zero conflicts simultaneously and both insert confirmed rows.

Backend engineers have several mechanisms to prevent double bookings, each carrying distinct trade-offs:

Mechanism How It Works Trade-Offs
Database Exclusion Constraints Uses PostgreSQL EXCLUDE USING GIST on tstzrange(start_at, end_at) scoped by vehicle_id. Guarantees zero overlapping active rows at the storage engine level; requires careful indexing when filtering out cancelled states.
Pessimistic Row Locking Executes SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the parent vehicles row before checking reservations. Serializes concurrent booking attempts per vehicle cleanly; increases lock contention on high-demand vehicles during traffic spikes.
Optimistic Concurrency Control Uses a version integer on the vehicle calendar and retries on UPDATE ... WHERE version = expected. High throughput under low contention; requires retry loops and degrades under heavy flash-crowd contention.
Temporary Holds + TTL Places a 10–15 minute held state during payment or provider review, paired with an idempotency key. Prevents users from losing a vehicle mid-checkout; introduces inventory lockup if malicious clients hoard holds without paying.

In practice, combining pessimistic locking on the parent vehicles record inside an ACID transaction with idempotency keys provides deterministic safety without complex retry storms:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import psycopg2

def create_reservation_hold(
    conn,
    vehicle_id: str,
    listing_id: str,
    customer_id: str,
    start_at: datetime,
    end_at: datetime,
    idempotency_key: str,
    hold_minutes: int = 15,
) -> dict:
    """
    Illustrative transactional reservation hold using PostgreSQL row-level locking.
    Assumptions: PostgreSQL database with READ COMMITTED isolation; UTC timestamps.
    Limitations: Serializes concurrent requests for the same vehicle_id; requires
    external payment/provider confirmation flow to promote 'held' to 'confirmed'.
    """
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    hold_expires_at = now + timedelta(minutes=hold_minutes)

    with conn:  # Begins transaction; commits on exit, rolls back on exception
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            # 1. Idempotency check for safe client retries
            cur.execute(
                """
                SELECT reservation_id, status
                FROM reservations
                WHERE idempotency_key = %s
                """,
                (idempotency_key,),
            )
            existing = cur.fetchone()
            if existing:
                return {"reservation_id": existing[0], "status": existing[1], "replayed": True}

            # 2. Lock parent vehicle row to serialize concurrent booking requests
            cur.execute(
                """
                SELECT operational_status
                FROM vehicles
                WHERE vehicle_id = %s
                FOR UPDATE
                """,
                (vehicle_id,),
            )
            vehicle = cur.fetchone()
            if not vehicle or vehicle[0] != "active":
                raise ValueError("Vehicle is not operationally available")

            # 3. Check for overlapping active holds or confirmed reservations
            cur.execute(
                """
                SELECT 1
                FROM reservations
                WHERE vehicle_id = %s
                  AND status IN ('confirmed', 'held')
                  AND (status = 'confirmed' OR hold_expires_at > %s)
                  AND start_at < %s
                  AND end_at > %s
                LIMIT 1
                """,
                (vehicle_id, now, end_at, start_at),
            )
            if cur.fetchone():
                raise RuntimeError("Booking conflict: overlapping reservation exists")

            # 4. Insert temporary hold atomically
            cur.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO reservations (
                    vehicle_id, listing_id, customer_id,
                    start_at, end_at, status, hold_expires_at, idempotency_key
                )
                VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, 'held', %s, %s)
                RETURNING reservation_id
                """,
                (
                    vehicle_id,
                    listing_id,
                    customer_id,
                    start_at,
                    end_at,
                    hold_expires_at,
                    idempotency_key,
                ),
            )
            reservation_id = cur.fetchone()[0]
            return {"reservation_id": reservation_id, "status": "held", "replayed": False}

Managing Multiple Provider Workflows

A multi-provider marketplace rarely serves a uniform supplier base. Commercial rental agencies manage multi-car fleets with dedicated dispatch teams, whereas individual owners listing a personal motorcycle or weekend sedan operate asynchronously and may require manual review before accepting a handoff.

If both the marketplace platform and the provider can mutate availability arbitrarily without clear boundaries, split-brain inventory states occur. Effective systems enforce strict ownership and event boundaries:

  • Provider-Scoped Mutations: Authorization middleware must enforce that provider_id claims match the owner of the target vehicle_id before allowing updates to pricing, pickup locations, or maintenance blocks.
  • Request-to-Book vs. Instant-Book Modes: Depending on provider settings, a customer request either confirms immediately upon payment authorization or transitions into a pending_provider_approval hold with a strict SLA timer.
  • Out-of-Band Availability Sync: When a local fleet operator rents a car to a walk-in customer, they must be able to create an offline_block interval on the vehicle calendar. If an offline block overlaps an unconfirmed hold, the system should automatically void the hold and notify the customer before payment capture.

* Symmetric Cancellation Handling: Cancellations initiated by either party must trigger deterministic state transitions, release date intervals atomically, and emit domain events for refund calculation and search index updates.

Designing a Search and Discovery Layer

Search queries in a regional rental marketplace combine geospatial filters, vehicle taxonomy, and temporal availability. A user browsing for motorcycle rental Dubai has fundamentally different discovery constraints than someone comparing options for car rental Abu Dhabi, motorcycle rental Abu Dhabi, or car rental Dubai.

To keep search latency low without serving stale availability, engineering teams typically separate discovery into two stages:

  1. Candidate Filtering (Search Index): An inverted index (such as OpenSearch or Elasticsearch) filters listings by emirate, delivery radius, category, pricing tier, and listing_status = 'published'.
  2. Real-Time Availability Verification (Relational Store): Before rendering final bookable badges or accepting a checkout intent, the API cross-references candidate vehicle_ids against the authoritative reservations table for the user's exact [start_at, end_at) window.

Displaying clear UI distinctions—such as "Available for your dates" versus "Listed in Dubai — select dates to verify availability"—prevents user frustration when popular vehicles are already booked during peak holiday weekends.

Handling Different Vehicle Categories

Treating every vehicle as a generic row with make, model, and daily_rate breaks down across diverse automotive segments. Two-wheelers, daily commuters, and high-value performance vehicles require category-specific schemas and validation rules:

  • Motorcycles and Sports Bikes: Search intents like Ducati motorcycle rental Dubai or sports bike rental Abu Dhabi involve rider-specific constraints that do not apply to sedans. Data models must capture engine displacement (cc), seat height, ABS/traction control equipment, included riding gear, and motorcycle-specific license class endorsements.
  • Standard Passenger Cars: Queries for car rental Dubai or car rental Abu Dhabi emphasize seating capacity, luggage volume, transmission type, fuel policy, and daily mileage allowances.
  • Luxury and Exotic Vehicles: Customers searching for luxury car rental Dubai or luxury car rental Abu Dhabi encounter stricter risk controls. The booking engine must enforce higher security deposit holds, minimum driver age thresholds (often 25+), multi-year license tenure checks, and higher excess mileage rates.

Using a JSONB category_attributes column paired with versioned JSON Schema validation per vehicle category allows the platform to enforce strict domain rules without proliferating dozens of sparse, nullable columns. Note that category taxonomy defines how vehicles are validated and discovered—it never implies live availability for any specific model until date-range checks pass.

Marketplace Architecture and Technology Choices

To isolate read-heavy discovery traffic from write-critical reservation transactions, a modular service boundary is effective. Note that the following diagram represents a conceptual architecture recommendation for marketplace engineers—not a claim regarding MotoShare Gulf's internal infrastructure or software stack.

Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Boundaries

  • Synchronous Paths: Availability checks, reservation hold creation, idempotency verification, and payment authorization must execute synchronously so the user receives immediate, deterministic feedback.
  • Asynchronous Paths: Search index updates, provider SMS/email notifications, invoice PDF generation, and analytics aggregation should run asynchronously via a transactional outbox pattern. If a notification provider experiences latency, it should never block or roll back a committed database reservation.

Supporting Rental Business Operations

For local rental agencies and independent fleet owners, marketplace visibility is only half of the operational picture. Providers still need day-to-day operational tooling to track fleet maintenance schedules, manage active reservation calendars, verify customer documents, reconcile security deposits, and monitor fleet utilization.

In its public positioning, MotoShare Gulf advertises free vehicle rental management software UAE alongside its consumer marketplace to help local rental businesses digitize fleet records, bookings, and daily operations. From a systems engineering perspective, unifying provider fleet management with marketplace availability eliminates the primary source of double bookings: manual spreadsheet syncs between an agency's back-office desk and its online listings. When a provider logs a walk-in booking or scheduled service directly inside their fleet dashboard, the underlying vehicle calendar updates immediately across all channels.

Engineering Lessons for Marketplace Developers

  1. Treat availability as date-dependent data. Never store availability as a static boolean flag on a vehicle record; always compute it against half-open time intervals and active reservation states.
  2. Keep reservation state transitions explicit. Enforce a strict finite state machine (held → confirmed → completed / cancelled) so invalid transitions—such as confirming an expired hold—fail fast.
  3. Protect booking operations against concurrency. Pair database-level locking or exclusion constraints with client idempotency keys to eliminate race conditions during simultaneous booking requests.
  4. Separate provider ownership from customer-facing listings. Anchor reservations to immutable physical vehicle IDs and provider ownership records rather than mutable marketing listings.
  5. Make failure and cancellation workflows part of the original design. Build hold expiration, offline provider blocks, and symmetric cancellation rollbacks into day-one schemas rather than patching them in after launch.

Conclusion

Reliable rental marketplaces—whether serving commercial fleets or peer-to-peer car rental UAE networks—succeed on data integrity rather than catalog volume alone. When inventory models separate physical vehicles from commercial listings, availability queries evaluate overlapping intervals accurately, and reservation writes execute inside atomic transactions, both providers and renters gain predictable outcomes. For backend engineers building two-sided booking platforms, investing early in explicit state machines and concurrency control prevents the edge-case failures that erode marketplace trust at scale.

title: How to Find Exposed API Keys in Your Vibe Coded App (a 5 Minute Check)
description:
If you built your app with Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Cursor or v0, there's a real chance something secret ended up in the code your browser downloads. Not because you did anything dumb. The AI just put the key where it made the feature work.

Short answer: to find exposed API keys in a vibe coded app, open your live site, open DevTools, press Ctrl+Shift+F (Cmd+Option+F on Mac) and search every loaded file for strings like sk_, sk-, service_role and secret. If a secret key shows up, it's public. Move it to the server and rotate it today.

That's the whole idea. Below is how I actually do it, what the results mean, and what to do if you find something.

Why vibe coded apps leak API keys

When you ask an AI builder to "add Stripe" or "call OpenAI", the fastest working version often calls the API straight from the frontend. It works on the first try, so nobody looks again.

The problem is that anything in your frontend is shipped to every visitor. Minified, sure. Hidden, no. Anyone can open DevTools and read it.

Build tools make this easy to miss. In Vite, any env variable that starts with VITE_ gets bundled into the client code (Vite docs). In Next.js it's the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix (Next.js docs). So VITE_OPENAI_KEY in your .env file isn't private. It's in the bundle.

The 5 minute exposed API keys check

You don't need any tool for this. Just Chrome or any Chromium browser.

  1. Open your live site, not localhost. Log in if most of the app sits behind a login, because some code only loads after that.
  2. Open DevTools (F12, or right click and Inspect).
  3. Press Ctrl+Shift+F on Windows/Linux or Cmd+Option+F on Mac. This opens a search across every file the page loaded.
  4. Search these one at a time:
    • service_role
    • sk_live and sk_test
    • sk- (OpenAI style keys start like this)
    • secret
    • apikey and api_key
    • Bearer
  5. Click around the app a bit, open the main pages, then search again. Lazy loaded chunks only show up after you visit them.
  6. Open the Network tab, reload, and click a couple of requests to your own API or to third party APIs. Look at the request headers. If an Authorization header carries a secret key from the browser, that key is public too.

Most of the time you'll get matches. Don't panic yet. Some keys are supposed to be there.

Which keys are fine to be public (and which aren't)

Usually fine in the browser:

  • The Supabase anon (publishable) key. Supabase built it to be public, and your Row Level Security policies are what protect the data (Supabase docs on API keys). Fine, as long as RLS is actually on.
  • Stripe publishable keys that start with pk_. Those are made for the frontend (Stripe docs).
  • The Firebase web config object. It identifies your project, and Firebase Security Rules do the protecting.

Never in the browser:

  • The Supabase service_role (secret) key. It skips RLS completely. Anyone with it can read and write every table.
  • Stripe secret keys, sk_live_ or sk_test_. Stripe's own docs say to keep them on the server.
  • OpenAI, Anthropic or any other AI API key. Someone copies it, and you pay for their usage.
  • Email provider keys (Resend, SendGrid, etc). These can send mail as your domain.

What to do if you find an exposed key

I'd do it in this order:

  1. Rotate the key first. Make a new one in the provider dashboard and delete the old one. Removing it from the code is not enough, because the old bundle may still be cached, and the key may already be in your git history.
  2. Move the call to the server. A Supabase Edge Function, a Next.js API route, a Replit backend route, whatever your stack has. The browser calls your endpoint, your endpoint holds the key.
  3. Check usage. Look at the provider dashboard for calls you don't recognize. For AI keys, set a hard monthly spend limit if the provider has one.
  4. Search again. Redeploy, hard refresh, run the Ctrl+Shift+F check one more time.

A prompt that usually works in Lovable, Bolt or Cursor:

Move every call that uses a secret API key out of the frontend into a server side function. The frontend should call that function instead. Read the key from a server only environment variable, not one with a VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix. Show me which files you changed.

Then check what it did. Don't just trust the "done!" message.

Exposed API keys checklist (copy this)

  • [ ] Ran Ctrl+Shift+F on the live site for service_role, sk_, sk-, secret, apikey, Bearer
  • [ ] Logged in and visited the main pages, then searched again
  • [ ] Checked Network tab request headers for secret keys
  • [ ] No secret keys in env variables that start with VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_
  • [ ] Any exposed key was rotated, not just deleted from code
  • [ ] Secret calls now go through a server function
  • [ ] Spend limits set on AI and email providers
  • [ ] RLS is on for every Supabase table (since the anon key is public anyway)

FAQ

Is the Supabase anon key safe to expose?

Yes, it's designed to be public. But it's only safe if Row Level Security is enabled with real policies on every table. With RLS off, the anon key can read your tables.

Can someone really find my API key in minified JavaScript?

Yes. Minifying shortens variable names, it doesn't hide strings. A key stays a plain string, and the DevTools search finds it in seconds.

I deleted the key from my code. Am I safe?

Not yet. Rotate it. Old builds, caches and git history can still have the old key.

Does this check cover everything?

No. It catches keys sitting in the frontend. It won't tell you if your database rules let user A read user B's data, which is the other big one in vibe coded apps.

A free self-check for the rest

I built ShipShield after seeing the same handful of problems over and over in AI-built apps. The free self-check is 10 yes/no questions, takes about two minutes, and needs no signup. It covers exposed keys plus the things this post doesn't, like RLS and who can see whose data.

You can run it here: shipshield.app

If you run the Ctrl+Shift+F check and find something weird, tell me in the comments. I'm curious what people actually find.

title: I Discovered How AI Coding Assistants Are Changing Software Development
description:
A few years ago, building software meant spending hours writing code, searching through documentation, debugging errors, and figuring out why a particular function refused to work. Even a relatively small feature could take an entire afternoon, especially when I encountered unfamiliar frameworks or programming concepts.

Today, things are changing.

AI coding assistants are becoming an important part of modern software development. They can suggest code, explain complicated functions, identify potential bugs, generate tests, and help developers move from an idea to a working solution much faster.

What interests me most is not simply how quickly these tools can generate code. It's how they're changing the way developers approach problems, learn new technologies, and manage their everyday work.

After exploring this growing technology, I found several interesting ways AI coding assistants are influencing software development.

1. Developers Can Spend Less Time Writing Repetitive Code

One of the first things I noticed about AI coding assistants is their ability to handle repetitive programming tasks.

Developers regularly write similar functions, validation rules, API requests, and database queries. Although these tasks are necessary, they can consume valuable time that could be spent solving more meaningful problems.

AI assistants can generate initial versions of these components based on simple instructions.

For example, a developer can describe a function that validates an email address or processes a user registration form. The assistant can suggest a possible implementation within seconds.

This doesn't mean developers should blindly accept everything generated. Instead, they can use the suggestions as a starting point, review the logic, and make adjustments according to the project's requirements.

I see this as one of the biggest advantages of AI-assisted development: less time spent on repetitive work and more time available for creative problem-solving.

2. Debugging Is Becoming More Accessible

Finding bugs can sometimes be more frustrating than writing the original code.

A small mistake in a variable, missing condition, or incorrect dependency can affect an entire application. Developers may spend considerable time tracing the problem before discovering its actual cause.

AI coding assistants can make this process easier by examining error messages, reviewing relevant code, and suggesting possible solutions.

For example, when a developer encounters an unexpected API response, they can provide the error message and relevant code to an AI assistant. The tool may identify an incorrect request format, missing parameter, or potential issue with the response handling.

What I find particularly useful is the ability to ask follow-up questions.

Instead of receiving only a suggested correction, developers can ask why the error occurred and how the proposed solution works. This turns debugging into a learning opportunity.

However, AI-generated explanations should still be checked against the actual application behavior. A convincing explanation does not always mean the suggested fix is correct.

3. Learning New Programming Languages Have Become Easier

Learning a new programming language or framework can feel overwhelming, particularly for beginners.

There are unfamiliar concepts, complicated documentation, and hundreds of examples to understand. Even experienced developers can struggle when switching to an entirely different technology stack.

AI coding assistants can act like interactive learning partners.
A beginner can ask for an explanation of a Python function, request a simple JavaScript example, or compare two approaches to solving the same problem.

For instance, instead of simply asking an AI tool to generate a React component, a learner can ask it to explain each section of the component and describe how the different parts interact.

This approach makes learning more practical because users can explore concepts through questions and examples.

I believe this is particularly valuable for people who want to develop their programming skills independently. The important thing is to understand the generated code rather than depending on it without learning the underlying concepts.

4. AI Is Helping Developers Work Across Different Technologies

Modern applications rarely depend on a single programming language or technology.

A typical project might involve a frontend framework, backend services, databases, APIs, authentication systems, and third-party integrations.
Working across all these components requires developers to understand how different technologies communicate.

AI coding assistants can help explain unfamiliar code, suggest integration approaches, and generate examples for different parts of an application.

For example, imagine developing an online shopping platform. The project may require product filtering, user authentication, payment integration, and inventory management.

An AI assistant can help developers explore possible approaches for each feature, generate sample API requests, and identify areas that need additional validation.

This can be useful in projects involving different business requirements, including ecommerce platforms such as ClothingRIC, where product discovery, customer experience, and website functionality all contribute to the overall shopping journey.

The assistant does not replace the need for proper architecture or technical decisions, but it can make exploring different implementation options easier.

5. Testing and Documentation Are Getting More Attention

Testing and documentation are essential parts of software development, but they are not always the most exciting tasks.

When deadlines become tight, developers may focus heavily on building features and leave documentation or additional testing until later.

AI coding assistants can help improve this process.
They can suggest unit tests, identify missing test scenarios, generate sample test data, and create initial documentation based on existing code.

For example, if a developer creates a function that calculates shopping cart totals, an AI assistant can suggest tests covering:

  • Empty shopping carts.
  • Multiple products.
  • Different quantities.
  • Discount calculations.
  • Invalid or missing values.

These examples can help developers consider situations they might otherwise overlook.

AI can also generate explanations of functions and suggest README sections describing installation instructions, dependencies, and usage.
Still, generated tests need to be reviewed. A test that simply confirms the current implementation is not necessarily a test that verifies the intended business requirements.

6. Popular AI Coding Assistants Are Offering Different Workflows

As I explored AI-assisted development, I noticed that different tools focus on slightly different workflows.

Some are designed to provide suggestions directly inside code editors, while others offer conversational coding experiences or more advanced assistance with entire projects.

A few notable examples include:

GitHub Copilot: https://github.com/features/copilot

GitHub Copilot helps developers with code completion, suggestions, and AI-assisted development directly within supported development environments.

Cursor: https://cursor.com/

Cursor is an AI-powered code editor that helps developers understand, modify, and work with codebases through AI-assisted interactions.

Claude Code: https://www.claude.com/product/claude-code

Claude Code provides an agentic coding workflow that can help developers explore codebases, edit files, and work through development tasks.

Windsurf: https://windsurf.com/

Windsurf offers an AI-powered development environment designed to help developers work with code through contextual assistance and agentic workflows.

What I find interesting is that these tools are not necessarily competing to solve exactly the same problem. Their features and workflows differ, so the right choice depends on the developer's experience, project complexity, preferred editor, and working style.

7. AI-Generated Code Still Needs Human Review

While AI coding assistants offer impressive capabilities, I don't think developers should treat them as completely reliable programming partners.

AI-generated code can contain incorrect assumptions, inefficient logic, security vulnerabilities, or compatibility problems.

For example, an assistant might generate a database query that works with sample data but performs poorly when the application handles thousands of records.

Similarly, generated authentication code may appear functional while overlooking important security requirements.

This is why human review remains essential.

Before using generated code in a real project, developers should:

  • Check whether the solution meets the actual requirements.
  • Review security and data-handling practices.
  • Test edge cases and unexpected inputs.
  • Check performance and scalability.
  • Verify compatibility with existing dependencies.
  • Understand the code before deploying it.

Another important consideration is privacy. Developers should avoid sharing passwords, API keys, customer information, or confidential source code with AI tools unless the relevant service and organizational policies explicitly permit it.

AI can speed up development, but responsibility for the final software still belongs to the people building and maintaining it.

8. The Developer's Role Is Evolving, Not Disappearing

One question I frequently come across when exploring AI development is whether these tools will eventually replace software developers.
My perspective is that the more important change is happening in the nature of the work itself.

Developers may spend less time manually producing repetitive code and more time understanding requirements, reviewing generated solutions, designing systems, testing functionality, and making architectural decisions.

Problem-solving, critical thinking, communication, and technical judgment are becoming even more important.

AI can suggest several ways to implement a feature, but developers must decide which approach is appropriate for the application.

A tool can generate a function, but understanding how that function affects the entire system requires broader technical knowledge.

This is why I believe learning programming fundamentals remains important, even as AI tools become more capable.

Final Thoughts: AI Is Changing How We Build Software

Exploring AI coding assistants has changed how I think about the future of software development.

These tools are making programming workflows more accessible, helping developers investigate errors, supporting learning, and reducing the time required for repetitive tasks.
However, faster code generation does not automatically mean better software.

The strongest results come when developers combine AI assistance with technical knowledge, careful testing, security awareness, and independent judgment.

I see AI coding assistants as tools that can strengthen a developer's capabilities rather than eliminate the need for developers.
The real advantage will belong to people who know how to ask better questions, evaluate AI-generated suggestions, and turn those suggestions into reliable solutions.

I'm curious: Have you started using AI coding assistants in your development workflow? Do they genuinely save you time, or do you find yourself spending more time reviewing and correcting their suggestions?

title: The EU Has an AI Act, the UK Has Regulators and No Bill
description:
Next Friday I start reading the AI Act one article at a time, and a single article is hard to follow without knowing where it sits, so this week is an overview of both regimes. The EU has one regulation of 113 articles that applies in every member state. The UK regulates AI through the laws and regulators it already had. Software sold in both has to satisfy both.

The EU's regulation is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, amended in July by the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. What it asks of you depends on who you are, what your system does, and when.

Who you are

Almost every duty in the Act is addressed to a provider or a deployer, so the two definitions in Article 3 decide most of what follows. Here they are, verbatim, in the format every article gets from next week. Select any part of the text and its plain reading and notes open underneath.

{{< act-excerpt act="article-3" >}}

You can be a provider without training a model. If your product calls a model API and shows the result to people under your name, you developed an AI system and put it on the market. The company that trained the model is the provider of a general-purpose AI model, which is a separate role with separate duties.

There are four more roles. An authorised representative is a person or company in the EU with a written mandate to act for a provider outside it. An importer brings a non-EU company's system onto the EU market. A distributor is anyone else in the supply chain who makes a system available. A product manufacturer puts an AI system on the market inside its own product. The Act calls all six "operators" (Article 3(8)).

What the system does

The Act sorts AI systems by what they are used for, and the duties rise with the risk.

  • Prohibited practices (Article 5). Banned outright since 2 February 2025: manipulative techniques that cause harm, social scoring, untargeted scraping of faces, emotion recognition at work and in schools, and several more. The Omnibus adds two more: systems that generate non-consensual intimate imagery, and systems that generate child sexual abuse material.
  • High-risk systems (Article 6). There are two ways a system becomes high-risk. The first is being a safety component of a product already regulated under the laws in Annex I, such as medical devices, machinery and toys. The second is a use listed in Annex III, which has eight areas, among them biometrics, employment, education, law enforcement and access to essential services, which is where credit scoring sits. Most of the Act's length is about these systems: risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, technical documentation and a conformity assessment before the system goes on the market.
  • Transparency duties (Article 50). Chatbots have to say they are AI, generated content has to carry a machine-readable mark, and deep fakes have to be labelled. This applies whatever the risk tier.
  • General-purpose AI models (Articles 51 to 55). Duties on the companies that train the models: technical documentation, a summary of the training content, a copyright policy, and more for models classified as carrying systemic risk.
  • Everything else. No obligations beyond AI literacy (Article 4), with voluntary codes of conduct encouraged under Article 95.

The fines follow the same order (Article 99). A prohibited practice costs up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Most other breaches, Article 50 included, cost up to €15 million or 3%. Giving a regulator incorrect or misleading information costs up to €7.5 million or 1%. For SMEs, and since the Omnibus for small mid-caps too, it is whichever figure is lower.

When it applies

The Act arrives in stages, and the Omnibus moved the biggest one. The high-risk obligations for Annex III systems were due on 2 August 2026 and now apply from 2 December 2027.

Date What applies
2 February 2025 The prohibitions in Article 5, and AI literacy in Article 4
2 August 2025 Duties for general-purpose AI models, the governance bodies, and penalties
27 July 2026 The Omnibus in force. Article 4 now asks providers and deployers to "take measures to support the development of AI literacy" and no longer to ensure it
2 August 2026 The Act's general application date, which brings in Article 50, and the Commission's power to fine model providers
2 December 2026 The end of the grace period for marking content from generative systems already on the market on 2 August, and the two new prohibitions
2 August 2027 Each member state has at least one AI regulatory sandbox running. General-purpose models already on the market before August 2025 have to comply
2 December 2027 High-risk obligations for Annex III systems
2 August 2028 High-risk obligations for systems in Annex I products
2 August 2030 Older high-risk systems intended for use by public authorities have to comply

The Commission fills in the detail with guidelines and codes of practice. For Article 50 there are guidelines published on 20 July 2026 and a Code of Practice finalised on 10 June. For general-purpose models there is a code of practice from July 2025. The guidelines on what counts as high-risk under Article 6 were published as a draft on 19 May 2026 and were still a draft when I checked on 12 November.

Who enforces it

Each member state names market surveillance authorities, and they enforce the Act for most systems. The AI Office, inside the Commission, has exclusive power over general-purpose AI models. The Omnibus gave it more: it is now also the only enforcer for AI systems built on a general-purpose model by the same provider, with exceptions that include products under Annex I and critical infrastructure, and for AI systems that are part of a very large online platform or search engine (Article 75(1)). A company that builds on its own model and sells across the EU is regulated by the AI Office rather than a national authority.

The UK has no AI act

The UK's approach comes from a white paper of March 2023, A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation. It gives existing regulators five principles to apply in their own sectors: safety, security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress. The principles are not law. The ICO applies them to personal data, the FCA to financial services, the CMA to competition, Ofcom to communications and the MHRA to medical devices, each using the powers it already had.

A bill has been discussed for two years and has not appeared. The King's Speech of 13 May 2026 contained no AI bill. Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights recommended one in September, and this month the AI minister said the government would look at regulation for the most advanced models if it turned out to be needed. I could find no bill, consultation or timetable.

Three things in the UK are more definite: the new rules on automated decisions, the AI Security Institute and copyright.

Automated decisions. Section 80 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 replaced Article 22 of the UK GDPR with Articles 22A to 22D, in force since 5 February 2026. They cover decisions "based solely on automated processing", meaning with "no meaningful human involvement", that have a legal or similarly significant effect on the person. Article 22B restricts such decisions when they use special category data. Article 22C sets the safeguards for the rest: tell the person, let them make representations, let them obtain human intervention, and let them contest the decision. The ICO's updated guidance went out for consultation on 31 March 2026 and has not been published in final form. For an engineer, 22C is the closest thing the UK has to an AI Act article.

The AI Security Institute. It tests frontier models before and after release and publishes research. It was renamed from the AI Safety Institute in February 2025 and is now part of the Cabinet Office. It is not set up in law and has no powers over anyone.

Copyright. UK law has no exception for commercial text and data mining, so training on copyrighted work for commercial use needs a licence. The Data (Use and Access) Act required the government to report on copyright and AI, and the report and impact assessment came out on 18 March 2026. They changed nothing in the law, and the government no longer has a preferred option.

Where the two meet

The AI Act applies to UK companies with EU customers. Article 2(1)(a) covers providers who place a system on the EU market "irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country", and Article 2(1)(c) covers providers and deployers in a third country "where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union". A product built in the UK with customers in Germany is covered.

The part of the Act most of those products meet first is Article 50, which has applied since August. This is its first paragraph, annotated the same way as the definitions above. The whole article follows next Friday.

{{< act-excerpt act="article-50" paras="1" >}}

Earlier posts

I wrote about these two regimes in February, from the architecture side. Architecting for Two Europes with Compliance-as-Code builds one platform for both, with the jurisdiction split in middleware, and its logging and oversight patterns are the ones to build towards for the high-risk date. What It Actually Takes to Fine-Tune an LLM in Europe covers copyright and text and data mining on both sides, and when fine-tuning makes you the provider of a new general-purpose model. The March copyright report left UK law as it was, so that post's advice to license for the UK and treat that as the standard for both markets still holds. A Practical Guide to the European Sovereign Inference Stack routes requests between the EU GDPR and the UK GDPR, and Securing the Open Source AI Supply Chain maps the technical documentation in Article 11 and Annex IV to MLOps tooling.

Next Friday

Next Friday, 20 November, is Article 50 in full, with every clause selectable and the Commission's guidelines and the Code of Practice cited by paragraph. Article 6, which decides whether a system is high-risk, follows on 27 November.

This is an engineer's reading and no substitute for legal advice.

title: Does My Bama Bound AI Clip Have a Glitch Frame? Finding Cuts, Flashes, Freezes and Skipped Frames in Python
description:
Checked November 13, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. Every clip in this post is a synthetic stand-in (a red "TEST BANNER" box swaying over a grainy green field, 720x1280, 30 fps, 8 s), not a real person and not a real generated clip.

People ask some version of this a lot: "There's a weird blink in the middle of my Bama Bound video. Is that a glitch, or did my editor do it?"

An AI clip is about eight seconds long (FAQ). At normal speed, a single odd frame is easy to feel and hard to find. You scrub, it's gone, you scrub back, you can't land on it. What you want is a list: frame 90, white flash, one frame long. Then you can look at exactly that frame, cut it, or send it to whoever made the clip.

This post builds that list with about 150 lines of Python, numpy and ffmpeg. I test it on five planted defects plus two clips that should come back clean, and compare it with ffmpeg's built-in scdet filter, which turned out to catch only two of the four defect types.

Four kinds of "jump", and what they look like in numbers

The whole method rests on one number per frame: how different is this frame from the one before it? Decode the clip very small (36 px wide, so film grain averages out), take the mean absolute RGB difference with the previous frame, and you get a 0-255 value. On my grainy test clip it sits around 1.1 for normal motion.

Defect What you see Shape of the difference curve
Hard cut the picture switches to a different shot one huge spike, and the picture stays different
Flash frame 1-3 frames of white/black/garbage a spike in, a spike out, and the frames either side match each other
Freeze motion stops, then resumes a run of near-zero differences
Skipped frames the banner "teleports" a little one moderate spike, a few times the usual motion

The skip is the sneaky one. Dropping 15 frames of a slowly swaying banner gave a difference of about 4 against a typical 1.1. That's visible to the eye, but nowhere near what a scene-cut detector is tuned for.

Judge each clip by its own motion

A fixed threshold doesn't work. A clip with lots of motion has big frame-to-frame differences everywhere. A calm one has tiny ones. So the script compares each difference with a rolling median over a one-second window around it. A spike counts when it is more than 4x that local median and above an absolute floor of 6. A skip counts at 2.5x local motion, 1.5x the clip's overall median and at least 1.0. A freeze is a run of frames under a tenth of the typical motion that lasts at least 0.3 s.

That 0.3 s number came from a false alarm, which I'll get to below.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""jumpcheck.py - find sudden jumps in a short clip: hard cuts, flash frames,
freezes and skipped frames.

It decodes the clip at a small size (default 36 px wide), measures how much each
frame differs from the one before it (mean absolute RGB difference, 0-255),
and compares every difference with the clip's own typical motion (a rolling
median), so a slow clip and a busy clip are judged on their own terms.

    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4            # human-readable report
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json     # machine-readable
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv d.csv  # per-frame differences

Exit code 0 = nothing found (keyframe pulses are listed but not counted),
1 = at least one cut/flash/freeze/skip, 2 = could not read clip.
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and numpy.
"""
import argparse, json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np


def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "stream=width,height,avg_frame_rate", "-of", "json", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    s = json.loads(out)["streams"][0]
    num, den = s["avg_frame_rate"].split("/")
    return int(s["width"]), int(s["height"]), float(num) / float(den)


def frames(path, w, h):
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-an", "-vf",
           f"scale={w}:{h}:flags=area", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    n = len(raw) // (w * h * 3)
    return np.frombuffer(raw[: n * w * h * 3], np.uint8).reshape(n, h, w, 3).astype(np.int16)


def keyframes(path):
    """Indices of I-frames. Low-bitrate encodes 'pulse' on every keyframe,
    which looks like a small skip but is just the encoder refreshing detail."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "frame=pict_type", "-of", "csv=p=0", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.split()
    return {i for i, t in enumerate(out) if t.strip(",") == "I"}


def diff(a, b):
    return float(np.abs(a - b).mean())


def analyse(path, small_w=36, spike=4.0, floor=6.0, freeze_ratio=0.1, min_freeze_s=0.3):
    W, H, fps = probe(path)
    small_h = max(2, round(small_w * H / W / 2) * 2)
    f = frames(path, small_w, small_h)
    n = len(f)
    kf = keyframes(path)
    min_freeze = max(2, int(round(min_freeze_s * fps)))
    d = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        d[i] = diff(f[i], f[i - 1])
    # typical motion around each frame: median of a 1-second window, excluding frame 0
    win = max(5, int(round(fps)))
    base = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        lo, hi = max(1, i - win), min(n, i + win + 1)
        base[i] = np.median(d[lo:hi])
    typical = float(np.median(d[1:])) if n > 1 else 0.0
    events, i = [], 1
    is_spike = lambda k: d[k] > max(spike * base[k], floor)
    while i < n:
        if is_spike(i):
            # flash: spike in, spike out within 3 frames, and the frames either side match
            back = None
            for k in range(1, 4):
                j = i + k
                if j < n and is_spike(j) and diff(f[i - 1], f[j]) < max(spike * base[i], floor) / 2:
                    back = j
                    break
            if back:
                events.append({"type": "flash", "frame": i, "frames": back - i,
                               "time": round(i / fps, 3), "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2)})
                i = back + 1
                continue
            # does the picture stay changed? compare a frame before with a frame after
            after = min(n - 1, i + 2)
            kind = "cut" if diff(f[i - 1], f[after]) > max(spike * base[i], floor) else "jump"
            events.append({"type": kind, "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        elif d[i] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
            j = i
            while j < n and d[j] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
                j += 1
            if j - i + 1 >= min_freeze:
                events.append({"type": "freeze", "frame": i - 1, "frames": j - i + 1,
                               "time": round((i - 1) / fps, 3),
                               "seconds": round((j - i + 1) / fps, 3)})
            i = j
            continue
        elif d[i] > max(2.5 * base[i], 1.5 * typical) and d[i] > 1.0:
            events.append({"type": "keyframe" if i in kf else "skip", "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        i += 1
    return {"file": path, "frames": n, "fps": round(fps, 3), "size": f"{W}x{H}",
            "typical_diff": round(typical, 3), "max_diff": round(float(d.max()), 2),
            "events": events}, d


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("clip")
    ap.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--csv")
    ap.add_argument("--width", type=int, default=36, help="analysis width in px (smaller = less grain)")
    ap.add_argument("--min-freeze", type=float, default=0.3, help="seconds of no change that count as a freeze")
    ap.add_argument("--spike", type=float, default=4.0, help="x typical motion that counts as a spike")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    try:
        rep, d = analyse(a.clip, small_w=a.width, spike=a.spike, min_freeze_s=a.min_freeze)
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, KeyError, IndexError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"could not read {a.clip}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if a.csv:
        with open(a.csv, "w") as fh:
            fh.write("frame,time,diff\n")
            for i, v in enumerate(d):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / rep['fps']:.3f},{v:.3f}\n")
    if a.json:
        print(json.dumps(rep, indent=2))
    else:
        print(f"{rep['file']}: {rep['frames']} frames @ {rep['fps']} fps, {rep['size']}, "
              f"typical frame-to-frame diff {rep['typical_diff']}, max {rep['max_diff']}")
        if not rep["events"]:
            print("  no cuts, flashes, freezes or skips found")
        for e in rep["events"]:
            extra = {k: v for k, v in e.items() if k not in ("type", "frame", "time")}
            print(f"  {e['type']:6} at {e['time']:6.3f}s (frame {e['frame']})  {extra}")
    real = [e for e in rep["events"] if e["type"] != "keyframe"]
    if any(e["type"] == "keyframe" for e in rep["events"]):
        print("  (keyframe = small pulse on an I-frame, usually encoder refresh; not counted)")
    return 1 if real else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Run it:

python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4          # report, exit 1 if anything found
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json   # for CI or a batch script
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv diffs.csv   # plot the curve yourself

Planting defects to test it

You can't trust a detector you've only run on clean clips. make_glitch.sh takes any clip and plants one known defect at a known frame:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Make a test copy of a clip with one known defect, to check a jump detector.
#   ./make_glitch.sh in.mp4 cut|flash|freeze|drop|lowbitrate N out.mp4
#   cut        N ignored: from 4 s on, the picture is flipped and hue-rotated (a "different shot")
#   flash      N white frames starting at frame 90
#   freeze     frame 150 held for N frames (same total length)
#   drop       N frames removed starting at frame 120 (clip gets shorter, motion jumps)
#   lowbitrate N ignored: CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames (encoder pulse, not a defect)
set -euo pipefail
in=$1; kind=$2; n=$3; out=$4
enc=(-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p)
case $kind in
  cut) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex \
        "[0:v]split[a][b];[a]trim=0:4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a2];[b]trim=4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,vflip,hue=h=120[b2];[a2][b2]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,fps=30[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  flash) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "drawbox=0:0:iw:ih:color=white:t=fill:enable='between(n,90,$((90+n-1)))'" \
        "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  freeze) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[a][b]freezeframes=first=150:last=$((150+n-1)):replace=150[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  drop) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "select='not(between(n,120,$((120+n-1))))',setpts=N/30/TB" -an -r 30 "${enc[@]}" "$out" ;;
  lowbitrate) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 38 -g 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  *) echo "unknown kind $kind" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "wrote $out ($kind $n)"

The base clip comes from a small synthetic generator (make_field_test_clip.sh: gradient sky, noisy field, red box with white text swaying on a sine, beeps over a hum). It's in the same folder as the scripts.

Results

Same base clip, one defect at a time:

Test clip jumpcheck.py found Exit
clean clip, grain 18 nothing (typical diff 1.07, max 1.54) 0
hard cut at 4.0 s cut at frame 120, diff 102.3 vs local 1.12 1
1 white frame at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 1 frame 1
2 white frames at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 2 frames 1
frame 150 held 15 frames freeze at 5.0 s, 0.5 s 1
15 frames dropped at 4.0 s skip at frame 120, diff 4.06 vs 1.11 1
clean clip, no grain nothing (typical 0.245) 0
clean clip scaled to 480x854 nothing 0
clean clip re-encoded CRF 38, keyframe every 30 7 keyframe pulses listed, not counted 0
file that doesn't exist error message 2

For comparison: ffmpeg's scdet

ffmpeg ships a scene-change filter, so the obvious question is why not just use it:

ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf "scdet=threshold=10,metadata=print:file=scd.txt" -f null -

On the same planted clips at threshold=10:

Defect Highest lavfi.scd.score Flagged?
clean 0.17 no
hard cut 24.5 (frame 120) yes
1 white frame 36.8 (frame 90) yes, but only the entry. The exit frame scored low, so it looks just like a cut
15-frame freeze 2.4 no
15 dropped frames 0.9 no

That isn't a bug. scdet is built to find scene changes, and its score is roughly "how much did the frame difference jump compared with the previous difference". The return from a flash is a big difference right after another big difference, so it scores low. Freezes and small skips aren't scene changes at all. If all you need is real cuts, scdet is fine. To tell a flash from a cut, or catch the quieter defects, you need the raw curve.

Two false alarms that shaped the defaults

1. Low-bitrate keyframe "pulses." I re-encoded the clean clip at CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames. The first version of the script reported seven "skips" at frames 29, 58, 87 and so on, exactly 29 frames apart. ffprobe -show_entries frame=pict_type showed an I-frame at every one of them. At low bitrate, every keyframe refreshes detail the P-frames had smeared away, and that registers as a small jump. The script now asks ffprobe for I-frame positions, labels those events keyframe and leaves them out of the exit code.

The cost of that choice is that a real skip landing on a keyframe gets hidden. This happened once in the dataset grid I mention below. Before I made the test clip deterministic, a 10-frame drop got labelled keyframe because x264 had put an I-frame right at the jump. If you have a clip that already feels wrong, also read the keyframe lines.

2. Slow motion looks like a freeze. With grain turned off, the test banner moves less than a pixel per frame at the slow ends of its sway. After encoding, some frames come out identical. The first version flagged eight "freezes" of 3-7 frames (0.1-0.23 s) in a perfectly fine clip. Raising the minimum to 0.3 s removed all of them and still caught the planted 15-frame freeze. A 0.1 s pause in an AI clip is rarely what people mean by "it froze".

Where it stops working

  • Tiny skips are invisible. On the grainy clip, dropping 1, 2 or 5 frames wasn't detected. The motion jump is smaller than the grain. On the grain-free clip, 5 dropped frames were caught (diff 1.59 vs typical 0.244) but 1-2 weren't. Freezes of 3 and 6 frames were not reported (by design, under 0.3 s); 9 and 15 were. A full grid of these cases is in the dataset linked at the end.
  • A cut to a similar-looking shot can slip through. My cut fixture flips the picture and rotates the hue, so it's an obvious change. A cut between two nearly identical framings won't produce a big spike.
  • The freeze after-effect. When a freeze ends, the motion catches up in one frame. On the grain-free clip that catch-up was also reported as a skip. It isn't a second defect, just the other end of the same freeze.
  • Thresholds were tuned on synthetic clips. Real footage with camera shake will need --spike raised.

What to do with the list

  • It's your own edit. Look at the reported frame first. Flashes and freezes usually come from a transition, a bad cut point or a dropped frame in the export. Trim with frame accuracy (re-encode, don't stream-copy) and run the check again.
  • The clip came out of the generator like that. The studio's help page separates a failed generation from one that looks wrong. Looking different from your photo isn't a failed order on its own. If you write to support, a frame number and a timestamp make the report concrete. The address is on the help page.

For reference, the pricing page listed these per-clip prices when I checked on November 13, 2026: 480p $7.98, 720p $9.98, 1080p $16.98, 4k $24.98, tax added at checkout. Check the page itself before you rely on them.

Measured grid

I ran the planted defects at several sizes (flash 1-3 frames, freeze 3-15, drop 1-15) on a grainy and a grain-free source, with fixed random seeds so it reproduces exactly. The 30 rows are in the bamabound-guides dataset on Hugging Face (config jump_detection), along with the script that rebuilds them.
