title: Architecting Real-Time Event Reporting Dashboards for Middle East Mega-Events
description:
When engineering the digital backbone for 10,000+ delegate exhibitions in Riyadh and Jeddah, the transition from basic CRUD apps to enterprise data pipelines is severe.

As part of advanced mega events training in the Middle East for system architects, the primary focus is shifting away from batch data processing (daily CSV exports) toward real-time telemetry. When CTOs demand live visibility over their exhibition floor, developers must build a highly responsive event analytics dashboard capable of ingesting massive concurrent hardware and software events.

Here is how we engineer these live data pipelines for Saudi Vision 2030 mega-events.

  1. Ingesting Fragmented Telemetry

A modern mega-event generates data from multiple disparate sources:

Digital: State-machine transitions from VIP booking portals (e.g., a meeting status changing from pending to approved).

Physical (IoT): Edge-computed RFID handshakes as attendees walk through passive UHF gates or tap interactive kiosks.

To power a live event reporting dashboard, we cannot rely on direct synchronous database writes from edge devices, as venue network latency will cause massive API blockages.

  1. The Asynchronous Data Pipeline

Instead, we decouple the ingestion from the visualization layer:

Edge Compute: RFID gates resolve the UID locally using edge-cached SQLite databases to ensure sub-5ms physical access.

Message Queue: Telemetry payloads (Timestamp, UID, Zone ID) are dispatched asynchronously to a message broker (like Redis or Kafka) rather than writing directly to the primary relational database.

Stream Processing: Background workers consume these queues, validate the payloads, and update the central data lake.

Live Push: To keep the frontend dashboard strictly real-time without suffocating the server with AJAX polling, we utilize WebSockets (or Server-Sent Events for one-way telemetry). The frontend React/Vue dashboard listens to these streams and updates the zone capacity graphs and VIP conversion funnels instantly.

The Value of Unified Architecture

The ultimate goal of technical mega events training in the Middle East is teaching engineers how to eliminate data silos. By routing all physical IoT telemetry and digital state machines through a centralized message queue, you provide operations directors with a flawless, single source of truth.

When your dashboard updates the exact second an attendee walks into a VIP lounge, you have successfully built enterprise-grade event architecture.

(Review the complete backend architecture behind our live reporting systems at StampIQ.sa)

title: How to Run Two Claude Desktop Accounts on One Mac (With Separate Dock Icons and Shared Context)
description:
I run my daily operations and recurring routines inside Claude Desktop's Code tab: morning check-ins at 08:45, weekly planning, Telegram community digests, and weekly SEO and AEO checks for this blog.

Running everything on a single account has a structural flaw. Paid Claude plans have a session limit that resets every five hours, plus weekly limits. When a heavy coding or video-rendering session burns through that session limit in 45 minutes, every scheduled task on that account hits the same wall and stalls.

I wanted two Claude accounts running in parallel on the same Mac mini:

  1. Account 1 (Routines): my existing account, left completely untouched, so all scheduled tasks, mail connectors and morning check-ins keep running on autopilot.
  2. Account 2 (Engineer): a second account dedicated to hands-on coding, debugging and content work.

And I needed two things most multi-account guides skip: the two accounts had to share the same project memory and skills without duplicating scheduled tasks, and they needed different icons in the macOS Dock so I wouldn't click the wrong window twenty times a day.

Short answer

You don't need to log out and back in, and you don't need to migrate your existing scheduled tasks. Leave your original Claude.app untouched for routines, and launch a second instance for daily work by passing both --user-data-dir (which isolates the Electron desktop app) and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (which isolates the Claude Code engine). To give the second window its own teal Dock icon and an "Engineer" label without breaking Apple's code signature, launch an unmodified APFS clone (cp -cR) at ~/Applications/Engineer.app through a small launcher, and symlink only skills, agents and projects between the two config folders.

Why --user-data-dir alone isn't enough

Most guides for running multiple Claude accounts focus either on the terminal CLI or on the chat window. If you use the Code tab inside Claude Desktop, two separate layers store your login and state:

Layer Setting What it isolates
Claude Desktop (Electron) --user-data-dir Desktop login, claude_desktop_config.json (MCP servers), the sidebar session list
Claude Code engine CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR Code tab credentials (a macOS Keychain entry), scheduled-tasks/, projects/, settings.json

Where each account keeps them:

Layer Account 1 (Routines) Account 2 (Engineer)
Claude Desktop ~/Library/Application Support/Claude ~/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work
Claude Code ~/.claude (variable left unset) ~/.claude-work

If you only pass --user-data-dir, the Desktop window opens a new account, but the Code tab inside it still uses ~/.claude and bills your original account. To isolate both, you have to pass both.

One macOS Keychain trap: leave CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR unset for your original account. Pointing it at ~/.claude explicitly can make Claude Code look up a different Keychain entry than the default, so your existing login seems to disappear. Only set the variable for the second account.

What didn't work: editing Info.plist, and a plain AppleScript launcher

Before landing on the working setup, I hit two dead ends that come up in almost every forum thread on this:

  • Dead end 1: editing Info.plist and re-signing the app. Some guides suggest duplicating Claude.app, changing CFBundleName and CFBundleIdentifier in Info.plist, replacing the binary with a wrapper script, and running codesign. On recent macOS and Electron builds, modifying any file inside the signed bundle strips Anthropic's entitlements. The app crashes on launch with EXC_BREAKPOINT (SIGTRAP) inside Electron Framework.
  • Dead end 2: a plain AppleScript launcher pointing at /Applications/Claude.app. An osacompile applet that runs open -n -a "/Applications/Claude.app" works without crashing. But even if you paste a custom icon onto the launcher in Finder, the launcher exits in a tenth of a second and /Applications/Claude.app is what stays in the Dock. You end up with two identical orange Claude icons in the Dock and in window switchers.

The fix: an unmodified APFS clone, a launcher and a recolored icon

The trick is to separate the launcher from an unmodified APFS clone:

  1. Copy /Applications/Claude.app to ~/Applications/Engineer.app with cp -cR. On APFS this creates a clone: it finishes instantly, uses no extra disk space, and leaves every file inside Contents/ untouched, so Gatekeeper and Electron never complain.
  2. Attach a custom icon to the outside of the bundle with macOS's NSWorkspace API. Finder stores custom icons in an extended attribute (com.apple.FinderInfo and an Icon\r file), outside the code-signing seal.
  3. Create a tiny launcher at /Applications/Engineer.app that starts ~/Applications/Engineer.app with --env "CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=..." and --args "--user-data-dir=...".

Because the running process is ~/Applications/Engineer.app, the Dock shows its custom icon and Engineer as the tooltip.


The two icons I keep in the Dock: the original Claude app for routines, and the recolored Engineer clone for hands-on work. Both icons are taken from the apps on my Mac.

In the real Dock, hovering over each icon shows its own name:


Hovering over the teal icon: Engineer.


Hovering over the orange icon: Claude.

Step 1: Create the isolated Engineer app and launcher

Open Terminal and run:

mkdir -p "$HOME/Applications" "$HOME/.claude-work" "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work" &&
rm -rf "$HOME/Applications/Engineer.app" "/Applications/Engineer.app" &&
cp -cR "/Applications/Claude.app" "$HOME/Applications/Engineer.app" &&
osacompile -o "/Applications/Engineer.app" \
  -e 'do shell script "open -n -a \"$HOME/Applications/Engineer.app\" --env \"CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.claude-work\" --args \"--user-data-dir=$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work\""'

Step 2: Recolor the original Claude icon to teal

Instead of hunting for a third-party PNG, you can use macOS's built-in CoreImage (CIHueAdjust) from Terminal. It takes Claude's official icon, keeps the transparent rounded corners and the white starburst, rotates the orange background 180 degrees to teal, and applies it to both Engineer.app bundles:

osascript -l JavaScript -e 'ObjC.import("Cocoa"); ObjC.import("CoreImage"); var ws = $.NSWorkspace.sharedWorkspace; var orig = ws.iconForFile("/Applications/Claude.app"); orig.setSize($.NSMakeSize(512, 512)); var ci = $.CIImage.imageWithData(orig.TIFFRepresentation); var f = $.CIFilter.filterWithName("CIHueAdjust"); f.setValueForKey(ci, "inputImage"); f.setValueForKey(3.14159, "inputAngle"); var rep = $.NSCIImageRep.imageRepWithCIImage(f.valueForKey("outputImage")); var img = $.NSImage.alloc.initWithSize($.NSMakeSize(512, 512)); img.addRepresentation(rep); ws.setIconForFileOptions(img, "/Applications/Engineer.app", 0); ws.setIconForFileOptions(img, ObjC.unwrap($.NSHomeDirectory()) + "/Applications/Engineer.app", 0);' && killall Dock Finder

If you prefer emerald green instead of blue, change 3.14159 to 2.1.

Step 3: Sign in to the second account without the deep-link mix-up

Claude Desktop signs in through your browser and passes the login back through a claude:// deep link. If two Claude instances are open at the same time, macOS often hands that callback to the wrong window.

For the first login only:

  1. Quit your original Claude app (Cmd + Q).
  2. Open Engineer from /Applications and sign in with your second Claude account (or use the email verification code instead of clicking the magic link).
  3. Switch to the Code tab inside Engineer and confirm that /status shows your second account.

Keeping both accounts in sync (without duplicating scheduled tasks)

Two isolated folders mean the new account starts empty: none of your installed skills, subagents, MCP servers or conversation transcripts are there.

The key is selective symlinking:

ln -sfn "$HOME/.claude/skills" "$HOME/.claude-work/skills" &&
ln -sfn "$HOME/.claude/agents" "$HOME/.claude-work/agents" &&
ln -sfn "$HOME/.claude/projects" "$HOME/.claude-work/projects" &&
cp "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json" \
   "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work/claude_desktop_config.json"

Here is why this split works:

  • What stays separate (scheduled-tasks/ and credentials): local scheduled tasks live under ~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/<task-name>/SKILL.md. By not symlinking scheduled-tasks/, all routines stay on Account 1. If you symlinked that folder, both open apps would fire every scheduled task twice.
  • What is shared on disk (skills/, agents/, projects/): Claude Code stores session transcripts and per-project auto memory (MEMORY.md) under ~/.claude/projects/, grouped by working directory, regardless of which account paid for the tokens. Symlinking projects/ lets either account resume or search conversations started by the other.
  • Project-level context (CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md): because both accounts open the same project folders on disk, shared files like CLAUDE.md, Now.md and project logs are read and updated by both accounts in real time.

Pairing each Claude account with its own Chrome profile

Several of my scheduled tasks read signed-in pages in Chrome through the Claude in Chrome extension. If two Claude instances try to share a single Chrome profile, they fight over the connection.

A Claude Desktop instance connects to Chrome through Anthropic's bridge and only sees Chrome extensions signed in to the same Claude account. That makes isolating browsers straightforward:

  1. Leave your original Chrome profile as it is. Its Claude in Chrome extension is already signed in to Account 1 (Routines). Keep the web sessions your scheduled tasks read (Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, Telegram Web, analytics dashboards) logged in there.
  2. Create a second Chrome profile for Engineer. Install the Claude in Chrome extension in the new profile and sign the extension in to Account 2.
  3. Lock the pairing once. With both Chrome profiles open, type /chrome inside an Engineer Code session (or ask it to switch browser) and approve the connection in the new Chrome window. Claude remembers the paired browser for future sessions.

Two gotchas to keep in mind

  1. Launch order matters (Claude.app first, Engineer.app second). Both apps share the same internal CFBundleIdentifier, so clicking the stock orange Claude.app icon while Engineer is already running tells macOS LaunchServices to focus the running Engineer window instead of starting a new process. Always start your main Claude.app first (it runs your background routines anyway, so it stays open all day), then launch Engineer.app. Because the Engineer launcher passes open -n, it always opens its own window.
  2. After a Claude Desktop update, refresh the clone. When /Applications/Claude.app auto-updates, your APFS clone at ~/Applications/Engineer.app stays on the previous build until you re-run the cp -cR and icon commands above.

Checklist

  1. Keep Account 1 (scheduled tasks and routines) on the default /Applications/Claude.app and ~/.claude.
  2. Create an unmodified APFS clone at ~/Applications/Engineer.app and a launcher at /Applications/Engineer.app that passes both --env "CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.claude-work" and --args "--user-data-dir=$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work".
  3. Run the CoreImage one-liner to give Engineer a teal Claude icon in the Dock and window switcher.
  4. Quit the main app once, sign in to Account 2 inside Engineer, then reopen the main app.
  5. Symlink skills, agents and projects from ~/.claude to ~/.claude-work, copy claude_desktop_config.json, and leave scheduled-tasks unlinked.
  6. Sign a second Chrome profile's Claude extension in to Account 2 and pair it with /chrome.

If you're building AI-native workflows around your business, or want a hand setting up a system like this without breaking your existing tools, get in touch.

title: Building SupportMeet: The First Months Are Hard to Describe From Inside. What Worked, What Broke
description:
The hardest design problem in the first version of SupportMeet was not matching. It was language.

A new parent in the first months is living a day that looks simple from outside and feels completely different from inside. Bottles gather by the sink, laundry moves in constant rounds, and the night stops belonging to sleep. From outside, people send congratulations and ask for photos. Inside, the days can feel long, repetitive, and strangely quiet, even with a baby breathing in the next room.

That gap shaped almost every early decision, and it broke a few of them first.

What was built

SupportMeet at https://supportmeet.com is a free peer support site where people share what they are going through and are matched with circles who have lived the same thing. For new parents, the circle is not a general parenting feed. It is a small group in the same early weeks, where someone can say the feeding is not going as planned, or that the house feels lonely at midday, and be read by people who were awake for the same feed last night.

Three choices mattered most. The site is private by default, so an honest post is not a public performance for coworkers or relatives. Matching is by lived stage, not by topic keywords, because week three and month five are different worlds. And circles sit alongside practical help and listings of professionals and programmes nearby, so a worry shared at night can still lead to a sensible next step in daylight.

What broke

The first prompts were too polished. Asking people to share an update produced the same bright summaries they were already sending family. The posts that actually helped started when the prompt got plainer: what did today actually look like. Small, lived details followed from that. How another parent handled the evening stretch when nothing settled the baby. What helped on the first trip out alone. How partners divided the night so both could get one longer stretch of rest.

Broad matching broke too. Putting every new parent in one circle mixed people in the first two weeks with people sleeping through the night, and the advice stopped landing. Narrower circles meant slower first replies in some cases, and that trade was worth making. A reply from the wrong stage can sound like a verdict. A slower reply from the same stage sounds like company.

The congratulations problem was subtler. Many new parents feel they should only share the bright parts, so a support space has to make the tired parts sayable without turning them into a crisis. The fix was tone, set in the circle itself: no polished update needed, no verdict offered, practical notes welcome alongside honest ones.

What the numbers look like

The honest measure at this stage is not traffic. It is whether a first post gets a reply from someone in the same stretch of life, and whether that reply contains a specific detail the poster can use tonight. Generic encouragement does not pass that test. A note about how one household split the night feeds does.

That is a stricter bar than page views, and it is the right one for a support product. A circle that produces one usable detail and one moment of recognition has done its job, even if it never grows large.

What stayed

New parenthood is often described as a beginning, and it is. It is also a season that asks a lot, quietly and every day. Having company from people in the same season does not make it perfect. It makes it less solitary, and that difference is the whole product.

The lesson that carried over to every other circle on the site is simple: match on the lived stage, keep the space private by default, and write prompts plain enough that the real day can be described in them.

title: CloudWatch Logs retention policy for the whole account
description:
A CloudWatch Logs retention policy is one of those settings nobody thinks about on the first deployment. Every Lambda function writes logs, and CloudWatch keeps them forever by default. After a few years of Serverless you end up with hundreds of log groups, and half of them belong to functions that no longer exist.

Since November 9, 2026, you can fix that centrally. An account-level retention policy defines how long logs stay in all log groups or in a selected subset. That sounds like a checkbox in the console. However, there is one detail in it that can delete data without warning. In this article I show you how the rules work, how to roll them out safely with a dry run, and how to manage them as code with AWS CDK.

In short

CloudWatch Logs can now set retention through policies for the whole account or for prefixes such as /aws/lambda. When several policies match, the longest one wins. The catch: a policy also replaces longer settings on individual log groups, so every change deserves a dry run first.

What you will learn in this article

  • How account-level policies decide the retention of log groups
  • Why a 90-day baseline can delete some logs earlier than you expect
  • How to check the impact first with a dry run and a small TypeScript tool
  • How to manage the policy as code with AWS CDK

Why log retention gets forgotten so often

CloudWatch Logs stores log data indefinitely by default. The documentation says so, and in day-to-day work you hardly notice. A Lambda function creates its log group /aws/lambda/<function-name> on the first invocation if you did not define it in your infrastructure code. It then says “Never expire”, and nobody ever looks at it again.

In addition, these log groups stay behind when you delete a stack. The function is gone, the logs remain. That costs storage, and it is also a privacy topic: logs like to contain email addresses, IP addresses or order numbers. The GDPR includes the principle of storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)), and “forever” is rarely a good answer to it. This is not legal advice, but it is a good reason to stop postponing the topic.

Until now you had two options. Either every team sets retention per log group in code. Or a platform group builds a Lambda function that catches new log groups via EventBridge and sets a retention afterwards. Both work, both have gaps. That is exactly where the new feature comes in.

How a CloudWatch Logs retention policy works

An account-level retention policy is an entry per account and Region that you create through the PutAccountPolicy API with the type RETENTION_POLICY. It has four parts:

Part Meaning Allowed values
Name unique name in the account free text, must not start with aws/
Retention how long log events are kept 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922, 3288, 3653 days or NEVER_EXPIRE
Enforcement mode does the rule also apply to existing log groups? RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY
Selection which log groups no filter (all) or LogGroupNamePrefix="/aws/lambda"

You can create up to 20 of these policies per Region. The feature costs nothing extra, and according to the announcement it is available in all commercial Regions except Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Important: a policy only applies in the Region where you create it. If you work in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1, you need it twice.

The longest policy wins

Unlike other account-level policies in CloudWatch, retention policies may overlap. If several match a log group, the one with the longest retention applies. NEVER_EXPIRE counts as the longest. This leads to a nice pattern: one baseline for everything, longer periods for certain prefixes, and exceptions that never expire.

Example with three policies: the longest matching policy determines the effective retention.

The catch: longer settings get replaced too

Now comes the part you should not skim. A matching account-level policy fully replaces the setting of the log group. That works in both directions. If a log group keeps data for ten years and you create a 90-day baseline for everything, CloudWatch deletes everything in it that is older than 90 days. The documentation explicitly warns about this.

The opposite case is surprising as well. Many teams deliberately use 7 or 14 days for Lambda logs. Account-level policies, on the other hand, require at least 30 days. If such a log group falls under your baseline, it suddenly gets 30 or 90 days and costs more storage than before. So a baseline is a fixed value for everything it matches, and it is no upper limit.

RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY?

With RETROACTIVE, the policy applies to every matching log group, including existing ones. With NEW_ONLY, it only applies to log groups created after the policy. Existing ones keep their own setting. NEW_ONLY is the cautious start, yet it does not clean up the old leftovers. I would begin with a dry run for RETROACTIVE and decide after that.

Two timing details: a new or updated policy only takes effect after about 24 hours. Until then, the old value applies. Also, CloudWatch typically deletes expired events within 72 hours, in rare cases later. From the moment they expire, though, they no longer count towards storage costs.

🎬 How CloudWatch Logs determines the effective retention of a log group – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Step by step: roll out retention with the AWS CLI

This is how I would introduce a CloudWatch Logs retention policy in an existing account. You need:

  • AWS CLI v2 in a recent version whose put-account-policy command knows the --dry-run parameter
  • the permissions logs:PutAccountPolicy and logs:PutRetentionPolicy, for deleting logs:DeleteAccountPolicy and logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy, for reading logs:DescribeAccountPolicies and logs:DescribeLogGroups
  • an idea of which logs must stay longer (audit, billing, contracts)

1. Take stock

First, check which log groups never expire today and how much they store:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].[logGroupName, storedBytes]' \
  --output table

The result is a table with names and stored bytes. Write down the log groups that should deliberately live longer. Those are exactly the ones that need their own policy in a moment.

2. Create the exceptions first

Create the longer periods before the baseline. That way there is no moment in which only the short baseline applies. In this example, the fictional bike rental keeps its audit logs for two years:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name audit-2y \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 731, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --selection-criteria 'LogGroupNamePrefix="/bikerental/audit"'

3. Check the baseline with a dry run

Next comes the baseline for everything. With --dry-run, CloudWatch saves nothing. Instead, it reports how many log groups would keep data longer, shorter or unchanged:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name baseline-90d \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 90, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --dry-run

The response contains a dryRunResult object with the fields decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount, increasedRetentionLogGroupCount and unchangedRetentionLogGroupCount. It also lists up to 20 of the largest affected log groups. For example, you immediately see whether a large archive group would get shorter. If decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount is greater than zero, look closely: those are the log groups that lose data.

4. Create it and check after 24 hours

If everything looks right, send the same command without --dry-run. After about a day, describe-log-groups shows the effective retention and the name of the policy that decides it:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda \
  --query 'logGroups[].[logGroupName, retentionInDays, retentionPolicyName]' \
  --output table

The retentionPolicyName field only shows up when an account-level policy applies. If NEVER_EXPIRE applies, retentionInDays is missing from the response. To list all policies, run aws logs describe-account-policies --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY.

A TypeScript tool for plan and dry run

The dry run returns counts and the 20 largest log groups. Often that is enough. But if you want to see the complete list of groups that lose data before an approval, a small tool helps. It loads all log groups and existing policies, recalculates the rules locally and then also asks for the real dry run.

Its core is pure logic without AWS calls and therefore easy to test. The effectiveRetention function implements both rules from above: the longest matching policy wins, and it replaces the log group’s own value.

// src/retention.ts
// Pure planning logic for account-level CloudWatch Logs retention policies.
// No AWS calls in here, so everything can be unit-tested offline.

/** Retention values (in days) that account-level policies accept. */
export const ALLOWED_DAYS = [
  30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922,
  3288, 3653,
] as const;

export type Retention = number | "NEVER_EXPIRE";
export type EnforcementMode = "RETROACTIVE" | "NEW_ONLY";

export interface RetentionPolicy {
  name: string;
  /** Log group name prefix; undefined = all log groups in the account. */
  prefix?: string;
  retention: Retention;
  mode: EnforcementMode;
  /** When the policy was created (epoch ms). Needed for NEW_ONLY. */
  createdAt: number;
}

export interface LogGroupInfo {
  name: string;
  /** Retention set on the log group itself; undefined = never expire. */
  retentionInDays?: number;
  creationTime: number;
  storedBytes: number;
}

export type ChangeKind = "shorter" | "longer" | "unchanged";

export interface PlannedChange {
  group: LogGroupInfo;
  before: Retention;
  after: Retention;
  kind: ChangeKind;
  /** Name of the policy that decides the retention after the change. */
  decidedBy?: string;
}

/** Parses CLI input like "90" or "never" into a valid retention value. */
export function parseRetention(input: string): Retention {
  const value = input.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (value === "never" || value === "never_expire") return "NEVER_EXPIRE";
  const days = Number(value);
  if (!Number.isInteger(days) || !(ALLOWED_DAYS as readonly number[]).includes(days)) {
    throw new Error(
      `Invalid retention "${input}". Allowed: ${ALLOWED_DAYS.join(", ")} or "never".`,
    );
  }
  return days;
}

/** Builds the policyDocument string for PutAccountPolicy. */
export function buildPolicyDocument(retention: Retention, mode: EnforcementMode): string {
  return JSON.stringify({ retentionInDays: retention, enforcementMode: mode });
}

/** Builds the selectionCriteria string, or undefined for "all log groups". */
export function buildSelectionCriteria(prefix?: string): string | undefined {
  if (prefix === undefined || prefix === "") return undefined;
  if (prefix.includes('"')) throw new Error("Prefix must not contain double quotes.");
  return `LogGroupNamePrefix="${prefix}"`;
}

/** Reads a policy as returned by DescribeAccountPolicies. */
export function parsePolicy(p: {
  policyName?: string;
  policyDocument?: string;
  selectionCriteria?: string;
  lastUpdatedTime?: number;
}): RetentionPolicy {
  const doc = JSON.parse(p.policyDocument ?? "{}") as {
    retentionInDays?: Retention;
    enforcementMode?: EnforcementMode;
  };
  const match = /LogGroupNamePrefix\s*=\s*"([^"]*)"/.exec(p.selectionCriteria ?? "");
  return {
    name: p.policyName ?? "unknown",
    prefix: match?.[1],
    retention: doc.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE",
    mode: doc.enforcementMode ?? "RETROACTIVE",
    // The API only returns lastUpdatedTime, which is the best approximation we have.
    createdAt: p.lastUpdatedTime ?? 0,
  };
}

/** Does a policy apply to a given log group? */
export function policyMatches(policy: RetentionPolicy, group: LogGroupInfo): boolean {
  const prefixOk = policy.prefix === undefined || group.name.startsWith(policy.prefix);
  const modeOk = policy.mode === "RETROACTIVE" || group.creationTime >= policy.createdAt;
  return prefixOk && modeOk;
}

/** Compares two retention values. NEVER_EXPIRE is the longest. */
export function compareRetention(a: Retention, b: Retention): number {
  const toNumber = (r: Retention) => (r === "NEVER_EXPIRE" ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY : r);
  return toNumber(a) - toNumber(b);
}

/**
 * Effective retention of a log group: if at least one account policy matches,
 * the longest matching policy wins and REPLACES the log group's own setting
 * (even if that setting was longer). Otherwise the log group's own value counts.
 */
export function effectiveRetention(
  group: LogGroupInfo,
  policies: RetentionPolicy[],
): { retention: Retention; decidedBy?: string } {
  const matching = policies.filter((p) => policyMatches(p, group));
  if (matching.length === 0) {
    return { retention: group.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE" };
  }
  const winner = matching.reduce((best, p) =>
    compareRetention(p.retention, best.retention) > 0 ? p : best,
  );
  return { retention: winner.retention, decidedBy: winner.name };
}

/** Simulates adding (or replacing) a policy and lists the effect per log group. */
export function planChange(
  groups: LogGroupInfo[],
  existing: RetentionPolicy[],
  candidate: RetentionPolicy,
): PlannedChange[] {
  const after = [...existing.filter((p) => p.name !== candidate.name), candidate];
  return groups
    .map((group) => {
      const before = effectiveRetention(group, existing).retention;
      const next = effectiveRetention(group, after);
      const diff = compareRetention(next.retention, before);
      const kind: ChangeKind = diff < 0 ? "shorter" : diff > 0 ? "longer" : "unchanged";
      return { group, before, after: next.retention, kind, decidedBy: next.decidedBy };
    })
    .sort((a, b) => b.group.storedBytes - a.group.storedBytes);
}

/** Groups the plan by kind, e.g. for a short summary. */
export function summarize(plan: PlannedChange[]): Record<ChangeKind, number> {
  const summary: Record<ChangeKind, number> = { shorter: 0, longer: 0, unchanged: 0 };
  for (const change of plan) summary[change.kind] += 1;
  return summary;
}

/** Human-readable bytes (base 1024). */
export function formatBytes(bytes: number): string {
  const units = ["B", "KiB", "MiB", "GiB", "TiB"];
  let value = bytes;
  let unit = 0;
  while (value >= 1024 && unit < units.length - 1) {
    value /= 1024;
    unit += 1;
  }
  return `${value.toFixed(unit === 0 ? 0 : 1)} ${units[unit]}`;
}

The command line uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3. Starting with version 3.1165.0, @aws-sdk/client-cloudwatch-logs knows the dryRun parameter and the retentionPolicyName field. Install and run it like this:

npm install
npx tsx src/cli.ts inventory
npx tsx src/cli.ts plan --name baseline-90d --days 90
npx tsx src/cli.ts apply --name baseline-90d --days 90 --yes

The expected output of plan looks roughly like this. Every line with SHORTER is a log group that keeps less data after the change:

Local plan: 2 shorter, 41 longer, 12 unchanged
  SHORTER         3653 -> 90           8.0 GiB  /bookshop/archive
  SHORTER NEVER_EXPIRE -> 90           5.0 GiB  /aws/lambda/search
Dry run (AWS): matched 55, shorter 2, longer 41, unchanged 12, not analyzed 0

There are two limits you should know. If a policy already applies to a log group, the API only shows the policy value and no longer the group’s own one. And for NEW_ONLY, the tool uses the time of the last update as an approximation. If the numbers differ, trust the AWS dry run. The Vitest tests cover the rules, for example that NEVER_EXPIRE always wins.

Retention policy as code with AWS CDK

A setting that affects this many log groups belongs in version control. There is one catch: as of this writing (November 10, 2026), the CloudFormation resource AWS::Logs::AccountPolicy does not list the RETENTION_POLICY type yet. Until that changes, an AwsCustomResource helps in AWS CDK. It calls putAccountPolicy on create and update and deleteAccountPolicy on delete.

// lib/log-retention-stack.ts
// CloudFormation's AWS::Logs::AccountPolicy does not list RETENTION_POLICY yet,
// so this stack calls the CloudWatch Logs API through an AwsCustomResource.
import { Stack, type StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import * as iam from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam";
import {
  AwsCustomResource,
  AwsCustomResourcePolicy,
  PhysicalResourceId,
} from "aws-cdk-lib/custom-resources";
import { Construct } from "constructs";

export interface RetentionRule {
  /** Unique policy name, must not start with "aws/". */
  name: string;
  /** Log group name prefix; leave empty for all log groups. */
  prefix?: string;
  /** 30, 60, 90, ... 3653 or "NEVER_EXPIRE". */
  retention: number | "NEVER_EXPIRE";
  mode?: "RETROACTIVE" | "NEW_ONLY";
}

export class AccountRetentionPolicy extends Construct {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, rule: RetentionRule) {
    super(scope, id);

    const params: Record<string, string> = {
      policyName: rule.name,
      policyType: "RETENTION_POLICY",
      policyDocument: JSON.stringify({
        retentionInDays: rule.retention,
        enforcementMode: rule.mode ?? "RETROACTIVE",
      }),
    };
    if (rule.prefix) {
      params.selectionCriteria = `LogGroupNamePrefix="${rule.prefix}"`;
    }

    const putCall = {
      service: "CloudWatchLogs",
      action: "putAccountPolicy",
      parameters: params,
      physicalResourceId: PhysicalResourceId.of(`retention-${rule.name}`),
    };

    new AwsCustomResource(this, "Policy", {
      onCreate: putCall,
      onUpdate: putCall,
      onDelete: {
        service: "CloudWatchLogs",
        action: "deleteAccountPolicy",
        parameters: { policyName: rule.name, policyType: "RETENTION_POLICY" },
      },
      policy: AwsCustomResourcePolicy.fromStatements([
        new iam.PolicyStatement({
          actions: [
            "logs:PutAccountPolicy",
            "logs:PutRetentionPolicy",
            "logs:DeleteAccountPolicy",
            "logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy",
          ],
          resources: ["*"],
        }),
      ]),
      installLatestAwsSdk: false,
    });
  }
}

export class LogRetentionStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    // Baseline for everything in this account and region.
    new AccountRetentionPolicy(this, "Baseline", { name: "baseline-90d", retention: 90 });

    // Longer retention for audit logs of the fictional bike rental.
    new AccountRetentionPolicy(this, "Audit", {
      name: "audit-2y",
      prefix: "/bikerental/audit",
      retention: 731,
    });
  }
}

Run npx cdk synth to check the template and npx cdk deploy to roll it out. Expected result: two resources of type Custom::AWS and one IAM policy with exactly the four Logs actions. If you delete the stack, the policies disappear as well. A dry run of delete-account-policy shows you beforehand what will then apply to each log group.

A tip from the architecture corner: once prefixes decide about retention, log group names suddenly become an architecture decision. Write the convention down, for example in an architecture decision record. Otherwise an audit log will eventually end up under a prefix that cleans up after 90 days.

Common mistakes with log retention

  • Creating the baseline before the exceptions. The exceptions go in first, otherwise only the short period applies for a moment. The 24-hour delay softens that a bit, but I would not rely on it.
  • Skipping the dry run. A look at decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount takes seconds. Deleted logs do not come back.
  • Trusting the value in your code. If your team sets 14 days in a CDK stack, but an account-level policy applies, the policy value wins. Every team should know that.
  • Forgetting Regions. Each Region needs its own policies, including the one where only “a little bit” runs.
  • Granting too many permissions. AWS recommends giving logs:PutAccountPolicy only to administrators who own logging for the whole account.
  • Starting several dry runs at once. Only one dry run can run per account at a time. Scripts that check in parallel will get errors.

Keeping an eye on cost and security

The policies themselves are free. What changes is the storage cost of log data, and it can move in both directions. Old log groups without expiry get cheaper, while short Lambda log groups below 30 days may get more expensive. How much that means for you follows from the inventory in step 1 together with the CloudWatch Logs price list.

Security is mostly about control. Whoever may change account-level policies can indirectly delete logs. Treat these permissions like delete permissions. For logs with a legal retention requirement, I would also check whether they belong in a central log archive account to which application teams have no write access.

My take

To be honest: I have been waiting for this for a long time. “Never expire” as the default was always a poor compromise for Serverless accounts with many small functions. Finally there is a built-in solution, without a custom cleanup Lambda.

Still, I would like different semantics. A baseline that replaces longer values on individual log groups is handy for platform teams and surprising for application teams. An option like “only set it if nothing is set” would save a lot of discussions. Until then, communication is the only fix: tell the teams that their value in code no longer has the last word. And put it into your runbook before someone searches for logs during an incident that no longer exist.

My suggestion for the start: a 90-day baseline with RETROACTIVE, exceptions for audit and contracts created first, everything checked with a dry run and managed as code. That takes an hour and cleans up years of leftovers.

FAQ

How long does CloudWatch Logs keep logs by default?

Indefinitely. Without its own setting and without an account-level policy, log events never expire.

Can I set a 7-day retention with an account-level policy?

No. Account-level policies require at least 30 days. Shorter periods still only work per log group, and only as long as no account-level policy applies to that group.

Does the retention policy cost extra?

No, according to AWS there are no additional costs for the policies. Only the storage costs of the log data change.

How do I delete a retention policy again?

Use aws logs delete-account-policy --policy-name <name> --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY. Add --dry-run to see the effect of the deletion first.

Your next step

Run the inventory from step 1 in your most important account today. The number of log groups set to “Never expire” is usually argument enough. If you are working on costs anyway, my article about NAT gateway costs with Lambda fits right in.

Now it is your turn: which baseline retention do you consider sensible, and which logs have to stay longer in your setup? Let me know in the comments.

All code from this article, ready to run: smirowstanitzok/sascha-ms-examples

  • Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide: Working with log groups and log streams
  • Amazon CloudWatch Logs API Reference: PutAccountPolicy
  • AWS CloudFormation: AWS::Logs::AccountPolicy

title: Why I Treat My Personal Notion Templates Like a Database Schema
description:
As software engineers, we spend our days designing database schemas. We normalize tables, set up foreign keys, and obsess over data integrity. It’s beautiful, logical, and it works perfectly in production.

So, naturally, when I started building my own productivity system in Notion, I applied the exact same logic. I created a relational masterpiece. I had a Tasks table with a relation to Projects, which was related to Areas of Life. I had rollups, formulas, and linked views.

It looked like a well-architected microservice. It was also completely useless.

The Problem with Over-Normalization
In databases, over-normalization leads to slow queries because you have to JOIN 10 tables just to get one piece of data.

In productivity, over-normalization leads to decision fatigue. If I wanted to add a task like "Buy milk," I had to decide: Is this a project? Is it an area? What's the energy level? What's the priority?

I was spending 15 minutes a day just doing data entry. My brain was spending more energy managing the system than actually doing the work. I was experiencing massive "cognitive load" just trying to open my dashboard.

The Refactor: The Flat Table
I decided to refactor my entire system. I deleted all the relations and rollups.

Now, my task manager is a single, flat table. It has only three columns:

Task Name (String)

Status (Select: To Do, In Progress, Done)

Date (Date, optional)

That's it. No complex JOIN logic. No dependencies.

If I need context, I just write it in the task name (e.g., "Buy milk for Project X"). I use a simple filter: Status != Done. When a task is checked off, it disappears from my view.

Why This Works Better Than Relational Databases
Low Friction: Adding a task takes 2 seconds.

No Dependency Hell: If I don't update my "Life Areas" database, my daily task list still works perfectly.

Mental Clarity: A flat list is easy to scan. A relational dashboard requires cognitive parsing.

The Lesson
We love building complex systems because it makes us feel like good engineers. But good engineering is about solving a problem with the least amount of complexity necessary. Your personal life doesn't need a relational database. It needs a list.

If you want to see how I structure this minimalist approach (with a few clever formulas for prioritization), I’ve shared my exact schema in the ADHD Daily Planner.

How do you structure your tasks? Are you a relational database person or a flat list person? Let me know!

title: 175 MB of Substrings to Read One Column
description:
I had a boring little job: a pile of CSV-shaped lines in memory, and I needed one number out of each — the amount column, third field, that's it. The rest of the row was along for the ride. I wrote the obvious loop, it gave the right total, and I moved on. Then the allocation profiler lit up on that exact loop and I went back to look. A million rows in, and I'd minted somewhere north of a hundred megabytes of garbage to read a single integer per line. Every other field I split out, I threw straight away.

Here's the loop that did it:

long total = 0;
foreach (string line in lines)
{
    string[] fields = line.Split(',');
    total += long.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
}

line.Split(',') is doing precisely what I asked and nothing I wanted. For each row it allocates a string[] to hold the pieces, then allocates a fresh string for every field it finds, four of them on my data, copying the characters out of the original line into each one. I read fields[2] and let the array and the other three strings fall on the floor. Four columns, five allocations a row, one of them actually used.

The split that doesn't cut anything out

The span-based Split has been around for a couple of versions now and it works on a different idea. Instead of handing you new strings, it tells you where the pieces are. You give it a destination buffer of Range values, it fills in the start and end of each field, and you slice the original line yourself when you want to look at one. Nothing gets copied. Nothing gets allocated.

long total = 0;
Span<Range> ranges = stackalloc Range[8];
foreach (string line in lines)
{
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
    int count = span.Split(ranges, ',');
    ReadOnlySpan<char> amount = span[ranges[2]];
    total += long.Parse(amount, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
}

The stackalloc Range[8] buffer sits on the stack and gets reused on every iteration — one buffer for the whole loop, not one per row. span.Split writes the field boundaries into it and returns how many it found. span[ranges[2]] is a view over the amount field, still pointing into the original line's characters, and long.Parse has had a ReadOnlySpan<char> overload for ages, so it parses that slice straight without a substring in between. The row never becomes an array, the fields never become strings, and the only thing that leaves the loop is the running total.

The numbers

A million rows, built in memory, parsed best-of-7 in a container. Not a lab — I care about the ratio between the two, not the absolute milliseconds on whatever box this ran on.

rows                 : 1,000,000
string.Split sum     : 4,998,543,546
Span<Range> sum      : 4,998,543,546
sums match           : True

string.Split  best   :     75.7 ms   alloc   174.7 MB
Span<Range>   best   :     32.1 ms   alloc     0.0 MB

The sums matching is the part I care about most. Same answer, so this is a fair fight and not a trick where I quietly dropped work. On that footing the span path ran in a bit under half the time and allocated essentially nothing. The 174.7 MB the naive loop burned is all throwaway: arrays and substrings created and collected inside a single pass. Dropping it doesn't just save memory, it saves the GC the job of walking all that back out later, which is a chunk of where the time goes too.

I'll admit I expected the allocation win and only hoped for the speed one. Getting both was the nice surprise.

When I'd leave Split alone

I would not reach for this everywhere, and I'd push back on anyone who tried. If you actually need the fields as strings — you're stashing them in a list, returning them, putting them in a dictionary — then the span version just means you call .ToString() on each slice and you've bought back every allocation you saved, plus more awkward code. The ranges approach pays off exactly when you read the fields, use them, and let them go without keeping them around. Parsing to a number, comparing, summing: yes. Collecting rows into objects you hold onto: no, Split into strings is honest about what you need.

The other caveat is size. At a few hundred rows none of this registers; the naive loop allocates a rounding error and you'd never see it in a profile. This only became worth touching because the row count had three commas and a half-decent chance of growing. Reaching for stackalloc Range[] on a cold path nobody runs in a loop is effort spent making code harder to read for zero measured gain, and I think that trade is a bad one often enough to say it out loud.

One real gotcha: size the Range buffer for the most fields you expect, because Split stops once the destination is full and folds the rest of the line into the last range. Eight slots for four columns gives me headroom; a buffer that's too small turns into a silent correctness bug, not an exception.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. It's a plain net10.0 console app — one Program.cs, nothing else, build and run with dotnet run -c Release.

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Globalization;

const int Rows = 1_000_000;
var lines = new string[Rows];
var rng = new Random(42);
string[] regions = ["emea", "apac", "amer", "latam"];
for (int i = 0; i < Rows; i++)
{
    int amount = rng.Next(1, 10_000);
    lines[i] = $"{i},{regions[i & 3]},{amount},{(i % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 0)}";
}

_ = SumWithSplit(lines);   // warm up both paths before timing
_ = SumWithRanges(lines);

const int Trials = 7;
var (splitSum, splitMs, splitBytes) = Measure(() => SumWithSplit(lines), Trials);
var (rangeSum, rangeMs, rangeBytes) = Measure(() => SumWithRanges(lines), Trials);

Console.WriteLine($"sums match        : {splitSum == rangeSum}");
Console.WriteLine($"string.Split  best: {splitMs,8:F1} ms   alloc {splitBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),7:F1} MB");
Console.WriteLine($"Span<Range>   best: {rangeMs,8:F1} ms   alloc {rangeBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),7:F1} MB");

static long SumWithSplit(string[] lines)
{
    long total = 0;
    foreach (string line in lines)
    {
        string[] fields = line.Split(',');
        total += long.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    }
    return total;
}

static long SumWithRanges(string[] lines)
{
    long total = 0;
    Span<Range> ranges = stackalloc Range[8];
    foreach (string line in lines)
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
        span.Split(ranges, ',');
        total += long.Parse(span[ranges[2]], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    }
    return total;
}

static (long sum, double bestMs, long bytes) Measure(Func<long> work, int trials)
{
    long sum = 0;
    double best = double.MaxValue;
    long bytesForBest = 0;
    for (int t = 0; t < trials; t++)
    {
        GC.Collect();
        GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
        GC.Collect();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        sum = work();
        sw.Stop();
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        if (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds < best)
        {
            best = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
            bytesForBest = after - before;
        }
    }
    return (sum, best, bytesForBest);
}

Have you swapped a hot Split over to ranges, or found a spot where it wasn't worth the trouble? I'd like to hear where the line fell for you.

— still benchmarking the boring loops nobody asked me to touch

title: LED strip flickers only at low brightness? My 10-minute debugging order
description:
A strip that is stable at 100% but flickers at 20% is not necessarily defective. Low brightness is where dimming method, controller resolution, power supply behavior, and wiring noise all meet.

This is the order I use before replacing anything.

1. Find out what is actually doing the dimming

A PWM controller, a phase-cut wall dimmer, and an addressable controller creating dimming in software are three different systems. A lamp-rated wall dimmer feeding an ordinary LED strip supply can produce exactly this symptom, and no change to the strip will solve it.

For a low-voltage DC strip, I want a compatible constant-voltage supply and a PWM controller on the DC side. If there is a phase-cut dimmer on the AC side, every component has to be designed for that chain.

2. Check whether the flicker follows the output level

Set the controller to a fixed low level and watch for a minute. Then raise it slowly.

Regular pulsing at one brightness often points to PWM frequency or limited dimming resolution. Random flashes while the level changes can be a control or signal issue. A brief drop when another load switches on points me toward the supply and wiring instead.

A phone camera can help reveal pulsing, but I do not use it as the only test. Cameras add their own sampling artifacts.

3. Measure the DC bus at the strip

Measure at the strip terminals, not only at the supply. Compare full brightness and the problematic setting.

A loose terminal or undersized lead can sit unnoticed at low current and become unstable when the load changes. I also check that the supply is not operating below a required minimum load. Some supplies need a small stable load to regulate cleanly.

4. Separate PWM flicker from data flicker

With analog white or RGB strip, the controller switches the power rails. With WS2812 or similar pixels, the power rail stays on and the controller sends data. Those failures look similar from across the room but need different fixes.

For addressable pixels, I check the ground shared by the controller and pixels, the data resistor, and the first pixel before touching the rest of the run. For PWM strip, I check the controller's output frequency and whether it supports the frequency I need.

This comparison of PWM and pixel control is a useful reference when choosing the control method: https://suntechlite.com/pwm-vs-spi-led-lighting/

5. Bypass one component at a time

My fastest useful test is a short known-good strip on the same controller. Then the original strip on a known-good controller. One variable at a time.

If the short strip flickers too, the original run is probably innocent. If the problem stays with the original run, I inspect connectors, damaged sections, and the first powered joint.

I replace the strip only after those tests point to it. Most low-brightness flicker complaints I see are compatibility or control problems, not dead LEDs.

title: osFoundry는 왜 Codex CLI에 변경을 푸시하지 않고 리소스마다 커서로 폴링하게 할까
description:
osFoundry MCP 서버에서 "뭔가 바뀌면 알고 싶은" 클라이언트가 쓸 수 있는 걸 이 Mac에서 토큰 없이 전부 두드려 봤다.

$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 watch_sim.py
== Part 1: live wire, 8 calls each, ms ==
initialize                   HTTP 200  median  414.7  p90  757.8
tools/list                   HTTP 200  median  606.8  p90  716.7
resources/subscribe          HTTP 200  median  450.6  p90  550.2
GET (stream)                 HTTP 405  median  423.9  p90  475.4
tools/call poll (no token)   HTTP 401  median  322.0  p90  463.9
initialize capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}
resources/subscribe -> {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}
GET body -> ''
poll without token -> isError True | Authentication required
rate limit headers: limit 2000, reset in 61 s

푸시 경로는 세 개 다 닫혀 있다. initialize가 선언하는 건 tools뿐이고 그마저 listChanged: false라서, 툴 목록이 바뀌어도 알려 주지 않는다. resources/subscribe는 "Method not found"다. Streamable HTTP 서버라면 서버→클라이언트 스트림을 열어 줄 MCP URL로의 GET은 405를 돌려준다. 남는 건 읽기 전용 툴 하나뿐이다.

{"name": "poll_resource_events",
 "description": "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session.",
 "inputSchema": {"properties": {
     "resource_type": {"enum": ["message_channel", "note", "knowledge_base", "record_channel", "room",
                                "gitnest_repository", "agent_session", "team_session", "loop_session",
                                "graph_session"]},
     "resource_id": {"type": "string"},
     "after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}},
   "required": ["resource_type", "resource_id"], "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": false},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:read"]}]}

핵심은 "one granted"와 "resume from an event sequence" 두 표현이다. 이 글에서는 이 두 표현을 클라이언트 쪽을 Python으로 다시 만들어서 확인한다. 이 Mac에는 codex 바이너리가 없어서 클라이언트 역할은 스크립트가 했다. osFoundry 서버 코드는 공개돼 있지 않다. Part 1과 2는 라이브 서버고, Part 3은 재현이라 응답 모양과 활동 빈도는 재현 쪽에서 정한 값이다.

왜 푸시가 아니라 폴링일까, 특히 Codex라면

Codex CLI는 상주 프로세스가 아니다. 실행하면 돌고, 턴 하나를 처리하고, 끝나거나 사용자 입력을 기다린다. 푸시를 받으려면 세션과 세션 사이에도 누군가 귀를 열고 있어야 하는데, 노트북에선 대개 아무도 없다. 시퀀스 커서는 이런 생활 방식에 딱 맞는다. 클라이언트는 리소스마다 정수 하나만 들고 있다가, 내키는 때 돌아와서 그 뒤로 무슨 일이 있었는지 물으면 된다.

위의 ms 숫자는 일본에서 Apple M1으로 잰 거라 서버보다 경로 얘기에 가깝다. 더 중요한 건 레이트 리밋 헤더다. 인증 안 된 응답에 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000이 붙고, 리셋은 61초쯤 뒤다. 로그인한 클라이언트도 같은 한도인지는 확인 안 했다. 그래도 리소스 30개를 30초마다 폴링해 봐야 분당 60요청이다. Codex로 변경을 지켜볼 때 발목을 잡는 건 서버 부하가 아니라 Codex 자신의 턴 수다. 폴링 한 번이 곧 모델이 툴을 부르고 결과를 읽는 한 턴이다.

폴링해도 되는 대상은 어떻게 찾을까

호출 두 개면 되고, 스키마만 봐도 설계 의도가 꽤 드러난다.

list_granted_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=[] props=[]
list_project_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['project_id', 'resource_type'] props=['project_id', 'resource_type', 'search', 'offset', 'limit']
poll_resource_events     osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['resource_type', 'resource_id'] props=['resource_type', 'resource_id', 'after_sequence', 'limit']
59 tools on server; these three = 591 of 12662 tokens (4.7%, cl100k_base)
poll_resource_events types: 10 | list_project_resources types: 9 | only pollable: ['graph_session']

list_granted_resources는 인자를 하나도 안 받고, 억지로 넣으면 스키마가 튕긴다.

list_granted_resources   no arguments           ok
list_granted_resources   project_id passed      REJECT additionalProperties

클라이언트가 뭔가를 요청하는 툴이 아니라, 서버가 "네가 가진 건 이거다"라고 알려 주는 툴이다. initialize의 instructions도 "Use list_granted_resources first."로 시작한다. 돌아오는 건 연결에 추가된 프로젝트와 개별로 허용된 리소스다. 웹 클라이언트(ExternalAssistantsPanel.tsx)로 치면 Projects 영역과 "Older individual access" 영역이다.

list_project_resources는 resource_type이 필수다. "이 프로젝트 안에 있는 거 전부" 같은 목록은 없어서, 전체를 파악하려면 타입마다 한 번씩 아홉 번 불러야 한다. 한 타입에 50개가 넘으면(limit 최대 50, offset으로 페이지 넘김) 더 늘어난다. 설명문에는 프로젝트 단위 접근의 유일한 예외도 적혀 있다. "Ordinary Message channels require a separate invitation."

graph_session은 폴링은 되는데 목록에는 안 나온다. Graph는 오너의 데스크톱에 있고, 오너가 데스크톱 앱에서 공유한 다음에야 list_graph_sessions로 들어온다.

커서는 왜 서버가 아니라 클라이언트가 들고 있을까

osFoundry에는 두 방식이 다 있다. 에이전트 네트워크의 wait_for_messages는 커서를 서버가 들고 있어 준다. "Without after_sequence it resumes where your last call stopped"라고 돼 있고, timeout_s로 최대 50초까지 롱 폴링도 된다. poll_resource_events에는 둘 다 없다. timeout_s는 튕기고 설명엔 "resume from"뿐이니, 번호는 클라이언트가 챙겨 와야 한다.

wait_for_messages props: ['after_sequence', 'timeout_s', 'limit'] timeout_s max 50 | poll_resource_events has timeout: False
poll_resource_events     timeout_s 30           REJECT additionalProperties

서버가 커서를 들고 있으면 듣는 쪽이 하나일 땐 편하다. 그런데 연결 하나를 클라이언트 둘이 같이 쓰면 깨진다. 같은 로그인으로 터미널 두 개에서 Codex를 열면 딱 그 상황이다. 재현에서 채널 이벤트 600개를, 랜덤하게 번갈아 폴링하는 터미널 두 개에 흘려 봤다.

two terminals, client cursor: A saw 600/600, B saw 600/600
two terminals, server cursor: A saw 305/600, B saw 295/600

연결마다 서버가 커서를 하나 들고 있으면, 한쪽이 커서를 밀 때마다 다른 쪽은 그만큼 놓쳐서 각자 절반 정도만 본다. 요청에 after_sequence를 넣는 방식이면 둘 다 전부 보고, 서버는 읽는 쪽 상태를 하나도 안 들고 있어도 된다. 여러 툴이 제각각 읽어 가는 리소스 로그라면 커서 주인은 클라이언트가 맞다.

스키마상 after_sequence는 필수가 아니지만, 빼면 어떻게 되는지는 어디에도 안 적혀 있다. 거기 기대지 말자. 번호를 저장해 두고 매번 보내는 게 안전하다.

페이지가 꽉 차면 몇 번 불러야 할까

limit은 100이 끝이다. 대량 임포트 뒤라면 노트 하나에 이벤트가 수백 개 쌓여 있을 수 있다. 마지막 시퀀스부터 다시 부르고, 페이지가 꽉 차지 않은 채로 올 때까지 반복해서 비운다.

burst of 350 events, limit 100:  4 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  50:  7 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  20: 18 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350

100으로 부르면 된다. 재현에서 응답 크기는 빈 페이지가 17토큰, 이벤트 하나짜리가 41토큰이었다(cl100k_base). 모양은 재현 쪽 거지 osFoundry 게 아니지만, 자릿수 감은 충분하다. 빈 폴링은 읽는 비용이 싸고, 폴링 비용은 거의 턴 수로 정해진다.

리소스 30개를 얼마 간격으로 폴링해야 할까

재현에서는 프로젝트 하나에 목록으로 뽑을 수 있는 아홉 타입의 리소스 30개를 두고 활동량을 한쪽으로 몰았다. 바쁜 게 3개(분당 이벤트 1개), 적당한 게 7개(10분에 1개), 조용한 게 20개(2시간에 1개). 빈도는 가정이다. 8시간짜리 하루를 시드 5개로, 가상 시계 위에서 돌렸다.

every 30 s, all 30                 calls/hour   3600  empty  94.7%  seen late median   14.9 s  p90   27.0 s  max     30 s  (1843 events/day)
every 5 min, all 30                calls/hour    360  empty  78.0%  seen late median  150.9 s  p90  271.1 s  max    300 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 10 min    calls/hour    502  empty  70.2%  seen late median   34.9 s  p90  206.4 s  max    599 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 30 min    calls/hour    420  empty  65.3%  seen late median   35.6 s  p90  238.4 s  max   1799 s  (1843 events/day)
server window for comparison: 2000 requests per ~61 s

고정 30초는 빠르지만 95%가 헛방이다. 시간당 3,600번 부르고 거의 다 비어 있다. 고정 5분은 싸지만, 바쁜 채널까지 포함해서 전부 느리다. 리소스별 백오프(빈 폴링마다 그 리소스의 간격을 두 배로 늘리고, 이벤트가 오면 처음으로 되돌림)는 호출 수를 싼 쪽에 가깝게 맞추면서 지연 중앙값은 빠른 쪽에 가깝게 유지한다. 바쁜 리소스는 30초에 머물고 조용한 것만 멀어지기 때문이다. 대가는 상한값이다. 30분으로 두면 조용한 리소스의 첫 변경은 최대 30분까지 기다릴 수 있다.

Codex 입장에선 이 표가 오히려 타이머를 아예 안 돌릴 이유가 된다. 사람이 "뭐 바뀌었어?"라고 물을 때 저장해 둔 커서로 한 바퀴 돌면, 지켜보는 리소스 하나당 호출 한 번으로 그 시점까지의 변경을 지연 0으로 잡는다. 백오프 표는 Codex든 뭐든 계속 지켜보게 돌려 두는 스크립트를 위한 거다.

오너가 접근을 회수하면 어떻게 될까

오너가 4시간 07분 시점에 프로젝트를 뺐다고 하자. 커서 30개가 전부 이제 못 읽는 리소스를 가리킨다. 문제는 클라이언트가 그걸 언제까지 폴링하느냐다.

owner removes the project at 4 h 07 min (30 resources lose access):
  re-list grants every 10 min    failed polls after removal  180, list_granted_resources calls 25
  re-list grants every 60 min    failed polls after removal 3180, list_granted_resources calls 5
  re-list grants on first error  failed polls after removal    1, list_granted_resources calls 5

타이머로 그랜트를 다시 확인하면 호출이 늘거나, 실패하는 폴링을 수천 번 쌓거나 둘 중 하나다. 처음 거절당한 순간을 "그랜트 다시 읽기" 신호로 쓰면 실패 한 번과 list_granted_resources 호출 한 번이면 끝난다. 그다음 목록에서 사라진 리소스의 커서를 버리면 된다. 나중에 오너가 프로젝트를 다시 넣어 주면 그 리소스들은 처음부터 새로 시작한다.

스키마는 어디서 막을까

나머지 케이스도 라이브 inputSchema에 jsonschema(Draft 2020-12)로 돌려 봤다.

list_project_resources   no resource_type       REJECT required
list_project_resources   limit 50               ok
list_project_resources   limit 51               REJECT maximum: limit
list_project_resources   graph_session          REJECT enum: resource_type
list_project_resources   search 101 chars       REJECT maxLength: search
poll_resource_events     no after_sequence      ok
poll_resource_events     graph_session          ok
poll_resource_events     after_sequence -1      REJECT minimum: after_sequence
poll_resource_events     limit 100              ok
poll_resource_events     limit 101              REJECT maximum: limit
poll_resource_events     resource_type project  REJECT enum: resource_type

다들 제일 먼저 해 보는 게 resource_type: "project"다. 프로젝트는 로그를 가진 리소스가 아니라, 리소스를 보이게 해 주는 그랜트 단위다.

스크립트 전체는 M1에서 20.2초 걸렸고, 그중 대부분이 네트워크 호출 40번이었다. 유저 CPU 시간은 0.91초였다.

직접 만든다면

  • 로그는 리소스마다 하나로 두고, 커서는 클라이언트가 들게 한다. 연결 하나를 둘이 읽어도 이벤트를 뺏어 가지 않고, 서버는 읽는 쪽 상태를 저장할 필요가 없다.
  • 그랜트 목록은 인자 없는 전용 툴로 만들고, 클라이언트가 거기서 시작하게 한다. 찾을 수 있는 건 오너가 허용한 것뿐이어야 한다.
  • 페이지 크기에 상한을 두고, 다 비우는 법(마지막 시퀀스부터, 덜 찬 페이지가 올 때까지 다시 부르기)을 정해 둔다.
  • 백오프는 전역이 아니라 리소스별로. 바쁜 건 빠르게, 조용한 건 싸게.
  • 폴링이 처음 거절되면 그랜트를 다시 읽고, 사라진 커서는 재시도하지 말고 버린다.
  • 커서는 이벤트를 처리한 다음에 기록한다. 중간에 죽어도 건너뛰는 게 아니라 다시 읽게 된다.

연결마다 툴이 어떻게 정해지는지는 툴 스코프 페이지, 프로토콜의 짧은 정의는 MCP 용어 설명에 있다.

title: Keeping a local Pinnacle odds book over WebSocket in Python (snapshot + deltas)
description:
Most odds feeds are built for polling: you ask for the whole board every few seconds and diff it yourself. A push feed works the other way round, and the client code gets simpler once you treat it as a tiny state machine. This post walks through that pattern for Pinnacle prices using PinnFeed, a WebSocket and REST API I work on (disclosure up front).

The model: snapshot, then deltas

After you connect and subscribe, the server sends three kinds of data messages:

  1. welcome, with your plan limits.
  2. A chunked snapshot of every event and market that matches your filters, split into parts of up to 400 events. The last part has "final": true.
  3. A stream of delta batches. Each change is either upsert (replace the object) or remove (the market was suspended or settled, or the event ended).

There is also a heartbeat: the server sends ping every 20 seconds and closes connections that stay silent for 60 seconds, so you answer with pong.

That means the whole client is: keep two dictionaries (events by id, markets by id), apply upserts and removes, and don't trust the book until the snapshot says final.

A minimal local book in Python 

# pip install websockets
import asyncio, json, os, websockets

events, markets = {}, {}
book_ready = False

def apply_change(c):
    store = markets if c["kind"] == "market" else events
    obj = c.get("market") or c.get("event")
    if c["op"] == "upsert":
        store[obj["id"]] = obj
    elif c["op"] == "remove":
        store.pop(obj["id"] if obj else c.get("id"), None)

async def main():
    global book_ready
    async with websockets.connect(
        "wss://pinnfeed.io/v1/stream",
        additional_headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["PINNFEED_KEY"]},
        compression="deflate",
    ) as ws:
        await ws.send(json.dumps({
            "type": "subscribe",
            "sports": ["soccer"],
            "markets": ["moneyline", "total"],
            "live": True,
        }))
        async for raw in ws:
            msg = json.loads(raw)
            t = msg["type"]
            if t == "ping":
                await ws.send('{"type":"pong"}')
            elif t == "snapshot":
                for e in msg.get("events", []):
                    events[e["id"]] = e
                for m in msg.get("markets", []):
                    markets[m["id"]] = m
                book_ready = msg.get("final", False)
            elif t == "delta" and book_ready:
                for c in msg["changes"]:
                    apply_change(c)

asyncio.run(main())

A few notes from writing this:

  • Wait for final: true. If you act on the first snapshot part you will think most markets are missing.
  • Sending subscribe again replaces the subscription and triggers a fresh snapshot, so reset your dictionaries when you change filters.
  • Ask for compression. The compression="deflate" option negotiates permessage-deflate, which matters when you subscribe to whole sports.
  • Every outcome already carries a no-vig fair price next to the decimal and American prices, so you don't have to remove the margin yourself before comparing against another book.

Polling is fine for prototypes

If you only want to see which prices are moving, the REST side has a GET /v1/drops endpoint that returns the biggest shortening per outcome over a rolling window (1 to 60 minutes, with a minimum drop percentage):

curl -H "x-api-key: $PINNFEED_KEY" \
  "https://pinnfeed.io/v1/drops?sport=soccer&live=true&minutes=10&min_pct=5"

On the free plan REST responses are delayed by 30 seconds, which is enough to build and test the logic before you need a live stream.

Where to go next

  • The full message reference (subscribe fields, snapshot and delta shapes, raw frames): PinnFeed WebSocket protocol docs
  • A complete small project that turns drops into Telegram alerts: pinnfeed/dropping-odds-telegram on GitHub

PinnFeed is not affiliated with Pinnacle. If you use odds data for betting, it is for adults (18+) only, and no data feed guarantees a profit.
