title: Why your prompt cache never hits, and what it saves
description:
A prompt cache pays only when the start of every request is identical and calls come often enough. The usual reasons it misses, and a way to check.

A prompt cache lets the API remember the beginning of a request, so the next request that starts with exactly the same text does not pay full price to process it again. When it works, repeated calls get cheaper and start answering sooner. When it does not, you pay for the marks you added and get nothing back, and no error tells you so. The only sign is a usage counter that stays at zero. This guide explains what has to be true for a hit, the five ordinary reasons for a miss, and a short routine for finding out which one applies to you.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/prompt-caching-misses?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: Python While Loop: Display Odd and Even Jersey Numbers
description:
In a school sports event, students wearing ODD jersey numbers enter the ground first. After they finish, students wearing EVEN jersey numbers enter the ground.

Let's use Python to display the order.

Displaying Odd Jersey Numbers

odd_no=1
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

odd_no=1
while odd_no<=10:
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

output 1 3 5 7 9

even_no=2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

even_no=2
while even_no<=10:
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

output 2 4 6 8 10

combined program
print("Odd Jersey Numbers:")

odd_no=1
while odd_no<=10:
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

print("\nEven Jersey Number:")

eeven_no=2
while even_no<=10:
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

Output:

Odd Jersey Numbers:
1 3 5 7 9

Even Jersey Number:
2 4 6 8 10

title: Flattening a PDF form? Keep an editable copy before you send it
description:
A customer fills in a PDF request form, downloads it, and emails it back. Your reviewer needs a copy to read. The customer may still need to correct an address tomorrow. Those are different requirements, even when both files look the same on screen.

Flattening can be useful for a delivery copy, but it should not silently replace the working document. The useful question is: what must the next person be able to do with this particular copy?

Three states that are easy to confuse

A PDF may contain interactive form fields, ordinary page text, and annotations. Typing something over a blank line does not necessarily create a field that another system can read as form data.

For an existing interactive form, distinguish these states:

State What the next person needs What to verify
Editable working copy Correct values or continue filling The saved file still contains the expected fields and values
Read-only field configuration Stop normal field editing in a cooperating viewer Field behavior and your viewer's handling of the setting
Flattened delivery copy Read the filled appearance without using the original interactive controls Values remain visible after reopening; the targeted controls are no longer interactive

Read-only flags and flattening are not interchangeable. Neither is a cryptographic guarantee that a PDF cannot be altered with other software. If the requirement is to detect changes or control access, evaluate signatures, permissions, and application authorization separately.

Make the copy decision before choosing the export operation

Suppose you are building an equipment request form. The applicant enters an item code, a quantity, and a delivery note. A reviewer can send it back for changes, then approve a particular revision.

Keep a working PDF for the revision process. After approval, create a delivery derivative only if the recipient needs that format. A practical sequence is:

  1. Start from the intended form template revision.
  2. Fill values, finish the active field edit, and run the application's validation.
  3. Save the editable PDF as a new revision.
  4. Reopen that saved revision and confirm the field values.
  5. Make a separate derivative and flatten the intended form content.
  6. Reopen the derivative in the recipient's viewer and compare the visible values.
  7. Deliver only the verified derivative while retaining its connection to the editable revision.

The ComPDF Web form operations cover creating and filling interactive fields as well as flattening forms. The PDF component performs those document operations. Your application still decides which revision was reviewed, who can create a delivery copy, and which file a download button returns.

Use the exact API and save behavior documented for the Web SDK version installed in your project; a method copied from a desktop SDK is not automatically a Web SDK call.

Save first, then derive from that saved revision

A subtle failure happens when an application saves the working copy and creates the final copy from different document states. The screen may show the last change while the saved file still contains an earlier value.

Treat the saved working revision as the input to the delivery operation. Do not use the original template again, and do not overwrite it with the filled result. When the reviewer requests a correction, create a new working revision and regenerate the derivative from that revision.

Workflow illustration. Revision records belong to the application, not the PDF engine.

One possible application record is:

{
  "submissionId": "request-127",
  "templateRevision": "equipment-v3",
  "workingRevision": 4,
  "workingFile": "requests/request-127/r4/editable.pdf",
  "deliveryFile": "requests/request-127/r4/delivery.pdf"
}

These are application-defined fields, not a ComPDF response schema. Their purpose is to let you answer a concrete question: which editable revision produced this delivered PDF? A file path or a name containing final is not approval evidence on its own.

Keep export separate from successful persistence: obtaining PDF bytes does not mean your server has stored them, authorized access, or recorded the revision.

Use values that expose handoff mistakes

Do not validate only with a short name and a selected checkbox. Use a small form that makes errors visible:

  • An identifier such as 00127. It should remain the same identifier; the application must not treat it as a number and remove leading zeros.
  • A zero quantity or amount, where allowed. It must not disappear because application code treats zero as an empty value.
  • An optional blank field. A blank is different from inserting a default value or the text null.
  • A long delivery note. Check whether the actual viewer and field configuration show all required content, including on the flattened copy.
  • Selected and unselected checkboxes. Confirm the visible state matches the saved data, rather than assuming the first radio option or default appearance is correct.
  • Characters your recipients use. Include the relevant language and punctuation, then check the saved appearance.

For each case, inspect both copies after closing and reopening them. The working copy should preserve the required field editing behavior. The delivery copy should preserve the intended appearance and the intended flattening scope. Compare the content at normal reading and print sizes, not just in a tiny preview.

If the field value is correct but some text is clipped, that is still a failed delivery for a reader who needs the missing text. Revisit the field layout, font settings, or text limits before regenerating the copy.

Check what you are flattening

Form fields, annotations, and drawn signatures can travel through different operations. Flattening forms does not justify a claim that every annotation has been flattened or that a cryptographic signature remains valid.

Choose the scope explicitly, inspect the output, and test any signed-document workflow separately. Do not use flattening as redaction: text that should be removed needs an appropriate removal workflow, not simply a less interactive presentation.

Likewise, a PDF that looks filled is not proof that submission data was stored in your database. If you need structured values for downstream processing, collect and validate them deliberately before removing the controls you depend on.

Let the recipient's task decide the deliverable

Keep the editable copy when corrections, field extraction, or continued form filling are part of the workflow. Consider a flattened derivative when a recipient needs the confirmed visual form and no longer needs the interactive controls. Keep both only when the workflow has a reason for both, with access and retention rules appropriate to each.

The acceptance test is straightforward: can the next person do their job with the delivered file, and can your team trace it back to the exact working revision? Once those answers are clear, filling, saving, and flattening become deliberate document operations rather than a single ambiguous “export” button.

For the export step, follow the Web SDK document saving guide, then apply the reopening checks above to your own form and recipient viewer.

title: 為什麼 osFoundry 讓 Codex CLI 針對每個資源輪詢 cursor，而不是主動推送變更？
description:
想知道「什麼東西變了」的 client，osFoundry 的 MCP server 能給的就只有下面這些。在這台 Mac 上、不帶 token 執行：

$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 watch_sim.py
== Part 1: live wire, 8 calls each, ms ==
initialize                   HTTP 200  median  414.7  p90  757.8
tools/list                   HTTP 200  median  606.8  p90  716.7
resources/subscribe          HTTP 200  median  450.6  p90  550.2
GET (stream)                 HTTP 405  median  423.9  p90  475.4
tools/call poll (no token)   HTTP 401  median  322.0  p90  463.9
initialize capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}
resources/subscribe -> {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}
GET body -> ''
poll without token -> isError True | Authentication required
rate limit headers: limit 2000, reset in 61 s

三條 push 的路都關著。initialize 只宣告了 tools，其他什麼都沒有，而且是 listChanged: false，所以連 tool 清單變動都不會通知。resources/subscribe 回的是 "Method not found"。對 MCP URL 發 GET，也就是 Streamable HTTP server 原本會開出 server 到 client 串流的地方，回傳 405。剩下的只有一個唯讀 tool：

{"name": "poll_resource_events",
 "description": "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session.",
 "inputSchema": {"properties": {
     "resource_type": {"enum": ["message_channel", "note", "knowledge_base", "record_channel", "room",
                                "gitnest_repository", "agent_session", "team_session", "loop_session",
                                "graph_session"]},
     "resource_id": {"type": "string"},
     "after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}},
   "required": ["resource_type", "resource_id"], "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": false},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:read"]}]}

"One granted" 的資源、"resume from an event sequence"。這篇接下來就是在講這幾個字，client 端則用 Python 重建。這台機器沒有安裝 codex 執行檔，所以由 script 扮演 client。osFoundry 的 server 程式碼沒有公開：Part 1 和 Part 2 打的是正式環境的 server，Part 3 則是重建版本，回應格式和活動頻率都是它自己設定的。

為什麼 Codex 特別適合用輪詢，而不是 push？

Codex CLI 不是 daemon。你執行它，它才會跑，做完一個 turn 之後就結束，或是停下來等你。Push channel 需要有東西在你的 session 之間持續監聽，而在筆電上，這個東西往往不存在。Sequence cursor 剛好符合這種使用方式：client 每個資源只記一個整數，想回來的時候再回來，問「這個號碼之後發生了什麼」。

上面的毫秒數是在日本用 Apple M1 量的，所以反映的多半是網路路徑，而不是 server 本身。更重要的是 rate limit header。未驗證的回應帶有 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000，大約 61 s 後重置。登入後的 client 是否有同樣的額度沒有另外確認，但就算每 30 s 輪詢 30 個資源，也才每分鐘 60 個請求。限制 Codex 監看程式的不是 server 負載，而是它自己的 turn：每一次 poll 都是一次 tool call，模型得發出去、再讀回來。

Client 怎麼知道自己可以輪詢哪些資源？

靠兩個呼叫，而 schema 本身就透露了不少設計思路：

list_granted_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=[] props=[]
list_project_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['project_id', 'resource_type'] props=['project_id', 'resource_type', 'search', 'offset', 'limit']
poll_resource_events     osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['resource_type', 'resource_id'] props=['resource_type', 'resource_id', 'after_sequence', 'limit']
59 tools on server; these three = 591 of 12662 tokens (4.7%, cl100k_base)
poll_resource_events types: 10 | list_project_resources types: 9 | only pollable: ['graph_session']

list_granted_resources 完全不接受參數，schema 也把加參數的路堵死了：

list_granted_resources   no arguments           ok
list_granted_resources   project_id passed      REJECT additionalProperties

這是 server 告訴 client 它擁有什麼，而不是 client 去要求什麼。initialize 的 instructions 第一句就是 "Use list_granted_resources first." 回傳的內容是加到這個連線的 project，以及個別授權的資源。在 web client（ExternalAssistantsPanel.tsx）裡，對應的是 Projects 區塊和 "Older individual access"。

list_project_resources 一定要帶 resource_type。沒有「列出這個 project 裡所有東西」的方式，所以要盤點完整內容，每種類型就要呼叫一次，總共九種；某個類型超過 50 筆的話還要更多次（limit 上限 50，用 offset 分頁）。它的 description 還補充了 project 存取的唯一例外："Ordinary Message channels require a separate invitation."

graph_session 可以輪詢，但不能列出。Graph 存在 owner 的桌面上，要透過 list_graph_sessions 進來，而且前提是 owner 已經從桌面 app 分享出來。

為什麼 cursor 由 client 持有，而不是 server？

osFoundry 兩種都有。Agent network 上的 wait_for_messages 會幫你記住 cursor："Without after_sequence it resumes where your last call stopped"，而且支援 timeout_s 最多 50 的 long polling。poll_resource_events 兩者都沒有。timeout_s 會被拒絕，description 也只寫 "resume from"，所以號碼要由 client 自己帶：

wait_for_messages props: ['after_sequence', 'timeout_s', 'limit'] timeout_s max 50 | poll_resource_events has timeout: False
poll_resource_events     timeout_s 30           REJECT additionalProperties

Server 端持有 cursor，對單一監聽者來說很方便。但只要兩個 client 共用同一個連線就會出問題，而你用同一個登入在兩個終端機開 Codex 時，正好就是這種情況。重建版本讓 600 個 channel 事件經過兩個隨機輪流輪詢的終端機：

two terminals, client cursor: A saw 600/600, B saw 600/600
two terminals, server cursor: A saw 305/600, B saw 295/600

每個連線一個 server 端 cursor 的話，每個終端機都會替另一個把 cursor 往前推，結果各自只看到大約一半。Request 裡帶 after_sequence 的話，兩邊都能看到全部，server 也完全不需要保存每個讀取者的狀態。對於可能被多個工具各自讀取的資源 log 來說，cursor 交給 client 才是對的。

Schema 沒有把 after_sequence 設為必填，也沒說省略時代表什麼。不要依賴這個行為。把號碼存下來，每次都帶上。

一整頁要花多少次呼叫？

limit 最多 100。大量匯入之後，一則 note 可能有好幾百個事件在等。要清空，就得從最後一個 sequence 繼續呼叫，直到回來的頁面不滿為止：

burst of 350 events, limit 100:  4 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  50:  7 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  20: 18 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350

就設 100。在重建版本裡，空白頁的回應是 17 個 token，一個事件是 41 個，用 cl100k_base 計算。這是重建版的格式，不是 osFoundry 的，但數量級已經足以說明：空的 poll 讀起來很便宜，所以輪詢的成本主要在 turn 的次數。

Codex 應該多久輪詢一次 30 個資源？

重建版本給一個 project 30 個資源，涵蓋九種可列出的類型，活躍度刻意不平均：3 個很忙（每分鐘一個事件）、7 個普通（每 10 分鐘一個）、20 個冷門（每 2 小時一個）。這些頻率是假設值。它在模擬時鐘上用五個 seed 跑一個 8 小時的工作日：

every 30 s, all 30                 calls/hour   3600  empty  94.7%  seen late median   14.9 s  p90   27.0 s  max     30 s  (1843 events/day)
every 5 min, all 30                calls/hour    360  empty  78.0%  seen late median  150.9 s  p90  271.1 s  max    300 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 10 min    calls/hour    502  empty  70.2%  seen late median   34.9 s  p90  206.4 s  max    599 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 30 min    calls/hour    420  empty  65.3%  seen late median   35.6 s  p90  238.4 s  max   1799 s  (1843 events/day)
server window for comparison: 2000 requests per ~61 s

固定每 30 s 很快，但 95% 是浪費：每小時 3,600 次呼叫，幾乎都是空的。固定每 5 分鐘很省，但到處都慢，連最忙的 channel 也一樣。以資源為單位的 backoff，也就是每次 poll 空手而回就把該資源的間隔加倍、一有事件就重置，呼叫次數接近省錢方案，延遲中位數又接近快速方案。原因是忙碌的資源一直維持在 30 s，冷門的則逐漸拉長。代價在上限：設 30 分鐘的話，冷門資源的第一個變更可能要等上半小時。

對 Codex 來說，這張表主要是在說明根本不需要計時器。有人問「改了什麼？」的時候，用已存好的 cursor 跑一輪，每個監看的資源只花一次呼叫，而且到那一刻為止的所有變化都能零延遲回答。Backoff 排程是給那種要讓 Codex 或其他東西持續監看的 script 用的。

Owner 撤銷存取權限時會發生什麼事？

Owner 在 4 h 07 min 把 project 移除。這時 30 個 cursor 全都指向連線讀不到的資源。問題是 client 還會繼續輪詢多久：

owner removes the project at 4 h 07 min (30 resources lose access):
  re-list grants every 10 min    failed polls after removal  180, list_granted_resources calls 25
  re-list grants every 60 min    failed polls after removal 3180, list_granted_resources calls 5
  re-list grants on first error  failed polls after removal    1, list_granted_resources calls 5

用計時器檢查授權，要嘛多花呼叫次數，要嘛浪費掉好幾千次失敗的 poll。把第一次被拒的 poll 當成「重新讀取授權」的訊號，只需要一次失敗加一次額外的 list_granted_resources。接著把資源已經不在清單上的 cursor 全部丟掉。如果 owner 之後又把 project 加回來，client 就從頭開始處理那些資源。

Schema 會在哪些地方擋下 client？

剩下的情況，用 jsonschema（Draft 2020-12）對照正式環境的 inputSchema 檢查：

list_project_resources   no resource_type       REJECT required
list_project_resources   limit 50               ok
list_project_resources   limit 51               REJECT maximum: limit
list_project_resources   graph_session          REJECT enum: resource_type
list_project_resources   search 101 chars       REJECT maxLength: search
poll_resource_events     no after_sequence      ok
poll_resource_events     graph_session          ok
poll_resource_events     after_sequence -1      REJECT minimum: after_sequence
poll_resource_events     limit 100              ok
poll_resource_events     limit 101              REJECT maximum: limit
poll_resource_events     resource_type project  REJECT enum: resource_type

resource_type: "project" 是大家最先會試的。Project 不是一個有 log 的資源，而是讓資源變得可見的那個授權。

整個 script 在 M1 上花了 20.2 s 的實際時間，包含 40 次網路呼叫。User CPU 時間是 0.91 s。

如果你要自己實作

  • 每個資源各自維護一份 log，cursor 交給 client 持有。這樣同一個連線上的兩個讀取者就不會互相搶走事件，server 也不必保存讀取者狀態。
  • 授權清單給它一個專用、不帶參數的 tool，並讓 client 從那裡開始。Discovery 應該只回傳 owner 授權過的東西。
  • 限制每頁大小，並說明怎麼清空（從最後一個 sequence 繼續呼叫，直到拿到不滿的一頁）。
  • Backoff 以資源為單位，不要全域套用。忙碌的資源保持快速，冷門的變得便宜。
  • 第一次 poll 被拒時，重新讀取授權，把已經消失的 cursor 丟掉，而不是一直重試。
  • 處理完事件之後才把 cursor 寫回去，這樣當機時事件會重播，而不是被跳過。

osFoundry 如何決定每個連線能拿到哪些 tool，請看 tool scope 頁面。協定的簡短定義在 MCP 詞彙條目。

title: A practical portrait review workflow and crop-boundary check
description:
A profile photo has a small job: help another person recognize you and get a sense of how you present yourself. That can be harder than it sounds. A picture that looks appealing at full size may be unreadable on a phone, while a technically sharp image may feel too formal for the setting. Instead of searching for one perfect portrait, build a small set of honest, varied images and review them together.

AI Dating Photo Generator is a browser-based tool that creates dating profile portraits from your own photos, lets you choose a scene, and offers a way to review or refine results. If you decide to explore the ai dating profile photo generator, treat generated images as options to evaluate rather than as proof of what you look like in every situation. I am associated with the project, and this guide was drafted with AI assistance. Examples are hypothetical, and it does not claim independent product testing or guaranteed results.

Start with recognition, not decoration

Before changing a background or choosing an outfit, decide what a viewer should be able to recognize. A clear view of your face, an expression that feels natural, and a recent appearance are more important than a dramatic location. A useful first image should still make sense at the small size at which most people will encounter it.

Compare a candidate with a recent, unedited photograph. Check features that matter for recognition, including the shape of your face, hairstyle, facial hair, and any distinctive marks you normally show. Lighting and a different camera angle can change how someone looks, but a generated image should not make a meeting in person feel like a surprise. If you would need to explain that the picture represents an old hairstyle or a substantially different appearance, choose a more current alternative.

Gather a useful source set

When selecting input images, use photographs you have permission to upload and share. Prefer images of yourself over pictures containing other people. A varied source set can include a straight-on portrait, a gentle three-quarter angle, and a picture in even daylight. Avoid relying entirely on images with heavy filters, deep shadows, face coverings, or very low resolution.

More files are not automatically better. Review each photo for focus, current appearance, and whether your face is large enough to distinguish. Set aside any image whose ownership or consent is uncertain. If a group photograph is your only option, consider taking a fresh individual picture instead of uploading other people’s faces unnecessarily.

Keep the original files in a private location. Before using any external service, read its current terms and privacy information, including what it says about uploads, retention, deletion, and permitted uses. Do not assume that a file disappears immediately after you close a browser tab. If the available information does not meet your comfort level, use an offline photo or another method instead.

Choose a setting that supports the subject

A background should add context without competing with your face. A simple outdoor scene, an uncluttered room, or a neutral wall can be easier to read than a busy street full of signs and strangers. Think about the mood you want to convey: relaxed, approachable, creative, or active. A setting can suggest a mood without making a factual claim about your occupation or lifestyle.

Review the boundaries where hair, clothing, and shoulders meet the background. Generated portraits may contain odd edges, inconsistent shadows, or details that look plausible at a glance but not on inspection. Look at hands, jewelry, glasses, fabric patterns, and objects close to the body. If a feature looks wrong, refine or discard the image rather than hoping nobody notices.

A convincing scene is not necessarily an accurate one. Avoid selecting a location that implies you visited a place or participated in an activity if you did not. A neutral illustrative setting is easier to interpret honestly than a picture that appears to document a specific trip or event. When in doubt, pair a generated portrait with real, recent photographs that show your everyday appearance.

Check light, color, and framing

Good lighting reveals the face without flattening every detail. Look for a balance between visible eyes, natural skin tones, and enough contrast to separate the subject from the background. Very bright highlights can erase detail, while strong backlighting can turn a face into a silhouette. Color should feel consistent across the image; a warm face against an implausibly cool shadow may be distracting.

Test the crop before deciding. Leave some space around the head and shoulders so the image can survive different app layouts. A square preview may crop differently from a tall profile card. Keep important facial features away from the extreme edges, and verify that hair or the top of the head is not unintentionally cut off.

Look at the image on both a larger display and a phone. At a large size, inspect artifacts. At a small size, ask whether the expression is readable and whether the subject stands out from the background. A photo can pass one test and fail the other. Keep only images that work in the context in which they will be seen.

Build variety across a set

A profile usually benefits from more than several nearly identical close-ups. Consider a clear primary portrait, a different angle or setting, and a candid or activity image that reflects something you actually enjoy. Each picture should contribute information rather than repeat the same expression in a slightly different crop.

Variety does not mean presenting incompatible versions of yourself. A collection that switches dramatically between ages, hair colors, body shapes, or styles can undermine recognition. Place images side by side and ask whether someone meeting you would reasonably identify the same person in all of them. Keep your real appearance as the reference point.

If an activity photo includes friends, ask for their permission before publishing it. Avoid showing documents, address details, workplace identifiers, vehicle plates, or other information you do not intend to disclose. You can crop a photograph to reduce incidental exposure, but check that the resulting image still makes sense and does not misleadingly change the context.

Use a short review checklist

A repeatable checklist is more useful than endlessly comparing minor differences. For each candidate, answer the following questions:

  1. Is the picture recent enough to represent my current appearance?
  2. Can a viewer see my face clearly at the expected display size?
  3. Are the eyes, hands, accessories, and background free of distracting artifacts?
  4. Does the image avoid implying an experience, place, or identity that is not mine?
  5. Do I have permission to use every visible person’s image and the underlying photograph?
  6. Does this picture add something distinct to the rest of the set?
  7. Am I comfortable with the platform receiving and displaying the image?

If an answer is no, decide whether a simple crop or a different candidate addresses the problem. If not, leave it out. This process is not a score for attractiveness; it is a way to reduce confusion, privacy risks, and avoidable visual distractions.

Get feedback without outsourcing the decision

A trusted friend can notice a misleading crop or an expression that does not look like you. Give them a narrow question, such as whether they would recognize you from the first image or which of two crops is clearer on a phone. Broad requests for a rating can produce conflicting opinions without helping you make a practical choice.

Remember that friends may have different preferences from the people you hope to meet. Treat their feedback as information, not a rule. You remain responsible for selecting pictures that feel comfortable, accurate, and consistent with the expectations of the app you use. Check that app’s rules on altered or generated images before uploading.

A small crop-metadata check

A developer building an internal review workflow can start by validating declared crop coordinates before recording a review. The function below only checks integer bounds against supplied dimensions. It does not open a file, identify a person, verify consent, inspect image metadata, or detect manipulated content. Coordinates use a top-left origin and a half-open rectangle: a crop ending exactly at the right or bottom edge is allowed. This is a standalone teaching example, not a feature of the product mentioned above.

def check_crop(width, height, left, top, crop_width, crop_height):
    values = (width, height, left, top, crop_width, crop_height)
    if any(type(value) is not int for value in values):
        return False
    if width <= 0 or height <= 0 or left < 0 or top < 0:
        return False
    if crop_width <= 0 or crop_height <= 0:
        return False
    return left + crop_width <= width and top + crop_height <= height

I ran six local synthetic cases for full-frame and edge-aligned crops, overflow, negative offsets, zero size, and a Boolean argument. Those cases establish only that this function returns the expected Boolean for the supplied values; they are not tests of an image editor or service. A production pipeline would also need to define orientation, units, metadata provenance, error handling, and data retention before using such a check. Keep consent records separate and do not log private photographs just to test a rectangle.

For example, (800, 600, 10, 20, 790, 580) is within bounds, while increasing the crop width to 791 extends one pixel beyond the declared right edge. The function deliberately rejects Boolean values even though Python treats bool as a subclass of int; this is a policy choice for this example rather than a universal validation rule. If an application accepts other numeric types or rotated coordinates, specify those rules explicitly and test them separately.

Maintain the profile over time

Revisit your pictures when your appearance or circumstances change. A new haircut, glasses, or a different everyday style may make an older image less useful as a primary portrait. You do not need to replace every picture at once; review the set periodically and swap out anything that no longer feels representative.

Keep a small private shortlist of approved images and their original sources. This makes it easier to update a profile without repeating the entire selection process. Remove files you no longer want to retain, and use any available deletion controls on services where you uploaded them. The result should be a profile that is easy to recognize, considerate of other people’s privacy, and comfortable for you to maintain.

title: I ranked 7 Android cloud services by one question: will the device still be the same device in three months?
description:
Disclosure first: I work with DuoPlus, on the growth side. So yes, it's on this list, and yes, it's near the top. I'll tell you where it falls short too, and I checked every other product's claims against its own website this week instead of going from memory.

Why this list exists: most cloud phone and device cloud roundups rank by "how many devices" or "how cheap." That's not what breaks for the teams I talk to. They're small QA shops, two-person dev teams, agencies looking after a dozen client apps. The question that actually costs them time is boring: when I open this Android environment next month, is it still logged in, still configured, still mine? Or am I starting from zero again?

So that's the ranking criterion. Fit for small dev/QA teams and agencies that need stable, isolated Android environments that last. Not gaming, and not one-off test runs (though some tools below are great at those).

1. DuoPlus

https://www.duoplus.net/share/market

DuoPlus gives you real ARM Android cloud phones, on Android 10, 11, 12 and 15. Each one is an isolated, independent device environment with its own data and login state, and it stays a fixed, long-term environment, so the phone you set up for a client in March is the same phone in June.

The part agencies care about is handover. You can share a device with a teammate in one click and they pick it up already logged in. When someone goes on leave, nobody spends an afternoon re-entering passwords and waiting on 2FA codes from the client.

Other things I actually use: per-device proxy and region settings, local environments in 150+ countries/regions, bulk install/uninstall/launch of apps across a batch of devices, root, and an API. Billing is per-minute. There are browser, desktop and mobile clients. There are also cloud numbers, which I use for testing our own app's signup and OTP flows without passing someone's personal SIM around the office.

Fits: agencies holding client app accounts long-term, small QA teams that want persistent devices they can hand to each other, anyone doing regional checks.

Drawbacks, honestly: it's Android only, so if your release checklist includes iOS you need a second tool. And it's not a test-automation grid with built-in reporting. If what you want is "upload APK, run Espresso suite on 40 device models, get a video per failure," the next three entries do that better.

2. Genymotion SaaS

https://www.genymotion.com/

Genymotion is the one I'd point a pure dev team at. Their site lists Genymotion SaaS ("optimized for team work, CI/CD and agentic AI"), a PaaS version on AWS, Alibaba, GCP and Azure, and Genymotion Desktop for PC and Mac. Integrations they name: Detox, GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Bitrise, Jenkins.

These are Android virtual devices built to be spun up from a pipeline, and they also pitch browser-based support and demo use.

Fits: dev teams that want Android devices wired into CI, plus support teams that need to reproduce a customer's bug from a browser tab.

Less ideal when: you need one specific device to hold a client's logged-in state for months and get passed between people. That's not what a CI emulator is shaped for.

3. AWS Device Farm

https://aws.amazon.com/device-farm/

Real physical phones and tablets hosted by AWS. You can run automated tests (Appium, Espresso, Calabash, or their built-in suite with no scripting), do manual remote sessions, and get videos, logs and performance data back. You can set location, language and network conditions.

The interesting bit for this list: their private device lab option gives you iOS and Android devices for your exclusive use and, per their page, lets you persist settings between sessions. That gets much closer to "my device stays my device."

Fits: teams already on AWS who need real hardware coverage, including iOS, hooked into Jenkins or Android Studio.

Less ideal when: you're a five-person agency without anyone who wants to own AWS config. And the shared pool is built for test runs, not long-lived logged-in accounts.

4. BrowserStack App Live

https://www.browserstack.com/app-live

BrowserStack says 30,000+ real iOS and Android devices. You can upload dev APK/AAB/IPA builds or install production apps from the stores, debug with logs and crash reports, and test on up to four devices at once. Their Custom Device Lab adds exclusive device access with options like app persistence and SIM binding.

Fits: QA teams who need wide model coverage across iOS and Android, fast.

Less ideal when: the job is keeping a handful of long-term environments for ongoing client work. You'd be paying for breadth you don't use, and persistence lives in the custom lab tier, not the default.

5. GeeLark

https://www.geelark.com/

GeeLark offers ARM-based cloud phones for Android apps plus multi-account browser profiles for web, both in one workspace. Team features are solid on paper: team members can be added free, roles and permissions, operation logs, groups/tags/notes for organising profiles. They also mention MCP so you can connect an AI agent to manage the phones and profiles, and they list GPS/SIM simulation across 150+ countries.

Fits: social and marketing teams who want phones and browser profiles managed side by side, with scheduling and AI content tools on top.

Less ideal when: you're a dev/QA team. A big chunk of the product is about posting, content generation and engagement automation, which you'll pay attention to (and maybe pay for) without needing.

6. VMOSCloud

https://www.vmoscloud.com/

VMOSCloud runs Android cloud phones with a strong lean toward social media automation: an AI workflow feature that turns text prompts into actions, a Synchronizer that mirrors one device's actions across many, and a Team Hub with roles and permissions. Their homepage lists Google Play Integrity, SafetyNet and Widevine L1. "App Test" appears in their industry list, though most of the page is about growing social accounts.

Fits: operators running many social accounts who want synchronized control.

Less ideal when: you want a dev-first tool. I'd also read their data policy closely if you plan long-term use: their FAQ says data is automatically deleted once the subscription ends, which is fine, just plan exports around it.

7. Redfinger

https://www.cloudemulator.net/

One of the older names. Redfinger has Android, Windows, web and iOS access, a Redfinger for Business line, and servers in the US, Taiwan and Singapore. Their site mentions device simulation for testing alongside gaming and cross-border marketing.

Fits: individuals and small teams who want a simple cloud Android device on several platforms.

Less ideal when: you need team handover and region coverage beyond those three server locations.

Honourable mentions: LDCloud and UgPhone

Both are positioned mainly for gaming. LDCloud (https://www.ldcloud.net/) leads with 24/7 AFK play, multi-instance and sync operation. UgPhone (https://www.ugphone.com/) lists tiers on Android 10, 12 and 13 with servers in places like Hong Kong, Germany, Japan, the USA and Singapore. For client QA work, I wouldn't start here.

How I'd actually choose

If I'm honest, the decision usually comes down to one question. Is the device disposable (run tests, throw away) or durable (holds state, gets handed between people for months)?

Disposable: Genymotion, AWS Device Farm, BrowserStack. Pick by whether you need iOS and how much CI you already have.

Durable: that's where DuoPlus, GeeLark, VMOSCloud and Redfinger sit, and I'd rank them by how painless handover and regional setup are for a non-engineer on your team. That's why DuoPlus is first on my list.

Plenty of teams end up with one of each. What hurts is using a disposable tool for durable work and wondering why everyone keeps logging in again.

If you've ranked these differently for your own team, I'd like to hear why in the comments, especially if you run client work on BrowserStack's custom lab.

title: How Shopify Killed Third-Party Cookies (And How to Build Embedded Apps with App Bridge 4.0 in 2026)
description:
If you’ve tried building an embedded Shopify app recently using older Express or cookie-based session tutorials, you probably ran into the dreaded blank white screen on Safari, iOS, or modern Chrome.

Here is why that happens—and how the modern 2026 Shopify stack completely solves it with App Bridge 4.0 and Header-Based JWTs.

The Death of Third-Party Cookies in Iframes

Historically, Shopify apps ran inside an <iframe> on admin.shopify.com. Developers set traditional HTTP cookies to maintain merchant sessions:

However:

  1. Apple Safari ITP (Intelligent Tracking Prevention) blocks all cross-site cookies inside iframes by default.
  2. Google Chrome Privacy Sandbox has systematically phased out third-party cookie access.
  3. If your app attempts to read document.cookie or expects session cookies in an embedded iframe, the request fails silently, leaving merchants with a broken spinner or white screen.

The Modern Solution: App Bridge 4.0 & Cryptographic Session Tokens

In modern Shopify architecture, we never use cookies. Instead, authentication relies on short-lived, cryptographically signed JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) generated directly by Shopify's frontend client.

Step 1: Client-Side Token Injection

With Shopify App Bridge 4.0, you don't even need bulky npm packages on the frontend. A single script tag in your root document handles everything:

<script 
  src="https://cdn.shopify.com/shopifycloud/app-bridge.js" 
  data-api-key="YOUR_SHOPIFY_API_KEY">
</script>

App Bridge automatically intercepts all native window.fetch requests and injects a 60-second signed JWT in the request headers:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

Step 2: Backend JWT Verification

On your backend (React Router / Remix or Node), you verify the token using your SHOPIFY_API_SECRET and extract the authenticated shop domain:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export async function verifyShopifySessionToken(request: Request) {
  const authHeader = request.headers.get("Authorization");
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
    throw new Response("Unauthorized: Missing Bearer Token", { status: 401 });
  }

  const token = authHeader.split(" ")[1];
  const [headerB64, payloadB64, signatureB64] = token.split(".");

  // Verify HMAC SHA-256 signature against your App Secret
  const calculatedSig = crypto
    .createHmac("sha256", process.env.SHOPIFY_API_SECRET!)
    .update(`${headerB64}.${payloadB64}`)
    .digest("base64url");

  if (calculatedSig !== signatureB64) {
    throw new Response("Forbidden: Invalid Token Signature", { status: 403 });
  }

  const payload = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(payloadB64, "base64url").toString("utf-8"));

  // Extract authenticated merchant domain
  const destUrl = new URL(payload.dest);
  return { shop: destUrl.hostname };
}

No cookies. No Safari ITP blocks. 100% reliable across every modern browser.

Want the Complete Zero-to-Production Guide?

Building a production-ready Shopify app in 2026 involves more than just auth. You need:

  • GraphQL Admin API Leaky Bucket rate-limit handling & cursor pagination
  • Webhook HMAC verification with Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ)
  • Prisma Multi-Tenant Database modeling
  • Shopify Billing API for recurring SaaS subscriptions
  • Multi-stage Docker & Fly.io zero-cost cloud deployment

I compiled everything into a comprehensive 59-page engineering handbook:

👉 Get The Modern Shopify App Development Blueprint on Gumroad

It includes complete starter code, architectural blueprints, and a 25-point App Store pre-flight checklist.

Drop any questions below about App Bridge 4.0 or GraphQL Admin API—happy to help!

title: Normalizing U.S. Company Names Before You Match Them
description:
Company names from different sources rarely agree character for character. "The Acme Group, L.L.C.", "ACME GROUP LLC" and "Acme Group" could be one entity or three. A normalized name gives you a stable comparison key, as long as you remember what the key discards.

What usually needs cleaning

Case and spacing. Pick one case, trim the ends, and collapse repeated spaces.

Punctuation. Periods, commas, and quotes are noise. Curly and straight apostrophes should end up identical, or be removed. An ampersand is safest as the word "and."

Accents. "Peña" and "Pena" should compare equal. Unicode normalization followed by an ASCII fold handles the common cases.

Legal endings. LLC and L.L.C., Inc. and Incorporated, Corp. and Corporation, Co. and Company, Ltd. and Limited, plus LP, LLP, and PLLC. Map the spellings to one short form and move it out of the name into a field of its own. It tells you the entity type, and "Acme Inc" and "Acme LLC" can be two separate legal entities.

A leading "The". Sources disagree on whether to keep it, so the key should not depend on it.

Trade names. A string like "Acme Group LLC dba Bright Path" holds two names. Split on dba, d/b/a, aka, or fka and keep both parts, labeled. Matching on the trade name alone can attach a record to the wrong legal entity.

Same name, different state

Identical names across states are common, because each state checks name availability only against its own registry. A key that ignores the state will merge strangers. Put the state, or the registry the record came from, into the key, and treat a cross-state match as a lead to confirm with other fields.

A teaching example

This is a teaching example, not production code. It returns the state, the core name, the entity-type ending, and any trade name found after dba, aka, or fka.

import re
import unicodedata
ENDINGS = {"INCORPORATED": "INC", "CORPORATION": "CORP", "COMPANY": "CO", "LIMITED": "LTD"}
ENDINGS.update({e: e for e in ("LLC", "INC", "CORP", "CO", "LTD", "LP", "LLP", "PLLC")})
ALIAS = re.compile(r"\b(?:D[./]?B[./]?A|A[./]?K[./]?A|F[./]?K[./]?A)\b\.?", re.I)

def words(text):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", text).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode()
    text = text.upper().replace("&", " AND ").replace(".", "").replace("'", "")
    return re.findall(r"[A-Z0-9]+", text)

def company_key(raw, state):
    legal, *alias = ALIAS.split(raw, maxsplit=1)
    core = words(legal)
    ending = ENDINGS.get(core[-1], "") if core else ""
    while core and core[-1] in ENDINGS:
        core.pop()
    core = core[1:] if core[:1] == ["THE"] else core
    return state.upper(), " ".join(core), ending, " ".join(words("".join(alias)))

Two calls show the behavior, including an edge case:

company_key("The Acme Group, L.L.C. d/b/a Bright Path", "tx")
# ('TX', 'ACME GROUP', 'LLC', 'BRIGHT PATH')
company_key("Peña & Co.", "or")
# ('OR', 'PENA AND', 'CO', '')

The second result leaves a dangling AND, because "& Co." is really part of how that firm writes its name. Rules like these are blunt, and every ruleset produces cases like this one.

Order matters as well. Split off the trade name before removing punctuation, or "d/b/a" falls apart into loose letters that look like part of the name.

To keep the rules honest, build a small table of pairs you know are the same entity and pairs you know are not, and rerun it whenever you change a rule. A fix for one case often breaks another.

What the key throws away

Normalization is lossy on purpose. Store the raw name next to the key, keep the ending and the trade name as separate fields, and never treat an equal key as proof of identity. Confirm with something the name cannot fake: a registry ID, a formation date, or a principal address.

This post was drafted with the help of AI tools.

title: ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection & Recovery Logic
description:
ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection & Recovery Logic

Understanding R01: The Most Common ACH Return

When an ACH debit fails because the originating account lacks sufficient funds, the NACHA network returns code R01. It's the most frequent return developers encounter in production payout systems—accounting for roughly 30–40% of all ACH returns in typical fintech volumes.

Understanding R01 isn't just about reading an error message. It's about building retry logic, deciding whether to escalate to customer support, or routing the transaction to an alternative rail (like RTP or Visa Direct). This guide walks through detection, handling, and recovery patterns.

What R01 Actually Means

R01 = Insufficient Funds

The originating bank verified the account exists and is valid, but the account holder doesn't have enough money to cover the debit at the time the bank processed the batch. This is different from:

  • R03 (No Account): The account number doesn't exist.
  • R04 (Invalid Account Number Format): The routing or account number is malformed.
  • R10 (Unauthorized): The account holder revoked authorization for ACH debits.

R01 fires during the bank's batch processing window, typically 1–2 business days after you submit the ACH entry. The return itself arrives as a separate ACH file, usually within 1–2 additional business days.

Return Timing and Reconciliation 

Day 0: You submit ACH debit (e.g., 2:00 PM EST)
Day 1: Bank batches and processes (overnight)
Day 2: Return file arrives (if R01 triggered)
Day 3: You detect return and can take action

This 2–3 day lag is critical: your payout status must remain "pending" until settlement is confirmed, not just when the debit is submitted.

Handling R01 Programmatically

1. Detection & Logging

When your ACH processor (SFTP, API, or bank portal) delivers return files, parse the ACH 920 (return) record. Extract the return code and trace number:

{
  "trace_number": "123456789012",
  "return_code": "R01",
  "amount": 50000,
  "originating_account": "1234567890",
  "return_date": "2025-01-15",
  "reason": "Insufficient Funds"
}

Log this immediately. Flag the payout record as status: "returned" with the return code.

2. Retry Logic

R01 is often transient. A developer's retry strategy might be:

  • Immediate retry (same day): Don't retry immediately; wait 2–3 business days.
  • Delayed retry (Day 5–7): Re-submit the same ACH entry. The account may have received deposits.
  • Max retries: Typically 2–3 retries before escalating to manual review.

Store retry metadata:

{
  "payout_id": "po_abc123",
  "return_code": "R01",
  "retry_count": 1,
  "next_retry_date": "2025-01-20",
  "status": "scheduled_retry"
}

3. Alternative Rails

If retries exhaust, consider routing to a faster rail:

Rail Settlement Cost Reversible? Best for
ACH (R01 retry) 1–2 days $0.25–$1 Yes, 60 days Budget-conscious, non-urgent
RTP (Real-Time Payments) <30 seconds $1–$3 No Urgent, high-value
Visa Direct 30 min–4 hours $0.50–$2.50 Yes, 120 days Card-based, mid-speed

If the customer has a linked debit card on file, Visa Direct may succeed where ACH R01 failed.

4. Customer Notification

Don't silently retry. Notify the user:

Subject: Payout Failed — Insufficient Funds

Your payout of $500 to account ending in 7890 failed because 
the account has insufficient funds. We'll retry on Jan 20. 
If it fails again, we'll contact you for an alternate method.

Production Checklist

  • [ ] Parse ACH return files (920 records) daily.
  • [ ] Distinguish R01 from R03, R04, R10 in your logic.
  • [ ] Implement 2–3 retry attempts, spaced 3–5 days apart.
  • [ ] Store retry metadata for audit trails.
  • [ ] Offer alternative rails (RTP, Visa Direct) after 1–2 failed retries.
  • [ ] Send templated customer notifications.
  • [ ] Monitor R01 frequency; >5

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Turn PDFs into Clean Markdown for ChatGPT and RAG (Without Uploading Them)
description:
If you've ever pasted a PDF into ChatGPT or Claude and got an answer about the wrong section, the model probably wasn't the problem. The text was.

A PDF doesn't store "a heading", "a table" or "a paragraph". It stores pieces of text placed at positions on a page. When you copy that text out, you get whatever order the PDF happens to keep it in, and the structure is gone. For an LLM, and even more for a RAG pipeline, structure is half the information.

This post covers what goes wrong, what clean Markdown for AI should look like, and a short Python chunker that splits it for retrieval while keeping page numbers.

Disclosure: I built QuickCatPDF, the free converter I use in the examples. The format and the chunking code work with any converter that produces similar Markdown.

What breaks when you copy text out of a PDF

Copy and paste from a typical report and you'll usually see some of these:

  • Lines broken mid-sentence, because every visual line ends with a newline.
  • Two columns mixed together, line by line.
  • The page header and footer repeated on every page ("Annual Review 2026 · Page 7").
  • Tables flattened into a run of numbers with no idea which value belongs to which column.
  • Words split by hyphens at line ends ("docu- ment").
  • Links gone. In a PDF, a link's address isn't part of the text at all. It's stored separately as an annotation on top of the page, so plain copy-paste only gives you the visible words.

None of this stops a model from reading the text, but it makes it worse at finding the right part and at quoting numbers from tables correctly.

What "clean Markdown for an LLM" looks like

Markdown is a good middle ground: models read it naturally, it's compact, and it keeps the structure that matters.

---
title: "Annual Review 2026"
source: "annual-review.pdf"
pages: 4
---

<!-- page 1 -->

# Annual Review 2026

## Introduction

Revenue grew in every quarter...

## Results by quarter

| Quarter | Revenue | Growth |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 1.2M | 4% |
| Q2 | 1.4M | 17% |

<!-- page 2 -->

A few details are worth copying, whatever tool you use:

  1. Front matter naming the source file and page count. When you paste several documents into one chat, the model knows which is which.
  2. Page markers as HTML comments (<!-- page 2 -->). Models read them, rendered Markdown hides them, and your RAG answers can cite a page.
  3. Real headings (#, ##, ###) instead of bold lines.
  4. Pipe tables, so every value stays in its row and column.
  5. No page furniture: page numbers and repeated headers and footers removed, hyphenated words joined, wrapped lines merged into single paragraphs.

Three questions people keep asking

"How do I keep headings when converting PDF to Markdown?"
Most converters detect headings from the text's size and weight. That works when the PDF's headings are visibly larger or bold. If a document's headings are the same size and weight as the body text, there's no signal to detect, and they come out as plain paragraphs. In that case, add the ## markers by hand for the main sections. It takes a minute and makes a big difference for chunking.

"How do I keep tables?"
Pick a converter that outputs pipe tables, then check one table against the original. Tables without lines (columns separated only by white space, like bank statements) are the hardest case for any tool.

"Why are my hyperlinks lost?"
Because of the annotation point above: the address isn't in the text layer. A converter has to read the link annotations and match them to the words underneath. Plain copy-paste and many text extractors skip that step.

Chunking for RAG without losing page numbers

Headings are natural chunk boundaries, and the page comments let every chunk carry the page it started on. Here's a small, dependency-free chunker:

import re

def chunk_markdown(md: str, max_chars: int = 4000):
    """Split Markdown on ## headings, keeping the page number each chunk starts on."""
    md = re.sub(r"\A---\n.*?\n---\n", "", md, flags=re.S)  # drop front matter
    page = 1
    chunks, current, heading = [], [], None

    def flush():
        text = "\n".join(current).strip()
        if text:
            chunks.append({"heading": heading, "page": start_page, "text": text})

    start_page = page
    for line in md.splitlines():
        m = re.match(r"<!-- page (\d+) -->", line)
        if m:
            page = int(m.group(1))
            if not "".join(current).strip():
                start_page = page
            continue
        if line.startswith("## ") or sum(len(l) for l in current) > max_chars:
            flush()
            current, start_page = [], page
            if line.startswith("## "):
                heading = line[3:].strip()
        current.append(line)
    flush()
    return chunks

Each chunk comes back as {"heading": "Results by quarter", "page": 1, "text": "..."}, ready to embed. Store heading and page as metadata, and your answers can say "see page 1, Results by quarter" instead of pointing at the whole document.

If you prefer page-sized chunks (useful for contracts and forms), split on the <!-- page N --> comments instead.

Watch your token budget

A rough rule for English is about 4 characters per token, fewer for other scripts. That's close enough to decide whether a document fits in one prompt or needs chunking. Treat it as an estimate, not an exact count.

Doing it without uploading the PDF

Many PDFs you'd want to ask an AI about are exactly the ones you shouldn't hand to random websites: contracts, financial reports, internal docs. You'll decide later where the text goes. The conversion step doesn't need to send it anywhere.

The converter I built, QuickCatPDF's PDF to Markdown for LLMs, runs in the browser:

  1. Drop in up to 20 PDFs.
  2. Keep Front matter and Page markers as comments ticked.
  3. Optionally limit the Pages.
  4. Click Convert to Markdown, then copy or download. It shows the character count and a token estimate.

In my test, a 4-page report converted in about half a second into 4.6 KB of Markdown. Scanned PDFs are read with OCR in the browser too. You can check that nothing is uploaded: load the page, turn on airplane mode, and convert.

For plain Markdown for GitHub, Obsidian or Notion (with bold, italics, links and optional images), there's a separate PDF to Markdown tool.

Quick checklist

  • Don't paste raw PDF text into an LLM when structure matters. Convert to Markdown first.
  • Keep front matter and page markers, and drop the headers and footers.
  • Check one heading and one table against the original.
  • Chunk on ## headings and keep the page number as metadata.
  • Estimate tokens at about 4 characters per token for English.

What's the worst PDF you've had to feed into an LLM? Tables, multi-column layouts, scans? I'm collecting hard cases.

title: How to Test a $10 Bank Reconciliation Gap in SQLite
description:
The September 28 bank statement closes at $40. The books have a $350 deposit and a $300 payment, both cleared. Starting from zero, that leaves $50. The last line on the statement is a $10 service charge. That one is missing from the books.

A test with just those amounts is easy to fool. Forget the date filter and it still passes. Run the fee import once and you’ll never find out what a retry does. Give the fixture a $25 payment that cleared the next morning. Then deliver the September fee a second time.

The number to assert

For this test, the gap is the statement closing balance minus the cleared book balance at the cutoff. For this statement that starts at 4000 - (35000 - 30000) = -1000 cents. A negative result means the cleared books are higher than the bank. The statement line is what tells us why.

Save this block as reconcile.sql and run sqlite3 -bail :memory: < reconcile.sql. Each entry belongs to one checking account. Amounts are signed integer cents, dates are ISO dates, and cleared_on is the day the entry cleared the bank.

CREATE TEMP TABLE book_entry (
    bank_ref   TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
    cleared_on TEXT NOT NULL,
    cents      INTEGER NOT NULL
) STRICT;

INSERT INTO book_entry VALUES
    ('deposit-17', '2026-09-27',  35000),
    ('payment-18', '2026-09-28', -30000),
    ('payment-19', '2026-09-29',  -2500);

CREATE TEMP VIEW at_cutoff AS
SELECT 4000 - COALESCE(SUM(cents), 0) AS gap_cents,
       COUNT(*) AS cleared_rows
FROM book_entry
WHERE cleared_on <= '2026-09-28';

CREATE TEMP TABLE checks (
    step          TEXT NOT NULL,
    gap_cents     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    cleared_rows  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    expected_gap  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    expected_rows INTEGER NOT NULL,
    CHECK (gap_cents = expected_gap AND cleared_rows = expected_rows)
) STRICT;

INSERT INTO checks
SELECT 'fee missing', gap_cents, cleared_rows, -1000, 2 FROM at_cutoff;

INSERT INTO book_entry VALUES ('fee-20', '2026-09-28', -1000)
ON CONFLICT (bank_ref) DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO checks
SELECT 'fee recorded', gap_cents, cleared_rows, 0, 3 FROM at_cutoff;

-- The importer delivers the same bank line again.
INSERT INTO book_entry VALUES ('fee-20', '2026-09-28', -1000)
ON CONFLICT (bank_ref) DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO checks
SELECT 'fee replayed', gap_cents, cleared_rows, 0, 3 FROM at_cutoff;

SELECT step, gap_cents, cleared_rows FROM checks ORDER BY rowid;

fee missing|-1000|2
fee recorded|0|3
fee replayed|0|3

The last two rows are deliberately identical apart from the label. After the fee posts, $310 has gone out against $350 in. Replaying the same bank line should leave both the $40 balance and the count of three cleared entries alone.

Two ways to break it

Remove the WHERE line (keeping the statement’s final semicolon). The next morning’s $25 payment slips into September 28. The first gap flips from −$10 to +$15 and the first CHECK fails. On a fresh run, change only the replay’s reference from fee-20 to fee-21. The database accepts a fourth entry, the gap becomes +$10, and the last CHECK fails.

That second failure says something about the import contract. Two genuine fees can have the same date and amount. This example relies on a stable reference for a bank line. If references are unique only within an account, include the account in the unique key. If a bank later corrects the amount under an existing reference, that needs a correction path of its own.

ChatGPT drafted this article and its SQL. The example and both failure cases were tested with SQLite 3.43.2.
