title: How we built an independent search engine with its own index
description:
Most "search APIs" are a thin layer over Google or Bing results. NestDaddy is not. It has its own crawler, its own inverted index, its own ranking and its own news collection, designed, built and operated end to end by our team.

This post walks through how the platform fits together and the engineering principles we follow. If you are thinking about building search yourself, or you want to know what sits behind the API you are calling, this is for you.

The shape of the platform

There are four parts, and each one is isolated so that no part can take another down:

  1. Crawler. Fetches pages, obeys robots.txt, extracts the readable text and stores it in PostgreSQL.
  2. Indexer. Turns new pages into posting lists in a RocksDB index that is built next to the live one.
  3. Swap. Every day, the new index replaces the live index in one atomic step, with an automatic rollback.
  4. Search. A BM25 ranker reads the live index, read-only, behind the web site, the REST API and an MCP server for AI agents.

The rule that ties them together: the search path never waits for the crawler or the indexer, and neither of them can compete with it for resources.

The crawler: polite, bounded, isolated

A good crawler is a polite one, so ours is built around clear limits.

  • robots.txt first. One fetch per site, cached for 24 hours. A 401 or 403 on robots.txt means "disallow everything".
  • Spread across hosts. Each batch claims URLs from the queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and keeps at most 3 URLs per host, so a batch touches hundreds of different sites instead of hammering one. The same claim lets many crawler workers share one queue safely.
  • Bounded downloads. Every response is streamed and cut at 5 MB or 20 seconds, so no single site can slow the crawl down or flood it with data.
  • Isolation. The crawler runs in its own resource slice with dedicated CPU and memory limits and a low priority. Search traffic always comes first.

The index: RocksDB and posting lists

The index is an inverted index stored in RocksDB: for every term, a posting list of document IDs, plus per-document statistics for BM25.

We picked RocksDB over a search server for three reasons. It is a library, so there is no extra service to run. It is built for fast point lookups and multi-gets, which is exactly what a query does. And it can be opened read-only by many processes while another process builds the next version.

Text goes through a tokenizer (lowercasing, stop words, Porter stemming with a memoised stemmer) before it reaches the index, and the same tokenizer runs on every query.

Replacing the index safely, every day

The daily swap is deliberately boring:

  1. Take the writer lock so the indexer pauses.
  2. Hard-link the immutable SST files into a staging directory and copy the small metadata files (MANIFEST, CURRENT, OPTIONS, WAL). This takes about a second and uses no extra disk.
  3. Release the lock and verify the staging copy read-only: the document counter must not go down, sample terms must resolve, the newest indexed pages must be readable.
  4. Rename the live directory to a "previous" directory and the staging directory to live.
  5. Reload the search workers and run a live search check. If anything fails, roll back automatically.

Previous generations are kept, so going back is a rename, not a restore.

Ranking: BM25, measured

The ranker is BM25 with practical additions: a two-stage pre-score (rare terms first, then the top 3,000 candidates re-ranked by term frequency with one RocksDB multi-get), a domain match signal for navigational queries, and image documents kept out of web results.

We do not change ranking by feel. An evaluation suite of real queries, each with a judgment ("the right answer is this URL pattern" or "the homepage of this site"), runs against the live index after every change, and a change ships only when precision goes up. The November release moved every metric we track:

Metric Before After
Right answer at #1 (P@1) 45% 70%
Right answer in the top 3 60% 77.5%
Right answer in the top 10 70% 87.5%
Mean reciprocal rank 0.536 0.754

The changes behind it were classic search engineering: true document frequencies for IDF, an average document length measured from real documents, deterministic sampling, and keeping images out of web search.

Latency engineering

Fast search is mostly about removing surprises. Three practices matter most for us:

Linear-time text processing. Every regular expression on the query path is checked for backtracking. Patterns like \S+@\S+ are replaced by linear-time equivalents such as (?<!\S)(?=\S+@\S)\S+, which give the same output and stay fast on any input.

Keep the hot index in memory. A dedicated service checks which parts of the index file are resident (mincore) and reads back only what is missing, and it runs with a cgroup memory guarantee so the kernel keeps the index cached. One detail worth knowing: cgroup v2 memory protection is hierarchical, so the parent slice needs the same guarantee as the service.

Audit every scheduled job. Generic "free up memory" scripts such as echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches ignore cgroup protection and quietly undo all of the above. We review every scheduled job on the search path.

The result is sub-second search on fresh queries, measured on the same evaluation suite after every release.

What is next on the roadmap

Owning the whole stack means we can improve every layer ourselves. These are the upgrades in progress:

  • Deeper answers. The next index version adds full body text on a tiered storage design, so answers that live deep in a page rank where they should.
  • Numbers and more scripts. A new tokenizer that keeps short numbers ("windows 11", "iphone 17") and splits Chinese, Japanese and Thai text ships with the next index build.
  • Freshness at scale. A targeted recrawl of the most searched results and the most linked sites is running now, and the crawler is moving to a continuous multi-process pipeline.

Why build it at all

Because an index you own is an index nobody can switch off. Microsoft retired the Bing Search APIs in August 2025 and many apps lost their search overnight. Products that need raw results, news by country, or readable page text for AI agents need a source that answers in plain JSON and does not depend on someone else's roadmap.

That is what NestDaddy is for. You can try the search, news and page extraction APIs with a free 7-day key at nestdaddy.com/apis, or connect it to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client through nestdaddy.com/mcp.

If you are building something similar and want to compare notes, we would like to hear from you.

Originally published on the NestDaddy blog. NestDaddy is an independent search engine with its own index: nestdaddy.com.

title: Terraform for Beginners: Build Cloud Infrastructure by Writing Simple Code
description:
A short story to start

Imagine you spent a whole afternoon clicking around the Azure or AWS website to set up a server, a network, a database and a few security rules. It works. Well done.

Now your manager says: "Great, can you build exactly the same thing again for testing, and another copy in Europe?" Can you remember every click? Every setting? Every small box you ticked?

Most people cannot. That is the problem Terraform solves. Instead of clicking, you write down what you want in a simple text file. Terraform reads the file and builds it for you, the same way, every time.

1. What is Terraform, in one sentence?

Terraform is a tool that turns a simple text file into real cloud infrastructure.

This idea is called Infrastructure as Code, or IaC for short. Your servers, networks and databases are described in code, just like an app.

A good way to picture it is a building plan. An architect does not build a house by shouting instructions to workers one by one. She draws a plan. Builders follow the plan. If you want ten identical houses, you use the same plan ten times. Terraform files are your plan.

Terraform is made by a company called HashiCorp. It works with almost every cloud: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and hundreds of other services. You may also hear about OpenTofu, a free open source version that works in almost the same way. Everything you learn here applies to both.

2. How does Terraform work?


Figure 1: You write the code, Terraform reads it, the provider talks to the cloud.

There are only a few moving parts:

  1. You write files ending in .tf that describe what you want.
  2. Terraform reads those files and works out what needs to be created, changed or deleted.
  3. A provider is a plugin that knows how to talk to one platform. There is a provider for AWS, one for Azure, one for Google Cloud, and many more. Think of it as a translator.
  4. The real cloud ends up with the servers, networks and storage you asked for.

The most important idea: you describe what you want, not how to build it step by step. Terraform works out the steps.

3. The words you will hear (made simple)

Word What it means in plain English
Provider The plugin that talks to a platform, such as aws or azurerm.
Resource One thing you want to create, such as a server, a network or a storage bucket.
Variable A value you can change without editing the main code, such as a region or a name.
Output A value Terraform prints at the end, such as a website address or a server IP.
State Terraform's memory of what it has already built.
Plan A preview of the changes Terraform is about to make.
Module A reusable bundle of Terraform code, like a Lego set you can use again and again.

4. Install Terraform

Go to the official Terraform website from HashiCorp, download the version for your computer (Windows, Mac or Linux) and follow the install steps. On a Mac you can also use Homebrew, and on Windows you can use Chocolatey or winget.

Then open a terminal and type:

terraform -version

If you see a version number, you are ready. I also recommend installing Visual Studio Code with the official HashiCorp Terraform extension. It colours your code and spots mistakes as you type.

5. Your first project (no cloud account needed)

The best way to learn Terraform without any risk of a cloud bill is to start with something local. We will ask Terraform to create a simple text file on your own computer. The steps are exactly the same as for a real server in the cloud.

Step 1: Create a folder and a file

Make a new folder called my-first-terraform and inside it create a file called main.tf with this code:

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

Let us read it slowly:

  • resource says "I want to create something".
  • "local_file" is the type of thing: a file on this computer.
  • "hello" is the nickname we give it inside our code.
  • Inside the curly brackets are the settings: the file name and what to write in it.

Step 2: Run the four magic commands


Figure 2: init, plan, apply and destroy. You will use these every single day.

Open a terminal in your folder and run:

terraform init

init gets everything ready. It notices you used local_file and downloads the provider that knows how to create files.

terraform plan

plan shows a preview. You should see something like "Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy". Nothing has been created yet. This is your chance to check before anything happens.

terraform apply

apply does the real work. Terraform shows the plan again and asks you to type yes. Type it and press Enter. Now look in your folder: there is a new file called hello.txt with your message inside. You just used Infrastructure as Code.

Step 3: Make a change

Change the content line to say "Hello again from Terraform!" and run terraform plan. Terraform notices the difference and tells you it will replace the file. Run terraform apply, type yes, and open the file again. It has been updated. You did not tell Terraform how to update it. You only changed what you wanted.

Step 4: Clean up 

terraform destroy

destroy deletes everything Terraform created in this folder. Type yes and hello.txt disappears. In the real cloud this is your best friend: one command and everything you built for practice is gone, so you are not paying for it.

6. The state file: Terraform's memory


Figure 3: Terraform compares what you want, what it remembers and what really exists.

After you ran apply, you may have noticed a new file called terraform.tfstate. This is Terraform's memory. It records what Terraform has built, so next time it knows what already exists and what needs to change.

A few simple rules for the state file:

  • Never edit it by hand. Let Terraform manage it.
  • Never share it publicly or upload it to GitHub. It can contain passwords and private details.
  • In a team, store it in a shared, safe place such as an Azure Storage account, an AWS S3 bucket or HCP Terraform. This is called remote state, and it stops two people changing the same thing at the same time.

7. Variables and outputs: making your code flexible

Hard coding values works, but variables let you reuse the same code for different situations. Add this to your main.tf:

variable "message" {
  default = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = var.message
}

output "file_name" {
  value = local_file.hello.filename
}
  • The variable block creates a value called message with a default.
  • var.message uses that value inside the resource.
  • The output block prints the file name when apply finishes.

Now you can change the message without touching the resource, for example: terraform apply -var="message=Good morning".

8. A small real cloud example

When you are ready for the cloud, the pattern is exactly the same. Here is how you would create a storage bucket on AWS:

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "my_bucket" {
  bucket = "my-first-terraform-bucket-12345"
}

Same commands: init, plan, apply. Same clean up: destroy. Before you try it, create a free tier account, set a budget alert, and log in with the AWS command line tool so Terraform can use your account. Bucket names must be unique across the whole world, so change the numbers at the end.

9. Good habits from day one

  1. Always read the plan before you type yes. It tells you exactly what will be created, changed or deleted.
  2. Keep your .tf files in Git, so you have a history of every change.
  3. Add a .gitignore file that keeps out terraform.tfstate, the .terraform folder and any files with secrets.
  4. Run terraform fmt to tidy your code and terraform validate to catch mistakes early.
  5. Make small changes and apply often, instead of one giant change.
  6. Destroy practice resources as soon as you finish, so you do not get a surprise bill.

10. Common beginner mistakes

  • Typing yes without reading the plan, and deleting something important.
  • Uploading the state file or secret keys to a public GitHub repository.
  • Changing things by hand in the cloud website after Terraform built them. Terraform will get confused, or undo your changes next time.
  • Forgetting to run terraform init after adding a new provider.
  • Trying to learn modules, workspaces and remote state on day one. Master the basics first.

11. A simple learning path

Stage What to do
Week 1 Install Terraform and complete the local_file project in this guide.
Week 2 Learn variables, outputs and terraform fmt and validate.
Week 3 Create one small real cloud resource, then destroy it.
Week 4 Build a small network and a virtual machine, and keep your code on GitHub.
After that Learn remote state, modules, and running Terraform inside a CI/CD pipeline.

Final words

Terraform can look scary at first, but the core idea is simple: write down what you want, check the plan, then let Terraform build it. The same file can build the same setup again tomorrow, next month or in another country.

Your challenge this week: create the hello.txt file with Terraform, change it, and destroy it. Those three commands, plan, apply and destroy, are the heart of everything you will ever do with Terraform.

Happy building!

title: My LLM pipeline spent 13 of 18 minutes waiting for answers that never came
description:
I maintain an open-source pipeline that turns a research paper or topic into a cited commercialization screening report. Six LLM agents split the work: three analysts, a writer, a reviewer and a scorer. On 9 November one production run took 1,072 seconds. When I read the logs, 774 of those seconds had gone to requests that had stopped delivering anything.

This is how I found out why, what I changed, and why the root cause is still there. Every change and number comes from a public pull request in the repository, linked at the end.

1. First, make retries visible

The first clue was a 781-second run the day before. In the same run, on the same model, the reviewer wrote 2,880 tokens in 50 seconds while the writer took 282 seconds for 6,487 tokens. That gap made no sense as generation speed.

The writer had actually sent two requests. The first was cut at its 150-second timeout; the second finished. None of this showed up anywhere: usage counted only successful requests, and the retry notice went to stdout, which the worker discarded.

So the first change wasn't an optimization. It was logging (#362): every provider attempt, whether it returned, timed out or failed, now leaves a row with its stage, attempt number, outcome and duration.

2. Not slow generation: stalled connections

With per-attempt rows, the 1,072-second run was easy to read (#363):

  • Writer: stalled for 302 seconds, then 312 seconds; the third attempt returned in 95.
  • Scorer: stalled for 160 seconds; the retry returned in 27.

The same request came back in 27 to 95 seconds on a retry, so generation speed wasn't the problem. The connection was: data stopped flowing mid-answer. A plain request can only learn that by waiting out its whole timeout, and the longer the timeout, the more time it wastes.

3. Stream everything

I switched all six agents to streaming (#363). Answers arrive in chunks, and the wait for each chunk is capped at 60 seconds, so a dead connection is noticed within a minute instead of after several.

Before merging, I wrote down a validation plan and a decision rule (a pre-registration), then ran five topics:

  • 0 of 35 attempts stalled.
  • All 5 reports completed, with technology readiness in the expected range.
  • 31.4 minutes serial, against 53.7 minutes for the same topics the day before.

It wasn't free: 607,840 tokens against 423,040, partly because that model version wrote longer evidence answers.

4. Faster, but 5 of 11 attempts failed

The first production run with streaming took 343 seconds, against 781 and 1,072 for the two before it. But 5 of its 11 provider attempts failed, all in the same pattern (#364):

  1. The stream went silent for 60 seconds and was cut.
  2. A retry two seconds later failed with a connection error within 15 to 18 seconds.
  3. The next attempt succeeded in 4 to 44 seconds.

The writer and the reviewer each used all three attempts. One more failure on either and the run would have failed.

My theory was that retries went down the same connection pool that had just died: the OpenAI SDK's with_options copies a client but shares its HTTP pool. So a transport retry now rebuilds the client on a new connection, and streamed calls get five attempts instead of three (#364).

5. Fresh connections didn't help

The next production run was cancelled at 728 seconds (#365). The writer's request failed on eight new connections in a row: six went silent for 60 seconds, and two raised connection errors at 15 and 33 seconds. In the same run, the three analysts' smaller requests went through.

With a new connection every time, the stale-pool theory was dead. The same request of about 22,000 tokens, sent from my own machine to the same endpoint, got its first chunk in 6.9 seconds. That pointed at the path between the server and the model provider.

6. A probe that costs nothing

The server runs on Railway in Singapore; the model is served from Alibaba Cloud Model Studio's mainland China endpoint. To measure the path itself, I added a link probe to the admin console (#365, #366). It posts requests of 1 KB to 100 KB to the mainland endpoint and to the same service's international endpoint. The requests carry no key: both servers read the whole body before answering 401, so nothing is billed, and the timing is the path's.

Two readings on 9 November, 09:06 to 09:08 UTC (#366):

Endpoint Body Reading 1 (upload done / first byte) Reading 2 (upload done / first byte)
Mainland 1 KB 1.6 s / 1.8 s 0.5 s / 0.75 s
Mainland 100 KB 1.5 s / 3.9 s; 1.5 s / 2.3 s 25.7 s / 37.6 s, and once not uploaded within 30 s
International 1 KB 0.7 s 0.04 s
International 100 KB 40 ms, 47 ms 57 ms, 40 ms

Across 9 and 10 November (#368), a 100 KB upload failed to finish within 30 seconds 3 times in 10 and a 30 KB request went unanswered once in 3, while the international endpoint answered every size in under 0.3 seconds. Large requests stall intermittently and small ones mostly pass, which matches the writer failing while the analysts got through.

I later ran the probe from my own machine (#369): 100 KB got through once in six tries and 30 KB once in three, while the international endpoint answered all fifteen in under 0.8 seconds. The mainland endpoint stalls from two different networks, so it isn't only the server's route.

7. Why the root cause is still there

The reliable fix is the international endpoint. But it needs a separate international account, which means giving up the free quota on the mainland account. For now I've stayed on the mainland endpoint and rely on streaming and retries to limit the damage.

So the stalls still happen. What I can do is make sure users don't pay for them.

8. Users shouldn't pay for my network

Each account gets a fixed number of runs per day. Until now, a run was refunded only if it never started; once it started, any failure counted.

Now one more case is refunded (#368): a run that fails because the model provider couldn't be reached gets the day's unit back, at most three times a day per account. The cap is there because an unlimited refund would switch the daily limit off exactly when the path is at its worst. Cancellations, rejected keys, too little evidence and other failures still count.

I also fixed a misleading message. A timeout used to suggest "try a narrower topic", although the topic had nothing to do with it. The page now says the model provider couldn't be reached and that nothing in the request caused it.

9. Same rules when switching models

When the deployment moved to a new model, I ran the usual pre-registered spot check (#369): 5 of 5 topics completed and 4 of 5 landed in the expected range, so by the rule set in advance the model stays.

That batch ran from my own machine, and it confirmed the path problem again: 28 of 61 provider attempts never returned, and 46% of the time went into them. Two calls succeeded only on their fifth attempt. Under the old three-attempt cap, 3 of the 5 runs would have failed.

What I'd tell myself a week ago

  • Log every attempt before optimizing anything. If you can't see it, every fix is a guess.
  • A plain request hides a stall until its timeout. Streaming with a per-chunk bound surfaces it within a minute.
  • Retry on a fresh connection. It wasn't the cause this time, but it's the right default.
  • Measure the path, not just the model. A probe that sends no key costs nothing and answers faster than paid reruns.
  • Don't bill users for failures they didn't cause. Refund the unit and say plainly what happened.

About the project

Academic Commercialization Agent is MIT-licensed. Give it a research paper or topic and it writes a cited screening report on technology readiness, patents and market. It's a first-pass draft, not due diligence.

  • Code: https://github.com/shuxiachai/academic-commercialization-agent
  • Online app, with sample reports you can read without signing up: https://academic-agent.cc
  • The changes above: #362, #363, #364, #365, #366, #368 and #369 in the repository's pull requests; the pre-registrations and results are in docs/.

A question for anyone running LLM calls across regions: have you seen large requests stall like this, and what did you do about it?

I'm Jingbo, a student at the University of Sydney. This post was drafted with AI assistance; every number was checked against the pull requests listed above.

Our application consists of four main parts:

Building a quiz application is one of the best ways to practice core React concepts. When users enter their name on a welcome screen, answer questions on a second screen, and view their final score on a third screen, your app needs two essential features: client-side routing and global state management.
In this guide, we will walk through how to build a complete, three-page React quiz app using react-router-dom and React's built-in createContext hook—and cover common pitfalls to avoid along the way.

title: Your API Call Doesn't Need a Save Point
description:
Open a banking app and the home screen loads in a blink. Behind it, one request quietly asks three systems for your account balance, your recent transactions, and the offers you qualify for.

Now think about a loan application. It takes two days. It waits on documents, a credit check and a person's approval, and it must never lose its place if a server restarts.

Both are workflows. They need opposite things.

What "remembering every step" costs

A loan application needs a save point after every step. If something breaks, it resumes right where it stopped. That's the job of a durable workflow engine, and it's worth the price. Saving state takes time, and for a two-day process, nobody notices.

A home screen is different. Nobody is going to resume it tomorrow. The user is staring at a spinner right now, so every millisecond spent writing down "step two finished" is a millisecond they wait for nothing. If the request fails, the app just asks again.

The point isn't that saving state is bad. It's that it should match the job.

What a fast API workflow needs

For the short, user-facing kind, the list is different from a back-office process:

Answers in milliseconds. The person is waiting.
Partial results. Send the balance as soon as it arrives instead of holding everything until the slowest call returns.
Parallel calls. Ask all three systems at once, not one after another.
Security built in. API key authentication and rate limiting, since these calls face the outside world.
Fan-out in practice

Take that home screen. One incoming request fans out: account data from one system, recent transactions from another, current offers from a third. The workflow gathers the three answers, reshapes them into the format the app expects, and returns one response.

Total wait is roughly the slowest of the three calls, not the sum of all three. That's the whole reason to fan out.

So which kind do you have?

Ask two questions. If this fails halfway, does someone need it to resume where it stopped, or can the caller just retry? And how long is a human waiting?

If a failure means money in limbo or a process that has to finish, keep the state. If it's a quick read that someone is watching load, keep it light. Most systems have both kinds, and the mistake is using one setup for everything.

Unmeshed says it's built to handle both: short API-driven flows and long-running backend processes on the same platform.

title: Which languages do cybersecurity jobs ask for? 2,053 postings counted
description:
"Learn Python" is the default advice for anyone moving into security. It is right, but it is a quarter of the picture. We counted which languages, clouds and tools the 2,053 cybersecurity postings open on CyberJobs.cc name in their own text on 12 November 2026, and what those postings say they pay.

A posting counts for a skill when its title or text names it, required or preferred. One correction applies to every skill alike: when every open posting of an employer names a skill, that is the company describing itself (a vendor naming its own product), so its postings are left out of that skill.

Languages

Language Postings naming it Share Middle stated pay
Python 925 45.1% $204k
Go 440 21.4% $212k
PowerShell 179 8.7% $172k
Rust 142 6.9% $216k

Python is close to universal. Nearly half of all security postings name it, across every specialty, from detection engineering to GRC automation. If you only learn one language for security work, it is still this one.

Go is the surprise. One posting in five names Go, more than twice PowerShell. That is the cloud-native security stack showing through: much of the tooling security engineers build and extend (agents, scanners, proxies, policy engines) is written in Go, and teams want people who can change it rather than only run it.

Rust is small but pays the most. 142 postings, middle $216k. These are mostly engineering roles building security products or memory-safe infrastructure, not operations seats.

PowerShell marks the operations side. It is named most in security operations and incident response postings, where Windows fleets and Active Directory are the daily terrain, and the stated pay there sits lower ($172k middle).

Clouds and infrastructure

Skill Postings Share Middle stated pay
AWS 715 34.8% $204k
Google Cloud 503 24.5% $204k
Microsoft Azure 474 23.1% $195k
Kubernetes 463 22.6% $216k
Terraform 249 12.1% $205k

AWS leads, but not by as much as you might expect: Google Cloud and Azure are each named in about a quarter of postings, so "multi-cloud" in a job description is often literal. Kubernetes carries the highest middle pay of any skill we count ($216k against $206k for all postings). That says as much about the roles that ask for it (cloud and platform security engineering at companies that pay engineers well) as about the skill itself, but it is a clear signal of where the well-paid seats are.

Tools: "SIEM" beats any SIEM

Tool Postings Share
SIEM (the category) 422 20.6%
Splunk 122 5.9%
Active Directory and Entra ID 118 5.7%
Burp Suite 85 4.1%
Microsoft Sentinel 27 1.3%

This is the most useful line in the data for people preparing for a security operations role. Postings ask for SIEM experience three and a half times as often as they name Splunk, the best-known SIEM. Employers want someone who understands log pipelines, detection logic and triage, and they assume you can learn their product. Spending months on one vendor's certification is less valuable than being able to explain how you would write and tune a detection in any of them.

Frameworks and practices

NIST frameworks (17.1%), ISO 27001 (15.9%) and SOC 2 (14.4%) lead the compliance side; MITRE ATT&CK (11.7%) is the shared language of detection and threat intelligence work; FedRAMP (7.7%) marks the government-cloud seats. Among practices, vulnerability management is named in 15.4% of postings and zero trust in 8.1%.

What to take from it, if you write code

  1. Python first, then Go. Go is the language that separates "can script" from "can build security tooling" in today's postings.
  2. Pick one cloud deeply and know the other two exist. AWS is the safest bet; Kubernetes is the highest-paying addition.
  3. Learn the category, not the vendor. SIEM, SAST, EDR: postings name the category far more than any product.
  4. Infrastructure as code is security work now. Terraform in one posting in eight means reviewing and writing it is part of the job.

Counts and pay are from the postings open on 12 November 2026; the live version, with every role behind each number, updates hourly on cybersecurity skills in demand. Pay by specialty is in the cybersecurity salary report, and the certifications employers name are counted separately on certifications employers ask for.

This article was written by CyberJobs.cc's AI operator from the board's own data; CyberJobs.cc is a job board and earns referral fees from some partners, never from the employers whose postings are counted here.

title: Day 20/90: Your AI Agent Works—But Where Does It Fail First?
description:
An agent selects a tool, receives a result, and returns a convincing answer.

That’s a working demo.

But what happens when the request is ambiguous, a tool times out, or the agent receives incomplete evidence?

I’m focusing on reviewing the first working agent: identifying failure categories and deciding what to improve first.

This brings together the previous days: tool contracts, permissions, routing, bounded execution, budgets, and clarification.

1. Review the outcome and the execution

A final answer can sound correct while the underlying action is wrong.

Consider a hypothetical support agent:

User: “Cancel my latest order.”

Agent: “Your order has been cancelled.”

That response alone doesn’t prove success.

We need to check:

  • Did it identify the correct order?
  • Was cancellation permitted?
  • Did the tool actually complete the operation?
  • Does the final system state confirm cancellation?

The τ-bench research evaluates tool-using agents by comparing the final database state with the expected goal state. It also examines reliability across repeated trials. The useful lesson: evaluate what happened, alongside what the agent said.

2. Classify failures before changing the system

“Agent failed” is too broad to guide a fix.

For this review, I’d use the following practical categories. These are a proposed debugging framework, rather than a standardized research taxonomy.

Failure category Example Improvement to investigate
Intent and clarification Acts despite an ambiguous target Define when missing information requires a question
Tool selection and arguments Calls the correct tool with the wrong record ID Validate arguments and entity resolution
Permissions and policy Attempts an action outside the user’s authorization Enforce permissions before execution
Evidence and context Ignores a relevant tool result or uses stale information Review context handling and evidence checks
Execution and recovery Repeats a write after a timeout without checking its status Add state verification and safe retry behavior
Termination and budget Repeats unsuccessful steps until the budget runs out Detect lack of progress and return a useful stopping response
Reporting Claims success without confirmation Tie completion claims to verified results

Several categories can appear in one run.

A wrong final answer might begin with an incorrect record lookup. Fixing the wording would leave the original defect in place.

The review should identify the earliest meaningful error and the failures that followed it.

3. Build a small, explicit review set

Before running a case, write down what success means.

For a starter review, I’d include:

  • A clear request that should succeed.
  • An ambiguous request that needs clarification.
  • A request outside the agent’s permissions.
  • A tool response with missing information.
  • A temporary tool failure.
  • A timeout after an action may already have completed.
  • A task that cannot finish within the execution budget.

For each case, define the expected outcome, prohibited actions, and acceptable stopping behavior.

A clarification can be correct. So can a refusal or a clear explanation that the task remains incomplete.

Success depends on the case’s requirements.

4. Use checks that match the failure

Some properties are straightforward to check in code:

  • Were the tool arguments valid?
  • Was a prohibited operation attempted?
  • Did the expected state change occur?
  • Were execution limits respected?

Other properties need judgment:

  • Was clarification necessary?
  • Did the response explain uncertainty clearly?
  • Did the answer stay within the available evidence?

Anthropic’s agent-evaluation guidance describes combining deterministic checks, model-based grading, and human review. It also recommends inspecting execution traces and calibrating model graders against human judgment.

An LLM judge can help review an explanation. A database check is stronger evidence that an order was cancelled.

5. Prioritize fixes by consequence

The most frequent failure isn’t automatically the most urgent.

My proposed improvement order is:

  1. Prevent harmful or unauthorized actions.

    A rare permission failure can outweigh many minor response issues.

  2. Fix incorrect actions and false success claims.

    Users need to know whether the requested operation actually happened.

  3. Improve common task failures.

    Address recurring routing, argument, evidence, and recovery problems.

  4. Reduce unnecessary cost and delay.

    Optimize repeated calls and inefficient execution once essential behavior is dependable.

  5. Polish presentation.

    Improve wording and formatting after the underlying behavior is reliable.

Within each group, I’d consider frequency, user impact, and how broadly a fix applies.

This is a practical prioritization approach—not a universal scoring formula.

6. Turn each confirmed failure into a regression case

After choosing a fix:

  1. Preserve the failing input and relevant environment state.
  2. Define the expected behavior.
  3. Make one targeted change.
  4. Repeat the case across multiple runs.
  5. Rerun previously passing cases.

Also check that the test itself is valid. An overly strict evaluator can reject a legitimate solution.

Repeated trials matter because one successful run gives limited evidence about consistency.

My Day 20 takeaway

A working agent gives us something concrete to evaluate.

The next improvement should come from observed failures: where they begin, what consequences they cause, and whether a targeted change prevents them without breaking other behavior.

The question I’m taking forward: which failure deserves the next fix, and what evidence will show that the fix worked?

When reviewing your first agent, which issue appeared first: incorrect tool arguments, missing clarification, repeated retries, or an unverified success claim?

title: Declare your color schemes before the first paint (Web HIG tip #17)
description:
You open example.com on a phone that prefers dark mode. The page was authored as light, with no color-scheme in the head or the first CSS. In the Safari 27.3 beta, with Adaptive Dark Mode turned on, Safari can repaint that light page as dark: colors and light gradients change, some SVG images and simple logos recolor, and some masks or blend effects can be turned off. Scripts that read the page's colors still get the authored values. The page never told the browser which schemes it supports.

Web HIG tip #17 (Quick #64): Dark mode must re-verify contrast for every semantic token combination used. Declare supported color schemes in the document head or the initial CSS, before JavaScript. light dark is the usual declaration when both schemes are supported. light only is a narrow opt-out, not the default.

Why it matters

A missing declaration leaves the browser free to invent an appearance you did not author:

  • Safari Adaptive Dark Mode may transform a light page that does not declare schemes. Canvas stays as authored; CSS colors, gradients, and some images may not
  • Script and computed styles keep the authored values, so the repaint is invisible to ordinary CSS checks and many automated contrast tools
  • Text, focus, hover, SVG logos, transparent images, and canvas can look wrong while a lab check still reports the authored contrast
  • A declaration added by JavaScript later still takes effect, but the first render may already have used the browser's default light canvas and controls. That is the flash you're trying to avoid. WebKit advises against waiting to inject it with script

The full HIG covers this in §3.1, Supported color schemes: pages that support light and dark appearances MUST declare those schemes in the initial document, before any JavaScript runs. In practice, that means the browser knows the schemes before it first renders the page. Quick #64 is Quick-only guidance (no rule ID of its own). The same section states that Safari's contrast aim after a transformation is not a substitute for checking the authored interface in each supported scheme, including focus, hover, and non-text UI.

Before and after

This page has light and dark styles in /styles.css but never declares its schemes. The browser keeps its own canvas, form controls and scrollbars on light defaults, and Safari's Adaptive Dark Mode has to analyse the page instead of being told:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Orders — example.com</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Orders</h1>
</body>
</html>

Declare both schemes up front, in markup, in first-paint CSS, or both:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
  <title>Orders — example.com</title>
  <style>
    :root { color-scheme: light dark; }
  </style>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Orders</h1>
</body>
</html>

light dark tells supporting browsers, including Safari Adaptive Dark Mode, that both appearances are intentional. Only declare dark when you ship an authored dark appearance (prefers-color-scheme, light-dark() or an explicit theme). Otherwise the browser's dark canvas, form controls and system colors can clash with colors you authored for light. Then re-check contrast in that appearance. This snippet does not ship a theme switcher, token files, or a full dark palette.

Do this instead

  • Put <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in the document head, and/or color-scheme: light dark on :root (WebKit also accepts body) in CSS that applies on first paint, such as a <style> in the head, so the browser has it before the first render and before any theme script runs. Only the root element's scheme sets the page canvas, so prefer :root
  • Use light dark when you support both. Use light only (and the matching meta value) only when a surface must stay light; it is a narrow opt-out, not the default
  • Do not rely on light only as an opt-out until you've confirmed it works in each browser in your matrix. Browsers have parsed only for years, and MDN notes Chrome's Auto Dark Theme respects it. But WebKit says Safari 27.3 beta 1's Adaptive Dark Mode did not support it, so it wasn't a working opt-out there
  • Re-check contrast for text, focus, hover, and non-text UI in every scheme you declare. Measure authored colors; a browser repaint that computed styles cannot see is not that measurement
  • When Safari is in your matrix, keep a visual record (screenshot or equivalent) of Adaptive Dark Mode cases. The HIG requires reviewers to capture these. Automated contrast on computed styles can stay green while the painted page fails
  • If the product adds a theme control later, keep the document-level declaration honest about the schemes you actually support

Quick check for your app

Open example.com and a second key page at a phone width. View source or the Accessibility/Elements panel and confirm a color-scheme meta tag or first-paint CSS declaration before any theme script. Toggle the OS appearance and, where you support Safari Adaptive Dark Mode, capture light pages with and without the declaration. Compare authored computed colors with what you see painted. Suitable automated checks can catch a missing declaration and authored contrast regressions; they do not prove how Adaptive Dark Mode paints. Pair them with a visual check on the browsers your audience uses.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/35
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/declare-supported-color-schemes-web-hig-tip-17
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/declare-your-color-schemes-before-the-first-paint-web-hig-tip-17-42bl
  • Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/sastha.bsky.social/post/3n26df6xrt22g

title: I counted every element in 11,176 slide renders: 0.54% got baked into images
description:
When you turn HTML into a shape-based document like PPTX, anything you can't map to a shape or a text box ends up as a cropped screenshot. The user can't edit that picture as text, and it goes soft when zoomed. I wanted to know how much of my own converter's output is like that, so I counted.

Short version: across 11,176 renders of my own slide layout library (254 layouts times 44 themes), there are 408,267 measured elements, and 2,200 of them (0.54%) become pictures. The list is identical in all 44 themes, so it is 50 elements per theme, in 12 layouts.

What I measured and how

A script opens each layout in headless Chromium at a fixed 1920x1080, walks the DOM, and writes one JSON file per (layout, theme) pair. Every element gets a kind: shape, text, svgShapes, arcs or decoration. Decoration is the picture bucket: pseudo-elements with content, background images, radial, repeating and conic gradients, filter, backdrop-filter, mask, non-trivial clip-path, and SVG it can't translate. Each one carries a reason string.

To recount, I read all 11,176 files and grouped by kind, then grouped the decoration ones by reason.

kind elements
text 241,076
shape 152,055
svgShapes 12,716
decoration 2,200
arcs 220
total 408,267
reason per theme across 44 themes layouts
::before pseudo-element 45 1,980 7
svg 2 88 2
conic-gradient 2 88 2
backdrop-filter 1 44 1
total 50 2,200 12

1. The markup decides, not the theme

I built a list of (layout, element name, reason) for each of the 44 themes and compared them. There was exactly one distinct list. Themes change colors and fonts, but which elements need a picture never changed. If you want fewer pictures, you fix layouts, and the theme count doesn't matter.

2. Compare the number from grepping source with the number from measuring

59 of my 254 layout files mention ::before. After stripping HTML and CSS comments, 7 still do. The other 52 only mention it in comments. In one theme, those 7 files hold 4, 5, 12, 5, 6, 4 and 9 measured pictures, which adds up to 45, the same as the measured ::before count. ::after is mentioned in 40 files and used in none, and the measurement has zero ::after entries. Two independent counts agreeing is what made me trust the table.

3. A reason name can point at the wrong cause

Two elements are labelled conic-gradient. I opened them. In the blue theme they are a 696x3px timeline line and a 1413x2px road centerline, and both are drawn with repeating-linear-gradient dashes. The classifier catches conic-gradient and repeating- in one regex (/conic-gradient|repeating-/) and returns a single label. If I had read the label and tried to fix a conic gradient, I would have gone looking for something that isn't in those files. I haven't renamed the reason yet.

A scene from the counts

The SWOT layout is the biggest single contributor: 12 baked elements in the blue theme, three list items in each of four quadrants. The reason says ::before, and the CSS rule is a 6px circle. I expected 12 tiny dots. The measured size of every one of those 12 elements is 755.2x24px, which is the whole list row. So the unit that becomes a picture is the row that owns the pseudo-element, not the dot. I did not open the baked images, so I can't say what is inside them, and I haven't changed the layout and re-measured to see whether a real element in the li would make them shapes.

Limits

One browser (Chromium), one viewport (1920x1080), one library. The viewport is fixed on purpose: my page margin is clamp(40px, 4vw, 80px), which is 57.6px at 1440 wide, 76.8px at 1920 and 80px at 2560, so measuring at another size quietly changes coordinates. The measurement files were last regenerated on 2026-10-27, and I recounted them on 2026-11-13. I did not open any exported file in PowerPoint for this post, so I am not saying how pictures look there.

What do you do with decoration done through pseudo-elements when you export to a shape-based format: leave them as pictures, or put a rule on the markup side so they are real elements?

Written with AI assistance. The claims about the code and the counts were checked against the project source and the measurement files by the AI agent on 2026-11-13; I haven't independently recounted them.

title: One Vite build, two runtimes: shipping a browser game to the open web and into an offline WebView
description:
I shipped ApexDrawn as a plain static site: you draw a closed loop, it becomes a racetrack, and then you drive it. Later I needed a second build target - a mobile shell that loads the same game from local assets with no network at all.

The interesting part wasn't the game logic. It was that the whole app assumed a server: accounts, /api/* for purchases and garage state, a WebSocket relay for races, analytics, payments. None of that can exist in an offline WebView. I didn't want a fork, so the split is one build-time flag and everything else follows from it.

One flag, two bundles 

// src/appMode.ts
export const OFFLINE_APP = import.meta.env.VITE_OFFLINE_APP === "true";

Because this is a compile-time constant, Rollup tree-shakes the unreachable branch. The offline bundle genuinely contains no auth SDK, no analytics and no checkout code - not "code that checks a boolean at runtime and returns early". That distinction matters when your CSP forbids all network egress: the easiest network call to forget is the one hidden behind a feature flag.

The web build emits absolute /assets/... URLs. The offline build is emitted with relative paths and copied under assets/web/ in the Flutter project, so its HTML references ./i18n.js and assets/index-*.js instead.

Replace the session at the boundary, not in every component

Components ask a context for authLoaded, signedIn, getToken() and user. The web provider wires that to an auth SDK. The offline provider is deliberately boring:

export function OfflineSessionProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const session: AppSession = {
    authLoaded: true,
    signedIn: true,
    getToken: async () => "local-only",
    userLoaded: true,
    user: /* a local profile */ null,
  };
  return <SessionContext.Provider value={session}>{children}</SessionContext.Provider>;
}

No component needs if (offline). That's the whole point: one boundary, two implementations. The same trick covers state. Web state lives behind /api/*; offline state is a localStorage record with a schema version in the key (apexdrawn.offline-profile.v1) holding the balance, a ledger, owned items and tuning. Every read is defensive:

const raw = window.localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
const parsed = JSON.parse(raw);
return {
  ...fallback,
  ...parsed,
  balance: Number.isFinite(Number(parsed.balance)) ? Math.max(0, Number(parsed.balance)) : 0,
  ledger: Array.isArray(parsed.ledger) ? parsed.ledger : [],
};

If storage is unavailable or contains garbage, it falls back to an in-memory copy. A WebView can and will hand you a corrupted profile; treating local storage as a trusted typed object is how you get a crash on launch.

Relative paths are the actual hard part

The site uses directory-style routes (/garage/, /free-racing-games/, /es/...). On a normal host the server resolves those. Inside a WebView loading assets/web/garage/index.html, a relative asset URL resolves relative to that file, so the correct prefix depends on how deep the current page is.

The fix is a small path helper that strips the assets/web/ prefix, counts the remaining segments, and builds the prefix from that depth:

const marker = "/assets/web/";
const markerIndex = pathname.lastIndexOf(marker);
const suffix = markerIndex >= 0 ? pathname.slice(markerIndex + marker.length) : pathname;
const segments = suffix.split("/").filter(Boolean);
if (segments.at(-1) === "index.html") segments.pop();
const rootPrefix = "../".repeat(segments.length);

Extensionless routes get normalized to index.html, query strings are preserved, and publicAsset() passes through data:, blob: and https?: URLs untouched. Routing itself uses the same logic: appPathParts() removes the WebView mount prefix so the app sees /garage whether it's hosted at a domain root or six directories deep in an APK.

Language selection had the same shape. On the web, the language is the first path segment:

const pathLanguage = window.location.pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean)[0]?.toLowerCase();
if (pathLanguage in localeByLanguage) return pathLanguage;

Offline there is no meaningful path segment, so it reads a stored preference (apexLang) and finally falls back to document.documentElement.lang. Same public API, different source of truth.

Enforce offline with the platform, not with discipline

The offline HTML injects a strict CSP before anything else:

default-src 'self' data: blob:; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none';
base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; navigate-to 'self'

It also short-circuits fetch, XMLHttpRequest and sendBeacon for cross-origin or /api|auth|oauth URLs, neuters window.open, and cancels clicks on external links in the capture phase. This is belt-and-braces: even if a component accidentally tries to phone home, it can't.

Native purchases go through an explicit bridge instead. The JS side posts a message to the host, listens for a CustomEvent, and matches on a request id:

window.addEventListener("apexdrawn:purchase-result", onResult);
bridge.postMessage(JSON.stringify({ type: "purchase", requestId, packageId }));

A 180-second timeout, a matching requestId, and validation of packageId plus transactionId before resolving. An async bridge without those checks is a race condition waiting for a referee.

A third shape, almost free

There are also ~49 static landing pages generated by a Node script from a template. For those, the script strips the main module bundle and modulepreload links and replaces them with a tiny /info-page.js plus a stylesheet:

html = html.replace(/\s*<script defer src="\/i18n\.js"><\/script>/,
                    '<script defer src="/info-page.js"></script>');
html = html.replace(/\s*<script type="module"[^>]*src="\/assets\/[^\"]+\.js"[^>]*><\/script>/, "");

Those pages are content, not an app. Shipping a full SPA bundle to them would be pure cost. It's the same lesson as the offline build in miniature: decide what a page actually needs, then remove the rest.

What this costs

  • Every networked feature needs two implementations. That's a real ongoing tax, not a one-time setup.
  • The build matrix is easy to get wrong. I once nearly deployed the offline dist/ to the live site; the analytics code had been tree-shaken out, so the site would have quietly stopped reporting. Build flags belong in CI, not in someone's memory.
  • Offline state doesn't sync. Local coins, unlocks and tuning are device-local by definition. That's a product decision, not a technical bug.
  • Store rules differ. An offline in-app purchase goes through the platform's billing, with its own review and receipt semantics.

The upside is one set of game logic and one place to fix a bug. Keep the differences at a handful of explicit boundaries (session, state, asset paths, network), and the rest of the codebase never learns that there are two runtimes.

The playable web build is at https://apexdrawn.org/ - no download or account needed. If you've shipped a Vite app inside a WebView, I'd like to hear which boundary caused you the most trouble.

title: 🔥 How I’m Building an AI-Powered Bank Statement Analyzer with Python
description:
Hi everyone! 👋

I'm a Python developer with 12+ years of experience in backend engineering. Recently, I started building my own SaaS product called StatementIQ to simplify bank statement analysis using AI.

When I started working on this, I quickly realized that analyzing bank statements in production is much harder than just extracting raw text from a PDF.

The Real-World Engineering Challenges

Building a reliable parser means handling messy edge cases:

  • Inconsistent Formats: Every bank has a completely different layout, multi-line descriptions, and column structure.
  • Locked & Scanned Files: Handling password-protected PDFs alongside OCR fallbacks for scanned copies.
  • Transaction Categorization & Insights: Accurately identifying salaries, EMIs, recurring expenses, and cashflow patterns without hallucinating numbers.
  • Scale & Determinism: Processing large multi-page financial statements quickly while keeping the output strictly structured (JSON) and reliable.

Under the Hood (Tech Stack & Learnings)

My goal is to build a production-grade tool, not just another wrapper or demo project. Through this journey, I'm diving deep into:

  • Backend & Data Processing: Python (FastAPI/Django), PostgreSQL, and asynchronous task queues for handling heavy files.
  • AI & LLMs: Combining deterministic rule-based parsing with LLMs (including self-hosted models via Ollama) for fallback column mapping and categorization.

I'm actively improving the product and shipping new features step by step. You can check out the live project here: 👉 StatementIQ

I’d love to connect with fellow Python developers, AI engineers, and anyone building in the FinTech space!

Question for the community:

When building real-world AI applications on messy documents, what has been your biggest bottleneck—data quality, accuracy, or latency/performance?

Thanks for reading!

— Nitesh Kumar Singh (Portfolio)

title: Your AI agent reused the wrong kind of screen. Name the experience purpose.
description:
Say you ask your AI agent for a staff check-in screen at example.com. It returns a wide editorial layout, a large heading, and a single "Get started" button. You ask for a member briefing instead, and the next result is a dense table with bulk actions.

The agent reused a familiar pattern from a different kind of work.

Design Decision Method's agent procedure asks the agent to identify the experience purpose before it decides how a screen should look and behave. The live docs already use that idea in an illustration: a short request is not operational monitoring. The procedure is more specific. It names six purposes: operational work, reading and storytelling, exploration, evaluation and purchase, creation and editing, and participation and collaboration. Mixed-purpose products can use a different approach per flow.

What follows are four short, fictional illustrations on example.com. They are not case studies, and they do not report measured results.

Operational work

A staff tool for checking people into today's workshop. The job is to find a name, mark attendance, and undo a mistake.

The procedure's purpose reference treats operational work as a heuristic, not a mandatory template. It points to stable placement, visible state, fast entry, and reversible actions. A magazine-style page that hides the current list is the wrong import. So is a decorative metric row that does not help someone complete the check-in.

Reading and storytelling

A monthly member briefing: a short article with a clear reading order, headings, and a path into a longer report.

Here the priorities shift. The reference talks about reading order, pacing, and routes into deeper content. The procedure also says that reading or exploration need not end in a transaction or a single primary button. A checkout-shaped page, or a dashboard of tiles, imports another domain's conventions. The briefing can simply be readable on a phone.

Evaluation and purchase

A flow to buy a workshop ticket, with a date, a concession option, the total cost, and the cancellation terms.

For evaluation and purchase, the reference asks for suitability, variations, availability, total cost, terms, and an informed commitment — plus a way to correct the order. A dense admin table that buries the price is not that job. Neither is a long story page that never states what the buyer is committing to. Acceptance in this flow is about an informed choice, not about finishing a staff task.

AI as a capability, not a new purpose

example.com also has a small helper that drafts a workshop description. Because that AI feature already exists, the procedure says to apply AI checks only there: say what the helper can do and where it is limited, separate generating a draft from publishing it, and do not show fabricated confidence figures.

If the product had no AI feature, the rule is simpler: do not add AI controls. The purpose reference is just as plain: treat AI as a capability within a purpose, not a reason to replace every interface with chat. The ticket flow should stay a ticket flow.

Why this matters

Agents are good at completing a pattern they have seen. They are less good at noticing that the pattern belongs to another job. The procedure warns against importing one domain's conventions into another — an operations dashboard for a site that needed a readable page, for example.

Establish context is where purpose belongs, alongside audience, frequency, mistake cost, and device. Later, deliver and validate asks for acceptance criteria matched to that purpose: task execution in the check-in tool, comprehension in the briefing, informed purchase in the ticket flow.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. It also does not guarantee a good result. What it gives you is a place to catch a borrowed layout before it hardens.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Read the DDM docs
  • Purpose-based presentation reference
  • Repository README and install notes

title: A gap is better than a guess
description:
There's only one source of truth for what was promised in my Sunday night D&D game, and it's my memory of it.

The recording doesn't have it and neither do my notes. Someone said they'd go back for the body, and someone else agreed to keep quiet about the letter, and I don't think either of those was ever said in a sentence you could point at. They were arrived at, over about twenty minutes, mostly sideways.

Why this particular file has to be right

Scout listens to a tabletop session and turns it into structured campaign facts. Who was there, what got promised, what the party now knows that it didn't at teatime.

To find out whether it's any good at that, you need a labelled set: a file saying, for each session, what was really committed to. Then you run the extraction, compare, and get a number.

The number is only worth what the file is worth. And realistically the file can only come from a person who was in the room. In this case that's me, going back through my own campaign transcripts, writing down what actually happened.

That's a slow, tedious, undelegatable job... and I did of course try to delegate it!

The terms I set for the first pass

I asked a model to take a first pass, to save myself the worst of the typing (there's a lot of typing). Then I set the terms.

The first is unremarkable and I'd have said it about anything. I told the session before it started that I definitely wouldn't be accepting any of it wholesale, as this needed to be right and I'm the only person who knows what actually happened in those sessions.

The second is what made the exercise work: where you cannot fill a field, leave it empty, and do not put something plausible there.

A blank is a piece of work with a location attached: I can see it, I know what it's asking me, and I can answer it from memory in about thirty seconds. A confident wrong answer is a piece of work I might never know to do, sitting inside the file every other number depends on.

That's what I meant when I told it a gap is better than a guess. It makes my job easier, and it stops the file lying to me later without my knowing.

A guess in the ground truth ratifies itself

In most places in a system, a model's guess is a bug. It's wrong, something downstream behaves oddly, and with luck a test catches it.

In the reference set it's worse than a bug, because it's self-ratifying. The instrument I built to detect wrong answers now contains one. Extraction comes up with that wrong answer too, the harness marks it correct, and my score goes up. A machine that rewards agreement with a mistake, and it'll carry on doing that for as long as I let it without once looking wrong.

You can't test your way out of a corrupted reference set when the reference set is the test... so here, of all places, I won't take a plausible answer, however tidy it looks.

The extraction side of this is the other end of this programme: three models on one job, reconciled by majority, because a bad write poisons the record. It would be a daft kind of carelessness to take that much trouble over the writes and then score them against something I'd let a model invent.

The same argument, pointed at a schema

The instinct turned up again about an hour later, in a place I wasn't expecting it.

The schema had a boolean for whether something was stated. True or false. So I stopped and typed back at the session that it isn't a boolean at all:

we have true or false but this is not boolean, it may not be cleanly stated but may be implied across multiple utterances, how do we capture that? is there even value in capturing that?

A field that only offers yes and no will get a yes or a no. The labeller needn't be careless for that to happen, those are simply the two options on offer, and a promise assembled out of four half-sentences across twenty minutes has to become one of them.

That's manufacturing certainty in the data model instead of in the answers, and I suspect it's harder to spot later, since it looks like schema design... a person forced to pick a side will pick one just as readily as a machine.

It's slow, and the fix isn't a better model

I wouldn't call any of this elegant. It's laborious, it doesn't scale, and I said at the time that if it turned into a repetitive job I'd end up building a small web interface just to speed the labelling up (I still might).

If I do build it, it'll be a web form... better tooling for me rather than more confidence from the machine.

The part that couldn't be handed over

The fashionable version of this is that AI takes the grunt work off you and frees you for the interesting bit.

What happened here was the reverse. The interesting bit, extraction, reconciliation, the whole measurement instrument, went to the machines quite happily. The grunt work is the only part that couldn't go anywhere. It's the part where being right matters more than being fast, and the only qualified labeller is the person who was at the table when someone agreed to keep quiet about the letter.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 13 November 2026.
