title: Node.js Account Deletion: Verified GDPR Erasure for User Avatar Images
description:
TL;DR: Treat the Express account-deletion handler as an orchestrator, not as proof of erasure: freeze the user's avatar mapping, delete every recorded asset by ID, read each ID back, and close the request only after every read confirms absence. Keep the deleted IDs and verification outcomes in an audit record. If quality and bandwidth are competing concerns elsewhere in the photo pipeline, settle that during upload or OCR; deletion must operate on the authoritative asset ledger, never on whatever compressed preview happens to be convenient.

For a B2B SaaS team, the practical service boundary is narrow. Node.js owns the user lifecycle and durable deletion state; a worker performs bounded external calls; the database remains the source of truth for which original photos, avatar variants, and OCR-derived images belong to the account. A successful DELETE response advances the workflow, but it does not finish it.

This is the decision rule: no complete mapping, no defensible deletion.

How should Node.js delete user images during account deletion?

The failure mode starts before the API call. A profile row may point at the current square avatar while an older original, a mobile crop, or an OCR input is still associated with the same user elsewhere. Deleting the visible avatar proves very little if the user-to-asset mapping is incomplete. The deletion job should therefore take an immutable snapshot of all known asset IDs after new uploads have been blocked, rather than repeatedly querying a relationship that can change underneath it.

Then comes the second trap: treating command acceptance as observed state. Networks fail between request and response, retries race, and providers differ in what a delete acknowledgement means. The safe sequence is deliberately boring: issue deletion by asset ID, follow it with a read of that same ID, classify the observed result, and retain the ID-level evidence. Trust the read.

Stop there.

For capacity planning, use calls rather than users as the unit. With N mapped assets, the happy path requires roughly 2N remote operations: one delete and one verification read per asset. Retries add load, and a verification delay stretches completion time. Set the erasure workflow's SLO around verified completion, then derive worker concurrency from the provider quota and the largest credible account, not from median avatar count. A queue depth that looks harmless in users can be large in assets.

Pick the ownership boundary before the vendor

The vendor choice matters less than retaining a complete local ledger. Still, the operational differences are real, particularly for a small platform team weighing on-call load against lock-in.

Option Interface and ownership model Operational trade-off Best fit
Cloudflare Images Image identifiers sit inside a managed image service Keeps delivery and image lifecycle in Cloudflare's control plane Teams already using Cloudflare for image delivery
ImageKit Media identifiers sit inside an image-management workflow Centers the decision on a dedicated image platform Teams that want image management and delivery together
Uploadcare File identifiers sit inside a managed upload and delivery workflow Moves upload handling into the same vendor decision Teams that want managed ingestion as well as media lifecycle operations
Cloudinary Media asset identifiers sit inside a managed image workflow Reduces image-pipeline machinery the application must own Teams that want transformations and lifecycle operations together
Infrai Image assets are addressed through one REST surface One key and one bill can reduce credential and invoice sprawl; the abstraction also increases dependence on that common API Teams consolidating several backend capabilities behind one control plane

Those are not interchangeable promises. Cloudflare Images, ImageKit, Uploadcare, and Cloudinary are dedicated media choices with different surrounding workflows; Infrai groups media with a broader backend surface. The Infrai discovery catalog reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules and runnable examples in ten languages, which is useful when the deletion worker is one of many integrations, but breadth does not remove the application's obligation to maintain ownership records. For this workflow, only the asset-ID delete and subsequent asset-ID read are material. A team should validate identifier semantics, deletion behavior, account-level access controls, and read-after-delete observations against the current documentation of whichever service it selects, because a familiar upload path does not prove that the erasure path matches this runbook.

The quality-versus-bandwidth decision belongs upstream: preserve whichever original and derived assets the product needs, record every resulting ID against the user, and apply retention policy explicitly. Do not infer ownership later from filenames, URLs, OCR text, or the current profile image.

Implement a bounded, verifiable deletion worker

The example below is Go because the worker is intentionally isolated from Express. Express can create the deletion job and wait for its durable state transition; the worker receives a frozen list of IDs. It uses exactly two media routes, sends an explicit method, retries 429 responses with Retry-After when available, and surfaces response bodies on other failures. No key is embedded in source.

The verification contract in this example is conservative: a read returning 404 confirms absence. Any other status, including 200, leaves the job open for investigation or another bounded attempt.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Client struct {
    httpClient *http.Client
    apiKey     string
    baseURL    string
}

func (c *Client) do(ctx context.Context, method, path string) (*http.Response, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, c.baseURL+path, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.apiKey)

        resp, err := c.httpClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return resp, nil
        }
        io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after bounded retries")
}

func (c *Client) deleteAndVerify(ctx context.Context, id string) error {
    path := "/image/delete/" + id
    resp, err := c.do(ctx, http.MethodDelete, path)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("delete %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    if readErr != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read delete response for %s: %w", id, readErr)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("delete %s returned %d: %s", id, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
    }

    resp, err = c.do(ctx, http.MethodGet, "/image/get/"+id)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("verify %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    body, readErr = io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    if readErr != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read verification response for %s: %w", id, readErr)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusNotFound {
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("asset %s still unverified; read returned %d: %s", id, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ids := os.Args[1:]
    if len(ids) == 0 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "provide at least one asset id")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    client := &Client{httpClient: &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}, apiKey: key, baseURL: strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/")}
    for _, id := range ids {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)
        err := client.deleteAndVerify(ctx, id)
        cancel()
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Printf("verified_deleted asset_id=%s\n", id)
    }
}

In production, do not pass IDs on a command line. Read them from the durable job snapshot, and write each transition to an append-only audit record containing the deletion-request ID, asset ID, attempt number, timestamps, HTTP outcome, and final verification state. Avoid storing image content, OCR output, bearer credentials, or response bodies that may contain personal data in that record. The point is evidence, not a second copy of the user's data.

The log line in the sample demonstrates the minimum useful correlation field. A real worker should use structured logging and should never mark the parent account request complete merely because the process exited zero once; completion is a database transition conditioned on every snapshotted asset reaching verified_deleted.

Verification, SLOs, and proof

Define three states clearly: deletion requested, deletion acknowledged, and deletion verified. Only the third satisfies the runbook. For a user with four avatar assets, the evidence set must contain four asset IDs and four successful absence checks; one missing row is an incomplete request, even if the other three finished quickly.

The useful service indicators are verified-completion latency, oldest unverified request age, verification failure rate, and retry volume. Page on a sustained threat to the erasure SLO or on requests approaching the policy deadline, not on every transient 429. A retry is expected control flow. An aging unverified asset is the risk.

One number changes the alert from noise into evidence: the age of the oldest job that has not reached verified completion. Aggregate success rates can stay green while a single large account remains stuck behind one overlooked derivative, so the dashboard needs both the population view and that worst-case clock. This also gives the on-call engineer a concrete starting point: open the frozen asset snapshot, compare it with the per-ID audit rows, and resume only the entries that lack a confirmed absence read.

Auditability also changes the deletion order. Preserve the workflow record while removing the media objects, then minimize that record according to the organization's retention rules after the request is closed. The retained proof should establish which identifiers were processed and what was observed, without retaining the deleted photos themselves.

Roll back the workflow, never the deletion

Deletion is irreversible, so rollback means halting safely and resuming from durable state. If verification does not confirm absence, keep the account in a restricted, deletion-pending state, stop downstream use of its media, and retry from the first asset that lacks proof. Do not recreate an image to make an application rollback look tidy.

Before rollout, run the worker against disposable assets and test four cases: all IDs verify absent, one delete is rate-limited, one read still finds an asset, and the worker stops halfway through the list. The last case is the important one. Restarting must skip IDs already recorded as verified, continue the remainder, and produce one coherent audit trail tied to the original request.

Roll out with a concurrency cap. Watch provider throttling, queue age, and database contention, then raise the cap only while the verified-completion SLO retains margin. This is where a capacity-planning reflex pays off: bandwidth used by normal avatar uploads and OCR should be budgeted alongside deletion traffic, since an account-closure spike should not starve the very reads needed to prove completion.

The final operational rule stays small: snapshot, delete, read, record. Everything else supports those four verbs.

References

  • Cloudinary Admin API, Delete resources: https://cloudinary.com/documentation/admin_api#delete_resources
  • Cloudflare Images API documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/images/
  • ImageKit API documentation: https://imagekit.io/docs/api-reference/
  • Uploadcare REST API documentation: https://uploadcare.com/api-refs/rest-api/v0.7.0/
  • MDN, Image file type and format guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Guides/Formats/Image_types
  • GDPR, Article 17, Right to erasure: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj

title: Game Feel in Jetpack Compose Without a Game Engine
description:
Cubbles is a block-placing puzzle with cute faces on the blocks, and almost all of its charm is feedback: a piece that settles with a bounce, a row that melts away in a wave, a sound and a buzz that grow with your streak. None of it needs a game engine. This post walks through how it is done in plain Jetpack Compose, what the numbers are, where the shortcuts are, and how two other games of ours solve the same problem differently.

Why a puzzle does not need an engine

An 8 by 8 board, three pieces in a tray and a drag gesture do not need physics, a scene graph or a game loop framework. What they need is a clock and a way to draw. Compose gives you both: a Canvas to paint on, and a frame callback to read time from. Everything below sits on those two things.

One Canvas, one clock

The game screen draws the board, the tray, the effects and the floating text in a single Canvas. A coroutine started with a launched effect loops forever: it waits for the next frame with withFrameNanos, ignores the frame time it is given, writes the current uptime in milliseconds into a state variable called now, and drops any finished effects from a list.

The important detail is where now is read. It is read inside the Canvas draw lambda, so each frame invalidates the drawing only, not the composition of the whole screen. The score text and the buttons around the board do not recompose sixty times a second. The board itself is a plain mutable object rather than observable state, so a small counter is bumped after each move to make the Canvas redraw. The cost of this design is honest: the loop never stops, even when no effect is running, because blinking eyes and the gently bobbing tray pieces also need a clock.

Effects are data, not animations

Instead of one Animatable per block, the game keeps a list of small effect objects. There is a sealed class with a start time and a duration, and subclasses for a placement pop, a line clear, a floating text, a screen shake, a particle burst, a color flash and a sweeping light. They are created at the instant a piece is dropped and appended to the list.

The drawing code turns each one into a progress value between zero and one, by subtracting the start time from now and dividing by the duration, and derives everything from that number. There is no coroutine per effect, nothing to cancel, and nothing that can drift out of sync with the board. Layering is free: a big clear simply adds several effects to the list.

Squash, stretch and the wave

A placed piece pops for 480 milliseconds. Its scale is one plus 0.28 times a sine over the first part of the animation, multiplied by one minus the progress, so it swells and settles with a fading amplitude. To be accurate, this is a damped swell rather than a volume-preserving squash and stretch: the blocks are rounded squares scaled uniformly, which is cheap and reads clearly at phone size.

The clear animation is where the personality is. Each cleared cell waits a delay of 28 milliseconds per step of Manhattan distance from the center of the piece you placed, so the clear spreads outward like a ripple and tells your eye where it began. Then the cell swells to 1.4 times its size during the first 30 percent of 380 milliseconds, shrinks to nothing, mixes toward white and fades its alpha, and wears a happy face until 70 percent of the way through. One smoothstep function, the classic three t squared minus two t cubed, is the only easing curve used anywhere in the file.

Faces are just a few arcs

Every block has a face drawn from circles, lines and arcs, with a mood chosen per frame: normal, happy, excited or sad. Blinking needs no state. The eyes close when the current time plus the cell index times 911, taken modulo 3700 milliseconds, is under 130, so each block blinks on its own schedule. The eyes also shift by four percent of the block size toward the finger while you drag, which is a small thing that makes the board feel alive.

Particles without a particle system

A particle here is an immutable object with a start position, a velocity, a size, a color and a spin. Nothing is updated per frame. The draw code computes the position in closed form from the elapsed time: start plus velocity times t, with a gravity term of half g times t squared added to the vertical axis, where g is sixteen cell heights per second squared. There is no pool and no per-particle state to maintain.

Counts are bounded by design. Each cleared cell emits 2 plus the hype level, capped at 4, particles, where hype is lines cleared plus the combo minus one. A board has 64 cells, so a single burst cannot exceed 384 particles. A perfect clear adds 90 pieces of confetti and a new record adds 70. A burst lives 1.1 seconds, shrinks to 40 percent of its size and fades out. Squares spin and circles do not. All randomness comes from a generator seeded with the event time, so effects are reproducible while debugging.

Floating text that stays readable

Floating text such as the score, the combo and the praise words rises with the same smoothstep, pops in with a quick overshoot and stays for 1.9 seconds. It used to vanish in one second and players missed it. The words are drawn with a dark outline made of eight shifted copies, because white text on a light bathroom-tile background is unreadable without one. A real bug lives here too: on very small screens a long praise word was wider than the space available, and a clamp call with an inverted range crashed the app. The fix was a small helper that never inverts the range, plus shrinking the text to fit.

Sound without sound files

There are no audio assets. At first use, a sound is synthesized into a short array of 16-bit samples at 22,050 Hz mono: a sine at the note frequency plus a second harmonic at 20 percent, multiplied by an exponential decay, with a 60-sample attack ramp, about three milliseconds, to avoid the click you get from starting at full amplitude. The arrays are cached by name, and each playback builds a static-mode AudioTrack with that array, tagged as game usage, and releases it from a position marker when it finishes.

Haptics that you can actually feel

The vibration class drives the vibrator directly. A comment in the code explains why: the standard view haptic call follows the user's touch feedback setting and was barely perceptible on many phones in the first release. Instead the game builds waveforms, with amplitude control where the hardware reports it and plain timings where it does not, and wraps the call so a missing vibrator never crashes anything.

The rule that keeps it honest

Feedback is cheap to add and easy to overdo, so the project notes set a rule: no effect for its own sake. The puzzle must stay readable and a bad moment must never feel like a punishment. In code that looks like this. A ghost of the piece and a highlight on the rows it would clear appear before you drop. The dragged piece is lifted 1.6 cells above your finger so that your hand does not hide it. Trays are generated so that a legal move always exists. And the game over screen only says how close you were to your best score when you are within 60 percent of it; otherwise it simply shows the best, so a poor run is not followed by a scolding.

One gap, stated plainly: Cubbles has no reduced-motion switch yet. Our bingo game does, and it shows the pattern. A setting is exposed through a composition local, and the confetti and the looping home screen animations check it and stand down.

The same ideas in two other games

Where the screen is made of widgets rather than one Canvas, the standard animation API fits better. In the bingo game, a drawn ball pops in with an Animatable and a bouncy spring, scaling from 0.2 to 1 while it rotates. The daub on a bingo card uses an animate-as-state call with a spring of damping 0.42 so it lands with a wobble. A rejected tap increments an integer key, and a launched effect on that key snaps a shake value to one and springs it back to zero, read inside a graphics layer so nothing recomposes.

In a space puzzle of ours, the frame loop moves each gate a fixed 38 percent of the remaining distance toward its target cell on every frame. It is the simplest possible smoothing and it feels good, with the caveat that the speed depends on the frame rate. A rule of thumb from all three: use the animation API for widgets, and time-derived drawing for free-form scenes.

What to take away

Keep effects as small data objects with a start time and a duration, derive everything from progress, read your clock inside the draw lambda, cap every effect, and let the game rules run ahead of the animation. You get a surprising amount of life from a few hundred lines of Canvas code and a sine function. If you want to see these numbers at work, Cubbles is the game they were tuned for.

FAQ

Can you build game feel in Jetpack Compose without a game engine?

Yes, for puzzle and casual games. One Canvas, a frame loop with withFrameNanos and time-derived drawing cover squash, particles and screen shake.

How do you avoid recomposing the whole screen every frame?

Read the clock state only inside the Canvas draw lambda. Then each frame invalidates drawing, not composition.

How are the sounds made without audio files?

They are synthesized once into short arrays of samples, cached, and played with a static-mode AudioTrack that is released when playback ends.

Why drive the vibrator directly?

The standard haptic call depends on the user's touch feedback setting and was hardly felt on many phones, so the game builds its own waveforms.

Does more feedback always make a game better?

No. Effects should never hide the puzzle or punish the player, so each one here has a cap and the game over screen avoids discouraging messages.

If you want to see this in action, Cubbles is free on Google Play and needs no account. More notes like this one live on my site.

title: Platform Engineering Companies to Know Before You Sign a Contract
description:
Choosing a platform engineering partner is harder than it looks, because the discipline sits at the intersection of cloud architecture, Kubernetes operations, developer experience, and governance, and few vendors are strong across all four. 80% of large software engineering organizations will have dedicated platform teams by the end of 2026, up from 45% in 2022, according to Gartner. This guide covers nine platform engineering companies and lays out the criteria buyers should use to separate a real platform practice from a rebranded staffing arrangement.

Executive Summary

Platform engineering is the discipline of building and operating the internal developer platforms, cloud infrastructure, and self-service tooling that let application, data, and AI teams ship reliably at scale. Done well, it replaces ad hoc provisioning and inconsistent environments with golden paths, built-in governance, and standardized Kubernetes and cloud operations, so developers spend less time on infrastructure and more time on features that matter to the business.

This guide covers 9 platform engineering companies and outlines how to assess partners based on Kubernetes and cloud-native depth, internal developer platform experience, multi-cloud fluency, delivery model, and long-term investment in the practice. It also compares how each company approaches governance, developer experience, and production support, so buyers can match a partner's strengths to their own maturity stage. The goal is a repeatable framework for picking a partner who treats your platform as a long-term product.

Who Is This Guide For?

  • CTOs and VPs of Engineering deciding whether to build an internal platform team or bring in a partner to accelerate the effort.
  • Platform and DevOps team leads evaluating vendors to fill Kubernetes, CI/CD, or internal developer platform (IDP) skill gaps.
  • Procurement and sourcing leads comparing proposals and needing a consistent framework for scoring platform engineering vendors.
  • Enterprise architects responsible for multi-cloud strategy who need a partner fluent across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.
  • CIOs sponsoring a broader cloud, data, or AI modernization program that depends on a stable platform layer underneath it.

Each of these roles is ultimately solving the same problem: finding a partner who can reduce developer friction and operational risk without locking the organization into one vendor's way of doing things.

What Is Platform Engineering & How Does It Work?

Platform engineering is the practice of designing, building, and operating the internal developer platforms and cloud infrastructure that application, data, and AI teams run on. Instead of every team reinventing its own CI/CD pipeline, Kubernetes configuration, or cloud landing zone, a platform team builds reusable, self-service components with governance and security built in. The result is commonly called an internal developer platform (IDP), and it is usually delivered through a developer portal, a service catalog, and a set of golden paths that developers can follow without filing a ticket.

Key Advantages of Platform Engineering:

  • Golden paths for developers through self-service portals and pre-approved workflows, cutting the need for manual tickets and one-off provisioning requests.
  • Faster, safer deployments by encoding CI/CD, security scanning, and compliance checks directly into the platform instead of leaving each team to build its own version.
  • Lower developer cognitive load by absorbing Kubernetes, multi-cloud, and observability complexity behind a curated internal developer platform instead of expecting every engineer to master it.
  • Consistent governance across environments, so security and compliance become platform defaults rather than manual checklists applied inconsistently from project to project.
  • Executive-level strategic priority, with 88% of technology executives now viewing platform engineering as crucial to meeting their organization's objectives, according to Platform Engineering.org.
  • Better retention of scarce engineering talent, since platform-oriented roles reduce the operational burden that pushes senior engineers toward burnout and turnover.

When To Use Platform Engineering?

Not every organization needs a dedicated platform team on day one, but a few recurring signals make the case clear.

  • Multiple product teams are independently reinventing CI/CD pipelines, Kubernetes configurations, or cloud landing zones.
  • Developers routinely wait on tickets for environment provisioning, access requests, or infrastructure changes.
  • The organization is scaling from a single cloud region or provider to a genuine multi-cloud footprint.
  • Compliance and security requirements are inconsistently applied across teams and need to be enforced as platform defaults.
  • AI and machine learning initiatives require standardized MLOps pipelines and governed infrastructure to move from proof-of-concept to production.
  • Leadership has approved a dedicated platform team but lacks the in-house Kubernetes or cloud-native depth to stand it up quickly.

How To Choose the Best Platform Engineering Partner?

Certifications and case studies matter, but the criteria below separate a real platform practice from a rebranded staffing arrangement.

  • Kubernetes and cloud-native depth: Look for certified engineers (CKA, CKS, CKAD) with real production experience, beyond vendor logos on a slide deck.
  • Multi-cloud and hyperscaler fluency: A strong partner should be able to design and operate across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud, not steer every engagement toward a single vendor's stack.
  • Internal developer platform (IDP) experience: Ask for concrete examples of self-service portals, golden paths, and developer experience metrics they have actually shipped.
  • Track record with regulated or high-compliance environments: If your organization operates under strict regulatory or data residency requirements, confirm the partner has delivered compliant platforms under similar conditions.
  • Delivery model and cost structure: Compare onshore governance paired with nearshore or offshore engineering against fully onshore or fully offshore models, and weigh the cost and communication tradeoffs of each honestly. Consulting and service-led partners face a different set of platform constraints than product companies do, a distinction Improving breaks down in Platform Engineering for Service-Based Organizations.
  • Market growth and long-term viability: With the platform engineering and internal developer platform market projected to grow from $10.44 billion in 2026 to $31.57 billion by 2031, according to Mordor Intelligence, confirm your partner is investing in the practice for the long term rather than treating it as a side offering.
  • Do they provide 24/7 production support and incident response, or only project-based delivery that ends at go-live?
  • Can they show a specific, quantified outcome, such as deployment time, uptime, or error reduction, from a platform engagement similar to yours?
  • How do they measure success: DORA metrics alone, or business outcomes like time-to-market and cost avoidance?

The bottom line: the right partner backs up its platform claims with certifications, named clients, and quantified outcomes.

Platform Engineering Companies Compared

Top 9 Platform Engineering Companies

1. Improving

Improving Enterprises builds and operates the cloud, data, and AI infrastructure that enterprise applications run on, with dedicated practices across hyperscaler cloud platforms, data and analytics platforms, AI infrastructure, and integration and application platforms. The firm holds more certified data streaming engineers in the Americas than any other partner, earning recognition as the 2025 Confluent Enablement Partner of the Year, and its Kubernetes practice includes 74 certified engineers across CKA, CKS, and CKAD specializations. Improving's platform work spans healthcare, energy and utilities, logistics, and retail clients running production Kubernetes, Kafka, and multi-cloud environments.

Why Is Improving the Best Platform Engineering Partner?

We pair consulting-led architecture with hands-on engineering delivery, so the same practitioners who design a platform strategy also build and operate it in production. Every certification and partnership below reflects work completed for a real client, not a logo agreement.

  • NPS 90+: among the highest in modern enterprise technology services.
  • 7.5-year average partnership length: built around long-term relationships, not one-off projects.
  • Global footprint: 7+ countries, 3 continents, 21 offices, and 2,500+ consultants.
  • Key verticals: healthcare, energy and utilities, logistics, retail, and financial services.
  • Platform stack: Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Confluent Kafka, Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft Fabric.
  • Relevant strengths: 74 certified Kubernetes engineers (51 CKA, 4 CKS, 19 CKAD), 2025 Confluent Enablement Partner of the Year, and co-chair contributions to KubeCon India and the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model.

Global Delivery Access

Platform engagements draw on practitioners who hold current CKA, CKS, and CKAD certifications and who also teach live technical sessions every week through Improving Talks, giving clients direct access to the same engineers building production Kubernetes, Kafka, and cloud environments for other enterprise accounts Improving's practitioners have also co-chaired KubeCon India in 2025 and 2026 and contributed directly to the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model, putting the firm's delivery teams inside the standards work that shapes the discipline.

McKesson needed to automate deployment of its Drug Serialization Repository across 29 distribution centers to meet a Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA) compliance deadline. Improving automated the deployment pipeline using GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Confluent Kafka, and MongoDB, cutting deployment time per location from four to six hours down to 33 minutes, hitting the federal compliance deadline across all 29 sites.

  • Key platforms/technologies: AWS, Azure, DevOps managed services, generative AI

Talent Pool Access: XenonStack operates from Dubai, Plano (Texas), and two locations in Punjab, India, giving it a footprint across the Middle East, North America, and South Asia.

Proven Track Record: XenonStack's client reviews specifically cite Kubernetes architecture and DevOps delivery for autoscaling cloud platforms and big data and AI solutions, with clients in education, IoT, and technology sectors describing production systems built and maintained over multi-year engagements.

9. RX-M

RX-M is a Cloud Native and AI training and consulting firm, and a charter member of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and a founding-class Kubernetes Certified Service Provider and Kubernetes Training Provider. The firm blends vendor-neutral training with hands-on platform engineering consulting, positioning itself as a way to both upskill internal teams and accelerate platform delivery.

Quick Facts

  • Headquartered: Miami, Florida, United States (with additional offices in San Francisco, California)
  • Team Size: 11-50
  • Key verticals: Fortune 100 enterprises across technology, finance, defense, and manufacturing
  • Key platforms/technologies: Kubernetes, CI/CD, internal developer platforms, agentic AI SDLC tooling
  • Relevant strengths: CNCF charter member, Kubernetes Certified Service Provider, Linux Foundation Authorized Training Partner

Why Consider RX-M? RX-M is best suited to organizations that need to build in-house Kubernetes and platform engineering capability through certification-grade training alongside, or instead of, outsourced delivery.

Talent Pool Access: RX-M's practitioners are active open-source contributors and authors who have trained engineers at organizations including Adobe, Cisco, GE, Dell, Lockheed Martin, and Wells Fargo.

Proven Track Record: RX-M's client logos span Fortune 100 companies across finance, technology, and defense, and its founding-class status as both a Kubernetes Certified Service Provider and Training Provider predates most competitors' cloud-native practices.

Choosing Your Platform Engineering Partner

These nine companies range from hyperscale integrators to specialized Kubernetes shops, but the strongest fit comes down to one thing: a partner who stays on to operate what they build. Improving has delivered exactly that for clients like McKesson, cutting a 29-site deployment from six hours down to 33 minutes per location under a hard regulatory deadline.

See how Improving's platform engineering team can do the same for your organization →

Frequently Asked Questions

1) What is the difference between platform engineering and DevOps?

DevOps is a set of cultural and technical practices that unite development and operations within individual product teams. Platform engineering centralizes that work into a self-service internal developer platform that multiple teams can use, reducing the need for every team to build its own tooling from scratch.

2) What certifications should we look for in a platform engineering vendor?

Look for Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS), and Certified Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD) credentials held by named engineers, alongside hyperscaler certifications such as AWS Solutions Architect Professional, Microsoft Azure Solutions Architect Expert, or Google Cloud Professional Data Engineer.

3) Can a platform engineering partner support multi-cloud environments?

Yes, but capability varies significantly by vendor. Confirm the partner has delivered production workloads on at least two of the three major hyperscalers (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud); certifications alone do not prove multi-cloud expertise.

4) How long does a typical platform engineering engagement take?

Initial platform builds commonly run 3 to 12 months depending on scope. Many organizations then keep their partner on for ongoing managed operations after go-live, continuing indefinitely.

5) What is a golden path in platform engineering?

A golden path is an opinionated, pre-approved workflow that makes the secure and compliant way to build and deploy software also the fastest and easiest option, so developers choose it because it saves them time, not because it is mandated by policy.

title: The App Opened. Did the Deep Link Reach the Right Screen?
description:
A practical iOS Universal Links and Android App Links QA matrix for mobile release teams.

A product manager taps an invitation link from a message. The app launches, which looks like success in a quick smoke test. Then the user lands on the home screen rather than the specific event, order, or workspace they were invited to view. The link technically opened the app, but it did not complete the user's task.

That gap is why deep-link QA must go beyond “Does the app open?” Real release testing asks whether the right user, in the right app state, reaches the intended content without losing context or seeing information they should not access.

First, agree on which link experience you built

On iOS, Universal Links associate an HTTPS domain with an app using Associated Domains and an apple-app-site-association file. On Android, verified App Links associate an app and website through manifest intent filters and a Digital Asset Links statement. These platforms have different verification and user-choice behavior; a link opening in the browser is not necessarily the same defect on every device. Apple's Associated Domains documentation, Universal Links debugging guidance, and Android App Links testing documentation are useful starting references.
Distinguish ordinary deep linking (the installed app opens a relevant destination) from deferred deep linking (a journey may continue after installation). Do not assume Universal Links or Android App Links alone guarantee post-install restoration of the original destination. Document whether deferred continuation exists, which provider handles it, and what fallback is expected when it does not.
There is also a legacy-link risk: Firebase Dynamic Links shut down on August 25, 2025. If an app or campaign still distributes those older links, treat them as a separate migration and regression question rather than as a current default implementation. Firebase Dynamic Links FAQ

Build a link-state matrix before testing

A useful test plan crosses link type, installation state, sign-in state, app state, and entry point. Start with these ten scenarios:

  1. Installed and signed in. Tap a valid link to a known item. Confirm the exact item, correct account, and correct screen, not merely an app launch.
  2. Installed but signed out. Open an invitation or private-item link. Login may be correct; after successful authentication, check whether the intended destination restores as required.
  3. Wrong account. Open a link while another user is signed in. Confirm a sensible denial, account-switch prompt, or approved alternative; never assume private content should display.
  4. Not installed. Tap the HTTPS link. Check documented web or store fallback. If a later install should preserve context, test that separately as deferred linking.
  5. Cold, warm, and background app. Repeat with app closed, already open on another screen, and resumed from background. Check navigation history and duplicate screens.
  6. Entry point variation. Open from an actual tapped message, email, browser page, and supported in-app WebView. Typing a URL into the address bar is not a substitute for tapping, particularly on iOS.
  7. Expired, removed, or malformed destination. Check for a clear error or safe fallback without a crash, endless spinner, or misleading success.
  8. Network interruption. Tap while offline or unreliable, then reconnect. Confirm recovery, retry behavior, and whether the original destination remains available.
  9. Install/update and domain changes. After a build update or domain change, repeat handling on target OS versions; verify entitlements, signing, and live domain association files match release configuration.
  10. Repeated and competing taps. Tap the same invitation twice or different links rapidly. Look for stale content, duplicate navigation, and wrong-item rendering.

Use a coverage table: link identifier, platform/OS/build, device, installation state, login state, source app, foreground state, expected destination, observed destination, result, and evidence. It turns a subjective report into a reproducible release decision.

The browser fallback matters as much as the app route

A web fallback is not automatically a failure. Apple's Universal Links guidance describes a browser path for people without the app, while Android's verification and user defaults influence which handler opens. Test against agreed requirements rather than assuming every tap must launch native UI.

If a visitor lands on a website, confirm the page matches the link intent, loads readable content, and gives the intended next action. If the destination was an RSVP, a generic homepage with no path back to the event is a poor experience even if no exception was logged.

Separate app behavior from platform association failures

When a link fails, begin with the symptom. Did it open the wrong app, remain in the browser, reach the wrong screen or lose context after login? Android documentation includes tools to check host verification and Digital Asset Links. Apple's TN3155 covers Universal Links debugging. Developers may need to review configuration; manual QA should supply the exact URL, source app, device/OS, account state, build, and result. Android App Links troubleshooting.

Avoid reporting every browser opening as “broken deep linking.” On iOS, tapping a link while browsing the same domain in Safari can behave differently from tapping it in another app, and user preferences affect handling. Capture the actual interaction used. A controlled repeat is more useful than a screenshot that merely says, “did not open.”

What a useful defect report looks like

Here is an illustrative example, not a client finding: “On Android device A, build 1.4.2, signed out, tapping a valid event-invitation HTTPS link from Gmail opens Login. After sign-in, the app opens Home instead of Event 482. Expected: return to the invitation or show the approved post-login fallback. Reproduced 3/3.” Attach a recording and sanitized link identifier. Never place live customer tokens or private invitation URLs in public content.

For a short pre-release cycle, prioritize links that influence signups, invitations, account verification, bookings, order status, and referrals. Test both platforms on real devices, then rerun critical paths after login, navigation, domain or build changes. A pass means the expected journey worked under documented conditions — not that all devices or future releases are guaranteed.

Testers HUB provides independent mobile functional, exploratory, compatibility, and regression testing on real iOS and Android devices, with reproducible defect evidence. If your release relies on links taking customers from messages or websites into app workflows, request a scoped review through Testers HUB Mobile App Testing Services.

Bottom line: A deep link that launches the app has passed only the first checkpoint. Destination, session, fallback, and recovery complete the test.

title: Building on a Broker API: Rate Limits, Safe Order Placement and Reconcile Loops for Option Sellers
description:
Building on a Broker API: Rate Limits, Safe Order Placement and Reconcile Loops for Option Sellers
The first script that places an order through a broker's API usually works. That is the dangerous part. A script that works once on a quiet morning with one order tells you almost nothing about what happens at 09:20 on expiry day, when it has to send four orders, one of them times out, the broker's server is slow, and your internet drops for eight seconds.

The code that decides what to trade is the small part of an automated system. The larger part is the code that deals with the fact that the outside world is unreliable: orders that are accepted but not confirmed, calls that are refused for going too fast, positions that do not match what you think you hold. Most of the money lost in home-built systems is lost there, and not in the strategy.

This guide is written for traders who are not full-time developers. It does not need much code. It explains the ideas you need to check, four in particular: staying within rate limits, placing orders so a retry cannot double your position, running a loop that compares your records with the broker's, and keeping logs you can actually use at the worst moment. The examples are about NIFTY and SENSEX weekly option selling, but the engineering is the same for any instrument.

The three books you are really keeping
Start with a mental model that makes the rest easy. At any moment there are three records of what you hold, and they can disagree.

Book What it says Who writes it
Intent What the strategy wants to hold right now Your rules
Ledger What your software has sent and believes was filled Your code
Broker's book What the broker says you actually hold and what orders exist The broker
In a perfect world the three match. In practice they drift apart, for ordinary reasons. An order was sent but the reply never arrived, so the ledger says nothing and the broker's book shows a fill. An order was rejected, but your code did not read the rejection, so the ledger says filled and the broker's book says nothing. You placed a manual trade on the broker's app, so the broker's book has a position that neither intent nor ledger knows about.

The broker's book is the only one that is legally and financially real. Margin, charges and settlement all follow from it. So the engineering aim is simple to state: make your ledger follow the broker's book, and make your intent act on the ledger only when the ledger has been checked against the broker's book. Everything else in this article is a method for doing that.

What to check on any broker API before writing code
Before you write a line, read the broker's documentation for six things. Do this for every broker you plan to use, as these details differ and change between versions.

Authentication and session life. Many broker APIs need a fresh login token every day, sometimes with a second factor. Your system needs a plan for the morning login, and an alert if it fails. A script that cannot log in at 09:10 is a missed day, or worse, a half-managed one.
Rate limits. How many requests per second and per minute, separately for order calls and for data calls. Also look for a daily order cap.
Order types and fields. Which order types exist, whether there is a field you can use to tag your own reference on each order, and how the status is reported.
Status values. The exact words the API uses for pending, open, filled, partly filled, rejected and cancelled. Your code has to handle every one of them.
Positions and order book calls. How fresh the data is, and whether it can lag behind a fill by a few seconds.
Error messages. What a rejection looks like and whether the reason is machine-readable.
If you are still at the stage of working out what is on offer and what the regulatory position is, one published overview of the algo trading API in India is a reasonable starting point for the wider picture. It cannot replace your broker's own documentation, which is the only source for the current limits and fields, so read both.

The rules about who may use an API and how have also been changing under SEBI's retail algo framework. Read the circulars yourself on sebi.gov.in and ask your broker what it needs from you, such as strategy registration or fixed IP addresses. Do not rely on a forum summary.

Rate limits: treat them as a budget
A rate limit is a promise that the broker will refuse some of your calls if you send too many. If your code is not written to expect that, it will eventually hit the limit at the worst time and behave in a way you did not plan.

Think of the limit as a budget and spend it on purpose. A short strangle with two hedges needs four order calls at entry. If your system also polls prices, checks the order book after each order and reads positions, the same minute can easily use dozens of calls. Add a retry loop that fires on every failure, and a single slow response can multiply the traffic exactly when the broker is struggling.

A simple call budget
Here is an illustrative budget. The numbers are made up. Replace them with your broker's current published limits.

Four design rules follow from the budget.

Put every API call through one gate. A single function that all calls use can count requests, sleep when needed and log each call. If calls are scattered around the code, nobody knows the total rate, and the first time you find out is when the broker refuses you.

Back off when you are told to slow down. If the API says you are going too fast, wait and then retry with a growing delay: 1 second, then 2, then 4, with a small random addition so that several parts of your system do not retry in lockstep. A fixed instant retry just makes the problem worse.

Rank calls by importance. Exit orders and the kill switch come first. Reports and nice-to-have data come last. If the budget runs short, the important calls must still go through. A simple way to do this is a priority queue, with exits at the top.

Know the daily cap. Some brokers limit the total orders per day. A strategy with re-entries and stop modifications can use more orders than you expect. Count them on a typical day and add a margin.

The cost of waiting
Rate limits and retries cost time, and time costs money, although less than people fear on the entry. EliteAlgo's desk study of 163 NIFTY and SENSEX weekly expiry sessions between January 2025 and July 2026 tracked the ATM straddle premium against its 09:16 level, averaged over all sessions. By 09:31 the average was 95.4% of the starting level. That is an average drop of 4.6% in fifteen minutes. On a straddle premium of 110 points, 4.6% is about 5 points, which on one NIFTY lot of 65 is roughly Rs 330. This is an average of many days with the strike held fixed. A single day can be far from it, and a fast move can go either way. The practical reading is that a delay of seconds is cheap compared with the cost of a wrong or doubled order, so it is right to let your system pause and check instead of rushing a retry.

Idempotent order placement: surviving the timeout
This is the most important idea in the article and the least known outside software teams. The word sounds technical. The meaning is simple: doing something twice should have the same effect as doing it once.

Placing an order is not naturally idempotent. If you send "sell 65 NIFTY call at market" twice, you sell 130. That matters because of a problem every network call has.

The three outcomes of an order call
When your code sends an order, there are three possible results, not two.

Accepted. The broker replies with an order ID.
Rejected. The broker replies with an error, and no order exists.
Unknown. You sent the request and got no usable answer. A timeout, a dropped connection, a garbled response. The order may or may not exist.
Most beginners' code handles the first two and treats the third as a failure: "it did not work, try again." If the order did in fact go through, the retry doubles the position. In a short-premium strategy, a doubled short leg is exactly the kind of mistake that turns a normal day into a bad one.

The rule for unknown
When the result is unknown, never retry blindly. Look first. Query the broker's order book and positions, find out whether the order exists, and only then decide. To make that lookup possible you need a way to recognise your own order.

Give every order your own reference. Before sending, generate a unique reference such as the date, the strategy name, the leg and a counter, for example 20261104-S1-CE-001. If the broker's API has a field for a tag or remark, put the reference there. After an unknown result, search the order book for that reference. If it is there, treat the order as sent. If it is not there after a short wait, it is safe to send again with the same reference.

Some APIs may offer a proper idempotency key that makes the broker ignore a repeated request. Many do not. Check your broker's documentation, and do not assume. If there is no such key, the tag-and-lookup method is your protection.

Order of operations for a multi-leg entry
With several legs, the order of the calls matters as much as each call. A safe pattern for a hedged short strangle looks like this.

  1. Check that the day, time, margin and daily-loss limit allow a new trade.
  2. Send the hedge (bought) legs first.
  3. Confirm each hedge is filled, by reading the order book, not by trusting the first reply.
  4. Only then send the short legs.
  5. Confirm the fills. Compare quantities with intent.
  6. If any step ends in unknown or partly filled, stop, alert yourself and do not continue to the next leg.

The rule behind this is that you should never be in a state where a naked short leg exists because a hedge is unconfirmed. Slower but safe beats fast but exposed.

Partial fills and price protection
Two more traps. A partly filled order is neither done nor failed. Decide in advance what you do: wait a set time, cancel the remainder, or top up. And a plain market order on a thin option strike can fill at a poor price. Many traders use a limit order with a small buffer to bound the damage, then handle the case where it does not fill. Either way, the rule is written down before the day, not invented when the screen is red.

The reconcile loop
The reconcile loop is a small program that runs while your strategy is live. Every few seconds, it compares the three books and raises a flag if they differ. Here is the idea in plain pseudocode. You do not need to understand any particular programming language to follow it.

every 10 seconds, and again after every order:
broker_positions = ask broker for open positions
broker_orders = ask broker for today's orders
ledger_positions = what my software believes it holds

for each instrument in either list:
    if broker quantity != ledger quantity:
        record a mismatch (instrument, both numbers, time)

if there is a mismatch:
    wait 3 seconds and check again    # the broker data may lag
    if the mismatch is still there:
        stop new orders
        alert me loudly
        apply the playbook for this kind of mismatch

Three details make the loop work in the real world.

Check twice before panicking. Some APIs show positions a few seconds after a fill. A mismatch that clears on the second look is just lag, and an alarm on every lag will teach you to ignore alarms. A mismatch that survives two looks is real.

Compare more than positions. Also compare open orders. A forgotten pending stop order in the broker's book that your ledger does not know about can fire later and open a position you did not intend. Include order status, quantity and price.

The loop must be able to stop the strategy. A reconcile loop that only prints a message is a decoration. It needs the authority to block new orders until a person has looked, and it should run even when the main strategy code is busy or has crashed. A separate process is the safest way.

Reconcile before the stops are trusted
A stop-loss rule is only as good as the position your software believes it has. If your system thinks it holds two lots and the broker holds four, a stop sized for two leaves half the risk unmanaged. So run a reconciliation before entry, after entry, after any stop or exit, and at the end of the day. The end-of-day one should confirm that you are flat if the strategy is intraday. A leg that was never closed overnight is a risk you should find at 15:35, not the next morning.

A mismatch playbook
Decide what to do for each kind of mismatch before it happens. During a live mismatch, you will be tempted to improvise, and improvisation under stress is how small errors grow.

Two rules cover the table. First, when in doubt, reduce risk and not increase it: pause, cancel pending orders, close if you must. Second, always correct the ledger to match the broker, never the other way round. The broker's book is what exists.

Logging: write for the person at 15:10
Logs are for the version of you who is looking at a problem at 15:10 with ten minutes to act. They need to answer one question fast: what has happened so far, and in what order?

A good log line is boring and complete. For every order action, record the time to the second, the strategy name, your own order reference, the instrument, side, quantity, order type, price, the request you sent, the exact reply or error you received, and the broker's order ID if one came back. For every reconcile run, record both sets of numbers, not just "OK".

What to keep and for how long
Raw requests and replies. Keep the full text, not your summary. When something odd happens, the exact wording of the broker's reply is often the clue.
Decisions. Log why the system did something: "Stop triggered, combined P&L minus Rs 2,700, limit minus Rs 2,600." A log of actions without reasons is a puzzle.
One file per day, with the date in the name. Plain text or CSV is fine. You will want to search and sort it.
Keep it for at least the period your tax and compliance obligations require, and longer if you can. Disk space is cheap and missing evidence is expensive.
Never log secrets. API keys and tokens do not belong in log files. Mask them.
Pair the logs with an alert channel you will really see, such as a message to your phone. Alerts should be few and meaningful: a failed login, a mismatch that persists, a rejected exit, a daily loss limit reached. If your phone buzzes twenty times a day for harmless events, the one that matters will be missed.

Time matters
Make sure the clock on your machine is accurate. Order timestamps, exit times and log lines are only useful if they line up with the exchange's clock. An unsynchronised computer that is off by a minute will make a time exit at 15:15 happen at the wrong moment and make your logs impossible to compare with the broker's records. Turn on automatic time sync and check it.

Testing without losing money
You can test most of this before real money is at risk, and you should. A test plan has four layers.

Dry run. The code runs the whole day's logic but sends no orders. It logs what it would have done. Compare the log with what you would have done by hand.
Paper or sandbox, if the broker offers it. Not all do, and some sandboxes behave differently from the live system, so do not treat a pass here as proof.
Smallest live size. Run a single lot of a cheap, liquid instrument. Real orders, real rejections, small cost.
Fault injection. Break things on purpose while the size is small. Switch off the internet for ten seconds in the middle of an order. Send an order with an invalid quantity. Place a manual trade in the broker's app and see if the reconcile loop catches it. Kill the script and restart it with a position open: does it recognise what it already holds, or does it enter again?
That last test, the restart with an open position, catches more real bugs than any other. A system that forgets what it holds after a restart will place a second set of orders. The fix is to rebuild the ledger from the broker's book on every start, before the system is allowed to do anything.

When your tests pass, run live at small size for several weeks before scaling. Keep the daily report, the mismatch log and the override log. If a month passes with no unexplained mismatch, you have earned a bit of confidence. If there are mismatches, each one is a free lesson from a cheap day.

Frequently Asked Questions
Can I trade through a broker API without knowing how to code?

Partly. No-code builders handle common cases. For custom checks, reconciliation and anything unusual, someone has to write code, whether you, a hired developer or a platform provider. If you hire help, agree in writing who owns the code and who is responsible when an order goes wrong.

What happens if my order request times out?

The result is unknown, not failed. Do not send it again straight away. Look up the broker's order book for your own order reference. If the order exists, treat it as sent. If it does not exist after a short wait, send it again with the same reference.

What is an API rate limit and what happens if I exceed it?

It is a cap on how many requests you can send in a period. If you go over it, the broker refuses some requests, and repeated violations may lead to a block. Route all calls through one gate that counts them, back off with growing delays, and keep the important calls, such as exits, ahead of the rest.

How often should I reconcile my positions with the broker?

Before entry, after every order, after every exit, at a steady interval while a position is open, and once at the end of the day. A common interval is every ten seconds or so, within your call budget. Check a second time before raising an alarm, since broker data can lag.

Is it safe to keep my API key in my script?

It is better not to. Keep keys and tokens in a separate configuration file or in environment variables, keep that file out of any shared folder or code repository, and never write secrets to logs. If a key is ever exposed, generate a new one at once.

Should I use market orders or limit orders for automated option selling?

Both have trade-offs. A market order is likely to fill but the price can be poor on a thin strike. A limit order bounds the price but may not fill. Many traders use a limit with a small buffer and a rule for the case where it does not fill. Decide in advance, and test it.

Conclusion
Building on a broker API is mostly an exercise in distrust. Distrust the reply that never came, the position screen that is a few seconds stale and the retry that might double an order. Keep three books and make the ledger follow the broker's. Treat rate limits as a budget, give every order a reference of your own, never retry an unknown result blindly, and run a reconcile loop that can stop the strategy. Write logs for the person who has ten minutes to fix something.

None of this makes a strategy profitable. It makes the system behave as designed, which is the only thing you can control. Test on small size, break things on purpose, and scale slowly.

Algo trading carries a real risk of loss, including more than you expected on a bad day. EliteAlgo is analytical software and not an investment adviser. Nothing in this article is investment advice, a recommendation to trade, or a promise of any result. Test everything on paper and with small size first.

title: Managed Services Partners: A Buyer's Guide to Choosing the Right Fit
description:
Choosing a managed services partner means handing over responsibility for the systems your business runs on every day, so the wrong fit shows up fast in downtime, security gaps, and frustrated internal teams. The global managed services market is projected to grow from USD 437.3 billion in 2026 to USD 847.4 billion by 2033, according to Grand View Research, as organizations shift routine IT operations to specialized partners. This guide profiles ten leading managed services companies and breaks down exactly what to evaluate before signing a contract.

Executive Summary

Managed services shift the day-to-day burden of running IT, from monitoring and patching to security operations and cloud licensing, onto a specialized partner operating under defined service levels. Done well, this frees internal teams from constant firefighting and gives leadership predictable costs, measurable uptime, and a partner accountable for outcomes.

This guide profiles 10 leading managed services companies and outlines how to assess partners based on service level commitments, security maturity, delivery model, and reporting transparency. It also covers how managed IT, managed security, and cloud licensing services differ from adjacent models like staff augmentation and traditional break-fix support. The goal is a repeatable framework for choosing a partner who stabilizes your environment today and scales with you tomorrow.

Who Is This Guide For?

  • CIOs and CTOs evaluating whether to outsource IT operations, security monitoring, or cloud administration to free internal teams for strategic work.
  • VPs of IT Operations who need a partner capable of meeting defined SLAs across infrastructure, endpoints, and applications.
  • IT Directors and Managers comparing managed services providers against the cost and risk of building an equivalent capability in-house.
  • Security and Compliance Leads assessing a provider's ability to strengthen threat monitoring and maintain regulatory alignment.
  • Procurement and Sourcing Leads building a shortlist and needing a consistent framework to compare vendors on cost, coverage, and delivery model.

Each of these roles shares the same underlying goal: reducing operational risk while making IT spend more predictable.

What Is Managed Services & How Does It Work?

Managed services is an arrangement where an external provider takes ongoing, contractual responsibility for specific IT functions, such as infrastructure monitoring, endpoint management, cybersecurity operations, or cloud licensing, in exchange for a recurring fee tied to defined service levels. Organizations get continuous monitoring, proactive maintenance, and a documented escalation path when issues occur, so support no longer waits for something to break first. The provider typically supplies the tooling, staffing, and processes, while the client retains oversight through regular reporting and governance meetings. This model shifts IT from a reactive cost center to a managed, measurable function.

Common delivery models include:

  • Fully managed IT operations, where the provider owns end-to-end monitoring, patching, and helpdesk support for an environment.
  • Managed security services (MSSP/MDR), focused on continuous threat monitoring, detection, and incident response.
  • Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) and licensing management, where the partner manages Microsoft 365 or Azure subscriptions, cost optimization, and configuration.
  • Co-managed IT, where the provider supplements an existing internal IT team without replacing it.
  • Application and platform production support, where the provider maintains uptime and performance for one specific system, narrower in scope than whole-estate IT operations.

Managed Services vs. Staff Augmentation vs. Break-Fix IT Support

These three models are often confused, but they carry very different accountability structures. Staff augmentation adds individual contractors or engineers under the client's own management and processes, useful for filling a skills gap but offering no service-level guarantee. Break-fix support means paying for help only when something fails, with no proactive monitoring and unpredictable costs. Managed services sits apart from both by combining ongoing, proactive operation of an environment with contractual SLAs the provider is accountable for meeting.

The bottom line: if predictable costs and proactive coverage matter more than direct day-to-day control, managed services is the model built for that trade-off.

How To Choose the Best Managed Services Partner?

  1. Defined SLAs and escalation paths: Insist on specific, written commitments on response and resolution times; vague language like "prompt support" should be a red flag. Ask how missed SLAs are tracked and remediated.
  2. 24/7 monitoring and incident response coverage: Confirm whether monitoring is truly around-the-clock or only during business hours, and who actually responds when an alert fires at 2 a.m.
  3. Security maturity and compliance alignment: A partner should be able to show how its monitoring and incident response practices map to frameworks relevant to your industry, and this matters more every year as the managed security services market grows at a 16.4% CAGR, according to Research and Markets.
  4. Onboarding and discovery process: A rigorous onboarding phase that documents your environment, priorities, and risks reduces the chance of blind spots once the contract starts.
  5. Reporting transparency and governance cadence: The best partners provide regular, readable reporting and scheduled governance meetings that give real strategic context, beyond a raw support ticket log.
  6. Licensing and cloud cost optimization: For organizations running Microsoft 365 or Azure, ask whether the partner actively audits and rightsizes licensing on an ongoing basis, beyond simply processing renewals.
  7. Delivery model and cultural fit: Understand whether support is onshore, nearshore, offshore, or blended, and whether that model matches your internal team's working hours and communication style.
  8. SLA accountability: Ask what happens if the partner misses an SLA, and expect a specific, contractual answer with defined remedies.
  9. After-hours incident handling: Ask how the partner handles a security incident outside business hours, since the answer reveals whether "24/7 coverage" is real or marketing language.

The bottom line: judge the right managed services partner on documented SLAs and a proven incident track record.

Managed Services Companies Compared

Top 10 Managed Services Companies

1. Accenture

Accenture delivers managed IT, security, and cloud operations at global scale, spanning infrastructure monitoring, cybersecurity operations, and application support for large, complex environments. Its managed services practice sits alongside a broad consulting arm covering digital transformation, AI and data, and cybersecurity, letting clients pair operational support with strategic technology initiatives under one contract.

Why Consider Accenture? Accenture suits large, multinational organizations that need a single managed services partner capable of covering every region and technology stack they operate in, backed by consulting depth for longer-term modernization planning.
