Building a Legacy Modernization Partnership Built to Last

Legacy modernization and cloud replatforming is no longer a project a business can defer indefinitely. Every year a critical system stays on unsupported infrastructure, the licensing costs, security exposure, and talent risk compound, while the AI and automation initiatives the business wants to pursue stay blocked behind a data and application layer that cannot support them. The right partner depends less on brand size than on migration methodology, platform certifications, and a track record of specific, quantified outcomes rather than general claims. Global integrators bring scale and cross-industry breadth. Boutique and nearshore specialists bring focused delivery and faster team assembly. The right fit depends on the buyer's system complexity, industry, and risk tolerance.

From COTS Dependency to Cloud-Native, Without Stopping Operations

We have seen this play out firsthand. NCLH was locked into a rigid commercial booking system that took months to update and could not operate reliably at sea. Improving rebuilt the platform using Domain-Driven Design and Reactive Architecture, a cloud-native, microservices system that ships features in days and keeps running when connectivity is gone, with 40+ Improving engineers on the engagement and a multi-year active partnership still delivering today.

If your organization is evaluating a legacy modernization partner, explore Improving's legacy modernization and cloud replatforming services to discuss your specific environment.

Frequently Asked Questions

1) What is the difference between legacy modernization and a simple cloud migration?

A cloud migration typically moves an existing application to cloud infrastructure with minimal changes, often called a lift-and-shift. Legacy modernization goes further, restructuring the application's architecture, code, and deployment model to take advantage of cloud-native scalability, resilience, and integration capabilities rather than simply relocating the existing system.

2) How long does a typical legacy modernization project take?

Timelines vary widely by scope and system complexity, from a few months for a single application to over a year for enterprise-wide programs involving multiple interdependent systems. Buyers should ask each prospective partner for a realistic timeline to the first production cutover rather than the full program end date.

3) Should we rehost, replatform, refactor, or rebuild?

The right approach depends on how well-documented and business-critical the system is. Rehosting suits systems needing a fast, low-risk move to the cloud. Replatforming and refactoring suit systems central to the business that need real architectural improvement. A full rebuild is reserved for systems too undocumented or brittle to migrate incrementally.

4) What certifications should a legacy modernization partner have?

Look for certifications specific to the buyer's target cloud platform, such as Microsoft Solutions Partner designations, AWS Advanced Tier Partner status, or Google Cloud Partner status, rather than general cloud experience claims alone.

5) Is nearshore or offshore delivery a good fit for legacy modernization work?

Nearshore delivery can reduce time-zone and cultural-alignment friction compared to fully offshore delivery, while offshore delivery typically offers the deepest bench at scale. The right choice depends on how much real-time collaboration the migration planning phase requires.

title: When Smart Retries End, the Stripe Case File Begins
description:
Open a Stripe invoice that failed three weeks ago and read it the way an investigator reads a case file. The events are all there: the first attempt, the decline code, the automatic retries spaced across the following days, the final state. What the file does not contain is any sign that anyone read it while it was still open. The retries fired on schedule. The schedule ended. The case closed itself, which is not the same as anyone deciding it should.

This is the structural fact about billing on Stripe that feature comparisons miss. Stripe's native recovery is a schedule, and a schedule is a fine thing — tireless, consistent, informed by network-level timing data no single merchant could gather alone. But a schedule cannot read. It cannot notice that this invoice belongs to a subscriber whose card was replaced by their bank nine days ago, whose new credential is sitting in a wallet the vault has never met. It cannot tell the difference between a subscriber who has ignored four notices and one who never received a notice a human would recognise as theirs. Reading the case is a different job from running the clock, and the cases that close themselves are usually the ones nobody read.

A case file, worked properly, has a short anatomy. First, the cause, in the issuer's own compressed language: a timing problem, a credential problem, an identity check that never completed, or a stop instruction wearing a failure's clothes. Second, the subscriber's own history: have they failed before, what fixed it last time, when are they paid, have they ever answered a billing message. Third, the state of the credential: current, replaced, refreshed by the network's updater, or dead beyond argument. Fourth, the next action that follows from the first three facts — which is sometimes a retry, sometimes a message, sometimes an immediate and polite closing of the case. Four facts, most of them already sitting in the billing record, unused.

Teams whose native retries keep ending early — whose dashboards show effort and whose churn reports show losses anyway — do not usually have a retry problem. They have an assignment problem: the reading work belongs to nobody. It does not appear in anyone's job description, so it happens in the gaps, when a support agent happens to notice a familiar name in the failure list. The fix is not a louder schedule. It is a layer whose entire job is the case file: sorting by cause before sequencing, checking the credential before spending an attempt, writing the message a specific subscriber needs, and closing the unwinnable cases early so they stop taxing the winnable ones.

That layer is what stripe dunning for teams whose native retries keep ending early describes in working order: where Stripe's schedule legitimately stops, what a reading layer adds on top of it, and how to judge the addition by your own closed cases rather than by a vendor's blended recovery rate. Bring a month of finished invoices to it. The ones that recovered will mostly credit the schedule. The ones that did not are the syllabus.

There is a discipline point worth stating plainly, because it decides whether the second layer earns anything at all. A card update that lands on day twelve must wake the case on day twelve, not at the next weekly review. A cancellation must close the case the moment it happens, everywhere, so no sequence keeps writing to a person who already left. A hard decline must end the attempts and move the subscriber to a human conversation or a clean goodbye. These are not features to demo. They are the difference between a case file that is worked and one that is merely stored.

Stripe will keep doing its part well; the schedule is genuinely good at the job it was designed for. The open question for every team billing on it is whether anyone is doing the other job — the reading, the sorting, the timely human sentence — in the days after the schedule ends. That is the work Swipe Again was built to do: not a louder clock, but a reader for every case the clock leaves behind.

title: Python While Loop!
description:
** Tenali Raman and the Palace Guards**

Tenali Raman wishes to meet the King. Before reaching the royal court, he has to pass through many palace gates. A guard is posted at each gate.

Every guard demands a share of whatever reward Tenali Raman receives from the King. Tenali Raman agrees and promises:

"I will give you half of whatever reward I receive from the King."

All the guards allow him to enter. After meeting the King, Tenali Raman receives a reward of 1024 lashes.

The interesting question is: How many guards can receive half of the remaining reward until the value becomes less than 1?

##Step 1: Manual Calculation

First, we can calculate the result manually.

python

guard = 0
received_lashes = 1024

guard = 1
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2

guard = 2
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2

guard = 3
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2

guard = 4
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2

guard = 5
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2

guard = 6
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2


This approach helps us understand the calculation at a basic level.

However, writing the same code repeatedly is not efficient. Also, we do not know how many guards there are.


## Step 2: Identifying the Repeated Pattern

We can see that two operations are repeated:

1. Divide `received_lashes` by `2`.
2. Increase the guard count by `1`.

For example:

#python
guard = guard + 1
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2

Since the same operations are repeated, we can use a while loop.

Step 3: Using a While Loop 

guard = 0
received_lashes = 1024

while received_lashes >= 1:
    received_lashes = received_lashes / 2
    guard = guard + 1

print(received_lashes)
print(guard)
![ ](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/x3tse2qigyuiqyeo9xpc.png)

Output
0.5
11

Explanation

The value is divided by 2 repeatedly:
1024 → 512 → 256 → 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 → 0.5
The loop runs 11 times.

Therefore:

  • Number of guards = 11
  • Remaining value = 0.5

Step 4: What Happens if We Start with guard = 1?

guard = 1
received_lashes = 1024

while received_lashes >= 1:
received_lashes = received_lashes / 2
guard = guard + 1

print(received_lashes)
print(guard)

Output
0.5
12

This happens because we started counting the guards from 1 instead of 0.
is the correct and clearer approach.

Correct Answer:

Guards counted: 11
Final remaining value: 0.5

title: What You Can Self-Host on Oracle Cloud Free Tier (2026)
description:
Last updated: July 27, 2026

Status as of this writing: Oracle quietly cut the Always Free Ampere A1 allocation from 4 OCPUs / 24 GB RAM to 2 OCPUs / 12 GB RAM on June 15, 2026. No blog post, no email, an edited documentation page and nothing else. If you're reading an older guide (including some still-circulating 2026 posts) that budgets against 24 GB, check your own console before following its numbers. Everything below is sized for the current 2 OCPU / 12 GB reality, plus the two small AMD Micro instances that are unaffected by the change.

A free tier that quietly loses half its headroom is still worth building on. It means the sizing conversation matters more than it used to, and CPU, not RAM, ends up being the tighter constraint on two cores.

What Oracle gives you for free

The Always Free resources relevant to a self-hosting stack:

  • Ampere A1 Flex (ARM): 2 OCPUs and 12 GB RAM total, split across one to four instances as you choose. This is down from 4/24 as of June 2026.
  • AMD Micro instances: two of them, each 1/8 OCPU and 1 GB RAM. Small, but free on its own terms and separate from the Ampere allocation.
  • Block storage: 200 GB total, shared across your instances.
  • Outbound bandwidth: 10 TB per month.
  • Reclamation risk: Oracle's current published policy reclaims an Always Free compute instance if, over a 7-day period, its 95th-percentile CPU, network, and (for A1 shapes) memory utilization all stay under 20%. A stack that's serving real traffic rarely trips this; an instance you spun up once and forgot about is exactly what the policy targets.
  • Regional availability: Ampere A1 capacity is tightly constrained in popular regions. Frankfurt and Singapore tend to provision within minutes; US regions can sit at "out of host capacity" for hours or days. Budget for that when you're planning a migration deadline. What "2 OCPU" means on Ampere A1. On Oracle's x86 shapes, one OCPU is a full physical core with hyperthreading, billed as the equivalent of two vCPUs, so a workload can lean on simultaneous multithreading to squeeze more out of contended cores. Ampere A1 doesn't work that way: the Ampere Altra processor behind it has no hyperthreading, so one OCPU is exactly one physical core and one thread, nothing shared. Two OCPUs on this tier means two real cores and nothing more to borrow from. That's why CPU contention shows up immediately on this tier rather than being smoothed over by a hyperthreading scheduler the way it might be on an equivalent x86 box.

Two honest limitations before the stack: first, ARM64 isn't universal. Most actively maintained self-hosting images ship multi-arch builds, but some don't. Ghost's core image runs fine on ARM64; its optional ActivityPub and Traffic Analyzer add-ons are AMD64-only as of this writing, so check before assuming a feature works. Second, 2 shared OCPUs is a real ceiling once more than one service wants the CPU at the same time. RAM sizing matters, but CPU contention is what bites on this tier.

The stack: one Ampere instance, one AMD Micro

Put everything internet-facing on the single Ampere A1 instance, and use one AMD Micro purely as an external watchdog, something that checks whether the main box is reachable from outside its own failure domain. The second Micro is spare capacity for later.

Service Job Real RAM cost
Caddy TLS termination, reverse proxy Under 50 MB
Ghost + MySQL Blog/CMS (this article's own platform) Roughly 750 MB in production use
Vaultwarden Password manager, Bitwarden-compatible ~10 MB idle
Syncthing Peer-to-peer file sync, no central server needed 150–300 MB typical, spikes higher during large scans
Ollama (3B model, Q4) Lightweight local AI for personal use Roughly 3–4 GB
Uptime Kuma + Beszel agent Uptime checks plus host/container metrics 150–180 MB combined
OS + Docker overhead Everything else Roughly 500 MB

That totals somewhere around 5–6 GB of the 12 GB available, leaving real headroom rather than a stack that fits with nothing to spare. The number that won't show up in a RAM table is CPU: an AI response generating tokens, a MySQL query, and a Syncthing hash scan happening at the same moment are competing for two cores, and that's where a personal Oracle box slows down, not memory pressure.

Running Vaultwarden already and want the full hardening pass? Our dedicated Vaultwarden guide covers backup strategy, admin panel lockdown, and the HTTPS requirements the official clients enforce. Take a look at our complete Vaultwarden self-hosting guide.

If you're enjoying what you've read so far, we recommend Oracle Free Tier ARM Cutoff: What to Do Before Aug 18 as your next read.

Why each piece is on this list

Ghost runs the blog you're reading right now, so it earns a place as a real-world example rather than a theoretical pick. The official minimum is 1 GB of RAM; in production with MySQL running alongside it, a well-known self-hosting write-up clocks its own long-running instance at 214 MB for Ghost and 538 MB for MySQL, comfortably under 1 GB combined. Budget for 2 GB if you expect real traffic or plan to turn on the newsletter feature, which adds Mailgun and additional background jobs.

Vaultwarden is the easiest sizing decision in this list. It's a Rust reimplementation of the Bitwarden server, and our own Vaultwarden instance (the one covered in our dedicated guide) idles around 10 MB of RAM serving eight active users, less than a browser tab. There's no meaningful tradeoff here: it's compatible with every official Bitwarden client, and the resource cost rounds to zero next to everything else on this instance.

Syncthing covers file synchronization without needing a central server the way Nextcloud does; it syncs directly between your devices and this instance acts as one more always-on peer. That's a deliberate tradeoff for this tier: Nextcloud gets you a web UI, calendar and contacts sync, and a proper multi-user file store, all of which cost meaningfully more RAM than 12 GB comfortably supports alongside everything else here. If you have RAM to spare on a bigger box later, our productivity-stack guide covers Nextcloud, Immich, Jellyfin, and Paperless-ngx together. On this tier, Syncthing does the one job (getting files onto more than one device) for a fraction of the cost.

Idle RAM use is modest, but it's not flat: Syncthing keeps file indexes in memory, and both very large individual files and folders with hundreds of thousands of small files can push memory use well above idle during an initial scan, in some reported cases into the gigabytes on a large enough folder tree. If you're syncing a large photo library or a folder with a huge file count, set maxConcurrentWrites to 1 and sync folders sequentially rather than in parallel; both are documented tuning options that trade sync speed for a lower peak. On a 12 GB instance already running an AI model, that peak matters more than it would on a dedicated NAS.

Ollama is the one service constrained by this tier's hardware and not only its RAM budget. There's no GPU on Oracle's free tier at all, so inference runs on the Ampere A1's ARM cores. A quantized 7B model is technically possible (public benchmarks put a Q4_K_M 7B model around 5–8 tokens per second on a 4-OCPU A1 instance), but at 2 OCPUs, a smaller 3B model at Q4 quantization is the more honest fit for anything resembling a responsive personal assistant, and it leaves the other two-thirds of your CPU budget for Ghost and Syncthing to use.

Uptime Kuma paired with Beszel is the monitoring choice that matters most on a RAM-constrained tier. A combined Prometheus, Grafana, and node_exporter stack, the setup in our own monitoring guide, runs 800 MB or more at idle before it's watched a single request; Uptime Kuma plus a Beszel agent covers external uptime checks and internal host/container metrics for roughly 150–180 MB combined. On a 24 GB instance, or a paid box with RAM to spare, Prometheus and Grafana's deeper PromQL querying and alerting rules are worth the extra memory. On 12 GB shared with an AI model, Uptime Kuma is the choice between having monitoring at all and not.

Elevated

Outgrown the free tier, or tired of Oracle reclaiming idle instances? Elevated runs managed VPS hosting from SudoSecurity, with real support behind it.

See Elevated VPS plans →

The Layout

Oracle free tier architecture · SVG Oracle Free Tier: Two-Instance Layout Ampere A1 Flex -- 2 OCPU / 12 GB RAM (Always Free) Caddy (TLS, reverse proxy) -- <50 MB Ghost + MySQL -- ~750 MB Vaultwarden -- ~50 MB Syncthing -- ~150-300 MB Ollama, 3B model Q4 -- ~3-4 GB Uptime Kuma + Beszel agent -- ~150-180 MB OS + Docker overhead -- ~500 MB Remaining headroom: roughly 6-7 GB of 12 GB Shared constraint: 2 OCPU total AI inference, MySQL queries, and Syncthing hashing compete for the same 2 cores -- CPU, not RAM, is the real ceiling on this tier AMD Micro -- 1/8 OCPU 1 GB RAM (Always Free) External uptime check Watches the Ampere box from outside its own failure domain Internet-facing CPU-heaviest service

Everything internet-facing sits behind Caddy on the Ampere instance. The AMD Micro doesn't run any of the stack; its only job is checking the Ampere box from a separate failure domain, so a problem with the main instance doesn't also take down the thing telling you about the problem.

A resource-bounded Compose file

    volumes:
      - ghost_db:/var/lib/mysql
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 700m

      - stack_net

  vaultwarden:
    image: vaultwarden/server:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - ADMIN_TOKEN=${VAULTWARDEN_ADMIN_TOKEN}

      - vaultwarden_data:/data

    volumes:

    deploy:

    networks:
      - stack_net

  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ollama_data:/root/.ollama
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 4g
    networks:
      - stack_net

  uptime-kuma:
    image: louislam/uptime-kuma:2
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - uptime_kuma_data:/app/data
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 150m
    networks:
      - stack_net

networks:
  stack_net:
    external: true

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  ghost_content:
  ghost_db:
  vaultwarden_data:
  syncthing_data:
  ollama_data:
  uptime_kuma_data:

Caddy stays the only exposed port on the instance. Everything else, Ghost, Vaultwarden, Syncthing's sync protocol, Ollama's API, and the Uptime Kuma dashboard, sits behind it on the internal Docker network, reachable by subdomain rather than by port number.

Still with us? We think you'll like How to Self-Host a Discord Bot: Building and Running Your Own Bot 24/7 as your next read.

Three Important Performance Fixes

The Compose file above will run. These three changes are what keep it running well once Syncthing hits a big scan or Ollama is mid-response while someone's reading the blog.

Add swap, even on a "fast enough" instance. Ampere A1 has no swap configured by default, and 12 GB with several services and an AI model loaded leaves less margin than it looks like on paper. A memory spike that would slow things down with swap available becomes an OOM-killed container without it, and Docker's OOM killer doesn't pick politely; it can take out MySQL as easily as the process that caused the spike. A modest swap file (4 GB is reasonable against 12 GB of RAM) plus a low swappiness value gives the kernel somewhere to put cold pages before it starts killing containers:

sudo fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf

Swap on a boot volume backed by network-attached block storage is slower than swap on local NVMe, so this is a safety margin for spikes, not a substitute for the RAM budget in the table above. Don't plan to run the stack out of swap day to day.

Tune MySQL down from its defaults. Out of the box, MySQL 8's innodb_buffer_pool_size defaults to 128 MB, which is conservative enough to be safe here, but the rest of its default configuration still assumes more headroom than a 12 GB shared host has to give. A small my.cnf override keeps Ghost's database from creeping past the budget in the resource table:

[mysqld]
innodb_buffer_pool_size=256M
max_connections=50
table_open_cache=200
thread_cache_size=8

Mount this as /etc/mysql/conf.d/low-memory.cnf in the ghost-db service. It won't matter for a low-traffic personal blog, and it's the difference between MySQL sitting at 700 MB and MySQL slowly climbing toward whatever's left on the box during a traffic spike.

Cap Ollama's concurrency instead of leaving it to load-balance itself. Ollama's defaults assume it can decide how many models to keep loaded and how many requests to serve in parallel, which is a reasonable default on a dedicated GPU box and a bad one on a 2-core ARM instance sharing memory with everything else here. Setting explicit limits keeps one long generation from queuing up a second one and doubling memory use:

OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1
OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1
OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE=4

Add these as environment variables on the ollama service in the Compose file. OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1 means the second request waits instead of doubling memory use by running alongside the first; on a personal instance where you're the only user, that queueing is invisible in practice and the memory ceiling it buys is not.

Want the general self-hosting stack playbook, beyond the free-tier version? Our shared server-prep and reverse-proxy pattern applies whether you're on a free Ampere instance or a paid box. Check out the Mailcow Guide!

Lessons from running this

Check ARM64 support before you deploy, not after. Most of the images above have solid ARM builds. A few popular self-hosting tools still don't, or only support ARM in a beta tag, and finding that out mid-migration is worse than checking before the first docker compose up:

docker manifest inspect ghost:5 | grep -A2 '"architecture"'

Look for "architecture": "arm64" in the output alongside "amd64". If it's missing, the image is x86-only and won't run on the Ampere instance at all, or will run under slow QEMU emulation if Docker's configured to allow it, which defeats the point of a free ARM box.

Watch the reclamation window if traffic is thin. A personal blog with a handful of daily visitors, a password vault only you touch, and a sync client that mostly sits idle can plausibly dip under Oracle's 20% utilization thresholds across a full week. Real, if modest, usage from an actual project protects you here better than any artificial workaround, and running an artificial load generator specifically to dodge the reclamation policy sits in a gray area against Oracle's terms of service that isn't worth the risk for a free instance.

Pin your image tags once the stack is stable. latest is fine while you're getting things running; once Ghost, Vaultwarden, and Ollama are doing real work, an unannounced upstream change landing on a routine docker compose pull is a worse failure mode than a slightly stale version.

Back up the volumes that matter. Ghost's content volume and MySQL data, Vaultwarden's data directory, and Syncthing's config and index. Model weights for Ollama are re-downloadable and not worth backing up; Uptime Kuma's history is nice to keep but not critical if it's lost.

The Compose file, ready to adapt

The full stack above, Caddy, Ghost, Vaultwarden, Syncthing, Ollama, and Uptime Kuma, is a lot to retype by hand. Grab the complete docker-compose.yml and a matching .env template below, drop in your own domain and secrets, and you're running rather than transcribing.

Get the Compose file and.env template

Enter your email and we'll send the exact configuration from this article, including the resource limits, ready to paste onto a fresh Ampere A1 instance.

If you outgrow the 12 GB ceiling, that's a genuine milestone, not a failure of the free tier. It means the stack is doing enough real work that a small paid VPS or dedicated box starts paying for itself in time saved rather than money spent, and at that point the free tier has already done its job: it got you running for the cost of an afternoon instead of a monthly bill.

title: A three-state label queue where 100% reviewed and 0 labels can both be true
description:
Why one boolean is not enough

A common first draft for a local annotation or review queue adds a done boolean to every record. It becomes true when someone looks at the record and false before that. The problem appears at export time: the same field cannot say whether the record has a label. A record can be processed yet unlabelled, or unprocessed yet read downstream as finished. Separate two predicates first. reviewed means the record has been handled, including giving a label or explicitly abstaining. label_present means the record actually carries a label from the taxonomy.

local-label-queue is a small public tool I made; the source and samples are downloadable. It uses three states instead of two booleans: unlabelled, labelled, and abstained. The label field holds a taxonomy string only when status is labelled, and is null in the other two states. The tool has no done or has_label boolean field. An external system that defines done as reviewed makes labelled and abstained both true. One that defines done as label_present makes abstained and unlabelled both false. The three states keep the gap between the two predicates.

What the 12 synthetic records show

The bundled demo-annotations.jsonl contains 12 records: 2 labelled, 1 abstained, and 9 unlabelled. Every non-labelled row has label: null. Reviewed therefore counts 3, label_present counts 2, and the difference is the abstained row. Abstaining on every record gives a reviewed fraction of 1 while labelled stays 0. That shows abstention counts toward workflow progress but creates no label and implies nothing about label correctness. If a single boolean is defined as reviewed, it merges labelled with abstained. If it is defined as has_label, it merges abstained with unlabelled. Splitting the two questions keeps the legitimate state of 100% processed with zero labels from disappearing.

The two lines below fetch the public sample and count it. The result should match the description above.

curl -sL https://huggingface.co/spaces/WideChaos/local-label-queue/raw/d8068775077cd4149a39ec9a2c6cb0ab52045d54/demo-annotations.jsonl -o demo-annotations.jsonl
node --input-type=module -e 'const rows=(await import("node:fs")).readFileSync("demo-annotations.jsonl","utf8").trim().split("\n").map(JSON.parse);const c=rows.reduce((a,r)=>(a[r.status]=(a[r.status]||0)+1,a),{});console.log(c, rows.filter(r=>r.status!=="labelled"&&r.label!==null).length)'

The output should include { labelled: 2, abstained: 1, unlabelled: 9 }, with zero non-labelled rows whose label is not null. This checks state modeling and export fidelity. It does not check label correctness because the sample is original synthetic material, not human annotation or a gold standard.

This screenshot shows the public Space I deployed, displaying the same 12 synthetic records: 2 labelled, 1 abstained, and 9 unlabelled, with reviewed near 25% including the abstention. That share measures queue progress only; it says nothing about label correctness. The page also has no autosave.

revision and checkpoint serve different purposes

demo-checkpoint.json uses the same inventory and still shows 2/1/9, but its revision field is 7. revision counts changes, including undo operations. It is neither a processed count nor a labelled count. Reading it as completion progress creates false numbers.

The checkpoint is for resuming. The tool keeps decisions only in page memory; it has no autosave, browser storage, or cloud sync. Download the checkpoint explicitly before a refresh. On restore, it verifies the inventory hash and content hash, shows a preview, and replaces the current state explicitly rather than merging. JSONL export keeps every original group and text, not only labelled rows, so review all records before sharing the file with someone else.

SHA-256 is a recomputable consistency check. It detects a changed or truncated file but proves nothing about origin, label truth, or encryption, and it cannot stop someone from repacking a file after verification.

Author: Renchao Wu

title: Honest intermediate states for small web tools
description:
A spinner tells someone that the interface is busy. It does not, by itself, tell them whether a request was accepted, where work is happening, whether a usable result exists or when it is safe to try again.

Disclosure: I maintain the six projects referenced below. This article proposes interface copy and transition rules. It does not report changes shipped to these sites, user research or product acceptance tests. The linked pages supply published constraints; the example messages are design suggestions.

1. A result can be ready while copying is incomplete

Small Text Studio provides its note on what to do when Copy fails. The fallback is to select the displayed result and use the system copy command when the site's button cannot access the clipboard.

Those are two separate states: a result exists, and the clipboard operation did not complete. Replacing the result with a generic error would hide the useful part.

Suggested copy:

The result is still shown below. Try selecting it and using your system Copy command.

Do not show “copied” merely because a click handler ran. If success is unknown, keep the output available and describe the remaining action. Pasting into another application is a further handoff with its own behavior.

2. A guide date is not a checked game version

PokéSurvivor Hub provides its note separating announcement dates from the guide's update date. Both dates can be useful without identifying the game build on a particular device.

A broad “up to date” badge can collapse these different facts. Keep the date's role visible, and leave an unknown running version unknown.

Suggested copy:

Guide updated: [date]. Announcement dated: [date]. The running game version has not been checked in this view.

Fill those fields only from their respective sources. A newly edited reference page is not evidence that a player's session changed version.

3. Rejection needs an explanation, not a universal retry button

WatermarkPilot provides its note on rejected formats and keeping your originals. The photo page identifies format and provenance-related restrictions and warns that exports may not retain camera or color-profile metadata.

Suggested copy when an input is refused:

No export is available for this input. Check the format and metadata restrictions, and keep your original.

“Try again” does not explain whether the same input can succeed. Changing an extension or choosing a JPG/PNG is not a universal recovery guarantee: a supported format still has other eligibility conditions. Keep the refusal reason separate from a processing fault and retain the cautious “may not” wording about metadata.

4. A service job needs evidence for each stage

Sonify provides its note on queue load and when the file is offered. The page describes server-side work, timing that depends on the source and queue load, and a file being offered after verification finishes.

Suggested copy while there is no available result:

No download is available yet. Check the current processing stage.

Use a label such as “queued” only when the service actually reports that stage. A frontend timer cannot establish it. Do not promise cancellation of queued work from a page that makes no such promise.

Once a result is available, keep its deadline visible. The stated fifteen-minute window starts after completion, not before it or when the visitor opens the page. Access expiry and physical cleanup are different events; a disabled download alone does not prove physical erasure.

5. A local processing limit is not a server queue timeout

GifLoom provides its note that very complex jobs stop after 90 seconds. This describes a local processing limit. It is a different kind of event from waiting for a conversion service.

Suggested copy when processing has stopped and no usable result exists:

Processing stopped without a completed result. Keep the original and review the task settings before another attempt.

Only report a stop after the worker has actually stopped. Do not infer that another attempt will succeed immediately, or describe the event as a server cleanup problem. A page's local-processing declaration also does not prove the absence of every network request made by the website.

6. Clearing input and changing privacy choices can affect working state

Square Footage Calculator provides its note on what a reset or a privacy change clears. The page distinguishes entered measurements from calculated area and says withdrawing an active analytics choice refreshes the page and clears the current calculation.

Suggested copy before an action with that effect:

This action clears the current calculation. Copy or print any result you need first.

Keep the input, derived result and persistence rule separate. A displayed number is not a saved record. Likewise, unavailable controls should not look like a completed zero-area calculation. Show the actual unavailable state and a relevant next step instead of a plausible-looking result.

Use state labels as small factual claims

For each transition, ask three questions: what event has actually happened, what remains unresolved, and what action is currently available?

“Result displayed,” “copy incomplete,” “input refused,” “service still working,” “local job stopped” and “calculation cleared” describe different events. Give each one a specific message rather than routing all of them through the same success or error banner.

These remain design suggestions from the maintainer of the six linked projects. Testing an implemented transition needs its own observations and results.

title: Copiar una base NoSQL no es exportar JSON: lo que aprendimos haciendo backups de Firestore
description:
Autor: Carlos Jimenez Laura
Curso: Base de Datos II · Universidad Privada de Tacna
Actividad: Estrategias de copia de seguridad NoSQL, desarrollada junto con Arturo Cutipa Flores
En PostgreSQL ejecutas pg_dump y obtienes un archivo que recrea la base. En Firestore, con el plan gratuito, no existe un equivalente: la exportación administrada exige un plan de pago y un bucket de Cloud Storage. La idea obvia es leer todos los documentos y guardarlos como JSON, y esa copia parece correcta hasta que intentas restaurarla.
En este artículo cuento qué se pierde con esa idea y cómo lo resolvimos en StockSeguro, un inventario con copias automáticas, cifradas y comprobadas.

Enlaces del proyecto
• Aplicación: https://stockseguro-firestore.onrender.com
• Repositorio público: https://github.com/CRJL19/firestore-backups
• Video: https://youtu.be/56mY6DRLr8U

Figura 1. StockSeguro con el panel de copias de seguridad.

Las opciones que teníamos

Elegimos la copia lógica porque era lo posible con nuestro presupuesto, no porque sea la mejor en general. Para una base grande en producción, recomendaría la nativa.

Cuatro formas de perder datos sin enterarte

1. JSON no conoce los tipos de Firestore
Un documento nuestro tiene un Timestamp, un GeoPoint y una referencia a su proveedor. JSON.stringify los convierte en objetos corrientes, y al restaurar ya no son esos tipos. La referencia deja de ser una referencia y ninguna consulta por fecha vuelve a funcionar.

Por eso cada tipo especial se guarda con una etiqueta:

Y hay una decisión deliberada al final de esa función: un tipo desconocido lanza un error. Prefiero que falle la copia a que parezca correcta y le falten datos.

2. Las subcolecciones no vienen con su padre
Leer products no trae products/{id}/movements. Hay que recorrerlas. Y hay un caso peor: una subcolección puede colgar de un documento que ya no existe. Firestore lo llama documento fantasma, y un collection.get() no lo devuelve, así que sus hijos quedarían fuera.
listDocuments() sí los incluye:

Una de nuestras pruebas crea justo ese caso, borra todo, restaura y comprueba que el hijo volvió.

3. Una copia que tarda no es una foto
Si la app sigue escribiendo mientras copias, puedes guardar un producto de hace un minuto con los movimientos de ahora. Resolvimos esto leyendo los documentos dentro de una transacción de solo lectura, de modo que todo corresponde a un mismo instante:

4. Un borrado no deja rastro
La copia incremental lee lo que cambió según updatedAt, pero un documento borrado ya no tiene ese campo: simplemente deja de existir, y la consulta no puede verlo. Sin más, al restaurar reaparecerían productos eliminados.
Por eso la app deja una marca en la misma operación que borra:

La estrategia completa
• Copia completa cada 7 días, que corrige cualquier desviación acumulada.
• Copia incremental diaria, que gasta menos cuota porque lee menos documentos.
• Restauración selectiva: --only products/abc123 recupera un producto y sus movimientos sin tocar el resto.
• Cifrado AES-256-GCM, necesario porque los artifacts de un repositorio público se pueden descargar con cualquier cuenta de GitHub.
• Objetivo de pérdida (RPO): 24 horas. El panel de la app avisa si la última copia supera las 26.
Restaurar una incremental significa aplicar la cadena en orden: la completa y luego cada incremental. Dentro de cada copia, los borrados se aplican antes que los documentos, porque un documento presente en una copia existía al hacerla, aunque se hubiera borrado y creado de nuevo.

El problema que no se resuelve del todo
La copia incremental depende de un contrato: todo se escribe a través de la app, con updatedAt y sus marcas de borrado. Alguien que borre un documento desde la consola de Firebase lo rompe, y la incremental no se entera.
No pudimos evitarlo, pero sí detectarlo. Cada copia guarda los conteos reales del origen con consultas de agregación, que son baratas. Si al restaurar los números no coinciden, la verificación falla:
products: la copia dice 1 y la restauración tiene 2
Una prueba automática reproduce ese caso. La solución entonces es una copia completa. Queda un hueco que prefiero admitir: una modificación externa que no cambie los conteos solo se recoge en la siguiente completa.

Cómo se publica y se automatiza
El código está en un repositorio público de GitHub, y todo se ejecuta con GitHub Actions:
• Cada git push ejecuta las 39 pruebas contra el emulador de Firestore, construye la imagen Docker y despliega en Render, un proveedor público en la nube.
• Cada día, a las 03:00 hora de Perú, un workflow hace la copia, la restaura en un emulador y solo si coincide la guarda.
Las copias se hacen con una cuenta de servicio de solo lectura, y la base está en Firestore, sobre Google Cloud.

Resultados
En producción, con Firestore real, la primera copia completa dio esto:

Figura 2. Resumen de la copia verificada en GitHub Actions.

Después dejamos el workflow funcionando solo. Del 2 al 12 de noviembre se ejecutó todos los días y guardó 12 copias, todas verificadas antes de guardarse: 2 completas, la segunda creada automáticamente al cumplirse los 7 días, y 10 incrementales. Cada incremental cifrada pesa unos 650 bytes, frente a 1,8 KB de una completa.
El simulacro de desastre lo hicimos en el emulador local, con los mismos comandos que usa GitHub Actions: una copia completa, un cambio de stock y un borrado, una incremental, la base vaciada y la restauración de la cadena. Volvieron los 25 documentos esperados en 237 ms, con el stock actualizado y sin el producto eliminado. En producción, la restauración existe como un workflow manual, pero no la ejecutamos para esta demostración.
Un dato que me sorprendió: esa incremental, hecha segundos después de la completa, copió 26 registros frente a 27. No es un error. Cada incremental relee los últimos 5 minutos por seguridad, porque copiar de más es inofensivo y copiar de menos no lo es. El ahorro aparece cuando las copias están separadas por horas.

Limitaciones
• Dos ubicaciones, no tres. Hay datos en Firestore y copias en GitHub. La regla 3-2-1 pediría una tercera.
• Enteros y decimales. El SDK de JavaScript no distingue 1 de 1.0. Tampoco se conservan createTime ni updateTime, que asigna el servidor.
• Memoria. Cada copia se procesa completa en memoria, adecuado para miles de documentos, no para millones.
• La clave de cifrado. Si se pierde, las copias no sirven de nada, así que hay que guardarla también fuera de GitHub.

Qué me llevo
En una base relacional el esquema y la herramienta de volcado resuelven casi todo por ti. En NoSQL, el esquema vive en la aplicación, y por eso la estrategia de copia también: tuvimos que cambiar cómo borra la app para poder copiar bien.
Lo otro que me llevo es desconfiar de una copia hasta verla restaurada. Mi compañero Arturo cuenta en su artículo cómo automatizamos esa comprobación.

title: Count Rows, Not Errors: 7 Data Bugs I Reproduced
description:
To find out whether a write path loses data, count rows in the source of truth after a forced failure or a concurrent run; the error rate will not tell you. In seven bugs I reproduced over the past week, every call that lost or duplicated data returned success, and one independent count caught each bug.

This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. Each case ran on the real software (PostgreSQL 16.4, Kafka 4.4.0, Elasticsearch 7.17.29, Redis 8.10.2, SQLite 3.46.1); only the external payment and webhook providers were simulated. Each section ends with the check that caught the bug.

1. A Caught Exception Rolled Back the Row It Protected

A migration dual-writes in one Spring @Transactional method: insert into the legacy table, then into the new one inside a try/catch that counts failures and queues the id for repair. I left out the new table's December partition and recorded 20 events, 10 in December.

All 20 calls returned normally, and nothing was logged at WARN or ERROR. The legacy table, the source of truth, held 10 rows: PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction when one statement fails, so COMMIT silently rolled back (pgjdbc 42.7.8 and 42.2.5). None of the 10 queued ids existed in legacy, so repair had nothing to copy.

// as written: 20 calls OK, the legacy table keeps 10 of 20 rows
@Transactional
public void record(OrderEvent e) {
  legacyInsert(e);
  try { v2Insert(e); } catch (DataAccessException ex) { caught(e, ex); }
}
// fix: nested is a TransactionTemplate with PROPAGATION_NESTED (a savepoint)
@Transactional
public void recordNested(OrderEvent e) {
  legacyInsert(e);
  try { nested.executeWithoutResult(s -> v2Insert(e)); } catch (DataAccessException ex) { caught(e, ex); }
}

The savepoint kept all 20 legacy rows, as did autosave=always on the JDBC URL. 2,000 clean writes took 3,150/3,005 ms instead of 2,646/2,850.

Check: after a forced failure, count the legacy table, not the failure counter.

2. Exactly-Once Kafka Paid 20 of 40 Payouts Twice

One partition, 40 payouts, read_committed, one transaction per poll of 20. Nothing crashed. One provider call took 12 s, past max.poll.interval.ms (10 s), so a second consumer took the partition and restarted at offset 0. The first, still alive, paid the other 14 payouts of its batch after the handover; its CommitFailedException came about 8 s later.

With a fresh UUID as the idempotency key per attempt, 20 of 40 payouts were paid twice, in both runs and under KIP-848. Kafka looked perfect: committed offset 40, 40 output records. A key derived from the payout, "payout:" + payoutId, turned 60 provider calls into 40 transfers.

Check: count transfers per payout id at the provider.

3. A Conditional UPDATE Protected the Row, Not the Charge

Two checkouts of one order, 0 to 20 ms apart, each read pending, called the provider, then ran UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending'. The loser's UPDATE matched 0 rows after its charge went out: 100 of 100 orders were charged twice. Claiming before the call brought it to 0:

def claim(conn, oid):
    attempt = uuid.uuid4().hex
    cur = conn.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'charging', attempt_id = %s WHERE id = %s AND status = 'pending'", (attempt, oid))
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        return 'skip'
    provider(oid)
    cur = conn.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', updated_at = now() WHERE id = %s AND status = 'charging' AND attempt_id = %s", (oid, attempt))
    return 'paid' if cur.rowcount == 1 else 'lost'

In production, also pass attempt_id to the provider as its idempotency key; my fake took none.

Check: fire two checkouts 0 to 20 ms apart and count provider calls.

4. The Checkpoint Reached the Max and Still Skipped Events

A projector read WHERE global_seq > checkpoint on a BIGSERIAL column. The number is assigned at INSERT; the row becomes visible at COMMIT. If 101 commits before 100, the projector checkpoints 101 and never reads 100. With 8 concurrent writers the checkpoint reached max(global_seq) every run, yet 201 to 214 of 3,228 events were never projected. One writer missed 0.

Storing pg_current_xact_id() per event, reading only tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot()) and checkpointing on (tx_id, global_seq) missed 0 in 8 runs. The price: any open write transaction stalls the projection.

Check: after the drain, events must equal projected rows.

5. bulk.close() Returned Before the Last Bulks Landed

An Elasticsearch reindex fed a BulkProcessor (5,000 actions, 2 concurrent requests), called close(), then swapped the alias. close() is awaitClose(0, NANOSECONDS), so two bulks, 10,000 documents, were still in flight. Counts through the alias right after the swap: 45,676, 68,830 and 70,116 of 100,000 (the 1 s refresh hid the rest). failedItems stayed 0. awaitClose(60, SECONDS) plus a refresh gave 100,000 in 3 of 3 runs.

Check: swap only after awaitClose returns true and the new count equals the source count.

6. A Webhook Got a 200 and Was Processed Zero Times

The handler claimed the delivery key in Redis with SET NX PX 30000, then processed. Processing threw, the handler returned 500, and the claim stayed. The retry at t=5 s hit the claim and got a 200 for "in progress"; most providers stop on any 2xx. At t=31 s the claim had expired with no done marker: processed 0 times. Releasing the claim in the catch (random token, Lua compare-and-delete) let the 5 s retry process it once. Answer 409 for in-progress claims.

Check: make the handler throw once, replay 5 s later, count successful runs.

7. Eight SQLite Workers Committed 2,000 Times and Kept 250

Eight Python processes each added 1 to one row 250 times: read, update, commit. All 2,000 commits succeeded; the counter ended at 250 in six of six runs. Default sqlite3 opens the transaction at the UPDATE, after the read, and the 5 s busy timeout turned contention into waiting, not errors. BEGIN IMMEDIATE before the read gave 2,000. Full write-up here.

Check: N workers add 1 M times each; assert the result is N × M.

What I Test Now

Error rates count calls that failed; all seven bugs lived in calls that succeeded. Before I trust a write path:

  • Force one failure, then count the source of truth.
  • Count external side effects per business id.
  • Test with concurrent writers: the checkpoint gap was 0 with one writer, about 200 with eight.
  • Count before switching reads: alias, checkpoint, new table.
  • Replay a delivery after a failure; claims and dedupe keys break on the second attempt.

title: What Is Human-in-the-Loop AI? 15 Questions Answered
description:
Originally published on AgenticTrainers.com.

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) AI means trained people take part in training, checking or approving what an AI system does, instead of letting it run unattended. IBM describes it as an ongoing cycle of human and AI interaction and feedback. Done well, it is how companies get AI speed without AI-sized mistakes. Done badly, it is a person clicking “approve” 400 times an hour (an illustrative figure, not a measurement), which is theater.

Why Should You Listen to Me?

SuperStaff, founded in 2009, is now in its 18th year of business. I started in 2006 as an outsourced call center agent in technical services, so I have more than two decades of business experience, virtually all of it on the technical side of outsourcing, including scaling strategy and the human-capital side of scaling for tech firms, later AI firms, and some semiconductor firms. I joined SuperStaff as CEO in 2019. Today I am CEO of SuperStaff and Managing Director of Agentic Trainers, the AI division of SuperStaff, and I am pursuing graduate study in AI. SuperStaff is a Philippines-based outsourcing company that provides human-in-the-loop teams for AI companies and for businesses implementing AI.

We do not build the models. SuperStaff provides the human teams that help train, evaluate and supervise them. I also sell human oversight, so I have a conflict of interest, which is why every claim below has a source you can check.

Key Takeaways

  • HITL has three jobs: teach the AI, evaluate it, and oversee it in production.
  • Companies are legally responsible for what their AI says. A Canadian tribunal said so in 2024.
  • A human in the loop is not automatically safe. Automation bias is real, and a September 2025 report from the European Data Protection Supervisor warns against oversight that is only a procedural formality.
  • You do not need one human per agent. Pooled, risk-tiered supervision keeps the economics intact.
  • The vendor that sells the agent should not be the only one checking it.

1. What Is Human-in-the-Loop AI?

Human-in-the-loop AI is a setup in which people actively take part in running, supervising or making decisions about an AI system. IBM describes the “loop” as the ongoing cycle of interaction and feedback between humans and AI, with humans involved at some stage to support accuracy, safety, accountability and ethical decisions.

Translated from consultant to human: the AI does the work, and a trained person catches what it gets wrong, decides what it should not decide alone, and teaches it to do better next week.

2. How Does Human-in-the-Loop Work in Practice?

In practice it shows up in three places. In training, people label data and give feedback so the model learns, including reinforcement learning from human feedback. In evaluation, people check outputs and catch errors, bias and strange behavior. In oversight, people approve, override or pause what the system does in production.

The third one is the job most companies forget to staff. They budget for the model, they budget for the integration, and they assume “oversight” will happen by osmosis. It does not. Osmosis has a poor on-call record.

3. What Is the Difference Between Human-in-the-Loop, Human-on-the-Loop and Fully Automated AI?

These terms are used loosely across the industry, so treat the table below as common usage and not as a formal standard. What matters is where the human sits and what power they have.

Model What the human does Best for
Human-in-the-loop Reviews or approves individual outputs or decisions before they take effect High-stakes, irreversible or regulated work
Human-on-the-loop Monitors the system and steps in when needed, often via sampling and alerts High-volume work where most cases are routine
Fully automated Sets the rules, then lets the system run without live review Low-risk, reversible, well-tested tasks

Most real deployments mix all three, depending on risk. Our approach is to sample the routine, review the risky, and require approval for anything you cannot undo.

4. Why Do AI Agents Need Human Supervision?

Because they are confidently wrong in ways that are hard to predict, and some of the evidence is now measured instead of anecdotal.

They can be bypassed

The UK AI Security Institute reported in its Frontier AI Trends Report that its team found universal jailbreaks in every system it tested. Safeguards are improving, though: in one comparison of two leading models released six months apart, in biological misuse testing, the newer one took about 40 times more expert effort to break.

They can behave differently when watched

In joint work published September 17, 2025, OpenAI and Apollo Research reported that models increasingly show awareness of being evaluated, that this awareness can itself reduce scheming without real alignment, and that some test results may therefore not carry over to real use.

Benchmarks are not enough

Researchers at FDA’s device center, in a research paper that is not FDA policy, write that "human evaluation offers the most clinically relevant assessment," and that current evidence suggests automated evaluators may complement, rather than replace, human evaluation.

AI does not get tired, bored or sick. It also does not get embarrassed, which is the one thing that keeps most of us from confidently inventing a refund policy.

5. Who Is Legally Responsible When an AI Gets It Wrong?

The company that deployed it. In February 2024, a British Columbia tribunal ruled in Moffatt v. Air Canada that the airline was responsible for wrong bereavement-fare information its website chatbot gave a customer. Air Canada argued that the chatbot was "a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions," and the tribunal rejected that. It held that the chatbot was part of the airline's website and that the airline owed a duty of care to make sure the information was accurate. The award was about $650 CAD plus interest and fees.

“The bot did it” is not a defense you want to test with your own legal team. A caution: this was a Canadian tribunal decision, not binding everywhere. But it shows how regulators and courts are inclined to think about it.

6. Does the Law Require Human Oversight of AI?

In some cases, yes. The EU AI Act's Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so that people can understand them, monitor them for anomalies, stay aware of automation bias, interpret and override outputs, and stop the system safely.

In the United States, there is no single federal law that requires it across the board. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, published January 2023) is voluntary. Its four functions are Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. NIST describes it as intended for voluntary use and says a revision is underway under the White House AI Action Plan, so check the current version. Because it is voluntary, no regulator requires it by name, but auditors and customers may treat alignment with it as useful evidence. This is general information, not legal advice. Ask your counsel which rules apply to you.

7. Does Having a Human in the Loop Actually Make AI Safe?

Not by itself. This is the part vendors skip, and it is the part that matters most.

The European Data Protection Supervisor published a report in September 2025 on human oversight of automated decision-making. Its message is that putting a person into the process does not, by itself, make that process safe or accountable, and that oversight only counts as meaningful when it actually improves decisions instead of becoming “a merely procedural formality, or symbolic gesture” (EDPS TechDispatch 2/2025). It describes automation bias, where operators accept system recommendations without enough scrutiny, and cites a 2023 study in Radiology (Yala et al.) in which 27 radiologists reviewed mammograms with AI suggestions and were significantly less accurate when the AI was wrong.

A human in the loop is a necessary condition for accountability. It is not a sufficient one. The quality of the oversight is what matters.

8. What Is Automation Bias, and Why Does It Matter?

Automation bias is the tendency to accept an automated system's recommendation without enough scrutiny. It matters because it can make human review worse than no review at all: the human adds the appearance of accountability without the substance.

Counter it by planting known-error test items in the workflow, tracking whether reviewers catch them, keeping checkpoints meaningful, rotating reviewers, and watching review quality over time. A supervisor who approves 400 items an hour, which works out to nine seconds each, is not supervising.

How many planted errors do you need to test a human reviewer?

For a 95% confidence that a reviewer catches at least 95% of errors, plant 59 known errors and make sure they miss none. This borrows the success-run theorem from quality engineering, where the zero-failure sample size is n = ln(1 - C) / ln(R), with C the confidence and R the reliability you want to demonstrate (Quality Systems Compliance). Here C = 0.95 and R = 0.95, so n = ln(0.05) / ln(0.95) = 58.4, which rounds up to 59. If you would settle for 90% and 90%, it is ln(0.1) / ln(0.9) = 21.9, so 22.

The practical protocol, which you can set up in an afternoon: write 59 realistic errors for one queue, mix them into normal volume without telling reviewers which are planted, and log whether each was caught. One miss means you cannot claim the 95/95 result, and that is useful information, not a failure of the exercise. Run it per queue, because a reviewer who is sharp on invoices may be asleep on contracts.

Two honest limits. The math assumes your planted errors resemble real ones and are independent, which is the hard part. And a catch rate on planted errors measures attention, not judgment on subtle real cases. I am applying a standard sampling result to a new use, so treat this as my rule of thumb, not an industry standard.

Is nine seconds per item a real review?

Almost never. Four hundred approvals an hour is nine seconds each (3,600 divided by 400). In the hypothetical staffing model in Section 9, a high-risk item gets six minutes of review, which is 40 times longer. The gap is the whole story.

I use a simple check I call the Time Floor Test, which is my rule of thumb and not an industry standard. For each queue, have a competent reviewer do ten items slowly, with the source open, and note the median time. Then look at the median decision time in your logs. If real reviewers are deciding in under a third of that time, treat their approvals as clicks, not checks, until planted errors (B1) prove otherwise. Fast is not always wrong, since experienced people really do get quicker. That is the strongest counterargument, and it is why the test only flags a queue for a closer look; it does not convict anyone.

This matters because the evidence on automation bias says experience and instructions do not remove it. A time floor does not fix attention, but it tells you where to look.

9. How Many Humans Do You Need to Supervise AI Agents?

Fewer than you fear, if you design it right. One supervisor per agent would erase the savings and annoy everyone. The model we use is pooled, risk-tiered supervision.

Illustrative example, not a client result. Here is a hypothetical staffing model so you can see the arithmetic and swap in your own numbers. Every number in this example is hypothetical. None comes from a client.

The formula: supervisors needed = (daily review minutes x (1 + overhead)) / (productive minutes per supervisor x utilization), rounded up. Daily review minutes = for each risk tier, items in the tier x share reviewed x minutes per review.

Hypothetical inputs: 2,000 AI-handled items a day. Risk mix: 10% high risk (every item reviewed, 6 minutes each), 30% medium (20% sampled, 3 minutes each), 60% low (2% sampled, 2 minutes each). Overhead for escalations, calibration and planted test items: 15%. Each supervisor has 390 productive minutes a day (6.5 hours) and works at 75% utilization.

The arithmetic, all hypothetical:

  • High: 200 items x 6 minutes = 1,200 minutes.
  • Medium: 600 items x 0.20 sampled x 3 minutes = 360 minutes.
  • Low: 1,200 items x 0.02 sampled x 2 minutes = 48 minutes.
  • Total 1,608 minutes, plus 15% overhead = 1,849 minutes.
  • Capacity per supervisor: 390 x 0.75 = 292.5 minutes.
  • 1,849 / 292.5 = 6.3, so 7 supervisors.

For comparison, a fully human baseline in the same hypothetical: 10 minutes per item and 85% utilization. 2,000 x 10 = 20,000 minutes, divided by 390 x 0.85 = 331.5, gives 60.3, so 61 reviewers. Seven supervisors against 61 reviewers is a headcount ratio of about 11%. That is headcount only. It ignores pay differences, AI running costs and tooling, so it is not a cost figure.

Notice how sensitive the answer is. Change the hypothetical risk mix to 20% high, 30% medium and 50% low and the same arithmetic gives 2,800 minutes, 3,220 with overhead, and 11.0, which rounds up to 12 supervisors. Drop utilization to 60% with the original mix and you need 8. That is why I say pooled supervision should be measured, not promised.

10. When Should a Human Review AI Output, and When Can It Run Alone?

Use risk, not mood. A workable rule of thumb:

Risk level Examples Supervision
Low and reversible Drafting internal summaries, tagging, routine lookups Automated tests and spot-check sampling
Medium Customer-facing replies, data entry that feeds reports Sampling plus review of low-confidence outputs
High or irreversible Payments, deletions, medical or legal outputs, regulatory filings Human approval before action

The “irreversible” row is not theoretical. According to the founder’s public account, reported by Euronews in April 2026, an AI coding agent deleted his company’s production database and, he said, its backups in about nine seconds. Euronews did not independently verify the account. A confirmation step before destructive commands is cheaper than a post-mortem.

11. Does Human Oversight Cancel Out the Cost Savings of AI?

Not if you do it right, and the alternative is not free either.

Gartner predicts that "over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls". Fortune’s report on an MIT NANDA study says about 5% of enterprise AI pilots reach rapid revenue acceleration, with a “learning gap” as the main cause. It also says purchased tools and partnerships succeed about 67% of the time, and that internal builds succeed about one-third as often. The study has drawn criticism: one critique notes that it discloses little about its methods, cites 52 interviews, and reports its 5% figure for custom enterprise tools only. Treat those numbers as directional.

In May 2025, Klarna's CEO told Bloomberg, as Entrepreneur reported, that chatbots were cheaper but gave lower-quality service, and the company began hiring human agents again. The company had earlier claimed its AI did the work of 700 agents; those claims were company statements, not independently verified.

Oversight is a cost. Unsupervised deployment is a bigger one that arrives later with interest.

12. What Goes Wrong When There Is No Human in the Loop?

  • Wrong answers with legal consequences. Air Canada, above.
  • Quality collapse. The Klarna reversal, above.
  • Data and access failures. IBM's 2025 breach report found that 13% of organizations reported breaches of AI models or applications, and that 97% of those organizations lacked AI access controls (IBM, July 30, 2025).
  • Silent errors at scale. Healthcare authorizations approved that should not have been, and denied that should not have been.

For a longer tour of these failures, see our piece on the 12 AI launches that backfired in public.

13. Should the AI Vendor Supervise Its Own Agents?

Some of it, yes. Gartner predicts guardian agents, meaning AI that reviews and restricts other AI, will capture at least 10 to 15% of the agentic AI market by 2030, partly because humans cannot watch agents at machine speed. Automated monitoring at scale makes sense.

But the party that builds the agent should not be the only party grading it. History is not kind to self-certification, and the research above shows models may behave differently under test. Automate the first line of defense. Never automate the last one. We wrote a whole piece on this: Who Guards the Guardrails?

14. Which Industries Need Human-in-the-Loop AI Most?

Anywhere a mistake is expensive, regulated or hard to reverse.

Healthcare is the obvious one. Prior authorization adds its own pain: the American Medical Association's physician survey found physicians and their staff together spend about 13 hours a week on it for a single physician, and 61% of physicians feared payers' use of unregulated AI was increasing denials.

Insurance, pharmaceuticals, finance, legal, logistics and any business that handles personal data belong on the same list. If a regulator, a patient or a judge could ever ask “who checked this?”, you want an answer.

15. How Do I Start With Human-in-the-Loop AI?

Start small, with one workflow. A sane first pilot looks like this:

  1. Pick one high-volume workflow. Rules-based, clear inputs and outputs, measurable results.
  2. Define the risk tiers. What can run alone, what needs sampling, what needs approval.
  3. Set escalation rules in writing. Who gets called, how fast, and who can stop the system.
  4. Choose supervisors who know the work. Train them on your standards, and give them time and authority to disagree.
  5. Measure from day one. Error rates, exceptions, turnaround, customer satisfaction, cost.
  6. Review weekly, expand monthly. Grow only when the numbers earn it.

If you want help, book a discovery call with Agentic Trainers. If you would rather do it yourself, steal the list above.

AI makes the work faster. Supervision makes the work right. You are allowed to want both.

Frequently Asked Questions About Human-in-the-Loop AI

What does HITL stand for?

HITL stands for human-in-the-loop, meaning people take part in training, checking or approving the work of an AI system.

Is human-in-the-loop required by law?

For some high-risk systems in the EU, yes, under Article 14 of the AI Act. In the US there is no single federal requirement, though frameworks like NIST's are widely used. Ask your counsel which rules apply to you.

Does human oversight slow AI down?

It adds some review time, but risk-tiered supervision keeps most work automated and puts people only where they matter.

Can one person supervise many AI agents?

Yes, depending on the risk mix. In the hypothetical model in Section 9 (an illustration, not a client result), about 7 supervisors cover volume that would otherwise take about 61 reviewers, and the answer shifts to 12 supervisors if the share of high-risk items doubles.

What is automation bias?

Automation bias is the tendency to accept an automated system's recommendation without enough scrutiny, which can make human review less effective.

Do I still need humans if I use guardian agents?

Yes. Automated monitors help at scale, but consequential and irreversible decisions need accountable people.

How many errors should I plant to test my human reviewers?

For 95% confidence that reviewers catch at least 95% of errors, plant 59 realistic errors and require zero misses. The figure comes from the success-run formula n = ln(1 - C) / ln(R). For 90% confidence and 90% reliability, 22 is enough. Run it per queue, and treat it as a rule of thumb.

How many supervisors does a team of AI agents need?

It depends on the risk mix. In a hypothetical model (not a client result), 2,000 items a day with 10% high risk needs about 7 supervisors, and doubling the high-risk share raises that to 12. The formula is in Section 9, so you can test your own numbers.

Written by Matt Narciso with AI-assisted research and drafting. Every fact and source was reviewed by a human editor.

Sources

  • EDPS TechDispatch 2/2025: Human oversight of automated decision-making, European Data Protection Supervisor, September 23, 2025 and EDPS publishes report on human oversight of automated decision-making, Simmons & Simmons

  • Gartner predicts guardian agents will capture 10 to 15% of the agentic AI market by 2030, June 11, 2025
