Disclaimer: This article is commentary and general information, not legal, compliance or financial advice. Statistics and rulings are drawn from the cited sources, several of which are secondary summaries; verify primary sources before relying on them. My company sells human oversight services, which is a conflict of interest I have disclosed above. The staffing model in this article is a hypothetical illustration, not a client result, and does not guarantee similar outcomes.

title: What to learn free before you pay for MERN stack training in Nepal
description:
You can learn the first part of the MERN stack for free: JavaScript, how HTTP works, a small Node.js server and basic SQL. Pay for MERN stack training only when you can do those four things, so the paid hours go to the parts that need a mentor.

MERN means MongoDB, Express, React and Node.js. Three of the four are JavaScript, and the free material for them is good. Here is the order we would follow, and how to tell when you are ready.

What does MERN stack training in Nepal teach?

A MERN course teaches you to build a whole web app in JavaScript. React draws the screen in the browser. Node.js and Express run the server and the API. MongoDB stores the data.

The only difference from PERN is the database. PERN swaps MongoDB for PostgreSQL. We compare the two in MERN stack vs PERN stack for web development training in Nepal.

Step 1: JavaScript, until you can read your own errors

Start with plain JavaScript, not React. Every later step is JavaScript, so a weak start makes everything after it slow.

The Odin Project is free and open source. Its Full Stack JavaScript path has a JavaScript course with 29 lessons and 12 projects. Do the projects, not only the lessons.

You are done with this step when an error message no longer scares you. Read the stack trace, find the line, fix it. That skill matters more than any framework.

Step 2: How HTTP works, in one evening

Every backend job is about requests and responses. The browser sends a request. The server sends back a status code, headers and a body.

Read MDN's "Overview of HTTP" guide once. Then open a terminal and run curl -i https://example.com. The -i shows the status line and headers above the page. Now 200, 404 and Content-Type stop being words and become things you have seen.

Step 3: A Node.js server with no framework

Before Express, write a server with Node.js alone. The official Introduction to Node.js page has one that is about ten lines long. It uses the built-in node:http module.

Save it as server.js and run node server.js. Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 and you see "Hello World". Then change res.statusCode to 404 and run curl -i against it again.

This shows you what Express does for you later. Express is a layer on top of this same idea. Our own course writes this kind of server in Week 3, before it touches Express in Week 4.

Step 4: Learn SQL, even though the M is MongoDB

This is the step most MERN learners skip, and we think that is a mistake. Learn basic SQL next to MongoDB.

Nepal job posts show why. A merojob post for an intern MERN stack developer, from July 2024, listed "Relational Database" in its required skills. A full stack React and Node.js post from July 2025 asked for "PostgreSQL (or MongoDB experience)" and the "ability to design and query relational schemas".

Mid-sized companies in Nepal often start with a written test at their office. It asks SQL questions on joins and normalisation, which means splitting data into clean tables.

The free PostgreSQL tutorial is the official one. Work through "Joins Between Tables" and "Aggregate Functions" in chapter 2. That is enough for a start.

How do you know you are ready to pay for MERN training?

You are ready when you can do all of these without a video open:

  • Write a function that uses map and filter on an array of objects.
  • Explain the difference between a 404 and a 500 response.
  • Run the Node.js server above and change what it sends back.
  • Write a SQL query that joins two tables and counts rows with GROUP BY.

If you can do these, a course will move faster for you. If you cannot yet, keep going free for a few more weeks. Paying early means paying for lessons you could have done free.

What is worth paying for?

Pay for the parts that are hard to check alone. The first is API design, with checks on every input. Then login, passwords and tokens done safely. Then database design, indexes and transactions. Last, putting an app online and keeping it running.

Free courses cover these too. What they cannot give is a person who reads your code and tells you what is wrong with it.

Saarathi Academy in Old Baneshwor, Kathmandu teaches the server half of this in its Backend Engineering course. It is 10 weeks of Node.js, TypeScript, Express, NestJS, PostgreSQL and MongoDB. It does not teach React. Batches have up to 10 students in the classroom, and the mentors still do the job they teach. Your first deploy is in Week 5, on your own subdomain of the academy's batch server.

What to do tonight

Copy the ten-line server from the Node.js page, run it, and break it on purpose. Change the port, change the status code, and read every error you get.

When you want to see the full week-by-week plan, read the Backend Engineering course page and the syllabus.

title: How we cut our homepage from 4 MB to 179 KB and reached Lighthouse 100
description:
Two PNG images made up almost all of quantumines.com's 4 MB homepage. Serving them as AVIF and WebP at the size each screen needs cut the page to 179 KB and the mobile Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) from about 17 seconds to 1.8 seconds. Self-hosted fonts with size-matched fallbacks, two colour fixes and an accessible-name fix took the remaining Lighthouse scores to 100. We made all of these changes on 10 November 2026 in one commit. This write-up lists each one, with the code, so another small team can repeat it in an afternoon.

Where did the 4 MB come from?

The network list in Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools answered that quickly. The homepage loaded a 2.0 MB PNG for the hero sculpture and a 2.1 MB PNG for the product artwork, both exported straight from a design tool at full quality. Everything else on the page, HTML, CSS, JavaScript and icons, was small. A 1.6 MB logo PNG was also referenced from our structured data, though not displayed.

On a phone over a throttled mobile connection, which is what Lighthouse simulates, two megabytes take many seconds to arrive. And because the hero is the largest thing on screen, it is the element LCP measures: until it finishes, the page counts as not loaded.

quantumines.com homepage before and after (Lighthouse mobile, 10 November 2026)

Measure Before After
Total page weight about 4 MB 179 KB
Largest Contentful Paint (mobile) about 17 s 1.8 s
Accessibility score 96 100
All four Lighthouse categories not all 100 100 / 100 / 100 / 100
Cumulative Layout Shift not recorded 0

Step 1: serve images as AVIF and WebP, at the right size

We exported each large image three times (480, 768 and 1,024 pixels wide for the hero) in AVIF and in WebP, and let the browser pick with <picture>, srcset and sizes. The 1,024-pixel hero dropped from 2.0 MB as PNG to 44 KB as AVIF; a phone downloads the 480-pixel AVIF, which is 12.5 KB.

<picture>
  <source type="image/avif"
    srcset="assets/hero-480.avif 480w, assets/hero-768.avif 768w, assets/hero-1024.avif 1024w"
    sizes="(max-width: 760px) 100vw, 55vw">
  <source type="image/webp"
    srcset="assets/hero-480.webp 480w, assets/hero-768.webp 768w, assets/hero-1024.webp 1024w"
    sizes="(max-width: 760px) 100vw, 55vw">
  <img id="hero-image" src="assets/hero-1024.webp"
    alt="Sculpture of mint metal, glass and textured stone"
    width="1024" height="1280" fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

Three details matter. The width and height attributes let the browser reserve the space before the image arrives, so nothing jumps. fetchpriority="high" tells it to fetch the LCP image before other images. And the hero is never lazy-loaded: lazy loading the largest image on screen delays exactly the thing LCP measures. The product artwork, further down the page, got the same AVIF and WebP treatment at 768 and 1,536 pixels.

The 1.6 MB logo in our Organization schema was replaced with a 512-pixel PNG of 137 KB. Search engines don't need more than that, and it no longer turns up in audits.

Step 2: self-host the fonts and stop the text from jumping

The site used Manrope and DM Sans from Google Fonts. That meant a render-blocking stylesheet request to another domain, then the font files from a third. We downloaded the variable versions of both (they are under the SIL Open Font License), serve them as WOFF2 from our own domain and preload them:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/manrope-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/dm-sans-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

With font-display: swap, text appears at once in a fallback font and switches when the web font arrives. The switch can move text, because Arial is wider or taller than the real font. So we defined fallback faces measured against Arial, with size-adjust and the ascent and descent overrides, and listed them right after the real font:

@font-face {
  font-family: 'Manrope Fallback';
  src: local('Arial'), local('Liberation Sans'), local('Helvetica');
  size-adjust: 94.9%;
  ascent-override: 112.4%;
  descent-override: 31.6%;
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}
--display: 'Manrope', 'Manrope Fallback', sans-serif;

Together with the image dimensions, this is why Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.

Step 3: fix the last accessibility points

Accessibility was at 96. Lighthouse flagged two things. Some muted text in the light theme was below the 4.5:1 contrast ratio that WCAG requires for normal text, so we darkened those colours until each passed. And the mobile menu button's accessible name didn't match its visible label "Menu", which confuses people who use voice control: they say what they see. Making the name match the label fixed it. Both changes took minutes; finding them is what the audit is for.

Step 4: cache by file type

Our Node server sets Cache-Control from the file extension. Fonts never change under the same name, so browsers may keep them for a year. Images can be kept for a week and refreshed in the background. HTML, CSS and JavaScript are checked again after an hour, so a deploy shows up quickly:

ext === '.woff2' ? 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable'
: /^(\.avif|\.webp|\.png|\.jpe?g|\.svg|\.ico)$/.test(ext)
  ? 'public, max-age=604800, stale-while-revalidate=86400'
  : 'public, max-age=3600'

Step 5: make the next page feel instant

Two newer browser features cost a few lines each. Speculation Rules tell Chrome to prefetch a same-site page when the visitor hovers over its link, so the click usually lands on a page that is already downloaded. We exclude anything with side effects or private data, such as log-in, the app, admin pages and the API:

<script type="speculationrules">
{"prefetch":[{"source":"document","where":{"and":[
  {"href_matches":"/*"},
  {"not":{"href_matches":["/login","/app/*","/admin/*","/api/*","/logout"]}}
]},"eagerness":"moderate"}]}
</script>

Cross-document view transitions add a short cross-fade between pages with one CSS rule, turned off for people who ask their system for reduced motion:

@view-transition { navigation: auto; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  @view-transition { navigation: none; }
}

Browsers that don't support either feature ignore them, so there is no downside for anyone.

How do we keep it at 100?

Scores drift as pages are added. Every time the site is rebuilt, we run Lighthouse on the homepage, the newest post and one product page, and fix anything below 95 before it goes live. New images must be AVIF or WebP with width, height and srcset. Each page's preview image for social media is generated at build time, so nobody uploads a multi-megabyte PNG by hand. The same discipline carried over to adding WebMCP for AI agents: the site still scores 100 in all four categories with it.

What would we tell another small team?

  • Open the network list before touching code. On most small sites one or two images are most of the weight.
  • Fix the LCP image first: modern format, right size, fetchpriority="high", never lazy.
  • Give every image width and height, and give web fonts a size-matched fallback. That is most of CLS.
  • Treat accessibility warnings as bugs. They are usually quick to fix and they affect real people.
  • Re-run the audit on every build, not once a quarter.

Frequently asked questions

Is AVIF supported in all browsers?

AVIF works in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari. The <picture> element falls back to WebP and then to the <img> source, so older browsers still get an image.

What is a good Largest Contentful Paint?

Google's Core Web Vitals treat an LCP of 2.5 seconds or less as good, measured at the 75th percentile of real page loads. quantumines.com's homepage measures 1.8 seconds in Lighthouse's mobile test.

Does a Lighthouse score of 100 guarantee good Core Web Vitals?

No. Lighthouse is a lab test on one simulated device. Core Web Vitals in Search Console come from real visitors' browsers. A high lab score makes good field data likely, but the field data is what Google uses.

Quantumines is a technology and product studio in Lahore, Pakistan, founded by Muhammad Ali Raza (Ali Arbi). We build websites and web apps for clients with the same standards; see our services.

Originally published on quantumines.com.

title: Spring Boot MCP Server Security: 2026-07-28 Spec Guide
description:
To secure a Spring Boot MCP server under the 2026-07-28 spec, treat it as an OAuth 2.1 resource server: keep the endpoint stateless, validate the JWT signature, issuer and audience, authorize each tool by scope, and demand step-up authentication for payment tools. On the login-server side, Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) replace Dynamic Client Registration.

I previously covered exposing a Java backend as an MCP server with Spring AI, which dealt with getting tools in front of an agent. Here the question is different: what changes once that agent can reach a payment API, and what the 2026-07-28 revision of the protocol means for whoever carries the pager for the server.

The authorization half of this is not news. The spec has framed MCP servers as OAuth resource servers since the 2025-06 revision. What the new revision changes is operational: it removes the session handshake and the open-registration fallback, the two things that made a remote MCP server painful to run behind a normal load balancer and a normal identity provider. If you have built PSD2 APIs, a lot carries over directly. Strong customer authentication step-up becomes an acr/auth_time challenge (RFC 9470). TPP consent scopes become tool scopes. The "which TPP is this?" question becomes the CIMD client ID. The mapping is almost one-to-one, and I use it below.

The plain-language version

If OAuth and MCP vocabulary is new to you, this section is the short glossary. Otherwise skip to the architecture.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI assistant ask another system "what can you do?" and get back a list of tools, for example "look up a payment" or "create a refund", which it can then call.

OAuth lets an application act for a user without ever seeing the user's password, the mechanism behind every "Sign in with Google" button. It involves a client (here, the AI application), an authorization server (the login system that hands out access tokens), and a resource server (the system that holds the data and inspects those tokens). Your MCP server is the resource server.

An access token is usually a JWT: a signed blob of claims saying who the user is, which scopes (named permissions such as payments:read) were granted, and which service the token was issued for. That last claim is the audience, and it is the one people forget. A token issued for the billing service must bounce off the payments service.

Two problems drove the 2026-07-28 changes.

Memory. Older remote MCP servers started a session: the client sent an initialize call, received a session ID, and every follow-up request had to land on the replica that remembered it. In practice that meant sticky sessions on the load balancer, and a user whose pod got rescheduled lost their conversation. The new revision drops the initialize handshake and the session ID, so each request is self-contained and any replica can serve it.

Introductions. Before an authorization server can show a consent screen, it has to know who the app is. The old fallback was Dynamic Client Registration (DCR, RFC 7591), where any app registers itself unattended. Across thousands of AI apps and one shared login server, that produces thousands of records nobody can vouch for. The revision deprecates DCR in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD): the app publishes a JSON file on its own domain and uses that file's URL as its client ID. The login server fetches it, reads the name and redirect addresses, and applies its own trust policy. No record exists on the login server until a human or a policy says yes.

What the changelog confirms, and what it leaves open

I read the official 2026-07-28 changelog on modelcontextprotocol.io and compared it with the project's release post. These points are firm:

  • The initialize handshake and session ID are gone from the core, which is the basis for the stateless transport.
  • DCR (RFC 7591) is deprecated in favour of CIMD (the changelog tracks this as PR #2858). It keeps working for backward compatibility and is slated for removal in a later version.
  • Issuer validation per RFC 9207 is added, so a client can tell whether an authorization response really came from the server it called.

Two things are not firm. The changelog gives no removal date for DCR, so I plan around "deprecated, not removed" rather than any calendar. And a few secondary write-ups list a registration priority order (pre-registered credentials, then CIMD, then DCR, then ask the user); I have not seen that order stated in the spec text, so I do not rely on it.

On Spring AI, my working position is this. Spring Security gives you everything in the OAuth half for free: resource-server JWT validation, SCOPE_ authorities, method security. Everything MCP-specific that I describe below as custom (protected resource metadata, audience binding, step-up guard, CIMD resolution) is code I wrote and run myself, because I did not find a Spring AI starter that provides it for me. If a newer release of the starters covers one of them, delete mine; the Spring AI changelog for your exact version settles that in a few minutes. For a broader view of what Java teams get when building agents on top of this, see my notes on Spring AI's new Agents project.

Architecture

Four moves. The client calls the MCP endpoint with no token and gets a 401 pointing at the server's protected resource metadata (RFC 9728), a JSON document naming the authorization server. The client then goes to that authorization server and presents its CIMD URL as its client ID. It returns with a token. Finally it calls whichever replica the load balancer picks, and that replica validates the token locally. Nothing on any instance remembers the client, which is what keeps scaling out dull, the quality I want most from infrastructure.

Step 1: a stateless endpoint behind a plain load balancer

At AirAsia we served around 130 million requests a day, and the rule that paid off most was refusing instance-local state. I have watched sticky sessions mask a capacity problem: one node runs hot while its neighbours idle, the dashboards average it out, and nobody notices until that node is replaced during a deploy and its users all get logged out at once. A stateless MCP endpoint lets you keep the same rule.

The security configuration is where statelessness shows up. No session, no CSRF cookie ritual, only bearer tokens:

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
class McpSecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain mcp(HttpSecurity http,
                            McpAuthEntryPoint entryPoint) throws Exception {
        http
            .securityMatcher("/mcp/**", "/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource")
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())          // bearer-only, no cookies
            .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                .requestMatchers("/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o
                .jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())
                .authenticationEntryPoint(entryPoint));
        return http.build();
    }
}

Turning CSRF off is defensible only because this path takes nothing but an Authorization header and never reads cookies. The day someone adds cookie auth to the same prefix, switch it back on.

Whether the MCP transport itself is stateless is a separate question from whether your security chain is. Spring AI has had a stateless Streamable HTTP server mode for a while, and that is where I would start. I could not match it against the final 2026-07-28 wire format from the release notes alone, so I test instead of trusting: run two replicas, alternate requests between them in an integration test, and treat any failure as hidden state. It is a ten-line test and it has caught session leaks for me more than once.

Step 2: publish protected resource metadata

The client needs to learn where to log in. RFC 9728 defines a well-known document for exactly that. This is custom code, and it is small:

@RestController
class ProtectedResourceMetadataController {

    private final McpSecurityProperties props;

    ProtectedResourceMetadataController(McpSecurityProperties props) {
        this.props = props;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource",
                produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    Map<String, Object> metadata() {
        return Map.of(
            "resource", props.resourceUri(),                 // e.g. https://mcp.example.com/mcp
            "authorization_servers", List.of(props.issuer()),
            "scopes_supported", List.of("payments:read", "payments:write", "mandates:read"),
            "bearer_methods_supported", List.of("header"));
    }
}

resource does double duty. It is also the identifier your tokens must carry as their audience, which the next step enforces.

Step 3: JWT validation with audience binding

This is the step where I have seen real damage. A resource server that checks signature and issuer but not audience will happily accept a token that was minted for a different service in the same realm. In open banking we called it a confused-deputy bug and it failed pen-tests. The typical way it arrives: a team reuses one realm for the internal admin API and the new agent-facing API, the agent's token is scoped fine, and nobody notices that the admin API never asked who the token was for. With MCP the exposure is wider, because the premise is that many different agents hold tokens.

Spring Security verifies signature and expiry by default. Audience binding takes a few lines of your own, expressed as a proper OAuth2TokenValidator so failures come back as standard invalid_token errors:

@Bean
JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(McpSecurityProperties props) {
    NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = NimbusJwtDecoder
        .withIssuerLocation(props.issuer())
        .build();

    OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> issuer =
        JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(props.issuer());

    OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> audience = token ->
        token.getAudience().contains(props.resourceUri())
            ? OAuth2TokenValidatorResult.success()
            : OAuth2TokenValidatorResult.failure(new OAuth2Error(
                "invalid_token", "Token audience does not include this MCP server", null));

    decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(issuer, audience));
    return decoder;
}

Two details matter. Compare against the exact resource URI, never a prefix match, or a hostile https://mcp.example.com.evil.net slips through. And the decoder downloads the issuer's signing keys and caches them, so a request does not trigger a network call and replicas share nothing. The flip side is key rotation: when the identity provider rolls its keys, a decoder holding a stale cache rejects good tokens until it refetches, so alert on a burst of signature failures right after a rotation rather than assuming the attack is real.

Step 4: where CIMD fits, and who does the work

This confuses people, so to be explicit: your MCP server never touches CIMD documents. The authorization server does. The client hands the authorization server a client ID that is an HTTPS URL, such as https://agent.example.org/client.json. The authorization server downloads it, checks that the client_id field inside equals the URL it came from, validates the redirect URIs, and shows the user a consent screen carrying the app's name.

For a Java team the work divides like this:

  • If you operate your own authorization server on Spring Authorization Server, expect to write a small RegisteredClientRepository that turns a URL-shaped client ID into a client by fetching and validating the document. I have not seen URL-form client IDs supported out of the box, so I plan on writing it.
  • If you use Keycloak, Entra, Auth0 or Okta, ask the vendor for their CIMD date in writing. Some will trail the spec by months, which is why you keep DCR on, behind rate limits, until they ship.
  • Whoever does the fetching, treat that fetch as hostile. The URL comes from a stranger, so block private address ranges, cap the body size, set short timeouts and refuse redirects. The SSRF mitigation post covers this class of bug, and CIMD is a textbook instance: a login server that downloads arbitrary URLs for people it has never met.

This is the validation I would put in front of that fetch:

record ClientMetadata(String clientId, String clientName, List<String> redirectUris) {}

class CimdResolver {

    private final HttpClient http = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER)
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .build();

    ClientMetadata resolve(URI clientIdUrl) throws Exception {
        if (!"https".equals(clientIdUrl.getScheme()) || clientIdUrl.getPath().isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("client_id must be an https URL with a path");
        }
        // Resolve and reject loopback, link-local and private ranges before connecting.
        SsrfGuard.assertPublicAddress(clientIdUrl.getHost());

        var request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(clientIdUrl)
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3)).GET().build();
        var response = http.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofByteArray());

        if (response.statusCode() != 200 || response.body().length > 16_384) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Metadata fetch rejected");
        }
        ClientMetadata meta = mapper.readValue(response.body(), ClientMetadata.class);
        if (!meta.clientId().equals(clientIdUrl.toString())) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("client_id in document does not match its URL");
        }
        return meta;
    }
}

The client_id equality check carries the whole design. Without it anyone can host a document claiming to be somebody else's app.

On the benefits over DCR: a DCR identity is a random string your server minted, which tells you nothing. A CIMD identity is a domain somebody controls, so you can rate-limit it, block it and put it in a report. For compliance work this is the real gain. I can finally answer an auditor's "who is this client?" with a name and a domain, not "whoever hit the registration endpoint".

Step 5: scope-based tool authorization

Authentication says who; authorization says what. In a tool protocol the natural unit is the tool. Enforce at the method that implements the tool, not at the HTTP path, because MCP routes every call through one endpoint and a path rule cannot distinguish get_payment from create_refund.

@Service
class PaymentTools {

    @Tool(description = "Look up a payment by its id")
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_payments:read')")
    PaymentView getPayment(String paymentId) {
        return payments.find(paymentId);
    }

    @Tool(description = "Create a refund for a settled payment")
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_payments:write')")
    RefundReceipt createRefund(String paymentId, BigDecimal amount) {
        stepUp.require(StepUpLevel.STRONG);   // see next section
        return refunds.create(paymentId, amount);
    }
}

Spring Security converts the token's scope claim into SCOPE_ authorities by default, so the annotation works without extra mapping; no string comparisons in the tool body. The trap is that @Tool discovery and Spring's method-security proxy must apply to the same bean. If the proxy is missing, @PreAuthorize is silently ignored and every call is allowed. So write a test that sends a token without payments:write and expects a refusal. That one test is the only thing standing between you and an open refund tool.

A second layer is easy to miss: the tool list itself. Filter it per caller, so an agent with read-only scope never even sees createRefund. A manipulated model has less to attempt, and agent behaviour gets more predictable.

Step 6: step-up authorization for high-risk tools

A scope granted at login is a blunt instrument. The user said yes to "payments" an hour ago in a chat about something else. Should an instruction injected through a web page be able to move money on the strength of that old yes? No.

Step-up authorization means the server asks for fresher or stronger proof before dangerous actions. The mechanism is a challenge: the server responds with a WWW-Authenticate header, and the client goes back to the authorization server for a token with the extra scope or a stronger authentication level. For "you lack the permission" the code is insufficient_scope, with the scope named in the header. For "log in again, more strongly", RFC 9470 defines the insufficient_user_authentication error built on the acr (authentication context class) and auth_time claims.

In PSD2 terms, this is SCA dynamic linking applied to an agent: the bank re-checks the customer at the moment of the risky act, not at session start. The mandate flows I built for recurring payments (see the Commercial VRP post) work the same way. An agent calling a payment tool is just a new caller of an old rule.

This part is custom code; I have not seen Spring AI ship a step-up primitive, so here is the guard I use:

@Component
class StepUpGuard {

    private static final Duration MAX_AGE = Duration.ofMinutes(5);

    void require(StepUpLevel level) {
        Jwt jwt = (Jwt) SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
            .getAuthentication().getPrincipal();

        boolean strongEnough = level.acceptedAcr().contains(jwt.getClaimAsString("acr"));
        Instant authTime = Instant.ofEpochSecond(
            ((Number) jwt.getClaim("auth_time")).longValue());
        boolean fresh = authTime.isAfter(Instant.now().minus(MAX_AGE));

        if (!strongEnough || !fresh) {
            throw new StepUpRequiredException(level, MAX_AGE);
        }
    }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
class StepUpAdvice {

    @ExceptionHandler(StepUpRequiredException.class)
    ResponseEntity<Void> challenge(StepUpRequiredException ex) {
        String header = "Bearer error=\"insufficient_user_authentication\","
            + " error_description=\"A stronger or more recent login is required\","
            + " acr_values=\"" + ex.level().primaryAcr() + "\","
            + " max_age=\"" + ex.maxAge().toSeconds() + "\","
            + " resource_metadata=\"" + props.metadataUrl() + "\"";
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)
            .header(HttpHeaders.WWW_AUTHENTICATE, header).build();
    }
}

Use whichever error code your authorization server and chosen MCP client both understand, and test the full round trip, since client behaviour on challenges is the least uniform part of this ecosystem. Keep the five-minute window in configuration so risk and compliance can change it without a deploy.

One rule I do not bend: the model never decides whether step-up happened. The guard reads the verified token and nothing the agent says.

Step 7: audit logging you can hand to a regulator

Each tool call by an agent is a decision taken on someone's behalf, and in a regulated setting somebody will later ask you to reconstruct it. DORA-style expectations boil down to: which user, which client, which tool, which arguments, what happened. The evidence side is in the DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code post.

An aspect over the tool methods keeps this out of business code:

@Aspect
@Component
class ToolAuditAspect {

    private static final Logger audit = LoggerFactory.getLogger("mcp.audit");

    @Around("@annotation(org.springframework.ai.tool.annotation.Tool)")
    Object record(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        Jwt jwt = (Jwt) SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
            .getAuthentication().getPrincipal();
        String tool = pjp.getSignature().getName();
        long started = System.nanoTime();
        String outcome = "ALLOWED";
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();
        } catch (AccessDeniedException | StepUpRequiredException e) {
            outcome = "DENIED";
            throw e;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            outcome = "FAILED";
            throw e;
        } finally {
            audit.info("tool={} sub={} client={} acr={} outcome={} ms={} trace={}",
                tool, jwt.getSubject(), jwt.getClaimAsString("client_id"),
                jwt.getClaimAsString("acr"), outcome,
                (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000,
                Span.current().getSpanContext().getTraceId());
        }
    }
}

Log the tool name and identifiers, but hash or mask arguments that contain account numbers. The trace ID links the audit line to the distributed trace, which is how a strange agent run actually gets debugged (see distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry). Ship the audit logger to an append-only store apart from application logs. For metrics and alerting on agent behaviour, see observability and guardrails for agentic AI backends.

Failure modes I test before launch

Authorization code is easy to get subtly wrong, so these negative tests run in CI:

  1. A validly signed token for a different audience is rejected with 401.
  2. A payments:read token calling createRefund is rejected with 403.
  3. A token with the right scope but a stale auth_time gets the step-up challenge, not a success.
  4. A CIMD document whose client_id differs from its URL is refused.
  5. A CIMD URL pointing at 169.254.169.254 or a private range is refused before any connection opens.
  6. Two replicas, alternating requests, behave identically.

If one of these cannot be written as a test, some state is still hiding in the design.

What I would do on Monday

For a team that already has an MCP server built the earlier Spring AI way:

  • Week one: add audience validation and the protected resource metadata. Both are small, they close the most dangerous hole, and they do not depend on any vendor catching up.
  • Week two: move tool authorization onto scopes with @PreAuthorize and filter the tool list per caller.
  • Week three: add the step-up guard to the two or three tools that move money or change a mandate, plus the audit aspect.
  • In parallel: ask your identity team for their CIMD plan with dates, and keep DCR enabled behind rate limits until it lands. DCR is deprecated, not removed, so there is a clock but no emergency.
  • Last: compare your Spring AI release notes with this list and delete whichever custom code the starters now cover.

None of this is exotic. I spent years on PSD2 consent flows and mandate APIs, and an AI agent is the newest kind of third-party provider: faster and less predictable than a human. The old controls (audience, scope, freshness, audit) still hold, and the 2026-07-28 spec lets you apply them without fighting the transport. More of my payments and AI backend work is under projects, with my background at experience.

If you are planning this migration and want a second pair of eyes on the threat model, send me the architecture through the contact section. If staffing is the open question, my remote developer hiring guide covers hiring a senior Java engineer for EU and ASEAN teams.

FAQ

What is an MCP server?

An MCP server is a program that offers a list of actions and data to an AI assistant through the Model Context Protocol. The assistant asks what the server can do, then calls those actions on a user's behalf.

How do I secure a Spring Boot MCP server?

Treat it as an OAuth 2.1 resource server. Use Spring Security's JWT resource-server support, add an audience validator, guard each tool with a @PreAuthorize scope, require step-up authentication on payment tools, and audit-log every tool call.

What is a Client ID Metadata Document?

A JSON file an AI application hosts at an HTTPS address, with that address serving as its client ID. The authorization server reads the file to learn the app's name and redirect addresses rather than requiring registration first.

Why is Dynamic Client Registration being replaced?

Open registration produces anonymous client records that are hard to trust or clean up. A metadata document ties the client to a domain you can check. DCR is deprecated, not yet removed.

Related Articles

  • Exposing a Java backend as an MCP server with Spring AI
  • Commercial VRP and UKPI Wave 1: mandates and recurring payments in Spring Boot
  • Observability guardrails for agentic AI backends in Spring Boot

title: CryptoPulse: Build a Real-Time Cryptocurrency Intelligence Platform on AWS
description:
What if your application could monitor Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other cryptocurrencies, detect unusual market activity, analyze historical trends, and send alerts automatically?

Cryptocurrency markets never sleep.

Bitcoin can experience a sudden price movement while Ethereum trading volume increases. Another cryptocurrency might attract unusual market activity within minutes.

For traders, analysts, and crypto enthusiasts, monitoring multiple exchanges and dashboards manually can quickly become overwhelming.

The challenge isn't simply collecting cryptocurrency prices. It's identifying meaningful market movements, preserving historical data, and notifying users when configured conditions are met.

That's the idea behind CryptoPulse – Cryptocurrency Intelligence, a serverless market-monitoring and analytics platform built using AWS.

In this project, we'll explore how to connect real-time market data ingestion, event processing, historical storage, SQL analytics, and automated notifications using AWS services.

1. What Are We Building?

CryptoPulse is designed to monitor cryptocurrency market activity and generate useful insights.

Its core capabilities include:

  • Real-time monitoring of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other supported cryptocurrencies.
  • Detection of configurable price fluctuations.
  • Identification of unusual trading-volume spikes.
  • Historical market data storage and analysis.
  • Automated email notifications when configured conditions are triggered.

For example, imagine these events:

  • Bitcoin moves more than 2% within 15 minutes.
  • Ethereum trading volume becomes three times its recent average.
  • Solana experiences an unusual price fluctuation.
  • A supported cryptocurrency experiences a sudden increase in trading activity.

CryptoPulse can evaluate these conditions and notify subscribed users.

The platform is designed for market monitoring and analytics, not guaranteed price prediction or automated trading.

2. AWS Architecture

The architecture follows an event-driven, serverless design.

       Cryptocurrency Exchange APIs
                    |
                    v
          Market Data Producer
        (Python / WebSocket Client)
                    |
                    v
          Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
                    |
                    v
               AWS Lambda
             Data Processing
                    |
          +---------+----------+
          |                    |
          v                    v
    Amazon S3             Amazon DynamoDB
    Raw Market Data       Latest Market State
          |                    |
          v                    v
    AWS Glue Catalog     DynamoDB Streams
          |                    |
          v                    v
    Amazon Athena         AWS Lambda
          |                    |
          v                    v
    S3 Query Results      Amazon SNS
                               |
                               v
                       Email Notifications

The main components are:

AWS Service Responsibility
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Real-time market data ingestion
AWS Lambda Event processing and market calculations
Amazon S3 Raw and processed historical data
Amazon DynamoDB Latest market state and alert records
DynamoDB Streams Trigger downstream alert processing
Amazon SNS Notification delivery
AWS Glue Data Catalog Dataset metadata and schemas
Amazon Athena Historical SQL analytics

The diagram represents the logical architecture. Each integration needs appropriate AWS configuration, IAM permissions, and event source mappings.

3. Step One: Collect Cryptocurrency Market Data

The first component is a market data producer.

We can build it using Python and connect it to supported cryptocurrency exchange APIs.

For continuous updates, WebSocket connections are useful because they allow the producer to receive market events without repeatedly polling an endpoint.

For example, CryptoPulse could monitor:

BTCUSDT
ETHUSDT
SOLUSDT
BNBUSDT
XRPUSDT

The exact feed depends on the metrics required.

Ticker streams can provide price and rolling market statistics. Individual trade streams can provide transaction-level information for custom volume calculations.

Before publishing events, normalize exchange-specific messages into a common structure.

Example event:

{
  "exchange": "example-exchange",
  "symbol": "BTCUSDT",
  "event_type": "ticker",
  "price": 68500.25,
  "volume_24h": 12500.75,
  "price_change_percent_24h": 2.85,
  "event_timestamp": "2026-11-13T09:30:00Z"
}

These values are illustrative, not live market data.

A consistent event format makes downstream processing easier, especially when supporting multiple exchanges.

4. Step Two: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

Once the producer collects market events, it publishes them to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.

Kinesis acts as the central ingestion layer.

Instead of connecting the producer directly to every processing component, events are published to a stream and consumed by downstream applications.

A useful partition key is the trading symbol:

BTCUSDT
ETHUSDT
SOLUSDT

This helps keep related records associated with the same shard and supports ordering within that shard.

Kinesis allows ingestion and processing capacity to be managed independently.

For production, consider:

  • Stream capacity and throughput.
  • Data retention requirements.
  • Consumer lag and iterator age.
  • Throttling and failed writes.
  • Producer retry and reconnection logic.

Exchange WebSocket connections can be interrupted, so the producer should be designed to reconnect and recover gracefully.

5. Step Three: AWS Lambda for Market Processing

AWS Lambda can consume Kinesis records through an event source mapping.

The processing function validates, transforms, and analyzes incoming market events.

Its responsibilities include:

  1. Validating incoming records.
  2. Normalizing exchange-specific fields.
  3. Calculating price changes and volume indicators.
  4. Updating the latest market state.
  5. Storing raw and processed information.

For example, a simple percentage price-change calculation looks like this:

def calculate_price_change(previous_price, current_price):
    if previous_price <= 0:
        return 0

    return (
        (current_price - previous_price)
        / previous_price
    ) * 100

Suppose Bitcoin's previous reference price was $65,000 and the current price is $66,300.

((66,300 - 65,000) / 65,000) × 100

= 2%

CryptoPulse can evaluate this result against a configured threshold.

One important detail: the system must define its monitoring window. A 2% change over one minute is different from a 2% change over 24 hours.

Use event timestamps and appropriate reference prices when calculating indicators.

6. Step Four: Amazon S3 for Historical Data

Real-time processing is useful, but historical information is equally important.

Amazon S3 provides durable storage for raw and processed market data.

A possible bucket structure:

cryptopulse-market-data/

    raw/
        exchange=binance/
            symbol=BTCUSDT/
                year=2026/
                    month=11/
                        day=13/

    processed/
        exchange=binance/
            symbol=BTCUSDT/
                year=2026/
                    month=11/
                        day=13/

    athena-results/

The raw zone preserves original or minimally transformed events. This is useful for auditing and reprocessing.

The processed zone contains normalized records for analytical queries.

Partitioning by exchange, symbol, and date can help reduce the amount of data scanned by Athena.

For larger datasets, consider Apache Parquet. Its columnar format can improve analytical query efficiency and help reduce scan costs.

Keep raw data, processed data, and Athena query results in separate prefixes.

7. Step Five: Amazon DynamoDB for Latest Market State

S3 is suitable for historical storage, but retrieving the latest price should not require scanning historical files.

Amazon DynamoDB can maintain the latest market state for each trading pair.

For example:

{
  "PK": "ASSET#BTCUSDT",
  "SK": "LATEST",
  "price": 66300.00,
  "volume_24h": 14500.50,
  "price_change_24h": 2.0,
  "updated_at": "2026-11-13T09:30:00Z"
}

The values are illustrative.

DynamoDB can also store alert records, including:

  • Asset symbol.
  • Alert type.
  • Observed value.
  • Configured threshold.
  • Event timestamp.
  • Notification status.

This makes it easier for the application to retrieve recent market information and alert history.

For production, design partition and sort keys around access patterns. Use conditional writes or other concurrency controls when multiple processing attempts could update the same market state.

8. Step Six: Detect Price Fluctuations and Volume Spikes

This is where CryptoPulse becomes more than a data collection pipeline.

Price movement detection

Suppose a user wants an alert whenever Bitcoin moves more than 2% within 15 minutes.

An illustrative rule:

IF 15-minute price change >= +2%
THEN create an upward movement alert

A downward movement rule could be:

IF 15-minute price change <= -2%
THEN create a downward movement alert

Thresholds should be configurable according to user preferences.

Trading-volume spike detection

A sudden increase in trading volume can indicate unusual market activity.

CryptoPulse can compare recent volume with a historical baseline.

Volume Ratio =
Recent 5-minute volume
/
Average 5-minute volume over baseline period

An illustrative rule:

IF Volume Ratio >= 3
THEN create a volume spike alert

This means recent volume is at least three times the selected baseline.

The comparison should use equivalent time windows and account for missing or incomplete data.

Historical indicators

The platform can also calculate:

  • Moving averages.
  • Percentage price changes.
  • Rolling trading volume.
  • High and low prices over selected periods.
  • Volatility measures.

These indicators help users explore market behavior, but they do not guarantee future price movements.

9. Step Seven: DynamoDB Streams and Lambda for Alerts

The architecture uses DynamoDB as the trigger for a second Lambda function.

This can be implemented using DynamoDB Streams.

When a market-state or alert record changes, DynamoDB Streams makes that change available to a downstream consumer.

A configured Lambda event source mapping invokes the alert-processing function.

Market Processing Lambda
          |
          v
     DynamoDB Update
          |
          v
    DynamoDB Streams
          |
          v
      Alert Lambda
          |
          v
       Amazon SNS
          |
          v
    Email Notification

The alert Lambda checks whether the event represents a valid notification.

It should verify:

  • The threshold condition was satisfied.
  • The alert is relevant to the user.
  • The notification has not already been sent.
  • The event is not an outdated update.

Use an idempotency key to reduce duplicate notifications. It could include the asset, alert type, monitoring window, and threshold configuration.

A cooldown period can also prevent repeated alerts for the same continuing market condition.

10. Step Eight: Amazon SNS for Automatic Notifications

Once the alert Lambda confirms that a notification should be delivered, it can publish a message to Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS).

SNS supports notification delivery to configured subscribers, including email endpoints.

Example notification:

CryptoPulse Market Alert

Asset: BTCUSDT

Alert Type: Price Movement

Observed Change: +2.0%

Monitoring Window: 15 Minutes

Event Time: 09:30 UTC

Status: Threshold Triggered

This is an illustrative message.

Users can receive alerts about significant price movements, unusual volume spikes, or other configured market conditions.

SNS handles notification delivery. The application logic determines whether a market event deserves an alert.

11. Step Nine: AWS Glue and Amazon Athena for Historical Analytics

Real-time notifications tell users when something happens. Historical analytics help them understand market behavior over time.

AWS Glue Data Catalog maintains metadata about datasets stored in S3.

A Glue crawler can inspect supported data and infer table metadata. Alternatively, teams can define schemas explicitly.

Amazon Athena uses the Glue Data Catalog to discover tables and query the underlying S3 data using SQL.

This allows CryptoPulse to analyze historical cryptocurrency data without managing a separate database cluster for every analytical workload.

Query recent Bitcoin records 

SELECT
    event_timestamp,
    symbol,
    price,
    volume_24h
FROM cryptopulse_market_db.market_data
WHERE symbol = 'BTCUSDT'
  AND year = '2026'
  AND month = '11'
  AND day = '13'
ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC
LIMIT 100;

The table and partition names are examples and must match the actual dataset registered in Glue.

Find records with high reported volume 

SELECT
    symbol,
    event_timestamp,
    volume_24h
FROM cryptopulse_market_db.market_data
WHERE volume_24h > 10000
ORDER BY volume_24h DESC;

This query uses an illustrative absolute threshold. A proper volume-spike analysis should compare recent volume against a historical baseline.

Where are Athena results stored?

Athena writes query results to a configured S3 output location, for example:

s3://cryptopulse-market-data/athena-results/

Remember the different responsibilities:

  • S3 stores market datasets.
  • Glue Data Catalog stores metadata and table definitions.
  • Athena queries S3 datasets using SQL.
  • S3 stores Athena query output in the configured results location.

Glue does not automatically transform the market records. It provides metadata that helps analytical services understand the data.

12. Production Readiness: What Should We Consider?

A production market-monitoring platform must handle interruptions, duplicate events, delayed records, and sudden increases in market activity.

Some important engineering considerations include:

Data validation: Validate prices, volumes, timestamps, symbols, and event formats before processing.

Duplicate handling: Use exchange trade IDs or event identifiers where available. Make processing idempotent so retries do not double-count trades or create repeated alerts.

Event ordering: Events can arrive late or out of order. Use exchange timestamps and sequence identifiers where available instead of assuming arrival order represents event order.

Failure handling: Configure Kinesis/Lambda retry behavior, record-age limits, and an on-failure destination where appropriate. Monitor iterator age and processing errors.

Alert reliability: Store alert state and notification status. Use idempotency keys and cooldown periods.

Security: Apply least-privilege IAM roles, encrypt stored data, and use AWS Secrets Manager for exchange credentials when authenticated APIs are required.

Cost management: Monitor Kinesis capacity, Lambda execution, S3 storage, Glue activity, and Athena data scanned. Use partitioning and columnar formats to help control analytical costs.

13. Implementation Roadmap

CryptoPulse can be developed in manageable stages.

Phase 1: Market Data Ingestion

  • Select supported exchanges.
  • Build a Python producer.
  • Connect to WebSocket market streams.
  • Normalize incoming events.
  • Publish records to Kinesis Data Streams.

Phase 2: Real-Time Processing

  • Configure Kinesis-to-Lambda integration.
  • Validate and process records.
  • Calculate price and volume indicators.
  • Store raw and processed events in S3.
  • Update DynamoDB market state.

Phase 3: Alert Engine

  • Configure DynamoDB Streams.
  • Build the alert-processing Lambda.
  • Add configurable thresholds and cooldowns.
  • Integrate Amazon SNS.
  • Test duplicate-event handling.

Phase 4: Historical Analytics

  • Organize S3 datasets.
  • Create Glue database and table definitions.
  • Configure crawlers or explicit schemas.
  • Run historical SQL queries using Athena.
  • Store query results in a dedicated S3 prefix.

Phase 5: Production Hardening

  • Add monitoring and alarms.
  • Configure retries and failure handling.
  • Secure credentials and permissions.
  • Implement data retention policies.
  • Test recovery and load behavior.

14. Future Enhancements

Once the core pipeline is operational, CryptoPulse can evolve with additional capabilities.

  • Multi-exchange comparison: Compare the same trading pair across supported exchanges.
  • Custom user alerts: Allow users to configure assets, thresholds, and monitoring windows.
  • Market dashboards: Display current prices, historical movements, volume trends, and alerts.
  • Advanced analytics: Add volatility analysis, moving averages, and other indicators.
  • Machine learning experiments: Explore anomaly detection using historical market data and validated models.
  • Portfolio monitoring: Add optional user-configured asset watchlists with secure authentication and privacy controls.

These are potential extensions, not features automatically provided by the initial architecture.

Conclusion

Cryptocurrency markets generate enormous amounts of continuously changing information.

Collecting that information is only the first step. The real value comes from processing it, identifying unusual activity, preserving historical records, and making useful insights accessible.

CryptoPulse demonstrates how AWS services can work together to build this type of platform.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides real-time ingestion. AWS Lambda processes incoming events. Amazon S3 stores historical data. DynamoDB maintains the latest market state. DynamoDB Streams supports event-driven alert processing. Amazon SNS delivers notifications. AWS Glue and Amazon Athena make historical analysis possible.

Together, these services provide a serverless foundation that can evolve as market-data volume and user requirements grow.

The goal of CryptoPulse is simple: don't just watch cryptocurrency prices—understand the market activity behind them.

Disclaimer: CryptoPulse is a conceptual market-monitoring and analytics project. It does not provide investment advice, guarantee price predictions, or execute trades.

References

  • Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Documentation
  • Using AWS Lambda with Amazon Kinesis
  • Amazon S3 Documentation
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog
  • Amazon Athena Documentation
  • DynamoDB Streams
  • Amazon SNS Documentation
  • Binance Spot WebSocket Market Streams

title: Automatización y despliegue de TechInventory con persistencia en CouchDB
description:
Autora: Gabriela Cohaila
Una aplicación puede funcionar en la computadora y aun así fallar al publicarse. En TechInventory, el requisito de usar Apache CouchDB añade una condición: los documentos deben sobrevivir al reinicio y al reemplazo de los contenedores. Por eso la elección del alojamiento depende de la persistencia, además del precio.
El proyecto combina React/Vite, Node/Express y CouchDB. Este artículo se concentra en cómo construir, verificar y preparar su publicación automatizada, y en distinguir una configuración disponible de un despliegue realmente observado.
Una sola aplicación dos servicios principales
El Dockerfile utiliza dos etapas. La primera instala las dependencias y compila React. La segunda incorpora la API, las dependencias de ejecución y los archivos compilados. Express entrega tanto la interfaz como /api, lo que evita configurar dos orígenes para esta demostración.
Compose inicia CouchDB y espera a que responda su comprobación de salud antes de iniciar la aplicación. El directorio de datos de CouchDB se monta en un volumen. Reconstruir la imagen de Express no reemplaza ese volumen.
Las credenciales se generan localmente con valores aleatorios y se guardan en .env, excluido de Git. Una imagen reutilizable no debe contener las claves del entorno donde terminará ejecutándose.
La validación forma parte del recorrido
El workflow CI instala con npm ci, ejecuta pruebas de API, compila el frontend y comprueba dependencias. Luego levanta los contenedores y ejecuta la prueba de integración contra CouchDB real.
La primera ejecución falló al iniciar CouchDB. El contenedor ajusta permisos de sus archivos y el montaje de configuración de solo lectura interfería con ese arranque. La solución fue copiar la configuración con el propietario correcto durante la construcción de una imagen derivada de couchdb:3.5.0. La ejecución CI #3 completó las seis pruebas de API y la integración real. Esta diferencia entre una prueba aislada y una prueba con el servidor real fue una evidencia concreta del proyecto.
El workflow de despliegue está preparado para iniciarse después de un CI exitoso en main. Utiliza el commit que pasó la validación, envía sus archivos al servidor por SSH y ejecuta Compose. Su activación requiere configurar el destino y secretos; no se publica un supuesto resultado mientras esos requisitos falten.
HTTPS y una base fuera de Internet
La configuración de producción agrega Caddy delante de Express. Caddy recibe tráfico en 80 y 443 y obtiene el certificado para el nombre DNS configurado. Express queda disponible solo en loopback del host y dentro de la red de contenedores. CouchDB no necesita un puerto público.
En producción la sesión usa una cookie Secure y HttpOnly. Las escrituras también requieren un token CSRF y el origen esperado. Usar HTTPS protege el transporte, pero no sustituye la autorización ni la validación de entradas.
Qué significa realmente gratuito
La documentación de Render indica que sus servicios web gratuitos tienen un sistema de archivos efímero y no admiten disco persistente. Hospedar CouchDB allí como si fuera una base duradera incumpliría el requisito del proyecto. Tener una URL accesible no compensaría perder los documentos al reiniciar.
Azure for Students ofrece crédito académico sin tarjeta. Antes de crear recursos hay que verificar elegibilidad, saldo, vencimiento, cuotas y límite de gasto en la cuenta concreta. Los créditos no convierten una VM en gratuita para siempre: la máquina, el disco y la IP consumen saldo mientras existan según sus tarifas aplicables.
La comparación y la decisión operativa se registran en docs/hosting.md. No se habilita pago por uso ni se retira la protección de gasto para completar esta tarea.
Cómo demostrar la automatización
La evidencia más clara sigue una secuencia pequeña: cambiar un texto visible, subir el commit, observar CI, observar CD y comprobar el cambio en la URL HTTPS. Conviene mostrar el identificador del commit y la ejecución correspondiente para conectar el resultado con el código.
Después se registra un equipo, se reinicia el servicio y se consulta de nuevo. Esa segunda secuencia demuestra persistencia, una propiedad diferente del despliegue automático. Las capturas deben excluir .env, claves SSH, cookies y pantallas con datos privados.
El proyecto incluye un guion de menos de cinco minutos. El video debe mostrar resultados reales; las pantallas pendientes se graban después de resolverlas, sin sustituirlas por imágenes ilustrativas.
Límites y siguientes pasos
La propuesta usa un solo servidor y no ofrece alta disponibilidad. El workflow preparado tampoco aplica una reversión automática si falla una versión nueva. Antes de usar el sistema con información importante se necesitan respaldos con restauración probada, monitorización y una operación de administración de cuentas más completa.
Automatizar no elimina la necesidad de revisar el resultado. Reduce pasos repetitivos y hace visible qué versión se probó y qué versión se intentó publicar. Esa trazabilidad es el principal aprendizaje de TechInventory.
Código y referencias
• Repositorio TechInventory
• GitHub Actions
• Limitaciones del alojamiento gratuito de Render
• Azure for Students
• Límite de gasto de Azure
• Volúmenes Docker
• HTTPS automático de Caddy
Resultado verificado de la demostración
El 12/11/2026 se publicó TechInventory con HTTPS en una VM Ubuntu de Azure for Students. El despliegue automático #4 terminó correctamente. También se ejecutó CRUD real desde la URL HTTPS y se comprobó que asset:LT-DEMO conservaba su identificador y revisión después de reiniciar Express y CouchDB. Los registros y capturas están en evidence.

Inventario real publicado por HTTPS

Despliegue automático exitoso
La URL utilizada fue https://techinventory-codexvex-20261112.eastus.cloudapp.azure.com. El alojamiento es temporal: se retira después de recopilar las evidencias para evitar consumo continuo de créditos. Esa dirección no debe considerarse un servicio permanente. El repositorio y los registros de Actions permiten revisar la construcción y el despliegue aunque el servidor se haya retirado.

title: Deleting your losers buys 4.1 points of hit rate: an audit protocol for model retirement
description:
Every prediction system eventually grows a lifecycle manager: models get born, promoted, demoted and killed. Ours has 8,789 model rows and a retirement pipeline that runs every two hours. For a long time the number we published was computed over whatever models happened to still exist at query time — a mistake whose size is measurable.

46,160 graded predictions carry a boolean hit. The all-cohort rate is 57.05% (26,334 correct). The rate over models still in a live lifecycle state is 61.17% (19,281 of 31,520). Nothing about the models changed between those queries — only the WHERE clause did. A 4.12-point swing produced entirely by bookkeeping. In a system that retires models automatically, survivorship bias is not an edge case; it is the default output. What follows is the audit protocol we now run before any retirement decision.

Where a model actually goes when it dies

There is no single "deleted" state. A model leaves the visible cohort through six different doors, and the aggregate rate treats each differently.

lifecycle_status models graded preds hits hit rate
evolving 2,165 31,105 19,001 61.09%
eliminated 2,708 7,950 3,586 45.11%
demoted 2,937 1,014 345 34.02%
retiring 589 330 196 59.39%
pending_retrain 56 318 90 28.30%
archived 170 — — —
hibernating 100 148 75 50.68%
active 24 415 280 67.47%
retraining 6 25 12 48.00%
(no ai_models row) 525 ids 4,854 2,748 56.61%

Three things stand out. First, the worst cohorts are also the smallest. demoted holds 2,937 model rows but only 1,014 graded predictions — 0.35 per model. pending_retrain holds 56 models and 318 predictions at 28.30%. These are not measured failures; they are barely-measured ones. A rule that fires on 0.35 observations per model is not selecting on quality, it is selecting on noise.

Second, eliminated is a real signal. 801 models, 7,950 graded predictions, 45.11% — 11.98 points below the evolving cohort on a sample worth reading.

Third: 4,854 graded predictions reference 525 model_id values that no longer exist in ai_models at all. Their score, 56.61%, is close to the pool average, and any metric written as JOIN ai_models silently drops every one of them. We also keep an ai_models_archive table with 4,054 rows, while archived_at is NULL on all 8,789 live rows — the primary table cannot tell you when anything was retired.

The audit query: publish two numbers, never one

The protocol: publish two numbers from one query so they cannot drift apart — the headline, and its complement over the full historical cohort including rows whose model row is missing.

-- Cohort audit: the same graded rows, seen through two different filters.
WITH graded AS (
    SELECT p.id,
           p.model_id,
           p.hit,
           p.created_at,
           COALESCE(m.lifecycle_status, 'hard_deleted') AS lc
    FROM ai_predictions p
    LEFT JOIN ai_models m ON m.id = p.model_id
    WHERE p.settled = TRUE
      AND p.hit IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT 'all_cohort'      AS view,
       COUNT(*)          AS n,
       SUM(hit::int)     AS hits,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2) AS hit_rate
FROM graded
UNION ALL
SELECT 'live_only', COUNT(*), SUM(hit::int),
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2)
FROM graded
WHERE lc IN ('evolving', 'active', 'incubating', 'validating')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'retired_cohort', COUNT(*), SUM(hit::int),
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2)
FROM graded
WHERE lc IN ('eliminated', 'demoted', 'archived');

     view      |   n   | hits  | hit_rate
---------------+-------+-------+----------
 all_cohort    | 46160 | 26334 |    57.05
 live_only     | 31520 | 19281 |    61.17
 retired_cohort|  8964 |  3931 |    43.85

The rule we now enforce: the delta between all_cohort and live_only is itself a monitored metric. Call it the retirement gap. When it grows, the pipeline is deleting measured failures faster than unmeasured models — flattering the published number without improving the system. Month by month:

month graded all-cohort live-only gap retired share of rows
2026-06 2,735 62.30% 62.94% +0.64 1.50%
2026-07 2,637 50.89% 58.94% +8.05 1.82%
2026-08 164 62.80% 70.37% +7.57 32.32%
2026-09 9,739 58.51% 62.13% +3.62 26.43%
2026-10 21,824 56.28% 60.85% +4.57 22.99%
2026-11 9,060 57.43% 60.95% +3.52 13.58%

The gap is not constant. It is smallest in the month when almost nothing had been retired and largest when a quarter of the pool was already gone. The full series runs between 50% and 62%, and part of the recent stability is the deletion of 23% of the evidence.

Why the survivors look better than they are

Hard deletion destroys the denominator. 525 model ids vanished from ai_models while their predictions stayed, so every JOIN-based metric silently excludes 4,854 rows — worse than a wrong number, because nothing in the output declares it.

Status filters are applied at read time, not write time. The same physical rows produce 57.05% or 61.17% depending on a WHERE clause chosen by a dashboard author, and no schema-level signal marks that the choice exists.

The leaderboard adds a minimum-sample filter on top. Of 4,681 models with any graded prediction, only 660 reach 20 and 170 reach 50; the median is 6. A "top models by hit rate" view is therefore almost entirely models whose whole record is under ten games, and sorting it descending returns 100% records: 388 with fewer than five graded predictions, 18 more between five and nine.

Here is the part that should end the argument. If every model were exchangeable at the pool rate of 0.5705, the expected number of perfect records is Σ p^n over the actual sample sizes:

models with n < 5   : expected 634.5 perfect records, observed 388
models with n >= 5  : expected  25.3 perfect records, observed  18

Observed is below the coin-flip expectation in both bands. A 4-for-4 record is not evidence of skill here — it is less impressive than chance would produce. Any rule that ranks on raw rate ranks a mixture of noise and sample size, and the models it rewards are the ones that guessed few times.

Make retirement append-only and auditable

The fix is not "stop filtering" — some views legitimately want the live cohort. The fix is to make the filter explicit, permanent and reversible, so excluded rows stay addressable. Retirement becomes an event, never a delete.

"""Retirement ledger: retirement is an event, never a delete."""
import hashlib, json, datetime as dt

def _h(prev: str, payload: dict) -> str:
    body = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256((prev + body).encode()).hexdigest()

def retire(cur, model_id: int, new_state: str, reason: str, evidence: dict):
    """Append one row. Never UPDATE ai_models.status, never DELETE."""
    cur.execute(
        "SELECT state, entry_hash FROM model_lifecycle_ledger "
        "WHERE model_id = %s ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1", (model_id,))
    row = cur.fetchone()
    prev_state, prev_hash = (row if row else ("born", "0" * 64))

    payload = {
        "model_id": model_id, "from_state": prev_state,
        "to_state": new_state, "reason": reason,     # 'eliminated_low_n'
        "evidence": evidence,                        # n, hits, rate, window
        "at": dt.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
    }
    cur.execute(
        "INSERT INTO model_lifecycle_ledger "
        "(model_id, from_state, to_state, reason, evidence, entry_hash, prev_hash) "
        "VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s)",
        (model_id, prev_state, new_state, reason,
         json.dumps(evidence), _h(prev_hash, payload), prev_hash))
    # projections may change; history may not
    cur.execute("UPDATE ai_models SET lifecycle_status = %s WHERE id = %s",
                (new_state, model_id))

With that ledger, the cohort view stops being a guess:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_model_cohort AS
SELECT m.id AS model_id,
       m.lifecycle_status AS current_state,
       COALESCE(f.first_retired_at, TIMESTAMPTZ 'infinity') AS retired_at,
       f.retirement_reason
FROM ai_models m
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT MIN(at) AS first_retired_at,
           (ARRAY_AGG(reason ORDER BY at))[1] AS retirement_reason
    FROM model_lifecycle_ledger l
    WHERE l.model_id = m.id
      AND l.to_state IN ('eliminated', 'demoted', 'archived')
) f ON TRUE;

Now "as of date D" is a temporal join instead of a status filter: a model retired in September still contributes its September predictions to every point-in-time metric, and the historical series can no longer be rewritten by a later decision. Three invariants belong in CI, each of which our bad state violated:

  1. COUNT(*) FROM ai_predictions p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ai_models m WHERE m.id = p.model_id) must be zero. Ours was 4,854.
  2. archived_at must be non-NULL for every row whose state is archived. Ours was 0 of 170.
  3. Every state change needs a ledger row, and the chain must verify from genesis. Ours had 1,185 rows with reactivated_at set and no recorded reason.

What a retirement decision actually needs

Judge a retirement rule on the predictions it would have removed, not on the leaderboard it produces afterwards. Report four numbers together for every candidate cohort: n, hits, rate, and the rate of the cohort that survives. A rule removing 8,964 rows at 43.85% from a pool running at 57.05% raises the published number by 3.18 points while deleting 19.4% of the evidence. Whether that trade is defensible depends on whether the rule fired on measured failure — and with demoted averaging 0.35 graded predictions per model, ours mostly did not.

The honest summary of our pool: 63.6% of model rows (5,587 of 8,789) have never produced a single graded prediction, the median model has six, only 170 clear fifty, and 253 models were fathered by parents that were later eliminated. A system that kills a parent but keeps its descendants runs a selection loop it cannot audit, because the descendants inherit a training word whose measured performance was negative and nothing records the inheritance.

Retirement is a data operation, not a UI operation. If deleting a row changes the headline metric, that metric is a function of your bookkeeping rather than your model quality — and the cheapest way to improve it is always to delete more.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+
