title: Which Backend Should You Choose for Your Mobile App?
description:
Which backend should you choose for your mobile app? Firebase and Supabase are the two backends this article compares, and they store data in different ways.

The problem: "I just need a backend, why is this so hard?"

You have an app idea. The guides you find name Firebase or Supabase, and they disagree with each other. One comparison says Firebase is cheaper, the next says Supabase is, and each one sounds sure.

So you pick the one you heard first. Then your app grows, and the backend fights you: reports need data from three places at once, the app stops working offline, or the monthly bill jumps for no clear reason.

The cause: the two backends store data in different ways

Firebase stores your data as documents. Think of each document as one card — one card per order, one card per user. That works when each screen reads one card.

Supabase stores your data in tables, the way a spreadsheet does, on PostgreSQL. You write SQL queries that join tables together. One query can join orders to customers and products and add up the total.

That difference is where the choice starts. If your app needs reports, an admin dashboard, or unplanned questions, SQL answers them with a new query. With documents, teams copy the fields each screen needs into each document, then update every copy when the source changes.

There are two more differences that matter on a phone. First, offline use. Firestore keeps a copy of the data on the phone, so the app can read and write offline, and Google turns this on by default for Android and Apple apps. Supabase has no built-in offline cache — you add a sync layer such as PowerSync. If yours is a field service or delivery app that must work in a dead zone, that gap alone can decide for Firestore.

Second, push notifications. Firebase includes Cloud Messaging, and it costs nothing on any Firebase plan. Supabase has no push service of its own. Its own guide sends push from Edge Functions through Firebase Cloud Messaging.

The minimum fix: which backend should you choose for your mobile app

1. Pick Supabase when your data is linked together

Go with Supabase when your app has orders, customers, products and payments that relate to each other, when you want SQL and row level security, and when you want a way out to plain PostgreSQL later. Supabase is open source, and a standard Postgres dump restores anywhere.

Watch one thing: a Supabase table without row level security switched on is readable and writable by any role with a grant on it. Since 30 October 2026, new tables in the public schema are not exposed to the data API at all until you add an explicit grant. Turn RLS on and write a row level security policy for every exposed table before real users arrive.

2. Firebase, when the phone must work offline

Firebase is the pick when the app must keep working with no signal, when each screen reads one self-contained document, and when you want the database, push notifications and crash reports in one Google project. It also fits chat apps and anything that needs live updates.

One catch: Firestore bills every document read, write and delete. Every query costs at least one read, even when it returns nothing. There is no hard cap — budgets and alerts do not stop usage. So read only the documents the screen shows, and never load a whole collection to show ten items.

3. Check the bill at your size, not at zero users

Both start free. Supabase free covers 50,000 monthly users and a 500 MB database, but a free project pauses after one week idle. Its Pro plan is $25 a month and covers 100,000 monthly users and 8 GB of disk.

Firebase Spark is free with no payment method: 1 GiB stored, 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes a day. Past that you move to Blaze, which is pay-as-you-go per operation.

In one cost model read on 2 November 2026, at 100,000 monthly users and 1,000 reads per user a month, the two came out close: about $100 a month on Supabase Pro and about $95 on Firebase with basic sign-in. Add multi-factor sign-in on Firebase and the same model put Firebase at about $370, because that needs the Identity Platform upgrade. Supabase includes basic multi-factor sign-in on every plan.

What NOT to do: do not pick a backend because an AI tool defaults to it, and do not pick a custom backend for your first version. Start on Firebase or Supabase, and move only when you can name what the managed backend cannot do.

When to get help instead of choosing it yourself

When your app takes payments or stores customer data, get a developer to plan the backend with you before you build. This is a choice that gets expensive to reverse once users sign up. My starting price for a small 4–5 screen app with Supabase is from $300.

If this is your app, contact me through https://israr-kundi.web.app

title: Should you proxy through Server Actions or call APIs directly?
description:
You've got a Next.js app, and it needs to talk to a backend that isn't Next.js, maybe a Python service, a Rails app, or plain Express. The first architectural decision you'll make, often without realizing it's a decision at all, is where that connection actually lives.

Some teams route every request through a Server Action and let Next.js sit in the middle. Others skip that step and have the browser call the backend directly. Both are common, both work, and picking wrong doesn't blow up right away. It just shows up later as latency nobody budgeted for, or a security gap nobody planned for.

This post walks through how each pattern works, then digs into the real trade-offs around performance, scaling, and security, so you can pick deliberately instead of by habit. It's written for developers who've built a Next.js app or two. You don't need to have used Server Actions before, the next section explains what they are.

There are two places the connection can live

The connection to your backend either runs through the Next.js server or skips it. A Server Action is an async function marked with 'use server' that runs on the Next.js server, but that a client component can call like a normal function. That makes it a natural middleman.

  • Pattern A: Server Actions as a proxy. The Next.js app becomes a middleman. Client components call Server Actions, which forward requests to the backend. This is the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) approach.
  • Pattern B: direct client-side calls. The browser talks straight to the backend, the same way client-side rendering has always worked.

Here's how a request travels in each.

A proxy adds a hop, a direct call skips it

The proxy pattern sends every request through the Next.js server on its way to the backend, while a direct call goes straight from the browser.

Server Actions as a proxy

  1. A user action in the app triggers a Server Action
  2. The Server Action runs on the Next.js server and calls the backend API
  3. The backend responds to the Next.js server
  4. The Server Action processes that response and sends it to the client

The path: client, Next.js server, backend API, Next.js server, client.

Under the hood, each Server Action becomes a POST endpoint on the page that uses it, identified by an action ID Next.js generates. Called from the client, it always goes over POST, regardless of what the action actually does.

Direct client-side calls

  1. A client component needs data
  2. Your JavaScript calls the backend directly with fetch or Axios
  3. The backend responds straight to the browser

The Next.js server serves the initial JavaScript bundle, then steps out of the way. Every request after that happens in the browser.

Each pattern wins on different things

Neither approach is better across the board. What matters is what you're optimizing for.

When Server Actions make sense

Secrets stay hidden. API keys and service tokens live on the server and never reach the browser.

Auth lives in one place. Every request can be validated against the user's session before it reaches the backend, instead of trusting each client call independently.

Client code stays simple. Components call functions instead of managing fetch calls, error states, and loading states by hand.

Cache invalidation is built in. After a mutation, calling revalidatePath or updateTag updates the UI in the same response. No manual cache bookkeeping.

When direct calls make more sense

Your backend already does the work. If the API already handles OAuth, JWTs, rate limiting, and CORS, a proxy layer adds a hop without adding much value.

Latency is the priority. Direct calls skip the extra round trip through the Next.js server, which matters for real-time features.

You want a thin frontend. If Next.js should just serve pages, direct calls keep it out of the request path entirely.

Developer experience, side by side

What you care about Server Action proxy Direct client calls
Client-side code Function calls Manual fetch setup
Type safety Typed at the call site, manual past the backend boundary Manual type definitions
Boilerplate Minimal, hooks manage state useState + useEffect
Cache invalidation Built in with revalidatePath Custom solution

That type safety row needs a caveat. "End-to-end, automatic" is the pitch when the whole stack is TypeScript, tRPC being the clearest example. The moment your backend is Python, Rails, or anything else, the automation stops at the Next.js boundary. The Server Action's own inputs and outputs are typed, but whatever the backend actually sends back still needs validating by hand, with something like Zod, unless you're maintaining matching types on both sides yourself.

Server Actions cost a hop and run one at a time

Server Actions add a network hop. There's no getting around that.

On serverless platforms like Vercel, that hop can push latency into the hundreds of milliseconds to low seconds, worse with cold starts. Direct calls go point to point, so they're faster by default.

That number is more a serverless characteristic than a Server Actions one. Run Next.js as a long-lived process next to your backend, same region, nothing scaling to zero, and the extra hop can cost single-digit milliseconds instead. If your own latency numbers look like the Vercel figures above, check what's actually adding the delay before blaming the pattern itself.

Here's a quick test. Fire three Server Actions from the client with Promise.all, each taking about a second on the server. How long until all three finish? Most people guess one second. It's closer to three.

Server Actions run one at a time. Trigger several at once and they queue up while the UI waits. The React docs say frameworks typically process one action at a time, and Next.js does. Direct calls with Promise.all really do run concurrently.

Don't use Server Actions for fetching data. Use Server Components or API routes with GET requests instead, Server Actions are built for mutations, and using them for reads gives up caching behavior you'd otherwise get for free.

A proxy centralizes load as well as logic

Centralizing data logic behind Server Actions is easier to maintain. One pattern, one place to update. The cost is that all that load lands on the Next.js server. As traffic grows, that server needs to scale with it, and on pay-per-invocation platforms the bill grows with it too.

Direct calls let frontend and backend scale independently. The Next.js layer stays thin and the backend absorbs its own load. The cost shows up later: fetching logic spreads across components, and tracing what calls what gets harder as the app grows.

A proxy hides more, but it's still attack surface

The proxy pattern is architecturally stronger on security, for a few concrete reasons:

  • API keys and tokens never touch the browser
  • The backend doesn't need to be publicly exposed, it can be firewalled to accept requests only from the Next.js server
  • CSRF protection comes built in
  • Authorization checks happen in one place, before anything reaches the backend

Going direct puts more of that burden on the backend itself:

  • JWTs stored in the browser are a target. Store them wrong and an XSS attack can steal them.
  • CORS has to be configured correctly, which is easy to get wrong.
  • The API needs its own rate limiting, input validation, and abuse protection.

None of that is unworkable, it's just work the backend now has to do on its own.

Neither pattern is immune to real vulnerabilities. CVE-2025-55182, the "React2Shell" vulnerability, allowed remote code execution via crafted payloads sent through the same POST/action-dispatch mechanism Server Actions use. The bug lived in React's own Flight protocol deserialization, not in anyone's Server Action code, but a proxy architecture still means treating Server Actions as endpoints that need patching and secure coding practices. The Next.js server can be the point of compromise too.

That's worth sitting with, because it cuts against the "proxy is just safer" framing above. Every layer between the browser and your data is also a layer that can be exploited, and a full Next.js server running action-dispatch logic is a lot more code than a stateless API behind tight CORS and short-lived tokens. The proxy pattern reduces what the browser can reach directly. It doesn't reduce the total surface, it just moves where the risk lives.

Pick by what you're optimizing for

Reach for Server Actions as a proxy when secrets need to stay hidden, when a centralized data access layer keeps the codebase easier to reason about, or when type-safe function calls matter more than shaving off a network hop.

Reach for direct client calls when the backend already handles OAuth, rate limiting, and CORS on its own, when latency is the constraint you're optimizing for, or when Next.js should stay a thin layer that just serves pages.

Most large apps use both

Large applications often use both. Server Actions cover sensitive operations, payment processing, account settings, anything touching secrets. Direct calls handle public, cacheable data like blog posts or product listings that don't need protection.


Sensitive calls take the extra hop through a Server Action to keep secrets on the server, while public data goes direct.

That split gets you the security of a proxy where it matters and the speed of a direct call where protection isn't the point.

FAQ

Do Server Actions really only run over POST?

Yes. Every Server Action, no matter what it does internally, gets invoked as a POST request. Next.js generates a hidden action ID and routes the call through that same mechanism, which is also part of why they don't get GET-style caching for free.

How do Server Actions protect against CSRF?

Two layers, by default. POST-only requests already sidestep most CSRF vectors, since SameSite cookies block cross-site POSTs in modern browsers. On top of that, Next.js compares the request's Origin header against the Host header and rejects the call if they don't match. You can widen that with the allowedOrigins option in next.config.js if you need cross-origin calls, but each origin you add is one more thing that has to be trusted.

What's the actual difference between revalidatePath and revalidateTag?

revalidatePath invalidates one specific route, and when a Server Action calls it, the response already carries the re-rendered page. revalidateTag(tag, 'max') works by tag instead. It marks every piece of cached data with that tag as stale, wherever it's used, and serves the old version while fresh data loads in the background, so the user doesn't see their change right away. When they need to, call updateTag(tag) in the Server Action instead, which expires the tag immediately. Reach for tags when the same data shows up in multiple places, and revalidatePath when you only need to refresh one page.

Can I run several Server Actions in parallel with Promise.all?

Not really, at least not the way you'd hope. Next.js's client sends Server Actions one at a time, waiting for each to finish before sending the next, and there's no setting to change that. The server itself doesn't queue them. If you need several things to happen at once, do the parallel work inside a single Server Action with Promise.all there, or move the read side to a Server Component or route handler instead.

Why do Server Actions feel especially slow on Vercel?

Serverless functions spin down when they're idle, and spinning one back up for the next request is what shows up as a cold start. That sits on top of the network hop a Server Action already adds. Keeping functions warm or moving latency-sensitive mutations closer to the edge helps, but it doesn't remove the extra hop.

Should I ever use a Server Action to fetch data?

Generally no. Server Actions are built for mutations, and fetching through one gives up the caching you'd get from a Server Component or a GET-based route handler. If a component just needs to read data, reach for those instead and save Server Actions for the writes.

Wrapping up

If you're optimizing for security and maintainability, the proxy pattern is the better default, even with the added latency. If you're optimizing for speed and a fully decoupled frontend, direct calls get you there, provided the backend can stand on its own as a public-facing API.

Most real applications end up mixing both rather than picking one architecture for everything. The important part is making that choice deliberately, based on what a given feature actually needs, rather than copying whatever pattern the last tutorial used.

Originally published at Notes by Sachintha.

title: Flutter + Node.js: how I plan a mobile MVP
description:
A mobile MVP has two jobs: reach real users fast, and stay cheap to change. Flutter helps with the first, because one Dart codebase gives you both an iOS and an Android app. A small Node.js API helps with the second, because your business rules live in one place that a web dashboard or a second app can reuse later.

I am a freelance full stack developer with more than 20 years in corporate IT. This is the order I work in when a founder asks me to turn an idea into a working app.

1. Write one sentence first

Who is the user, and what is the one thing they must be able to do? "A customer places an order and sees its status" is enough. That sentence decides your screens and your tables. Then sketch the data: for an order flow, users, products, orders and order items. Getting this right early saves the most rework.

2. Design the API before the screens

Keep it plain REST with JSON: POST /auth/login, GET /orders, POST /orders, PATCH /orders/:id/status. In Node.js I use Express or Fastify with PostgreSQL or MongoDB, validation on every route and one consistent error format. Document the endpoints from day one so the app, the dashboard and later integrations share one contract.

3. Keep the Flutter architecture simple

Three layers are enough: a data layer that calls the API, a layer that holds state, and the widgets. Riverpod is lighter to start with, Bloc is stricter for larger teams; either works if you use it consistently. Generate Dart models from your API shapes so a backend change shows up as a compile error instead of a crash on a user's phone.

4. Build the UI from a few reusable parts

A button, an input, a list tile and a loading state, used everywhere, make the app look consistent without a long design phase. Handle empty lists, slow networks and expired sessions early. Users meet those on day one.

5. Plan auth, payments and push notifications

  • Auth: short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens, kept in secure storage, never in plain preferences.
  • Payments: use a provider with a mobile SDK, such as Stripe, and let the API create and confirm the payment.
  • Push: Firebase Cloud Messaging covers both platforms; the API stores device tokens and sends a message when an order changes.
  • Third-party APIs: call them from the backend so keys stay secret and you can swap providers without a new app release.

6. Test what matters, on real phones

A few API tests for login, the core workflow and permissions, unit tests for the logic layer and widget tests for the main screens are enough for an MVP. Install weekly builds on real devices; simulators hide keyboard, notch and slow-network problems.

7. Automate the build and deploy

GitHub Actions can run tests and build the app on every push. The API runs in a Docker container behind HTTPS with secrets in environment variables and a daily database backup. Create the store accounts in your own name (Apple Developer $99 a year, Google Play a one-time $25) and leave time for review.

A realistic timeline

For a focused app with a small admin view: week one for scope, data model and API design; weeks two to four for core screens and endpoints, with an installable build each week; week five for payments, notifications and polish; week six for testing and store release. More user types or integrations add weeks.

Flutter or React Native?

Both can ship a good MVP. I lean to Flutter when you want a very consistent interface on both platforms and have no React mobile team. React Native makes sense if you already have React web developers to share.

Full guide with FAQ: How to Build a Flutter MVP Backed by a Node.js API

title: DuckDB: Analytics Queries on a File, Without a Server
description:
A small shop owner exports twelve orders to a CSV file and wants one answer: which city brought in the most money this week? The file sits on a laptop, the data fits in a spreadsheet, and yet getting the answer takes longer than it should. A spreadsheet means wrestling with filters and formulas, and the totals shift every time a row is added. A database server for a file this small is worse: installing, configuring, creating users, all for twelve rows. DuckDB sits in the middle. It is a small analytical database that runs inside your own program, reads the CSV directly, and answers with plain SQL. No server, no setup, no separate process to keep alive.

What I would check before using it

My first check is the shape of the question. DuckDB earns its place when the question is analytical: totals by group, rankings, running sums, joins across files. If the job is storing one record at a time and reading it back by key, SQLite or a JSON file is simpler, because that is not what an analytical engine is built for.

DuckDB shines on files from thousands of rows up to hundreds of millions, far beyond what a spreadsheet handles comfortably. For twelve rows it is still pleasant, because setup costs close to zero. For a dataset that no longer fits on one machine, or many writers updating the same tables at once, it is the wrong tool, and a server database or a distributed engine fits better.

DuckDB speaks SQL, so anyone comfortable with SELECT, GROUP BY, and window functions can use it on day one. A team that only knows pandas can get the same answers with a DataFrame, but SQL keeps the logic in one place when the analysis grows from one file to several.

DuckDB reads CSV, Parquet, and JSON files directly, and it can query a file without importing it first. That matters when the source file is produced by another system every day and copying it into a database would add a step that can break.

My verdict, as judgement: use DuckDB when you have files to analyse with SQL and no appetite for running a server. Skip it when you need many concurrent writers, or when the data has outgrown a single machine. The recommendation flips the moment the file becomes a shared, constantly updated system of record instead of a snapshot to analyse.

One small shop, run end to end

The example is a small online shop selling computer accessories. Its orders live in a CSV file with twelve rows: an order id, a city, an item, a quantity, and a price. The cities are Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad, and the prices are ordinary shop prices, from a Rs 650 cable to a Rs 7,200 monitor arm. The owner wants revenue per city, ranked, and a grand total. The whole script is short, and it reads the CSV straight into DuckDB without loading it into Python first.

import duckdb

csv_text = """order_id,city,item,quantity,price
1,Karachi,Wireless mouse,2,1450
2,Lahore,USB-C cable,5,650
3,Karachi,Mechanical keyboard,1,"1,250"
4,Islamabad,Laptop stand,3,2800
5,Lahore,Wireless mouse,1,1450
6,Karachi,Webcam,2,3900
7,Islamabad,USB-C cable,4,650
8,Karachi,Monitor arm,1,7200
9,Lahore,Laptop stand,2,2800
10,Islamabad,Mechanical keyboard,1,"1,250"
11,Karachi,USB-C cable,3,
12,Lahore,Webcam,1,3900
"""

with open("orders.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write(csv_text)

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("CREATE TABLE orders AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('orders.csv')")

Two rows in that file are deliberately messy, the way real export files are. Order 3 and order 10 carry the price as "1,250", with a thousands comma, and order 11 has no price at all, because the shop had not entered it yet. DuckDB reads the file and guesses the column types from the values it sees, and the comma in "1,250" means the price column comes in as text rather than a number. The describe output from the run shows this plainly:

Columns and types DuckDB inferred:
- order_id: BIGINT
- city: VARCHAR
- item: VARCHAR
- quantity: BIGINT
- price: VARCHAR

The thing that went wrong came next. The obvious query, summing the price after casting it to a number, failed on the very first comma:

Trying the obvious total, SUM(CAST(price AS DOUBLE)):
Conversion Error: Conversion Error: Could not convert string '1,250' to DOUBLE when casting from source column price

LINE 1: SELECT SUM(CAST(price AS DOUBLE)) FROM orders
                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The fix is to clean the value before casting it. REPLACE strips the comma, CAST turns the result into a number, and COALESCE turns the empty price into zero so the row still counts instead of vanishing from the total. The fixed query also ranks the cities with a window function, which is one query doing the grouping and the ranking together:

rows = con.execute("""
    SELECT
        city,
        COUNT(*) AS orders,
        SUM(quantity) AS items_sold,
        SUM(COALESCE(CAST(REPLACE(price, ',', '') AS DOUBLE), 0) * quantity) AS revenue,
        RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(COALESCE(CAST(REPLACE(price, ',', '') AS DOUBLE), 0) * quantity) DESC) AS revenue_rank
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY city
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
""").fetchall()
for city, orders, items, revenue, rank in rows:
    print(f"- {city}: {orders} orders, {items} items, Rs {revenue:,.0f}, rank {rank}")

Here is the real output from the run:

Total revenue per city (comma stripped, empty price treated as 0):
- Karachi: 5 orders, 9 items, Rs 19,150, rank 1
- Lahore: 4 orders, 9 items, Rs 14,200, rank 2
- Islamabad: 3 orders, 8 items, Rs 12,250, rank 3

Grand total revenue:
Rs 45,600

The numbers check out by hand. Karachi leads because of the Rs 7,200 monitor arm and two webcams, while Islamabad trails even though it sold eight items, because four of them were low-priced cables. Order 11, the one with the missing price, contributed three cables at Rs 0, which is honest about what the data actually says, but it is also a flag: a zero in the total is a reminder to go back and fill in the real price. A cleaner long-term fix is to pass thousands = ',' to read_csv so DuckDB parses "1,250" as a number on the way in, and then the REPLACE is not needed at all.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, trusting the types DuckDB guesses. The symptom is a Conversion Error on a cast, or a SUM failing because the column arrived as VARCHAR. The fix is DESCRIBE after loading, and declaring the types with the columns option in read_csv when the guess is wrong.

Second, letting NULLs eat your totals. The symptom is revenue lower than expected, with no error, because a missing price makes the product NULL, and SUM skips NULLs silently. The fix is COALESCE around the value, as in the example, and count NULL prices so you know how much is guesswork.

Third, forgetting that an in-memory database disappears. The symptom is a table that exists during the run and vanishes next time, because duckdb.connect() with no file name keeps everything in memory. The fix is to pass a file name, such as duckdb.connect("shop.duckdb"), when the data should survive.

Fourth, querying the file instead of the table. The symptom is a query that re-reads the CSV on every run, so a changed file rewrites old answers. The fix is loading the file once with CREATE TABLE AS, then querying the table.

My call on DuckDB

DuckDB is at its best when the data already exists as files and the question is analytical. Twelve messy orders became a ranked revenue table with two queries and no server, and the one real problem, a comma in a price, surfaced as a clear error with a clear fix. For a shared system that many people update at once, or data that no longer fits on one machine, reach for a server database instead. If your work looks like this shop, a pile of exports and a question about totals, try it on one real file and see whether the SQL reads more clearly than the spreadsheet it replaces. If it does, keep going.

Further reading

  • DuckDB Python API, https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/clients/python/overview.html
  • DuckDB CSV Import, https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/data/csv/overview.html

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/duckdb-analytics-queries-on-file.html

title: From CSS custom properties to Figma variables, with no plugin
description:
Figma can import design tokens as variables directly: open the Variables view, create a collection and drop a JSON file on it. The file has to be in the Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG) format, and Figma is picky about what it accepts. From Figma's help page on modes:

  • Colors must be sRGB or HSL objects (colorSpace, components, alpha, optional hex).
  • Dimensions must be in px. Anything in rem is not imported.
  • Font families must be a single name as a string. A fallback stack is not supported.
  • Numbers are fine, and nested names become folders: color.primary turns into color/primary.

Composite types like typography and shadow aren't on the list.

Most sites already have their tokens as CSS custom properties, so here is a small script that converts a :root block into a file that follows those rules.

The input

The :root block of Northwind Roasters, a fictional coffee shop site I use for demos. Shortened, but these are the real values:

:root {
  --color-primary: #c2410c;
  --color-background: #fffaf3;
  --font-body: "Hanken Grotesk", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif;
  --text-base: 1.0625rem;
  --leading-base: 1.6;
  --weight-base: 400;
  --space-16: 16px;
  --radius-lg: 10px;
  --shadow-sm: rgba(43, 29, 20, 0.08) 0px 1px 3px 0px;
  --gradient-1: linear-gradient(135deg, rgb(194, 65, 12), rgb(245, 158, 11));
}

The full block has 49 variables: 9 colors, 3 font stacks, 5 type sizes with line height and weight each, 13 spacing values, 5 radii, 3 shadows and a gradient.

The script 

import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const css = readFileSync(process.argv[2], 'utf8');
const vars = [...css.matchAll(/--([\w-]+):\s*([^;]+);/g)].map(([, name, value]) => [name, value.trim()]);

const hexToSrgb = (hex) => {
  const n = [1, 3, 5].map((i) => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255);
  return { colorSpace: 'srgb', components: n.map((c) => +c.toFixed(4)), alpha: 1, hex };
};
const toPx = (v) => {
  const m = v.match(/^(-?[\d.]+)(px|rem)$/);
  if (!m) return null;
  return { value: m[2] === 'rem' ? +m[1] * 16 : +m[1], unit: 'px' }; // Figma only takes px
};
const firstFont = (stack) => stack.split(',')[0].trim().replace(/^["']|["']$/g, '');

const tokens = {};
const skipped = [];
const put = (path, token) => {
  const keys = path.split('-');
  const group = keys.length > 1 ? keys.shift() : 'misc';
  (tokens[group] ??= {})[keys.join('-')] = token;
};

for (const [name, value] of vars) {
  if (/^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/i.test(value)) put(name, { $type: 'color', $value: hexToSrgb(value) });
  else if (name.startsWith('font-')) put(name, { $type: 'fontFamily', $value: firstFont(value) });
  else if (toPx(value)) put(name, { $type: 'dimension', $value: toPx(value) });
  else if (/^-?[\d.]+$/.test(value)) put(name, { $type: 'number', $value: +value });
  else skipped.push(name);
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(tokens, null, 2));
console.error(`converted ${vars.length - skipped.length}, skipped: ${skipped.join(', ')}`);

Run it with node css2figma.mjs styles.css > tokens.json. It reads the variables with a regex, which is fine for a :root block of plain values; it doesn't resolve var() references.

What came out 

converted 45, skipped: shadow-xs, shadow-sm, shadow-2xl, gradient-1

A few of the converted tokens:

"primary": {
  "$type": "color",
  "$value": { "colorSpace": "srgb", "components": [0.7608, 0.2549, 0.0471], "alpha": 1, "hex": "#c2410c" }
}
"base": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": { "value": 17, "unit": "px" } }
"body": { "$type": "fontFamily", "$value": "Hanken Grotesk" }

That's 9 colors, 3 font names and 33 numbers: 5 sizes, 5 line heights, 5 weights, 13 spacing values and 5 radii. Every token uses a type Figma lists as supported.

Each step of the conversion:

Colors. Divide each channel by 255: #c2410c is 194, 65, 12, which gives 0.7608, 0.2549, 0.0471. I keep the hex too, since Figma accepts it alongside the components and it's easier to read in a diff.

rem to px. --text-base: 1.0625rem becomes 17px. That multiplies by 16, which assumes the root font size is the default. If the site sets html { font-size: 62.5% }, use 10 instead, or you'll import every size 60% too big. Check getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).fontSize on the site first.

Font stacks. Only the first name survives: "Hanken Grotesk", ui-sans-serif, ... becomes Hanken Grotesk. Figma variables just hold the name, so nothing is lost there that Figma could use.

Shadows and gradients are skipped. In Figma they're effect and fill styles, not variables, so recreate those 4 by hand.

Two things that caught me out

JSON object key order. In the CSS the radii go md, lg, 2xl, 18, full. In the output they came out as 18, md, lg, 2xl, full. JavaScript objects always put integer-like keys first, in ascending order, before any other key, so 18 jumped to the front. The spacing group only has numeric names, so there it happens to look right. If the order in the file matters to you, for diffs or for how the folder reads in Figma, use non-numeric names like r18 or s4.

One name with no group. --space: 4px has no second part, so the script puts it in a misc group. Rename it in the CSS (--space-base) or in the JSON before importing, or you get a lonely misc/space folder.

Importing

  1. In Figma, open the Variables view and create a new collection.
  2. Drag tokens.json into it. Figma creates one mode for the file.
  3. For a dark theme, run the script on the dark :root values and import that file too: Figma makes one mode per file. A variable is only created if its token is in every file with the same type, so keep the names identical.
  4. To update later, right-click the mode and choose Import mode. Variables with matching names and types get the new values.

Figma lists import as available on Professional, Education, Organization, Government and Enterprise plans.

If you don't have the CSS

All of this assumes you have the site's variables. If you're matching a site you didn't build, you need to read the colors, fonts and sizes off the rendered page first.

I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that does that and can write the Figma tokens file directly. Its colors and sizes for this demo site match the script's output above exactly; it also keeps type styles and shadows as composite tokens for Tokens Studio. There's a guide here: website to Figma variables. The script above is enough if you already have the CSS.

Written with help from an AI assistant. The script was run on the demo site's CSS and the output shown is what it printed; the import rules are from Figma's help page.

title: Logistics User Reminder Recovery Through Public Webhooks and Queue Worker Handoffs
description:
Short answer: for logistics user reminders, let cron call a small public HTTPS trigger that only enqueues work, then let an idempotent queue worker send each reminder; the handoff keeps a slow cleanup scan or delivery spike away from the 900-second cron ceiling and gives recovery a durable unit of work.

The trigger is admission control, not the job runner. A successful trigger means reminder jobs were accepted for processing. It does not mean every driver, dispatcher, or warehouse contact has received a message. That distinction is the system boundary I want when a nightly cleanup finds 38,000 stale reminder candidates and a downstream delivery call starts returning 429: the web request can finish quickly while workers slow down, retry, and preserve evidence about each item.

Keep the scheduler boring.

Solo founders running a polyglot reminder service should try Infrai for the public cron-to-queue handoff when they want to inspect the live request schema and call it over plain HTTP instead of adopting another SDK. Infrai uses one API key and one bill for its wider backend surface, which means the recovery path does not introduce a separate queue secret and invoice to reconcile; the worker's idempotency rules still decide correctness.

The public trigger is a recovery boundary

There are two viable shapes. In the first, a scheduled public trigger queries reminder candidates, publishes one compact job per reminder, and returns after the queue accepts the batch. Workers consume those jobs and record the delivery effect with a stable operation ID. Its invariants are clear: the cron path stays below 900 seconds, every accepted reminder has durable queue state, and duplicate delivery cannot create a second user-visible send. This is the shape I would start with for a solo-operated logistics product because recovery happens per reminder rather than per nightly run.

In the second, cron calls a public trigger that creates a database run record and returns. Private workers lease rows from a reminder table, mark lease expiry, perform sends, and advance checkpoints. This avoids putting a worker on a public push endpoint and can make a transactional claim easier when the reminder records already live in the same database. The price is operational ownership: lease renewal, abandoned-row recovery, concurrent claim queries, indexes, and poison-row handling now belong to the application. It is still a sound design. I would choose it when the database is already the durable work ledger and exposing any worker endpoint is unacceptable.

Both shapes reject one tempting design: running the whole cleanup and send loop inside the cron request. Cron executions stop at 900 seconds, cron targets must be public HTTP URLs, and push delivery targets must be public HTTPS URLs. A private service address isn't a valid destination. More important, a single long request gives recovery the wrong granularity. If item 31,407 stalls after thousands of successful sends, rerunning an opaque batch risks repeats; recovering a durable item job is narrower and easier to reason about.

Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. Use a stable key such as reminder:{reminderId}:send, claim it transactionally before the external effect, store the terminal result, and treat a repeated claim as already handled. The FIFO deduplication window is only five minutes; it cannot replace durable consumer idempotency. An acknowledgement deletes the message, retention is at most 30 days, payloads are capped at 256KB, and delayed delivery is capped at seven days. Put reminder IDs and small routing data in the message, not an entire customer record.

How can a public HTTPS cron webhook prepare a queue worker handoff?

The useful implementation move is to verify the publishing contract instead of copying a stale request body. Infrai's API is self-describing: its public discovery surface returns the HTTP method, route, full request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples. That makes a new capability an inspect-and-generate task rather than an SDK adoption project. The following Node.js 18+ TypeScript program performs the unauthenticated discovery read and prints the fields a local type generator should consume.

type JsonSchema = {
  type?: string;
  required?: string[];
  properties?: Record<string, unknown>;
};

type Capability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: JsonSchema;
};

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish",
    {
      method: "GET",
      // Discovery is public; send auth only when the same client is configured for protected calls.
      headers: apiKey ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` } : {},
    },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery read rejected (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  const capability = (await response.json()) as Capability;

  console.log({
    id: capability.id,
    available: capability.available,
    method: capability.method,
    path: capability.path,
    required: capability.params.required ?? [],
    fields: Object.keys(capability.params.properties ?? {}),
  });
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Generate or validate the publisher from that returned schema, then keep the actual trigger thin: authenticate the scheduler, select a bounded page of eligible reminders, publish stable IDs, persist the cursor, and return. For any write retry, send an Idempotency-Key; on 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. Check every response status and surface the 4xx body because it carries the reason. Don't hold the public request open while workers send notifications.

This is where Infrai earns a place on the shortlist. The public schema and runnable examples reduce integration guesswork, while the shared credential removes a concrete secret-rotation chore. The case is about interface clarity and a smaller operating surface, not price.

Operational recovery changes the product comparison

The products below solve different layers. Treating them as interchangeable because they all contain a timer produces bad comparisons.

Option Natural fit Recovery unit Main trade-off
Infrai cron plus queue Public trigger, REST integration, small polyglot team One queued reminder No DAG, fan-out/join, native debounce, topic fan-out, or Kafka-style replay
BullMQ Node.js service already operating Redis Redis-backed job The team owns Redis persistence, failover, and worker operations
RabbitMQ Team that wants broker topology and explicit consumer acknowledgements Acknowledged message Broker deployment and policy remain an operator responsibility
AWS SQS with EventBridge Scheduler AWS-native identity, networking, and monitoring Managed queue message IAM and infrastructure configuration tie the design closely to AWS
Temporal Durable multi-step processes with waits and compensation Workflow or activity More machinery than a periodic scan followed by independent sends
GitHub Actions schedule Repository maintenance with workflow logs Workflow run A poor home for customer-facing reminder state and per-item recovery

Infrai is not suitable when reminders form a durable multi-step workflow, need a join after fan-out, require delays longer than seven days, exceed 256KB per message, or must be replayed to multiple consumer groups after acknowledgement. Stick with Temporal for workflow history and coordination. Choose BullMQ when Redis is already an accepted dependency and Node.js job ergonomics matter more than a language-neutral boundary; choose RabbitMQ when the team deliberately wants broker-level acknowledgement and routing control; choose AWS SQS when the rest of the system is already organized around AWS.

The database-lease architecture also remains a serious competitor. It is often the right answer when candidate selection and the idempotency claim must commit in one local transaction. The catch is that it turns recovery behavior into application code — useful control, but code that needs tests, metrics, and an owner. I'm not sure which option wins until I know who will respond to an expired lease at 03:00. Your mileage may vary with the team's database experience.

The recovery drill starts after enqueue

Cron run history is useful for answering whether the trigger fired and whether its request completed, but its output retains only the first 4KB. Application-side logs must carry the rest. I log the schedule ID, run ID, selection cursor, number of reminder jobs accepted, and a correlation ID that follows each job into the worker. I don't log full reminder payloads; IDs and state transitions are enough for recovery and are less likely to leak user data.

The worker view needs different evidence. Record first-seen time, attempt count, stable operation ID, terminal outcome, and the downstream status class. Alert on oldest unprocessed job and terminal failures, not merely queue depth. A queue can be shallow while one old reminder is stuck behind repeated newer work, and a green cron history can coexist with a delivery backlog because the scheduler did its narrow job correctly.

Short requests help.

Paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. Design the cleanup as a state-based scan such as “find eligible unsent reminders before this cursor,” not as “process exactly the records created during this second.” On resume, the next scan can rediscover eligible records without relying on a missed tick. The stable idempotency key then prevents rediscovery from becoming a duplicate user-visible send.

The operational checklist is prose because these checks belong together. Confirm that the cron URL is publicly reachable over the intended protocol and that it enqueues rather than sends. Keep its timeout at or below 900 seconds and bound each selection page. Verify the request contract through discovery during development, then pin generated types in source control. Make worker effects idempotent beyond the five-minute FIFO window. Keep delayed jobs within seven days and messages below 256KB. Finally, rehearse recovery from a missed schedule, a repeated delivery, a 429, and a worker restart; each exercise should end with the same reminder state and no second send.

The decision rule is compact: use the managed cron-to-queue shape when a public admission endpoint is acceptable and per-item recovery matters; use database leases when private workers and local transactional claims dominate; use a workflow engine when reminders stop being independent jobs. Cron wakes the system. It should not carry the system's work.

If this boundary fits your reminder service, start by checking the cron and queue recovery guide against your own trigger and worker invariants.

Sources

  • Infrai machine-readable capability index: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • GitHub Actions scheduled workflow triggers: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: How to structure a full-stack React + Motoko dApp on the Internet Computer
description:
Hey builders,

When you first start building on the Internet Computer Protocol (ICP), getting a basic "Hello World" canister running is pretty straightforward. The real headache starts when you try to scale that into a full-stack SaaS application with a multi-tool React frontend, user state tracking, and clean file handling.

While building VaultyPDF (a 15-tool on-chain PDF utility suite), I had to reorganize my project several times before finding a structure that didn't turn into spaghetti code. Here is the clean folder architecture I landed on for pairing React with Motoko.

1. Keep Backend Canisters Modular

Instead of stuffing thousands of lines of logic into a single main.mo file, separate your data types and helper functions early on:

src/
├── backend/
│   ├── main.mo          # Main entry point & public actor methods
│   ├── types.mo         # Custom user & document metadata types
│   └── storage.mo       # Stable memory & state management helpers

Using a dedicated types.mo file makes it much easier to keep your Motoko records aligned with your frontend JavaScript/TypeScript interfaces.

2. Isolate Frontend Canister Calls

Never call your backend actor directly inside your UI components. Create a dedicated service or hook layer in your React folder so your UI stays focused purely on rendering:

src/
├── frontend/
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── components/  # Reusable dark-mode UI cards & modals
│   │   ├── hooks/       # Custom hooks for auth & canister queries
│   │   ├── pages/       # Individual tool views (Merge, Split, Redact)
│   │   └── App.jsx      # Main dashboard layout & routing

3. Handle Heavy Client-Side Processing Locally

On-chain storage and compute are great for user profiles, audit logs, and document metadata. However, for heavy PDF manipulation (like merging pages or applying visual redactions), run the heavy lifting directly in the user's browser via JavaScript, and only send the verified metadata or final state hashes to your Motoko canister. This keeps your cycle burn rate low and makes the UI feel instant.

Want to skip the boilerplate setup?

Setting up the React routing, dark-mode SaaS dashboard UI, and Motoko canister bindings from scratch easily eats up a couple of weeks.

If you want a ready-to-deploy foundation for your own ICP project, I packaged my entire 15-tool codebase into a clean starter template:

👉 Check out the VaultyPDF React + Motoko Boilerplate on Gumroad

How do you guys usually organize your Motoko projects when the codebase starts growing? Drop your folder tips below!

title: Modelar para NoSQL: cómo construimos encuestas en vivo con Firestore y por qué una transacción nos estorbaba
description:
Autor: Carlos Jimenez Laura
Curso: Base de Datos II · Universidad Privada de Tacna
Actividad: Grupal 01-U2, NoSQL App Development, desarrollada junto con Arturo Cutipa Flores

Veníamos de trabajar con bases relacionales, y nuestro primer instinto fue pensar en tablas: una de encuestas, otra de opciones, otra de votos y un GROUP BY para los resultados. En Firestore ese diseño funciona mal. En este artículo cuento cómo construimos VotaYa, una app de encuestas con resultados en vivo, y qué decisiones cambian cuando la base de datos es NoSQL.

La actividad pedía evitar Redis, MongoDB, Neo4j y Prometheus, así que elegimos Google Cloud Firestore, una base de documentos.

Enlaces del proyecto
• Aplicación: https://votaya-firestore.onrender.com
• Repositorio público: https://github.com/CRJL19/votaya
• Video: https://youtu.be/isFjASR8LGw

Figura 1. Pantalla de inicio de VotaYa.

Por qué Firestore
Comparamos tres opciones que cumplían la restricción:

El emulador pesó mucho: nos permitió probar contra el motor real de Firestore sin tocar la nube ni gastar cuota.

En NoSQL se modela a partir de las consultas

La pantalla más visitada muestra una encuesta con sus resultados. Con un diseño relacional, cada carga contaría votos. En Firestore pagas por documento leído, así que contar 1 000 votos costaría 1 000 lecturas.
Por eso guardamos los contadores dentro de la propia encuesta:

Mostrar los resultados cuesta ahora una sola lectura, sin importar cuántos votos existan. Es desnormalizar a propósito: el dato se duplica y el trabajo se paga al escribir. En una aplicación donde se lee mucho más de lo que se vota, el cambio sale a cuenta.
Los votos van en una subcolección, y el identificador del votante es el identificador del documento. Así la unicidad la garantiza la propia clave, sin consultar antes.

La transacción que nos estorbaba

Mi primera versión del voto usaba una transacción, lo que parecía la opción correcta: leer la encuesta, leer si el votante ya existe, escribir ambas cosas.
Las pruebas pasaban, pero una llamaba la atención: 10 votos simultáneos tardaban 11,6 segundos en el emulador. Sin esa prueba de concurrencia no lo habríamos visto. La transacción leía el documento de la encuesta, de modo que los votos competían por él y se reintentaban una y otra vez.

Lo que resolvió el problema fue preguntarnos si de verdad necesitábamos leer dentro de la operación. No hacía falta:
• FieldValue.increment() suma sin conocer el valor anterior.
• create() falla por sí solo si el documento del votante ya existe.
Eso permite usar un batch atómico, sin lecturas y por tanto sin bloqueos:

Las dos escrituras ocurren juntas o no ocurren. Si alguien vota dos veces, create() falla, se cancela todo el batch y el contador no se infla, aunque las peticiones lleguen a la vez.

La cifra de producción incluye la red y el servidor, así que no es comparable con las otras dos. Lo importante es que los 10 votos se registraron y el total coincidió.
Hay una concesión: el estado de la encuesta se comprueba antes del batch, por lo que un voto que coincida justo con el cierre aún puede contar. En una encuesta es aceptable. En un sistema de pagos no lo sería.

Resultados en vivo sin gastar la cuota

Firestore puede avisar de cada cambio en un documento mediante listeners, y eso hace que los resultados se actualicen solos. El navegador no se conecta a Firestore directamente: el servidor escucha y reenvía por Server-Sent Events.

Figura 2. Encuesta con resultados en vivo.

Una primera idea era un listener por cada navegador, pero Firestore cobra cada documento entregado a cada listener. Con 50 personas mirando, cada voto costaría 50 lecturas. Por eso el servidor mantiene un solo listener por encuesta y lo reparte a todos los conectados; una prueba automática lo verifica.
El mismo razonamiento se aplicó al health check. Render lo consulta periódicamente y, si cada consulta leyera Firestore, gastaría cuota solo en comprobaciones. Separamos /api/health, que no toca la base, de /api/health/ready, que sí la comprueba.

Seguridad
• El navegador nunca habla con Firestore, y firestore.rules deniega cualquier acceso directo.
• Cerrar o borrar una encuesta exige un token que se entrega solo a quien la crea. En la base se guarda únicamente su hash.
• Hay límite de peticiones por IP y cabeceras de seguridad con Helmet.

Despliegue automático en la nube
La aplicación está publicada en Render, un proveedor público, con su base en Firestore, en Google Cloud. No la desplegamos a mano: cada git push a main ejecuta un workflow de GitHub Actions con tres pasos:

  1. Pruebas de integración contra el emulador oficial de Firestore.
  2. Construcción de la imagen Docker.
  3. Si ambos pasan, una llamada al Deploy Hook de Render, que publica la nueva versión. El despliegue automático propio de Render está desactivado (autoDeploy: false en render.yaml), de modo que el único camino a producción pasa por las pruebas. La credencial de Firestore se configura como variable de entorno en Render y nunca entra al repositorio.

Limitaciones
Prefiero dejarlas claras:
• Un voto por navegador, no por persona. Quien borre sus datos locales puede votar de nuevo. Evitarlo exigiría iniciar sesión.
• Escrituras por documento. Google recomienda no sostener más de una por segundo sobre un mismo documento, y aquí todos los votos actualizan el mismo. Una encuesta masiva necesitaría repartir los contadores en varios documentos.
• Borrar no es en cascada. Eliminar un documento no borra sus subcolecciones, así que usamos recursiveDelete.

Qué me llevo
Lo que más me sirvió fue dejar de preguntar "¿cómo guardo esto?" y empezar por "¿cómo se va a leer?". Y la transacción lenta me enseñó otra cosa: el diseño más seguro en apariencia no siempre es el correcto, y una prueba de concurrencia lo detecta antes que un usuario.
Mi compañero Arturo cuenta en su artículo la otra mitad del proyecto: cómo lo probamos y lo desplegamos de forma automática.

title: How to Scrape Goodreads with Node.js: Book Search, Rating Distributions, Reviews, Author Lists, and a Ratings Tracker (2026)
description:
Goodreads is still where most readers log what they read, so it's where the numbers are: how many people rated a book, how those ratings split across one to five stars, what the most-liked reviews say, and which of an author's books carry their reputation. If you build a reading app, do comp titles for a publisher, or just want to know whether a book you're about to pitch is growing, you'll want that data in a script.

Then you search for "Goodreads API" and find out it's gone. This post covers what's left officially, what goodreads.com hands a plain script today, and then builds goodreads.mjs, one Node.js file with no npm dependencies (built-in fetch and node:sqlite, so Node 22.13+). It has six commands:

  1. probe checks what goodreads.com returns to a script and reads the data embedded in a book page
  2. search finds books by title or ISBN
  3. book prints details and the full one-to-five-star rating distribution
  4. reviews pages through community reviews with a cursor and summarizes them
  5. author lists an author's books and shows how concentrated their ratings are
  6. track stores rating snapshots in SQLite and reports new ratings per day between runs

Every command was run on November 13, 2026 on a rented Linux VM (Node 24.22.1), and each output block below is pasted unedited from that session.

Read this first. Goodreads' Terms of Use forbid this kind of collection. Section 1 ("Use of Our Service") of the terms at goodreads.com/about/terms (last revised April 28, 2021) says your license to use the site does not include "any collection and use of any book listings, descriptions, reviews or other material included in the Service" or "any use of data mining, robots, or similar data gathering and extraction tools." So scraping Goodreads is against its terms, whoever does the fetching. Read the terms yourself and think about the legal risk for your use case before you run anything here, and use the official options below wherever they cover what you need. Reviews are also personal writing by real people: don't republish them, and keep only what you need.

Is there still a Goodreads API?

Not for new projects. In December 2020 Goodreads stopped issuing new developer keys and said it planned to retire the public API. Today goodreads.com/api just redirects to the homepage (you'll see the 302 in Step 1). Old keys you may find in blog posts and GitHub repos don't help a new project.

What you can still use without scraping:

  • Your own library export. Under My Books, "Import and export" gives you a CSV of your own shelves, ratings, and review dates. If you only need your own reading data, stop here.
  • Open Library. The Internet Archive's Open Library API is open and has ISBN, work, and author lookups. It has ratings too, but far fewer: on November 13 it had about 200 ratings for Project Hail Mary, versus about 1.94 million on Goodreads.

If you need Goodreads' own ratings, distributions, or reviews, there's no official route left. That's what the rest of this post is about.

Step 1: See what goodreads.com sends a script

Book pages are a Next.js app. The HTML contains a <script id="__NEXT_DATA__"> tag with the page's Apollo GraphQL cache, so you don't need to parse markup. The cache holds Book:..., Work:..., Review:..., and User:... entries. The rating statistics live on the work (all editions together), not on the edition you asked for.

#!/usr/bin/env node
// goodreads.mjs - Goodreads book, review, and author data in Node.js (22.13+), no npm dependencies.
// Usage: node goodreads.mjs <probe|search|book|reviews|author|track> ...
import { DatabaseSync } from "node:sqlite";
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

const KEY = process.env.SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY ?? "";
const API = "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/goodreads";
const UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/130.0 Safari/537.36";
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function get(url, headers = {}) {
  const r = await fetch(url, { headers, redirect: "manual", signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) });
  return { status: r.status, location: r.headers.get("location"), text: await r.text() };
}

function nextData(html) {
  const m = html.match(/<script id="__NEXT_DATA__" type="application\/json">(.*?)<\/script>/s);
  if (!m) throw new Error("no __NEXT_DATA__ on the page (layout changed or you got a block page)");
  return JSON.parse(m[1]).props.pageProps.apolloState;
}

function bookFromApollo(state) {
  const values = Object.entries(state);
  const book = values.find(([k, v]) => k.startsWith("Book:") && v.title)?.[1];
  const work = values.find(([k]) => k.startsWith("Work:"))?.[1];
  const reviews = values.filter(([k]) => k.startsWith("Review:")).map(([, v]) => v);
  return {
    title: book.title,
    isbn13: book.details?.isbn13,
    pages: book.details?.numPages,
    genres: (book.bookGenres ?? []).map((g) => g.genre.name),
    averageRating: work.stats.averageRating,
    ratingsCount: work.stats.ratingsCount,
    ratingsCountDist: work.stats.ratingsCountDist, // [1-star, 2-star, 3-star, 4-star, 5-star]
    textReviewsCount: work.stats.textReviewsCount,
    embeddedReviews: reviews.length,
  };
}

async function probe(bookId) {
  const page = `https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/${bookId}`;
  let real;
  for (const ua of ["curl/8.5.0", "", null, UA]) {
    const res = await get(page, ua === null ? {} : { "user-agent": ua, "accept-language": "en-US,en;q=0.9" });
    const label = ua === null ? "Node default UA" : ua === "" ? "empty UA" : ua.slice(0, 15);
    console.log(`GET /book/show/${bookId} [${label.padEnd(15)}] -> ${res.status}, ${res.text.length} bytes`);
    if (ua === UA) real = res;
  }
  const b = bookFromApollo(nextData(real.text));
  console.log(`  __NEXT_DATA__: "${b.title}" avg ${b.averageRating}, ${b.ratingsCount} ratings, dist ${JSON.stringify(b.ratingsCountDist)}`);
  console.log(`  genres: ${b.genres.slice(0, 5).join(", ")} | ${b.textReviewsCount} text reviews, ${b.embeddedReviews} embedded in the HTML`);

Step 2: A small API client

Reading the book page yourself works for a single book's stats. Paging through reviews means reverse-engineering the reviewFilters cursor that robots.txt asks crawlers to stay away from, and search results and author lists are more page types to parse, each of which can break on its own. So from here on, the script reads Goodreads through ScrapeAtlas*. Its OpenAPI spec lists five Goodreads routes: /v1/goodreads/search, /book, /book-reviews, /author, and /author-books. You call them with GET and pass your key in the x-api-key header. Each successful call, partial results included, costs 1 credit. Failed calls are free. Using an API doesn't change the terms: Goodreads' rules still apply to the data, whoever fetches it.

async function sa(path, params) {
  if (!KEY) throw new Error("Set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY first.");
  const qs = new URLSearchParams(Object.entries(params).filter(([, v]) => v != null && v !== ""));
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const r = await fetch(`${API}/${path}?${qs}`, { headers: { "x-api-key": KEY }, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(120_000) });
    const body = await r.json().catch(() => ({}));
    if (r.ok && body.success !== false) return body;
    const code = body.failure?.code ?? `http_${r.status}`;
    const retry = r.status === 429 || r.status >= 500;
    if (!retry || attempt === 3) {
      const err = new Error(`${path}: ${code} - ${body.failure?.message ?? r.statusText}`);
      err.code = code;
      throw err;
    }
    await sleep(2000 * attempt);
  }
}

// Accepts 54493401, "54493401-project-hail-mary", or a full goodreads.com URL.
function idOf(x) {
  const m = String(x).match(/(?:show\/)?(\d+)/);
  if (!m) throw new Error(`not a Goodreads id or URL: ${x}`);
  return m[1];
}

sa() retries 429 and 5xx up to three times and throws errors that carry the API's failure.code (for example not_found), so the commands can tell a missing book from a network problem. idOf() takes 54493401, 54493401-project-hail-mary, or a full book or author URL.

Step 4: Book details and the rating distribution

The average rating hides most of the story. Two books with a 4.2 can look completely different: one where nearly everyone gave 4 stars, and one that splits between 5 and 1. The distribution shows which one you have.

function ratingStats(dist) {
  const counts = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((s) => dist[s] ?? 0);
  const total = counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const mean = counts.reduce((a, c, i) => a + c * (i + 1), 0) / total;
  const share = (stars) => stars.reduce((a, s) => a + counts[s - 1], 0) / total;
  return { counts, total, mean, five: share([5]), low: share([1, 2]) };
}

function bar(n, max, width = 30) {
  return "#".repeat(Math.round((n / max) * width));
}

async function book(ref) {
  const { book: b } = await sa("book", { id: idOf(ref) });
  const st = ratingStats(b.ratingsDistribution);
  const max = Math.max(...st.counts);
  console.log(`${b.title} - ${b.authors.map((a) => a.name).join(", ")} (${b.work?.firstPublishedAt?.slice(0, 4) ?? "?"})`);
  console.log(`  ${b.format ?? "?"}, ${b.pages ?? "?"} pages, ISBN13 ${b.isbn13 ?? "-"}, ${b.publisher ?? "-"}`);
  console.log(`  avg ${b.averageRating} from ${b.ratingsCount} ratings (mean of distribution: ${st.mean.toFixed(3)}), ${b.reviewsCount} text reviews`);
  for (let s = 5; s >= 1; s--) {
    const n = st.counts[s - 1];
    console.log(`  ${s}* ${String(n).padStart(9)} ${(100 * n / st.total).toFixed(1).padStart(5)}%  ${bar(n, max)}`);
  }
  console.log(`  5-star share ${(100 * st.five).toFixed(1)}%, 1-2 star share ${(100 * st.low).toFixed(1)}%`);
  console.log(`  genres: ${b.genres.slice(0, 6).map((g) => g.name).join(", ")}`);
  const wins = (b.awards ?? []).filter((a) => a.designation === "WINNER");
  if (b.awards?.length) console.log(`  awards: ${b.awards.length} listed, ${wins.length} wins (${wins.slice(0, 3).map((a) => a.name).join(", ")})`);
  if (b.series?.length) console.log(`  series: ${b.series.map((s) => s.position ? `${s.title} #${s.position}` : `${s.title} (no position given)`).join(", ")}`);
  return b;
}

Step 5: Reviews with cursor pagination

/v1/goodreads/book-reviews returns 30 reviews per page and a nextCursor. Pass it back as cursor to get the next page. The function below stops when there's no cursor or a page brings nothing new, deduplicates by review ID, and can write everything to JSONL.

async function reviews(ref, pages = 3, out = null) {
  const id = idOf(ref);
  const seen = new Map();
  let cursor = null;
  let total = null;
  for (let p = 1; p <= pages; p++) {
    const res = await sa("book-reviews", { id, cursor });
    total = res.totalCount;
    let fresh = 0;
    for (const r of res.reviews) if (!seen.has(r.id)) { seen.set(r.id, r); fresh++; }
    console.log(`page ${p}: ${res.reviews.length} reviews (${fresh} new), totalCount ${res.totalCount}`);
    cursor = res.nextCursor;
    if (!cursor || fresh === 0) break;
    await sleep(500);
  }
  const all = [...seen.values()];
  if (out) writeFileSync(out, all.map((r) => JSON.stringify(r)).join("\n") + "\n");
  summarizeReviews(all, total);
  if (out) console.log(`saved ${all.length} reviews to ${out}`);
  return all;
}

function summarizeReviews(all, total) {
  const byStar = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((s) => all.filter((r) => r.rating === s).length);
  const words = all.map((r) => (r.text ?? "").split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const median = words[Math.floor(words.length / 2)] ?? 0;
  console.log(`\n${all.length} unique reviews of ~${total}; stars 5..1: ${byStar.slice(1).reverse().join(" / ")}; unrated: ${byStar[0]}`);
  console.log(`median length ${median} words; spoiler-flagged ${all.filter((r) => r.spoiler).length}; written by Goodreads authors ${all.filter((r) => r.reviewer?.isAuthor).length}`);
  const years = {};
  for (const r of all) years[r.createdAt.slice(0, 4)] = (years[r.createdAt.slice(0, 4)] ?? 0) + 1;
  console.log(`created per year: ${Object.entries(years).sort().map(([y, n]) => `${y}:${n}`).join(" ")}`);
  console.log("most-liked:");
  for (const r of [...all].sort((a, b) => b.likeCount - a.likeCount).slice(0, 3)) {
    console.log(`  ${r.rating}* ${String(r.likeCount).padStart(6)} likes  ${r.reviewer.name.slice(0, 28)}: "${(r.text ?? "").replace(/\s+/g, " ").slice(0, 70)}..."`);
  }
}

Two things here will mislead you if you don't know them:

  • The order isn't random. Reviews come in Goodreads' default order, which puts popular, much-liked reviews first. In these 120, 14 of the 116 star-rated reviews are 1 or 2 stars (12%).   • totalCount moves around. It came back as 265185 and 265252 on different pages of the same run, and the book's reviewsCount was 265795. Treat it as an estimate.

Also: rating is 0 when someone wrote a review without picking stars (4 here). Each review has both text and textHtml, and the HTML can contain images and quotes. reviewer.isAuthor marks Goodreads author accounts, which is useful if you want to separate fellow writers from regular readers. Two reviews are from 2020, before the book came out in May 2021. Those are most likely advance-copy readers.

Step 7: A ratings tracker in SQLite

A single snapshot can't tell you whether a book is gaining readers. Two snapshots can. track stores the totals and all five buckets for each book, then compares the newest snapshot with the previous one.

function openDb(file) {
  const db = new DatabaseSync(file);
  db.exec(`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS snapshot (
    book_id INTEGER, taken_at TEXT, title TEXT, avg REAL, ratings INTEGER, reviews INTEGER,
    s1 INTEGER, s2 INTEGER, s3 INTEGER, s4 INTEGER, s5 INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (book_id, taken_at))`);
  return db;
}

async function track(refs, dbFile = "goodreads.db") {
  const db = openDb(dbFile);
  const prevStmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM snapshot WHERE book_id = ? ORDER BY taken_at DESC LIMIT 1");
  const insert = db.prepare("INSERT INTO snapshot VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)");
  const now = new Date().toISOString();
  for (const ref of refs) {
    let b;
    try {
      ({ book: b } = await sa("book", { id: idOf(ref) }));
    } catch (e) {
      console.log(`${ref}: skipped (${e.code ?? e.message})`);
      continue;
    }
    const d = b.ratingsDistribution;
    const prev = prevStmt.get(b.id);
    insert.run(b.id, now, b.title, b.averageRating, b.ratingsCount, b.reviewsCount, d[1], d[2], d[3], d[4], d[5]);
    if (!prev) {
      console.log(`${b.title.slice(0, 34).padEnd(34)} first snapshot: ${b.ratingsCount} ratings, avg ${b.averageRating}`);
      continue;
    }
    const hours = (Date.parse(now) - Date.parse(prev.taken_at)) / 3.6e6;
    const added = b.ratingsCount - prev.ratings;
    const deltas = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((s) => d[s] - prev[`s${s}`]);
    console.log(`${b.title.slice(0, 34).padEnd(34)} +${added} ratings in ${hours.toFixed(1)}h (${(added / hours * 24).toFixed(0)}/day), +${b.reviewsCount - prev.reviews} reviews, avg ${prev.avg} -> ${b.averageRating}`);
    console.log(`${"".padEnd(34)} new ratings by star 5..1: ${deltas.slice().reverse().map((x) => (x >= 0 ? "+" : "") + x).join(" / ")}`);
  }
}
