                                   new ratings by star 5..1: +6 / +6 / +2 / +1 / +0

That's a useful result, because it shows a trap. Project Hail Mary and Sunrise on the Reaping didn't move at all in half an hour. That's almost certainly not because nobody rated them. Goodreads refreshes these counters in batches: between 04:01 and 04:04 UTC that morning, Project Hail Mary jumped from 1,938,620 to 1,938,684 ratings, then stayed exactly there for over half an hour, and the book page itself (fetched directly at 04:36 UTC) showed the same frozen number. The Martian happened to get a refresh in between, so its "768/day" is just 15 ratings extrapolated from a 28-minute window.

So don't run the tracker every few minutes. Run it once a day at the same time, and look at trends over a week or more. The per-star deltas are where it gets interesting over time: if a book's new ratings start landing in the 1- and 2-star buckets while the average still reads 4.4, the average is being held up by old ratings.

To run it every day, a cron line is enough:

15 6 * * * cd /opt/goodreads && SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY=... node goodreads.mjs track 54493401 214331246 18007564 >> track.log 2>&1

Each track run costs one credit per book. The database is a single snapshot table, so SELECT taken_at, ratings, s5, s1 FROM snapshot WHERE book_id = 54493401 gives you a chart-ready series.

The CLI 

const [cmd, ...args] = process.argv.slice(2);
const flag = (name, def) => {
  const i = args.indexOf(`--${name}`);
  if (i === -1) return def;
  const v = args[i + 1];
  args.splice(i, 2);
  return v;
};

try {
  if (cmd === "probe") await probe(idOf(args[0] ?? "54493401"));
  else if (cmd === "search") { const page = Number(flag("page", 1)); await search(args.join(" "), page); }
  else if (cmd === "book") for (const a of args) { await book(a); console.log(); }
  else if (cmd === "reviews") { const pages = Number(flag("pages", 3)); const out = flag("out", null); await reviews(args[0], pages, out); }
  else if (cmd === "author") { const pages = Number(flag("pages", 2)); await author(args[0], pages); }
  else if (cmd === "track") { const db = flag("db", "goodreads.db"); await track(args, db); }
  else console.log("usage: node goodreads.mjs <probe|search|book|reviews|author|track> ...");
} catch (e) {
  console.error(`error: ${e.message}`);
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

Gotchas I hit, collected

  • The official API is gone. /api redirects to the homepage. Old tutorials with key= URLs won't help.
  • Check the body, not the status. Empty UA → 403. Everything else gave a mix of 200, 202, and 503 within minutes, from the same IP.
  • Only 30 reviews per book page. More need the reviewFilters cursor, which robots.txt disallows.
  • Stats belong to the work. All editions share them. Key on work.id.
  • Title search returns summary spam. Search by ISBN, or check the author and ratingsCount.
  • Counts differ between surfaces. Search, book page, and author list can be a dozen or so ratings apart at the same moment.
  • Review order is popularity, not a sample. Low-star reviews are over-represented among the most-liked.
  • rating: 0 means no stars, not a zero-star review.
  • series[].position can be null, and publishedYear is often null for editions and box sets.
  • Bibliographies include anthologies and forewords. Filter on the first author's ID.

Wrapping up

  • There's no Goodreads API for new projects. Your own CSV export and Open Library cover some needs.
  • Book pages embed a full Apollo cache with rating distributions, genres, awards, and 30 reviews, but the site answers a script inconsistently.
  • The five-bucket distribution says more than the average does, and it lets you check your parsing.
  • Reviews show what's popular, not what's typical. Don't estimate sentiment from the first pages.
  • Two SQLite snapshots are enough to measure new ratings per day and which star buckets they land in.

What do you use Goodreads data for: reading apps, comp titles, or something else? I'd like to hear how you deal with the summary-book spam in search.

*I build it.

title: Toggle Switch Animation CSS: A Stretchy, Accessible Switch From a Checkbox
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

TL;DR: A good toggle switch animation in CSS starts with a real checkbox, so it works with keyboards and screen readers for free. Slide the knob with transform, fade the track colour, and add a short stretch to the knob while it moves. Finish with role="switch", a visible focus ring and a reduced-motion fallback. Or start from the Stretch Toggle in the Capture Motion gallery.

Toggles look simple, but they are one of the most touched controls in any settings screen. A flat jump from left to right works. A knob that leans into the move and settles feels like a physical switch. The extra polish costs about ten lines of CSS.

The markup: a checkbox and a label

Start with a native input. Do not build a toggle from a div and JavaScript. You would have to rebuild focus, keyboard support and form submission by hand.

<label class="switch">
  <input type="checkbox" role="switch" class="switch__input">
  <span class="switch__track" aria-hidden="true">
    <span class="switch__knob"></span>
  </span>
  <span class="switch__label">Email notifications</span>
</label>

The role="switch" tells assistive tech this is an on and off switch, not a checkbox in a list. Screen readers then announce "on" or "off" instead of "checked". The visible track and knob are decoration, so they get aria-hidden="true".

Hide the input visually, but keep it in the page so it can take focus:

.switch__input {
  position: absolute;
  opacity: 0;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
}

Avoid display: none here. It removes the input from the tab order and from the accessibility tree.

Toggle switch animation CSS: track and knob

Now style the track and the knob. Use custom properties so sizes stay in sync.

.switch {
  --w: 52px;
  --h: 30px;
  --pad: 3px;
  --knob: calc(var(--h) - var(--pad) * 2);
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 12px;
  cursor: pointer;
}

.switch__track {
  position: relative;
  width: var(--w);
  height: var(--h);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: #c9c9d1;
  transition: background-color 220ms ease-out;
}

.switch__knob {
  position: absolute;
  top: var(--pad);
  left: var(--pad);
  width: var(--knob);
  height: var(--knob);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: #fff;
  box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / .25);
  transition: transform 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}

Slide the knob

When the input is checked, move the knob across the track. The distance is the track width minus the knob and both paddings.

.switch__input:checked + .switch__track .switch__knob {
  transform: translateX(calc(var(--w) - var(--knob) - var(--pad) * 2));
}

Use transform, not left. It stays smooth because it avoids layout on every frame.

Change the track colour

The track colour is the main on and off signal. Make it clear.

.switch__input:checked + .switch__track {
  background: #17171c;
}

Check contrast between the knob and the track in both states. A pale grey off track on a white page can fail. A darker border on the track is a simple fix.

Add the stretch: the detail that makes it feel alive

A real knob does not teleport. A stretchy version widens while it travels, then snaps back to a circle when it lands. You can fake this with a short keyframe animation on the knob's width.

The trick is that the knob must stretch toward where it is going. Moving right, it grows on its right edge. Moving left, it grows on its left edge. Two keyframe sets handle that, one per direction.

@keyframes stretch-on {
  45% { width: calc(var(--knob) * 1.35); }
}
@keyframes stretch-off {
  45% {
    width: calc(var(--knob) * 1.35);
    margin-left: calc(var(--knob) * -0.35);
  }
}

.switch__knob {
  animation: stretch-off 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}
.switch__input:checked + .switch__track .switch__knob {
  animation: stretch-on 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}

Keyframes with only a 45% step animate from and back to the knob's normal size. The knob is pinned by left, so a wider knob grows rightward on the way on. On the way off, the negative margin-left shifts the growth to the left edge. Because the animation name changes on each flip, the browser restarts it every time.

Two trade-offs to know. Animating width and margin triggers layout, but on one small knob the cost is tiny. The off animation also plays once on page load, which most people never notice. If it bothers you, add a class to the switch after the first change and scope the animations to it.

Keep the peak stretch between 1.2 and 1.4 times the knob size. Beyond that, it reads as a bug, not a feature.

Timing guidance:

Part Duration Easing
Knob travel 220 to 300 ms Decelerating curve
Stretch peak About 40 to 50% of the travel Same curve
Track colour 180 to 240 ms ease-out

If you want a springy settle instead, CSS linear() can approximate a spring in pure CSS. Our guide on CSS linear() easing shows how to build one.

Accessibility: role, focus and reduced motion

A toggle that looks great but fails a keyboard user is a broken toggle. Cover these three points.

Role and label

You already have role="switch" and a visible text label inside the label. Clicking the text toggles the switch, and screen readers read the label. If the visible text is not enough context, add aria-describedby pointing to a helper sentence.

Focus ring

Because the input is hidden, show focus on the track instead:

.switch__input:focus-visible + .switch__track {
  outline: 2px solid #fb9f3d;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

:focus-visible shows the ring for keyboard users without flashing it on every mouse click. Space toggles a native checkbox, so keyboard support comes for free.

Reduced motion

Respect users who ask for less motion. Drop the stretch and shorten the slide, but keep the colour change.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .switch__knob {
    animation: none;
    transition-duration: 1ms;
  }
}

The state is still clear from the knob position and the track colour. Motion is decoration on top of that, never the only signal.

Quick accessibility checklist

  • [ ] Native input type="checkbox" with role="switch"
  • [ ] Visible text label inside the label
  • [ ] Focus ring on :focus-visible
  • [ ] On and off states differ by more than colour alone (knob position)
  • [ ] Contrast checked in both states
  • [ ] Reduced-motion fallback in place

A ready version: the Stretch Toggle in the Capture Motion gallery

Building it yourself is a good way to learn the parts. If you would rather start from a finished piece, the Capture Motion gallery has a Stretch Toggle. The knob leans toward where it is going, stretches on the way, and inverts the track as it lands.

From the gallery, you can customize it and then:

  • Send it to Figma as a Figma Motion timeline, with the keyframes and easing on tracks you can edit.
  • Copy it as code in CSS, Framer Motion or GSAP, or download it as HTML and React.

It sits next to other interactive components in the gallery. If you like the stretch idea, the liquid tabs animation uses the same leading-edge principle on a tab indicator. For a bigger gesture on a confirm action, see the slide to confirm button animation.

Seen a toggle on another site that you want to study? The Capture Motion extension can record its real keyframes, durations and easing, then export them to code or Figma. Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use.

FAQ

Should a toggle switch use a checkbox or a button?

A checkbox with role="switch" is the simplest robust choice. It works in forms, supports the Space key and reports its state. A button with aria-pressed also works, but you have to handle the state in JavaScript.

How long should a toggle switch animation be?

Around 220 to 300 ms for the knob travel. Shorter feels abrupt, longer feels sluggish on a control people flip often.

How do I make the knob stretch while it moves?

Animate scaleX or the knob width with a short keyframe that peaks near the middle of the move. Set transform-origin so the knob grows toward its direction of travel.

How do I keep the animation accessible?

Use a native checkbox with role="switch", a visible label, a :focus-visible ring and a prefers-reduced-motion fallback. Make sure the on state is clear from the knob position, not just colour.

Is there a ready-made animated toggle I can use?

Yes. The Stretch Toggle in the Capture Motion gallery can be sent to Figma as a Figma Motion timeline or copied as code.

title: Button Hover Animation CSS: Fill Sweep, Lift, Arrow Nudge and Glow
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

TL;DR: A good button hover animation in CSS is short, eased and honest about what the button does. Use 150 to 300 ms, an ease-out curve, and animate only transform, opacity and colour where you can. Below are four effects with code and the timing that makes them feel right. You also get a reduced-motion fallback and a faster way to copy a hover you like.

Buttons are the most hovered element on any page. A small, well-timed response tells the user "this is clickable, and it is ready". A slow or bouncy one feels laggy. The difference is rarely the effect itself. It is almost always the duration and the easing.

Start with a solid base button

Every effect below builds on the same base. Keep the transition on the base rule, not the :hover rule, so it plays both ways.

.btn {
  position: relative;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 8px;
  padding: 12px 20px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 10px;
  background: #17171c;
  color: #fff;
  font: 600 15px/1 system-ui, sans-serif;
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: transform 200ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1),
              box-shadow 200ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1),
              background-color 200ms ease-out;
}

List each property in transition. Writing transition: all is tempting, but it animates things you did not plan, like a width change from a font swap.

Four button hover animation CSS effects

Each effect suits a different job. Pick one per button style, not all four at once.

1. Fill sweep

A colour fills the button from one side. It reads as "you are about to commit to this", which suits primary actions.

.btn-sweep {
  overflow: hidden;
  isolation: isolate;
}
.btn-sweep::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  z-index: -1;
  background: #fb9f3d;
  transform: scaleX(0);
  transform-origin: left;
  transition: transform 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}
.btn-sweep:hover::before {
  transform: scaleX(1);
}

Animating scaleX on a pseudo-element is cheaper than animating width or background-position. The browser can run it on the compositor. If the text colour changes too, check contrast on both the start and end colours.

2. Lift and shadow

The button rises a few pixels and its shadow grows. It feels physical, and it works well on cards and secondary buttons.

.btn-lift:hover {
  transform: translateY(-2px);
  box-shadow: 0 8px 20px rgb(0 0 0 / .18);
}
.btn-lift:active {
  transform: translateY(0);
  box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / .18);
  transition-duration: 80ms;
}

Keep the lift small: 1 to 3 px. Larger lifts make a row of buttons look jumpy. The :active rule gives a quick press back down, which closes the loop.

Animating box-shadow repaints on every frame. On one button it is fine. On a grid of fifty cards, put the larger shadow on a pseudo-element and fade its opacity instead.

3. Arrow nudge

An arrow icon slides a few pixels in the direction of travel. It is the quietest of the four and suits links like "Read more" or "Next".

.btn-arrow svg {
  transition: transform 180ms ease-out;
}
.btn-arrow:hover svg {
  transform: translateX(4px);
}

Put the :hover on the button, not on the icon. The button is the bigger target, and the user hovers it first. This is the "hover the container, move the child" pattern.

4. Glow

A soft, coloured halo appears behind the button. It works on dark backgrounds and for one hero call to action per page.

.btn-glow::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: -6px;
  z-index: -1;
  border-radius: 14px;
  background: #fb9f3d;
  filter: blur(14px);
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 240ms ease-out;
}
.btn-glow:hover::after {
  opacity: .55;
}

The blur is set once and never animated. Only opacity changes, which keeps it smooth. Animating filter: blur() directly is much heavier.

Timing and easing: the part that makes it feel right

Most hover problems are timing problems. Use this table as a starting point.

Effect Duration Easing Notes
Fill sweep 220 to 300 ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1) Larger area, so slightly longer
Lift and shadow 150 to 220 ms ease-out Press back in about 80 ms
Arrow nudge 150 to 200 ms ease-out Small distance, short time
Glow 200 to 260 ms ease-out Fade only

A few rules hold across all four:

  • Stay between 150 and 300 ms. Under 100 ms, the user barely sees it. Over 300 ms, the button feels slow to respond.
  • Use ease-out for entering. The motion starts fast and settles, so the button answers the pointer right away.
  • Leave faster than you enter. A hover-out at about two thirds of the hover-in time feels tidy. Put a second transition on the :hover rule to make them differ.
  • Avoid bouncy springs on buttons. Overshoot is fun on toggles and tabs. On a button you hover many times a day, it gets tiring.

To make the exit faster than the entry:

.btn { transition: transform 140ms ease-in; }          /* leaving */
.btn:hover { transition: transform 220ms ease-out; }   /* entering */

The rule that applies is the one for the state you are moving into. That is why the faster value sits on the base rule.

If you want to go deeper on curves, our guide to CSS easing functions explained covers cubic-bezier() and steps() with examples.

Respect reduced motion and touch screens

Some users ask their system for less motion. Honour that with a media query. Keep the colour change, drop the movement.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .btn,
  .btn::before,
  .btn::after,
  .btn svg {
    transition-property: opacity, background-color, color;
  }
  .btn-lift:hover,
  .btn-arrow:hover svg {
    transform: none;
  }
}

On phones, a tap can leave a hover style stuck until the user taps elsewhere. Wrap hover-only motion in a hover media query:

@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) {
  .btn-lift:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }
}

Two more checks before you ship:

  • Give :focus-visible the same visual change as :hover, so keyboard users get the same feedback.
  • Never rely on motion alone to show state. A disabled button should look disabled even with no animation.

Copy a hover you like instead of guessing the values

You often see a button hover on a real site and want the same feel. Guessing is slow. You eyeball 200 ms, it turns out to be 320 ms, and the easing was a custom curve you would never have picked.

DevTools can help when the hover is a plain CSS transition. Force :hover in the Styles pane and read the rule. It gets harder when the hover is started by JavaScript, uses GSAP, or animates several layers with different delays. Our walkthrough on how to capture hover animations covers each case.

Capture Motion reads the real values for you:

  1. Open the page in Chrome and start the Capture Motion extension.
  2. Pick the button, or its container if an inner icon moves too.
  3. Play the hover. The extension triggers a real :hover state through the Chrome DevTools Protocol, attached only during the capture.
  4. Preview the capture. You see each animated property with its keyframes, duration, delay and easing.
  5. Export it. With a free account, copy the CSS, Framer Motion or GSAP code, or send it to Figma as a Figma Motion timeline.

It records CSS transitions and keyframes, the Web Animations API, GSAP and Lottie. That covers the cases where DevTools shows no timing to read. Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use. Take the timing and easing, then apply them to your own button.

A quick checklist before you ship

  • [ ] Duration between 150 and 300 ms
  • [ ] Ease-out on enter, slightly faster exit
  • [ ] Only transform, opacity and colours animate
  • [ ] :focus-visible matches :hover
  • [ ] Reduced-motion fallback in place
  • [ ] Hover motion wrapped in @media (hover: hover)
  • [ ] Contrast checked at both ends of a colour change

Want a ready example with stagger and hover? See the animated avatar stack build, or browse the gallery on capturemotion.dev.

FAQ

What is a good duration for a button hover animation in CSS?

Between 150 and 300 ms covers almost every case. Small moves like an arrow nudge sit near 150 to 200 ms. Larger fills can run to 300 ms. Past that, the button starts to feel slow.

Which easing should I use for button hovers?

Use ease-out or a curve like cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1) for the hover-in. It responds instantly and settles gently. For the hover-out, a slightly shorter ease-in or ease-out works well.

Why does my hover animation stutter?

You are probably animating layout or paint properties like width, top or filter. Switch to transform and opacity. For shadows and glows, animate the opacity of a pseudo-element that already has the shadow.

How do I make hover-out faster than hover-in?

Put the faster transition on the base rule and the slower one on the :hover rule. The browser uses the transition of the state the element is moving into.

Can I copy the exact hover timing from another website?

Yes. For plain CSS, force :hover in Chrome DevTools and read the rule. For JavaScript or GSAP hovers, a capture tool like Capture Motion records the real keyframes, durations and easing. Only copy from sites you own or have permission to use.

title: How to Find Slow Queries in SQL Server (DMVs and Query Store)
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Find the slow queries in SQL Server fast: ready-to-run DMV scripts for running queries, top CPU and reads, wait stats, plus Query Store reports.    Before you can tune anything, you need to know which queries are the problem. Users report "the system is slow", but the cause is usually a handful of queries. SQL Server already tracks everything you need to find them. This guide gives you the scripts I use first, in the order I use them.

1. What is running right now?

When the system is slow at this moment, start with live requests. This shows each running query, how long it has run, what it is waiting on and whether it is blocked:

SELECT
    r.session_id,
    r.status,
    r.start_time,
    DATEDIFF(SECOND, r.start_time, SYSDATETIME()) AS running_seconds,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.cpu_time,
    r.logical_reads,
    DB_NAME(r.database_id) AS database_name,
    t.text AS query_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id <> @@SPID
  AND r.session_id > 50
ORDER BY r.start_time;
  • A non-zero blocking_session_id means the query is waiting for another session's locks.
  • wait_type tells you what it is waiting for, such as locks (LCK_M_*), disk (PAGEIOLATCH_*) or parallelism (CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER).

2. Which queries cost the most overall?

For general slowness, the most useful view is total cost across all executions. A 50 ms query that runs 100,000 times an hour usually matters more than one 30-second report that runs once a day.

-- Top 10 queries by total CPU since they were cached
SELECT TOP (10)
    qs.execution_count,
    qs.total_worker_time / 1000                        AS total_cpu_ms,
    qs.total_worker_time / qs.execution_count / 1000   AS avg_cpu_ms,
    qs.total_logical_reads / qs.execution_count        AS avg_reads,
    qs.total_elapsed_time / qs.execution_count / 1000  AS avg_duration_ms,
    SUBSTRING(t.text, (qs.statement_start_offset / 2) + 1,
        ((CASE qs.statement_end_offset WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(t.text)
          ELSE qs.statement_end_offset END - qs.statement_start_offset) / 2) + 1) AS statement_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) t
ORDER BY qs.total_worker_time DESC;

Change the ORDER BY to qs.total_logical_reads DESC to find the queries that read the most data, which are often the ones missing an index.

Keep in mind that this view only covers plans still in cache. It resets on restart and loses queries whose plans were evicted, which is why Query Store is better for history.

3. Use Query Store for history and regressions

Query Store records query performance and plans over time inside the database. It is on by default in Azure SQL Database and for new databases in SQL Server 2022. In SSMS, open the database, expand Query Store, and use:

  • Top Resource Consuming Queries: the heaviest queries over any time window you pick.
  • Regressed Queries: queries that got slower, usually because their plan changed.
  • Queries With High Variation: queries whose duration swings a lot, a common sign of parameter sniffing.

The big advantage is history: you can compare "today, when it was slow" with "last week, when it was fine".

4. Check what the whole server waits on

Wait statistics show where SQL Server spends its waiting time overall, which points you to the type of problem:

SELECT TOP (10)
    wait_type,
    wait_time_ms / 1000.0 AS wait_seconds,
    waiting_tasks_count
FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats
WHERE wait_type NOT LIKE 'SLEEP%'
  AND wait_type NOT LIKE '%QUEUE%'
  AND wait_type NOT IN ('BROKER_TASK_STOP','CHECKPOINT_QUEUE','WAITFOR',
                        'XE_TIMER_EVENT','DIRTY_PAGE_POLL','HADR_FILESTREAM_IOMGR_IOCOMPLETION')
ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC;
  • PAGEIOLATCH_*: reading data from disk. Often too many reads, so look for missing indexes or scans.
  • LCK_M_*: blocking. Look at long transactions and locking patterns.
  • SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD with high CPU: CPU-heavy queries.
  • WRITELOG: transaction log writes. Look at many tiny commits or slow log storage.

Wait stats accumulate since the last restart, so compare snapshots taken a few minutes apart for a picture of current load. This filter list is a starting point; there are more harmless background waits you may want to exclude.

5. Pick one query and fix it

Once you have a shortlist, take the query with the biggest total impact, get its actual execution plan, and look for scans on large tables, key lookups, bad row estimates and warnings. Fix one thing at a time, and compare logical reads and CPU before and after.

Quick routine

  1. Slow right now? Check sys.dm_exec_requests for blocking and waits.
  2. Slow in general? Rank queries by total CPU and reads.
  3. Slower than last week? Use Query Store's Regressed Queries.
  4. Check wait stats to understand the type of bottleneck.
  5. Tune the top query, then measure again.

Related reading:

  • SQL Server Query Store: A Practical Beginner's Guide
  • How to Read a SQL Server Execution Plan
  • SQL Server Index Tuning for Beginners

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: Opening a 50 GB text file without reading it
description:
Most text editors open a file by reading all of it. That is fine for a source file and hopeless
for a 50 GB log: the work done before the first screen grows with the file, and no processor
saves you from that. BigText, a free and open-source editor for Windows, Linux and macOS, is
built on the opposite rule:

The time and memory of every operation depend on the text on screen, not on the size of the
file.

This article is about the five decisions that make that rule hold, what they measure at on a
50 GB file, and what I learned building the editor with an AI model.


BigText opens a 50 GB log at once, jumps to its end and its middle, searches it with a regular expression and follows a growing log.

A fast machine does not help

All the numbers below come from one machine:

Part
Model HP Z2 Tower G1i Workstation
CPU Intel Core Ultra 9 285, 24 cores
Memory 192 GB DDR5-5600
GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090
Disks 2 × 1 TB Samsung NVMe SSD
OS Windows 11 Pro

On a machine like this everything should be instant, and for years opening a big log, CSV export
or SQL dump was not. The editor would think for a long time, the window would freeze, sometimes
it would refuse the file.

The reason is simple. Notepad++ allocates a buffer for the whole file and warns above 2 GB that
opening it may take minutes
(source).
VS Code keeps roughly the size of the file in memory
(VS Code blog).
Reading a file from start to end and splitting it into lines is one sequential pass, usually on
one thread: one of the 24 cores works and the rest wait. The GPU has nothing to do with it.

That pass is easy to measure, because BigText makes it too, in the background, to build its line
index. For the 50 GB file it takes 17–18 seconds on this machine, with the file already in the
operating system's cache, that is, in RAM. An editor that makes this pass before it shows the
first line keeps you waiting at least that long in the best case. If the file does not fit in
memory, it does not open at all.

The problem is not the hardware but the algorithm. If the work before the first screen is
proportional to the file, no processor helps.

The idea: read what the screen needs

A screen holds fifty or sixty lines, a few kilobytes of text. Showing the first screen of a 50 GB
file does not require reading 50 GB. Five decisions follow from that.

1. The file is mapped, not loaded, and in windows

Memory mapping (mmap, MapViewOfFile on Windows) ties a file to the program's address space
without reading anything. The actual read happens when the program touches a byte, and only for
that page. Opening a file this way costs the same whatever its size.

There was a surprise here. On Windows, mapping a 50 GB file as one view costs almost 100 MB of
memory by itself: the system keeps 8 bytes of bookkeeping for every 4 KB page. Memory use
depended on the file size again; with a 50 GB file open the process took 205 MB.

So the single view became a cache of windows: 288 MB each, starting every 256 MB so that a line
near a boundary always fits in one of them, with at most six mapped at a time. Memory dropped from
205 MB to 107 MB and stopped depending on the file size.

2. Opening reads the first megabyte

When a file opens, a worker thread reads its first megabyte. From that sample it decides the
encoding (UTF-8, UTF-16, Windows-1251 and others), the line endings and whether the file is
binary. That takes 1.1–1.4 ms. Then the lines that fit on the screen are drawn, and the file is
open.

3. The screen is anchored to a byte offset, not a line number

An ordinary editor knows its position as "I am at line one million", and to know that it has to
count every line before it. BigText knows "I am at byte 26,843,581,344". The scrollbar is
proportional to bytes too. Jumping to the middle of the file counts nothing: it reads a few
kilobytes there, finds the nearest line start and draws.

The line number is shown at once anyway. At first it is an estimate with a ~ in front of it;
when the index reaches that part of the file, the exact number replaces it.

4. A sparse line index: one number per 64 KB

Storing where every line starts is expensive. My test file has 453,565,956 lines; a full table of
offsets would take 3.4 GB. BigText splits the file into 64 KB blocks and stores one number per
block: how many lines came before it.

file:   [ 64 KB ][ 64 KB ][ 64 KB ][ 64 KB ] ...   819 thousand blocks
index:     0        554     1,107    1,661   ...   lines before each block (example)

For the 50 GB file the index is 8.12 MB, 0.016 % of the file. "Go to line N" finds the block by
binary search and then scans at most 64 KB of text, counting newlines with SIMD.

The index is built in the background from the start of the file, at about 2.9 GB/s: 17–18 seconds
for 50 GB. The editor works normally meanwhile: scrolling, jumping and searching all work.

5. The UI thread never waits

The UI thread reads only the bytes on screen. Indexing, search, replace and save run on worker
threads, each with a progress bar and a cancel button. The goal is that no frame takes more than
16 ms. While the 50 GB file was being indexed, a page-down frame took 1.2 ms on average.

There is one more edge case. A file can be a single enormous line, such as a 2 GB minified JSON
document. Such lines are split softly every 64 KB, so working out any line never reads more than
128 KB.

Measurements

The numbers come from a release build of BigText 0.4.1 and its own benchmark
(bigtext --bench-ui). Each file was measured three times, with the files in the OS cache.

1 GB 10 GB 50 GB
Lines 9,069,553 90,713,192 453,565,956
Open request → first screen of text painted 31–32 ms 31–32 ms 31–35 ms
of which opening the file and detecting the encoding 1.3–1.4 ms 1.3 ms 1.3 ms
Background indexing 0.4 s 3.7 s 17.4–17.7 s
Index size 130 KB 2.03 MB 8.12 MB
Memory of the idle editor 98–99 MB 100–101 MB 107–109 MB

The important row is the second one: the file grew fifty times and the time to open did not
change. Six more runs on the 50 GB file gave 35 ms at worst.

Memory hardly changed either. Most of the 100 MB is the graphical interface itself: the core
without a window holds the 50 GB file and its index in 12.1 MB.

What the 30 ms means needs saying precisely. Opening the file and detecting the encoding take
1.2 ms and laying out the first screen of text 0.03 ms; the rest is waiting for the window's next
frames. The benchmark stops the clock when the editor has painted the text, which does not
include the frame reaching the monitor, and it opens the file in the program's first frame.

In a window that is already running there are two cases. With another file open, the 50 GB file
opened in a new tab in 10 ms. The first file opened into an empty window took 0.1–0.2 s to show:
the editor's own work is again a few milliseconds, and the rest is the GPU driver or the
compositor presenting the first frame with a document in it. The cause of that one slow frame is
not known yet; a second file in the same window paints in about 10 ms.

Other numbers on the 50 GB file:

  • Go to line before the index was ready: no frame above 2.1 ms.
  • Plain-text search: 4.0–4.3 GB/s, the whole file in 12 seconds.
  • Regular-expression search: 3.6–4.3 GB/s.


A regular expression found 830 matches in the 50 GB file in 15.5 seconds. The results list is under the text; a click jumps to a match.

Editing and saving

Viewing is half of it; big files also need editing. BigText uses a piece table, an old and proven
structure. The original file is never touched. Typed text goes into a separate buffer, and the
document is a list of pieces: "this part of the original, then this part of the buffer". A
thousand edits in a 50 GB file take a few kilobytes.

Saving streams the result into a temporary file in the same folder, flushes it to disk and only
then replaces the original atomically (ReplaceFileW on Windows, which keeps attributes and
permissions). If something fails on the way or the power goes off, the original stays intact.

The 25th gigabyte of the same file in hex view. Jumping there is instant too.

I built it with Claude

I built BigText with Anthropic's Claude model, through Claude Code. Claude wrote the code. My
part was to say precisely what was needed, check the result and choose the next step. Every one
of the 174 commits in the repository names Claude as co-author.

It started with one document: the goal of the program, eight architecture rules that must not be
broken, measurable speed targets and a list of edge cases that must not break it. It is in the
repository as prompt.md. Four of its requirements:

  • Never read the whole file into memory.
  • Never block the UI thread; no task on it may take more than 16 ms.
  • Do not use ready-made editor components: they all keep the whole document in memory.
  • Measure the speed targets and report real numbers.

Claude first wrote a plan (PLAN.md), then worked through it in stages: opening and viewing,
search, replace, editing and saving, encodings. After each stage it measured on the test files
and compared the result with the target.

  • 24 October, 09:46: the first commit.
  • 24 October, 14:38: version 0.1.0, five hours later.
  • 29 October: version 0.4.1, the one measured above.
  • 10–12 November: versions 0.5.0 to 0.7.3.

Today the project has 151 Rust files, about 70,000 lines of code including tests, 335 tests and an
in-app GUI self-test that drives the real window with synthetic mouse and keyboard input through
229 checks.

Four lessons:

  1. Make the goal measurable. Not "it should be fast" but "the first screen in under 200 ms" and "under 200 MB of memory with a 50 GB file open". A goal like that can be checked.
  2. Write the architecture rules down first. The decisions that mattered most were made before any code was written.
  3. Measurement beats guessing. Memory dropping from 205 MB to 107 MB was not in the plan; it came out of a measurement.
  4. Give the AI tests it can run itself. When the GUI self-test was added, it found four bugs, which were then fixed.

What else it does

Besides opening big files, BigText:

  • searches with regular expressions, filters lines like grep and replaces across the whole file;
  • follows growing logs like tail -F, jumps to a time, filters by level and opens logs on servers over SSH;
  • opens CSV and TSV as tables with sorting, statistics and pivots, and JSON with a structure view;
  • compares two huge files;
  • reads files inside .gz, .zst, .zip and .tar without unpacking them by hand;
  • highlights code in about two dozen languages and formats, with a folder side bar and go-to-file, for the files that are not huge.

Two logs compared: four differences in 425 thousand lines, found in 0.04 seconds.

Try it, or measure it yourself

BigText runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. It is free and open source under the MIT license, and
its interface is in eight languages. The test-file generator and the benchmark come with the
portable downloads:

gen-testfiles --only random-lines-10g.txt
bigtext --bench-ui testdata/random-lines-10g.txt --report report.txt

The 50 GB file is the 10 GB one joined five times.

  • Website: https://erkinbek.github.io/bigtext/
  • Downloads: https://github.com/Erkinbek/bigtext/releases/latest
  • Source: https://github.com/Erkinbek/bigtext

If you have a file your editor cannot open, try it in BigText and tell me how it went.

A note on this article: like the code, it was written with Claude, from the project's notes and measurements. I checked it before publishing, and the replies in the comments are mine.
