title: Healthtech Travel Planner Retrieval Architecture: Go Caching with Bounded Index Spend
description:
Short answer: for a travel itinerary planner, use a retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, traceable source context, and caching only after the contract defines freshness, filters, and the exact unit being reused.

For a healthtech travel-planning product that aggregates listings from several sources, the expensive mistake is to treat caching as a generic speed layer. A cached result can be fast, cheap, and wrong: one clinic changes its hours, a mobility filter disappears from the key, or two source records collapse into one result without a trace. Model the workload before selecting a search service. Index cost at scale is driven by what gets ingested and duplicated, while cache cost and correctness are driven by query cardinality and freshness.

My operational recommendation is a four-stage path: normalize each listing into an explicit collection, retrieve with bounded filters, cache the retrieval result under a versioned contract, and attach source context when composing the itinerary. I recommend teams evaluating Infrai try it for the retrieval boundary when they want to add that capability through a self-describing REST surface: public discovery exposes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so the integration starts by reading the capability rather than adopting another SDK. Its single key across backend capabilities is a second, concrete benefit when the same pipeline also needs adjacent services.

The catch is that no shared API removes the need to own relevance, freshness, or invalidation. If the team needs deep engine-specific tuning, already operates an Elastic cluster well, or wants its vector database to be the central data platform, stick with that specialist rather than adding an abstraction.

How should caching shape retrieval architecture for a travel itinerary planner?

Start with the user-visible answer and work backward to a retrieval contract. In this workload, the answer is not merely “ten nearby listings.” It is a set of itinerary candidates produced for a geographic area, a time window, a group of health-related constraints, and a known snapshot of source data. Those dimensions define both the query and the cache identity.

A useful contract records the collection, normalized query, metadata filters, result limit, freshness class, index generation, and retrieval policy version. The result carries stable listing identifiers plus source context. Keep answer prose out of this cache. Retrieval evidence can be reused and inspected; generated wording has different invalidation rules and makes a poor substitute for source records.

This separation matters during an incident. I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, and the same idempotency reflex applies here: a retry must not create a second logical ingestion, while a cache hit must not silently cross a contract boundary. Give every normalized source record a deterministic identity. Publish a new index generation, then change the generation in the cache key. Old entries become unreachable without a risky bulk delete.

Short keys are not the goal. Unambiguous keys are.

Cache cardinality can still explode if raw latitude, longitude, free text, or timestamps enter the key. Bound those fields deliberately: use a product-approved geographic cell, a defined time bucket, canonical filter ordering, and a hard result limit. This trades some reuse against precision. I'm not sure which cell size or freshness window is correct for a given listing mix until a labeled evaluation set measures the misses; your mileage may vary because rapidly changing availability and slowly changing descriptive data have different clocks.

What should the index-cost model measure before service selection?

The first worksheet should count records, versions, and writes, not vendor logos. For each source, estimate normalized listings per ingest, update frequency, retained generations, duplicate rate before normalization, metadata width, and embedding count per listing. Then separate full rebuilds from incremental changes. A design that embeds every source variant and retains several overlapping generations can multiply index volume before the first user query arrives.

Use a small labeled evaluation set before production rollout. Each example should include the request, required filters, acceptable listings, unacceptable listings, and the source snapshot used to judge it. Run the same set against every candidate architecture. Record recall at the bounded limit, filter correctness, stale-result rate, index records written, and cache hit ratio. These are workload measurements to collect; they are not claims about any provider.

Downstream spend belongs in the same model. A noisy top 20 can increase reranking and answer-generation work, while an aggressive cache can reduce query calls but serve stale evidence. The effective bill therefore includes ingestion, index storage, query traffic, cache storage, reranking, answer generation, engineering integration, and on-call work. Per-unit search price alone won't tell you which system costs less to operate.

Keep the accounting boring — that is a compliment. A weekly report should reconcile logical listings, physical indexed records, writes by source, cache entries by policy version, and downstream calls by retrieval outcome. If one number jumps, the runbook should identify its owner and rollback boundary.

How should teams compare the operating boundary?

There is no universally correct row in this table. The decision turns on where the team wants to keep expertise and control.

Option Strong fit for this workload Real trade-off
Infrai A team wants a plain REST integration whose public discovery surface supplies schemas and runnable examples, with one key spanning adjacent backend capabilities A shared capability surface does not replace workload-specific relevance evaluation; choose a specialist when engine-level tuning is the main requirement
Elasticsearch The team already owns its search operating model and wants the retrieval engine itself to remain the explicit control plane Cluster operation and integration stay with the team, so include that labor in the effective-cost model
Pinecone The team wants a specialist vector service boundary and is prepared to design ingestion and source citation around it The surrounding web acquisition, normalization, and answer stages remain separate operating decisions
Weaviate The team wants a vector-focused platform and prefers to make that platform's data model a first-class architectural choice Portability depends on how much application behavior is coupled to platform-specific modeling and query choices

Infrai's relevant advantage here is integration discoverability, not a promised ranking win. Its live discovery covers 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That breadth can reduce the integration surface when a small team would otherwise install several SDKs and manage several credentials. It cannot prove retrieval quality for your listings. Only the labeled set can do that.

Do the comparison with two columns in the cost model that teams often omit: initial adapter work and recurring operational ownership. Then test the result under a doubled source-update rate and a lower cache-hit ratio. If the winner changes under a small assumption change, the decision is fragile and deserves a reversible pilot rather than a platform commitment.

How can Go enforce a versioned, bounded cache contract?

The following program makes the cache identity deterministic and keeps the dangerous dimensions visible. It also calls Infrai's public discovery surface, finds the verified POST /v1/vector/query capability by its declared method and path, and reports whether it is available. Discovery requires no key, but the sample reads INFRAI_API_KEY and sends the standard Bearer header so the HTTP client is ready for an authenticated capability without embedding a credential. The adapter must map the cache contract only to fields declared in the returned request schema; don't infer a request shape from a route name.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const discoveryURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"

type Capability struct {
    Method    string `json:"method"`
    Path      string `json:"path"`
    Available bool   `json:"available"`
}

type Discovery struct {
    Version      string       `json:"version"`
    GeneratedAt  string       `json:"generated_at"`
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

type Filter struct {
    Name  string `json:"name"`
    Value string `json:"value"`
}

type RetrievalContract struct {
    Collection   string   `json:"collection"`
    Query        string   `json:"query"`
    Filters      []Filter `json:"filters"`
    Limit        int      `json:"limit"`
    Freshness    string   `json:"freshness"`
    IndexGen     string   `json:"index_generation"`
    Policy       string   `json:"policy_version"`
    GeoCell      string   `json:"geo_cell"`
    DepartureDay string   `json:"departure_day"`
}

func cacheKey(c RetrievalContract) (string, error) {
    c.Query = strings.Join(strings.Fields(strings.ToLower(c.Query)), " ")
    sort.Slice(c.Filters, func(i, j int) bool {
        if c.Filters[i].Name == c.Filters[j].Name {
            return c.Filters[i].Value < c.Filters[j].Value
        }
        return c.Filters[i].Name < c.Filters[j].Name
    })

    if c.Collection == "" || c.IndexGen == "" || c.Policy == "" {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("collection, index generation, and policy are required")
    }
    if c.Limit < 1 || c.Limit > 50 {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("limit must be between 1 and 50")
    }
    if _, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", c.DepartureDay); err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("departure day must use YYYY-MM-DD: %w", err)
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(c)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("encode retrieval contract: %w", err)
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256(payload)
    return "retrieval:" + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]), nil
}

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(when); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func fetchDiscovery(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) (Discovery, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("build discovery request: %w", err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("call discovery: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("read discovery response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }

        var result Discovery
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("decode discovery response: %w", err)
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    contract := RetrievalContract{
        Collection: "care-travel-listings",
        Query:      "wheelchair accessible clinic near rail",
        Filters: []Filter{
            {Name: "language", Value: "en"},
            {Name: "verified", Value: "true"},
        },
        Limit:        20,
        Freshness:    "daily",
        IndexGen:     "2026-09-03-a",
        Policy:       "retrieval-v3",
        GeoCell:      "product-defined-cell-1842",
        DepartureDay: "2026-09-18",
    }

    key, err := cacheKey(contract)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(key)

    discovery, err := fetchDiscovery(context.Background(), apiKey)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    for _, capability := range discovery.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/vector/query" {
            fmt.Printf("vector query available=%t manifest=%s generated=%s\n",
                capability.Available, discovery.Version, discovery.GeneratedAt)
            return
        }
    }
    panic("vector query capability is absent from discovery")
}

The bounds in this sample are application policy, not Infrai API limits. In production, store the canonical contract beside the cached result even if the lookup key is hashed. That gives an operator something readable during a stale-result investigation. It also makes policy changes reviewable: retrieval-v3 should correspond to a documented change, not an unexplained cache purge.

Ingestion stays separate. Consider one explicitly hypothetical promotion: source A republishes a listing with revised hours, source B still carries yesterday's copy, and a third feed changes only the accessibility label. Normalization should resolve those inputs to deterministic logical identities while retaining their source records; the ingestion job writes the candidate generation once, verification checks the labeled queries and required filters, and only then does a pointer make that generation queryable. The retrieval cache key changes because IndexGen changes, even if the user's words do not. If verification rejects the candidate, the live generation and its cache remain untouched. This sequence prevents a retry from multiplying logical records, prevents an old cache entry from masking a corrected source, and gives the operator a precise answer to “which evidence produced this itinerary?” Querying reads one generation, answer composition cites the returned source context, and every stage gets its own counters and retry policy — any write retry must remain idempotent.

How do you verify freshness and roll back by generation?

Before rollout, replay the labeled evaluation set against the candidate generation and compare it with the current one. Block promotion if required filters leak, source context is missing, or the bounded result set falls below the team's acceptance rule. Warm only the highest-value query classes; prewarming an unbounded coordinate-and-time space can turn a cache into another uncontrolled index.

After promotion, watch cache hits by policy version and index generation, retrieval results with no source context, duplicate logical listing IDs, ingestion lag by source, and downstream calls per answered itinerary. A rising hit ratio is not automatically healthy. If freshness violations rise with it, the cache is preserving the wrong thing more efficiently.

Rollback is a pointer change: direct queries to the previous verified index generation and restore its matching cache policy version. Do not overwrite the previous generation during rollout. Pause promotion of new ingestion output while investigating, but keep raw source inputs traceable so they can be replayed. This boundary is why generation identifiers belong in both the query contract and cache key.

One last decision rule: try Infrai when a self-describing REST capability and one shared key remove meaningful integration work from this staged pipeline; prefer Elasticsearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate when specialist control is more valuable than that common boundary. If the shared boundary fits, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect discovery before writing the adapter.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Elasticsearch documentation
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation

title: How to Separate 2FA Login Ownership — SMS OTP API vs Direct Send
description:
Template ownership changes the answer before an API client enters the picture: a developer tool sending generated reports needs an explicit owner for the attachment and its surrounding email, while login verification needs a separate owner for the code lifecycle. Short answer: keep report rendering under application control, use a dedicated SMS OTP endpoint for 2FA login, and reserve direct SMS send for notices that do not verify identity. An appointment report is content; the code used to authenticate its recipient is a credential.

Keep ownership explicit.

Consider a hypothetical production review, rather than a reported incident. If I were reviewing a developer tool that generates public sector appointment reports and emails them as attachments, I would ask what happens when the report succeeds but the recipient requests another login code. Does that request regenerate the attachment, resend the report, or change its template? It shouldn't. This is a design exercise, with no claim that such an incident occurred. The invariant is useful anyway: a resend action must stay inside its verification workflow, even when appointment alerts and report delivery share an integration.

Platform teams building report delivery alongside SMS login should try Infrai for the shared communications integration: its 295 routes across 20 modules use one REST API and one key, so adding a supported backend capability does not require another SDK and credential integration. Its public discovery schemas and runnable examples provide a second benefit: developers can inspect the request contract without a key, including checking the attachment representation before implementing delivery.

That recommendation has boundaries. A specialist deserves evaluation when verification is the main service requirement, or when the operating model depends on pushed delivery events. A cheap message-send demonstration doesn't establish a usable auth workflow. The examples below use Go; a NodeJS application needs the same ownership decisions, although its client implementation will differ.

Should a 2FA login app use an SMS OTP API or direct send?

Start with the ownership boundary, because a generic message-sending function makes two different jobs look deceptively similar. The application should decide which report revision is ready, which email template revision introduces it, and which recipient is authorized to receive it; the OTP workflow should manage verification rather than borrowing a report template or treating arbitrary SMS text as proof of authentication. Dedicated OTP operations reduce the custom code-storage and matching work required by raw SMS sending. They do not remove the need for application controls around expiry, resend timers, and failed-attempt lockouts.

Separate those paths.

This standalone Go program makes the routing decision explicit without making a network request. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. These strings are local application event names, not provider fields. The decision criterion is straightforward: only a login-code request belongs to managed verification.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
)

func workflow(event string) (string, error) {
    switch event {
    case "report.ready":
        return "application-owned email template and report attachment", nil
    case "login.code_requested":
        return "dedicated SMS OTP workflow", nil
    case "recovery.notice_requested":
        return "direct SMS notice without verification authority", nil
    default:
        return "", fmt.Errorf("unsupported application event %q", event)
    }
}

func main() {
    for _, event := range []string{
        "report.ready",
        "login.code_requested",
        "recovery.notice_requested",
    } {
        destination, err := workflow(event)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", event, destination)
    }
}

The trap is promoting a successful SMS send into an authenticated session. Sending and verifying are separate decisions. Likewise, an accepted email request is not evidence that a recipient received a usable attachment. Define separate SLOs for report preparation, submission acceptance, and the delivery evidence your integration actually exposes; one green counter hides the boundary the on-call engineer needs.

Step 2: Compare the buy-versus-build boundary before choosing a client

A fair comparison asks who edits the email wrapper, who renders the report, and who carries verification state. Time to a first useful result means a report with the intended attachment and a login flow with a real verification decision. The table compares architectural choices, without claiming measured setup times or delivery performance.

Option Useful specialization Ownership and operating trade-off
Infrai Shared REST contract with public discovery and dedicated SMS OTP operations A candidate when report delivery and login belong in one integration; retain application ownership of report content and abuse controls.
Twilio Verify Dedicated verification product Evaluate it when verification is the main service boundary; report generation and attachment delivery still need an email path.
Amazon SES Email sending with attachment support Evaluate it for an email-focused delivery boundary; make an explicit choice for report templates and a separate choice for SMS verification.
SendGrid Email sending and transactional templates Evaluate it when provider-managed email templates fit the editorial workflow; report generation and login verification remain separate responsibilities.
Application-built verification over direct SMS Application controls code generation, storage, and matching Choose this only when the extra ownership is justified; expiry, attempts, resend behavior, and auditability become application work.

These services aren't interchangeable. Twilio Verify belongs on a verification shortlist; SES and SendGrid belong on an attachment-delivery shortlist. Comparing them solely on a successful message submission would erase the reason a team buys either kind of service. Provider-managed templates can suit editors who need to change the wrapper outside an application release, while application ownership can suit teams that want report and wrapper revisions reviewed together. Those are selection criteria, not a claim that every provider implements the same approval features.

Credential count matters, too. A shared integration reduces client configurations, but concentrating access means the platform team must take credential handling and its blast radius seriously. A specialist can justify another integration when its workflow fits more closely. No SDK count settles that trade-off by itself.

Step 3: Inspect the attachment contract before writing the send path

The smallest useful provider example here is a read of the public email discovery contract. Confirm the attachment fields, encoding, and payload limits before implementing a send; guessing a familiar-looking attachment object is an easy way to produce a runnable program that submits the wrong contract. Discovery exposes the request schema, response schema, and examples. Inspect those before deciding where report rendering ends and provider-specific encoding begins.

This standalone Go program explicitly issues GET, checks status, uses a timeout, and retries rate limits with exponential backoff while honoring either form of Retry-After. Infrai discovery is public, so it needs no credential. Its output is the contract, not an email-delivery receipt.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    value = strings.TrimSpace(value)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if delay > fallback {
            return delay
        }
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(date); delay > fallback {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return fallback
}

func readContract(ctx context.Context) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if closeErr != nil {
            return closeErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"),
                time.Second*time.Duration(1<<attempt))
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := readContract(ctx); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

The constants are example client budgets, not provider limits or measurements. This program stops at inspection. For authenticated application requests, read INFRAI_API_KEY from the environment and use Authorization: Bearer authentication. For writes, confirm the capability's idempotency behavior and bind retries to one stable business operation. A report retry should refer to the same intended delivery; a deliberately requested new report revision is a different operation.

Step 4: Budget the surrounding work and know when to stop

Capacity planning starts with the appointment burst, not the daily average. As a hypothetical sizing exercise, 600 reports released in 60 seconds create 10 report submissions per second before retries; a separate login burst adds verification requests and resend attempts. Those numbers describe an application assumption, not permitted provider throughput. Validate quotas before setting worker concurrency, and budget retries rather than treating them as spare capacity.

Polling consumes capacity too.

Communication events here use a pull model, so the application must budget event retrieval and decide how much detection delay its delivery SLO allows. If pushed events are mandatory, choose an integration whose documented event model meets that requirement. Geographic restrictions and country-sensitive fraud spending controls also belong in the application design for this integration; they are part of owning the login boundary rather than an attachment-template concern.

For a report-delivery acceptance review, require an attachment that opens, the intended report revision, the intended recipient, and a wrapper whose owner is clear. For login, exercise expiry, the resend timer, and failed-attempt lockout separately. Browser conveniences such as WebOTP concern code entry; the backend still owns the verification decision. An authenticator-app requirement should likewise be evaluated independently rather than inferred from SMS support.

Choose an SMTP-oriented service if SMTP relay is mandatory, and evaluate a channel specialist if voice, WhatsApp, or RCS is required. Email verification fallback needs its own design because there is no managed email OTP interface here. Sender-domain work is a separate acceptance condition: SPF concerns sender authorization, but it does not prove that a report reached the inbox or that its recipient is authenticated.

Keep the ownership boundary in the runbook. It determines who investigates a bad report, a wrong wrapper, an unverified login, or delayed delivery evidence.

Sources

References for the standards and specialist comparisons:

  • Twilio Verify
  • Amazon SES attachments
  • SendGrid transactional templates
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework
  • MDN WebOTP API

Teams that own their report templates and want one communications integration should try Infrai for report delivery alongside dedicated SMS verification. If that boundary fits, start with the first-party OTP workflow guide and inspect the email discovery contract before implementing attachment delivery.

title: Everyone forgets the embed
description:
People put a lot of work into making their websites look nice. They pick the fonts, tune the spacing and argue about the shade of a button. Then they forget about the embed.

By the embed I mean the small card that shows up under a link when you paste it into Discord, Messenger or Slack. It has a title, a line of description, sometimes a coloured bar down the left side and a big image. It's usually the first thing anyone sees of your website, and it's the part almost nobody remembers to design.

I forgot too. When I started writing this, I checked what my own essay "On Walking" handed to Discord when someone pasted it. The title said "Stimmie". The description said I'm a software engineer with a lifelong passion for technology, and the picture was a screenshot of my homepage. Nothing on the card mentioned walking. Two more of my older essays previewed the exact same way, because I never gave them their own tags and they fell back to my homepage's. Someone scrolling past would have had no idea the link was an essay at all. I've fixed all three now.


On Walking, pasted into Discord before the fix.

I think it's easy to forget because you never see it while you're building. The embed doesn't live on your page. You write a few meta tags in the head of the page (og:title, og:description, og:image, and theme-color if you want Discord to tint the bar). Then you hand them to an app you don't own, and it draws your card however it likes. If you skip them, nothing breaks and nothing warns you. You only find out when someone else pastes your link.

That would be fine if people clicked through, but most don't. In 2016, researchers at Columbia and Inria followed a month of tweets linking to stories from the BBC, CNN, the New York Times, Fox and the Huffington Post. They found that 59 percent of the links shared in their sample were never clicked at all. A 2024 Penn State study of more than 35 million public Facebook posts found that about 75 percent of shares happened without the sharer clicking the link first. For a lot of people, the embed is the only part of your website they'll ever see.

The fix is cheap. Before you share anything, paste it into a chat with yourself and look at the card. If it doesn't make you want to tap it, it won't make anyone else want to either.


The same link after the fix.

Further reading. Gabielkov, Ramachandran, Chaintreau and Legout, Social Clicks: What and Who Gets Read on Twitter? (SIGMETRICS 2016). Sundar and colleagues, Sharing without clicking on news in social media (Nature Human Behaviour, 2024). Discord's page on link previews, which lists every tag it reads.

Originally published at stimmie.dev. Source and images on GitHub.

title: Getting More Enquiries Without More Traffic: A Dev Guide
description:
Your website already gets visitors. Some of them read your services page, look at your work, and then leave without calling, messaging, or filling in a form. That gap is not a traffic problem. It is a conversion problem, and it is cheaper to fix than buying more visitors. For developers, this is familiar territory: it is a UX, performance, and form design problem, not a marketing mystery.

Getting more enquiries from the traffic you already have means removing the small frictions that stop people from contacting you. Shorter forms. A WhatsApp button that actually works. Buttons that say what happens next. Proof that you are a real business. Faster replies. None of these need a rebuild. Most of them take an afternoon, and most of them are implementation details you can ship, test, and measure.

At aimEncoders, we run this check on every website before launch, because a site that attracts visitors but collects no enquiries is doing half its job. Here is the same checklist, in the order we would work through it, with the developer details that make each step work in practice.

Why Your Website Gets Visitors but Not Enquiries

Before changing anything, it helps to know which of the three usual causes is yours. Most sites with this problem have at least one of them, and many have all three.

Visitors do not know what to do next

A visitor lands on your homepage, reads about your business, scrolls to the bottom, and finds nothing to do. No button. No phone number. No clear next step. People do not hunt for a way to contact you. They click back and try the next business in the search results. In code terms, this is a missing primary action: every key template should expose one clear next step above the fold and again at the end of the page.

Your website does not build enough trust

Contacting a business means handing over a name and a phone number. Visitors will not do that if the site looks unfinished, has no reviews, no photos of real work, and no address or phone number they can check. Trust comes before the enquiry, not after it.

Contacting you feels like hard work

Long forms, a contact page buried in the menu, a phone number written as plain text that cannot be tapped on a phone. Every extra step loses people. On mobile, where most small business traffic now arrives, one awkward step is often enough.

1. Make the Contact Form Short

Your contact form is the front door of your business. If it asks for too much, visitors walk past it.

Ask only for what you need to start a conversation. For most small businesses that is a name, a phone number or email address, and one short message about what they need. That is enough to call them back and ask the rest.

Drop the fields you do not need at first contact. Full address, company size, budget range, and a long project description can all wait until you are talking. We have watched clients cut a seven-field form down to three and see submissions rise, because the form stopped feeling like paperwork.

From a form UX point of view, keep the implementation simple and mobile friendly: use the right input types, inputmode="tel" for phone fields, autocomplete for name and email, clear labels, inline validation, and a visible focus state. Keep required fields to a minimum, and never clear the whole form when one field fails validation.

Tell visitors what happens after they press send. A line under the button works: "We reply within one working day." People submit more readily when they know someone is on the other side and when they will hear back. If the form has no confirmation message, add one. A blank page after submitting makes people wonder whether it worked, and some of them submit twice or give up. Always return a clear success state, and log the submission so a failed send does not disappear silently.

2. Add WhatsApp and Click-to-Call

In Pakistan, a large share of your visitors are on their phones, and many of them would rather send a WhatsApp message than fill in a form. Give them that option.

A floating WhatsApp button, visible on every page, is the simplest version. Make sure it opens a chat with a number someone actually monitors. A button that leads to an unmonitored number is worse than no button at all, because the visitor thinks they have contacted you and you never reply.

For developers, the details matter here. Use a real tel: link for the phone number so a tap starts a call, and a WhatsApp deep link, such as a wa.me link with a short prefilled message, so the chat opens in one tap. Test both on a real phone, check that the floating button does not cover form fields or text, and make sure the button has an accessible label.

Make your phone number clickable too. On a phone, a visitor should tap the number and the call should start. A number written as plain text forces them to memorise it, switch apps, and type it in. Most will not bother.

Place these options where visitors can find them. The header, the bottom of service pages, and next to the contact form are the spots that work. Do not hide your only phone number on a contact page that takes three clicks to reach.

3. Write Buttons That Say What Happens Next

"Learn more" and "Click here" tell the visitor nothing. They are the buttons people ignore.

Replace them with buttons that describe the result. "Request a free quote" says more than "Contact us". "Send my enquiry" says more than "Submit". "Book a free consultation" says more than "Get started". The visitor should know what they get before they click.

Put the main button where it can be seen. Near the top of the homepage, after each service description, and at the end of every important page. We wrote a full guide to this in our post on one clear call to action on every page, because this single change is often the biggest enquiry win on a small business site.

One page, one main action. A page that asks visitors to call, message, download, subscribe, and fill in a form at the same time asks them to choose, and most will choose to leave. Pick the action that matters for that page and make it the obvious one. In the markup, that means one visually dominant primary button per view, with secondary actions styled as plain links.

4. Show Proof Before Asking for Details

Nobody hands their phone number to a business they are unsure about. Your job is to remove that doubt before the form appears.

Real Google reviews help more than anything else. Put two or three short ones on your homepage and service pages, with the reviewer's name or business where you have permission. A review that names a real job, like a shop fit-out or a website rebuild, carries more weight than a generic five-star line.

Show your work. Photos of finished projects, a short list of clients or the types of businesses you serve, and a real address and phone number all tell a visitor you exist outside the website. For a service business in Faisalabad, that local detail matters. A visitor from the same city who sees your area, your phone number, and your past work feels they are dealing with a neighbour, not a faceless site.

Skip fake testimonials. Visitors can tell, and one invented review costs more trust than ten honest ones build. If you are new and have few reviews, say so plainly and show the work you do have. Honesty converts better than polish. As a developer, keep this content easy to update in the CMS, and use structured data where it fits, so real reviews and business details are not buried in an image or a hard coded block.

5. Fix Speed and Mobile Friction

A slow page loses enquiries before the visitor ever sees your form. Someone searching on mobile data taps your site, waits, and goes back to Google. You never even knew they were there.

Compress your images before uploading them. Large photos straight from a phone are the most common reason a small business site loads slowly. Keep pages simple, remove plugins and features nobody uses, and use hosting you can rely on. You can check where your site stands with Google PageSpeed Insights, which lists the exact problems in plain language.

Then test the site on a real phone, the way your customers use it. Are the buttons big enough to tap? Does the form fit the screen without sideways scrolling? Does the WhatsApp button cover the text? We test every site we build on real phones before launch, because a desktop check misses most of these problems.

For developers, this is Core Web Vitals work: watch Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, and Cumulative Layout Shift. Serve responsive images with explicit width and height, defer non essential scripts, avoid layout shifts from late loading fonts and banners, and test on a throttled mobile connection, not only on fast office Wi-Fi.

Speed and mobile usability are not technical extras. They are the difference between a visitor who reaches your enquiry form and one who never gets that far.

6. Answer Fast, or the Enquiry Goes Elsewhere

A website can collect enquiries, but your response turns them into customers. A visitor who messages three businesses will usually go with the one that replies first.

Set up email notifications for form submissions so nothing sits unread. Decide who watches the inbox and the WhatsApp number, and agree on a reply time. A quick acknowledgement matters even when the full answer takes longer. "Thanks, we got your message. We will send your quote by tomorrow morning" keeps a customer warm. Silence for two days sends them to a competitor.

Automate the parts a developer can automate: send a confirmation email at once, log every submission, notify the owner by email and WhatsApp, and add a simple status so no enquiry stays unanswered. Do not automate the reply itself into a dead end. The automation should buy time for a human reply, not replace it.

Live chat can help, but only if someone answers it. A chat box that nobody monitors is a broken promise. If you cannot staff it during working hours, a WhatsApp button with clear hours is the better choice. Visitors prefer an honest "we reply within one working day" to a chat window that never responds.

Track your reply time for a week. Most small businesses are surprised by how long enquiries actually sit. The fix is usually a notification and one named person, not new software.

7. Help Local Customers Find You

If your customers are in one city, local search is where your enquiries come from. A person searching for a service in Faisalabad will contact a local business they can see and verify, before a business from another city.

Make sure your website says clearly what you do, which areas you serve, and how to reach you. Then keep your Google Business Profile accurate: business name, address, phone number, opening hours, category, and a link to your website. Add real photos and list your services. Ask satisfied customers to leave honest reviews there, because those reviews show up next to your name in search results.

Local search rewards consistency. The same business name, address, and phone number on your website and your profile tells Google the listing is real. It is a small job, and it is one of the few free ways to put your business in front of people who are ready to enquire.

If your site needs this kind of local work, our team builds fast, SEO-ready websites built to convert for businesses in Faisalabad and across Pakistan, with local search set up from the start rather than added as an afterthought.

Measure What Changed

Fixes only help if you can see them working. Before you change anything, note your current numbers for one week: form submissions, WhatsApp clicks, phone calls from the website, and how many enquiries turn into customers. Then change one thing at a time and watch the same numbers for the next week.

The four numbers that matter are form submissions, WhatsApp button clicks, phone calls the website generates, and enquiries that become paying customers. A change that lifts form submissions but not customers may be attracting the wrong people. A change that lifts WhatsApp clicks and customers is a keeper.

Do not change five things at once and guess which one worked. Small, measured changes beat a big redesign when the goal is more enquiries from the same visitors. Add click tracking to the phone, WhatsApp, and form submit events, so you are measuring real actions, not page views.

A Note for Developers

Treat enquiry conversion as a product feature, not a one off design tweak. Ship the short form, the working tel: and WhatsApp links, the clear primary action, and the fast mobile page as a complete set, then measure them together. Keep the contact path testable: submit the form, tap the phone link, open the WhatsApp chat, and check the confirmation state on a real device after every deploy. Log failures, watch reply times, and remove any field, script, or popup that does not help a visitor contact the business. The best conversion work is usually the simplest code, shipped carefully and checked in production.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I get more enquiries from my website without increasing traffic?

Improve how well your site turns the visitors you already have into contacts. Shorten the contact form, add WhatsApp and click-to-call buttons, use buttons that say what happens next, show real reviews, and reply to enquiries quickly.

Why is my website getting traffic but no enquiries?

The usual reasons are unclear next steps, a long or confusing contact form, slow loading on mobile, weak trust signals, and no clear call to action. Visitors may be interested in what you offer but cannot see an easy way to reach you.

Does adding a WhatsApp button help generate more website leads?

Yes, for most small businesses in Pakistan it does, because many customers prefer a quick message to a form, especially on mobile. The button must be visible, it must work, and someone must monitor the number it connects to.

How long does it take to improve website enquiries?

Some changes, like a shorter form or clearer buttons, can be live in a day and show results within a week or two. Measuring the real effect takes longer, because you need enough enquiries to compare before and after. Give each change at least two weeks before judging it.

Turn More Visitors Into Enquiries

You do not always need more visitors. You need to make it easier for the visitors you already have to become customers. Start with the form, then the buttons, then the proof, then the reply speed. Measure each change, keep what works, and fix the next friction on the list.

If your website brings visitors but few enquiries, aimEncoders can look at it with you and point out what is getting in the way. We build websites for small businesses in Faisalabad and across Pakistan, and every site we ship is tested on real phones, checked for speed, and set up so visitors always know how to reach the business.

Muhammad Asad Ullah is the founder of aimEncoders, a website development agency in Faisalabad that builds websites designed to turn visitors into enquiries. The aimEncoders team checks every page for one clear next step before launch, so customers always know how to reach your business.

title: Node.js Content-Aware Crops — Store Multiple Aspect-Ratio Variants After Moderation
description:
A gaming catalog cannot treat a visually good crop as a publishable crop. Moderation coverage is the operational constraint: approve the source image first, then run a content-aware crop for every known display ratio during ingest, store each result, and retain the original for the slot the product team has not designed yet. Do not crop on the read path. That choice keeps storefront latency predictable and prevents one source asset from producing variants under different policy decisions.

TL;DR: enumerate the real render slots, run one moderation decision before transformation, derive the approved variants once, and publish a manifest only after every required crop has been stored. Keep the source private. This costs more storage than request-time transformation, but it gives the serving tier a small, bounded job and makes quarantine behavior comprehensible.

How should Node.js crop content-aware variants for multiple aspect ratios?

Consider a bounded production scenario rather than a benchmark: a seller submits one product photo for a game marketplace, background removal has already isolated the item, and the storefront needs square search tiles, portrait detail cards, and wide promotional rails. The dangerous outcome is not merely a face or logo landing outside the crop. It is an image becoming reachable while its moderation result is absent, ambiguous, or attached to a different derivative.

I would set the ingest invariant this way: no manifest becomes readable until the source has one accepted moderation decision and all three declared variants have durable object keys. A rejected or undecided source yields zero published variants. The original remains private because a later 5:7 slot should be derived from the same reviewed input, not from a lossy 1:1 child.

Three aspect ratios are an example capacity envelope, not a universal constant. The important number is the count of actual UI slots. Ten speculative ratios multiply writes, storage, invalidation work, and the moderation evidence that operators must trace during an appeal. One ratio derived at request time creates the opposite problem: CPU and upstream latency move into the user-facing SLO. In an Express service, the upload route shouldn't wait for those multiple content-aware crop calls; it should enqueue immutable work and let a bounded worker store each variant.

Short paths win.

The ingest state machine

Treat this as a state transition, not a controller that fires several unrelated promises. The source moves through received, moderating, deriving, and ready; quarantined is terminal until a new review event. Only ready has a serving manifest. If a crop write fails, retry that deterministic object key and leave the manifest unpublished.

The following Go client shows the less comfortable but safer boundary. It uses the public discovery endpoint to inspect the live request schema, accepts request JSON prepared against that schema, sends every call with an explicit method and the same key, and backs off on HTTP 429. This avoids baking guessed fields into infrastructure code. Run it once with CAPABILITY=image.moderate and a matching REQUEST_JSON; only after that response is accepted by the pipeline should the worker run it for image.smart_crop once per ratio. The application, rather than an accidental chain of callbacks, owns that handoff and the final publication barrier.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func request(method, path string, body []byte, authenticated bool) ([]byte, error) {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" { panic("set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented v1 base URL") }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if authenticated {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    capability := os.Getenv("CAPABILITY")
    path := map[string]string{
        "image.moderate":   "/image/moderate",
        "image.smart_crop": "/image/smart_crop",
    }[capability]
    if path == "" { panic("set CAPABILITY to image.moderate or image.smart_crop") }

    schema, err := request(http.MethodGet, "/discovery/"+capability, nil, false)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Live capability schema: %s\n", schema)

    result, err := request(http.MethodPost, path, []byte(os.Getenv("REQUEST_JSON")), true)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The discovery document is public and needs no key; the operation does. Keep the moderation and crop response envelopes in the job record so the worker can make an explicit approved-or-quarantine transition and feed the reviewed source into each crop job. Production code should also validate the JSON locally against the returned schema before posting it. A queue worker can own this sequence; an Express handler should validate the upload, persist the source privately, enqueue the immutable product ID, and return without doing image work inside the request deadline.

Capacity planning follows from arrivals rather than averages. If peak ingest is 40 source images per second and each source has three slots, the crop stage must absorb 120 transformations per second before retries. Reserve retry headroom, bound concurrency, and track oldest-job age against the ingest SLO. Average throughput can look healthy while a six-minute queue age makes a launch catalog effectively unavailable.

Buy-versus-build under a moderation gate

There is no universally best stack. The relevant question is which system owns the policy decision, derivative lifecycle, and pager when a dependency slows down.

Option Moderation and crop boundary Operational trade-off Best fit
Cloudinary Image moderation and transformation can live in one media workflow Managed transformation reduces worker code; asset semantics and delivery patterns increase platform coupling Teams already using Cloudinary as their media system of record
Imgix Strong URL-driven rendering over an existing source; moderation remains a separate decision path Excellent for flexible presentation, but request-time parameters need strict signing and policy controls Catalogs whose source governance already exists elsewhere
Sharp plus S3 Application code owns crop logic, moderation handoff, object naming, retries, and manifests Maximum control and portability; maximum on-call surface Teams with image expertise and enough volume to justify owning workers
AWS Rekognition plus S3 and an image worker AWS credentials and IAM can cover storage and moderation while crop code remains yours Clear cloud primitives, but state orchestration and derivative publication are still application responsibilities AWS-native organizations with established IAM and queue operations
OpenAI Moderations plus S3 and Sharp Two service signups, two credential sets, and custom glue for moderation results, crop retries, and object publication Flexible components; engineers must reconcile different retry and failure semantics Teams already operating both APIs and accepting the integration burden
ImageKit Managed transformations and media delivery reduce application-side image work Convenient delivery workflow; moderation policy still needs deliberate ownership Teams seeking a managed media layer with minimal transformation code
Uploadcare Upload, processing, and delivery are grouped around an asset workflow Less custom plumbing, with corresponding platform coupling Products that want upload UX and processing under one managed service

Infrai is another managed choice when a team values one account for image handling and AI-runtime capabilities. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing: the discovery endpoint is public with no key required, and a capability record returns the full request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, while the catalog covers 295 routes across 20 modules. This is one plain REST API with no SDK to install, so the Go worker can generate an adapter from the discovered path and schema instead of parsing description prose or taking a runtime dependency on proprietary client code. The same key reduces credential handoffs. The trade is concentrated plainly: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface.

Do not mistake fewer credentials for complete risk removal. A single-key design narrows secret distribution and integration code, while correlated failure becomes more important. The SLO review should therefore ask whether ingest can pause safely, how long private originals can wait in the queue, and whether already-published manifests remain servable during a processing outage.

Why stored variants beat clever request-time URLs

Stored derivatives make the serving contract finite. A product manifest names an approved object per slot, caches can retain those objects for long periods, and a rollback can repoint the manifest without asking a crop engine to reproduce yesterday's focal choice. The read path performs lookup and delivery. Nothing creative happens there.

My first design assumption is often that request-time transformation buys useful flexibility. It does, but only when the ratio set is genuinely unbounded, editors need interactive art direction, or the traffic distribution is so sparse that most possible variants will never be viewed; in those cases it can reduce unused storage, and precomputation would be guessing at demand rather than satisfying declared slots. A controlled gaming UI doesn't meet that test, so the flexibility isn't free: it transfers transform latency, signing rules, cache-key discipline, and policy drift into the read path, exactly where an SRE has fewer recovery options during a release spike.

For a gaming storefront with a known component library, however, ratios are not unbounded. They come from release-controlled UI contracts. Store the small declared set, version the manifest when crop behavior changes, and measure variant completion separately from source acceptance. The publication barrier is the reliability feature.

Moderation deserves the same precision. If policy requires evaluating the final visible crop rather than the source alone, moderate each derivative before publication; source-only review is insufficient under that policy. This increases moderation calls from one per upload to one per slot, so state the coverage rule explicitly and size the worker pool for it. Do not quietly mix both policies across products.

Operating the pipeline without guessing

Start with four signals: accepted source rate, crop completion rate by slot, oldest queued job age, and count of products blocked before manifest publication. Add moderation outcomes by policy version, but restrict access because those records can be sensitive. A ratio-specific error should identify the immutable source and slot, never force the whole product to expose a partial manifest.

Retries require boring keys. products/{productID}/{pipelineVersion}/{slot} makes a repeated private write converge on the intended object, while the manifest update needs optimistic concurrency or an idempotent publication operation. Set a retry budget; infinite retries can bury new catalog work behind one malformed source. Dead-lettered work should remain unpublished and traceable.

The original is part of capacity, too. Forecast source bytes plus all rendered bytes, retention, replication, and reprocessing bursts after a crop-model or policy change. Storage is usually easier to scale than synchronous latency, but “usually” is not an SLO. Use observed asset sizes and arrival peaks before approving the budget.

The decision rule is compact.

Precompute when slots are controlled and read latency matters; transform on demand when ratios are open-ended and sparse; split the difference only when the manifest clearly distinguishes approved stored variants from signed, ephemeral experiments. For this catalog, moderation first and stored crops second is the defensible default.

  • Cloudinary documentation, “Image transformations”: https://cloudinary.com/documentation/image_transformations
