title: Crypto Withdrawal Risk Monitoring: How CDC Helps
description:
When a withdrawal sits in review, the customer wants to know when it will go through. Your team needs an answer too. Sometimes, the risk service is still waiting for the account data it needs to decide.

Imagine a customer changes their security settings, adds a withdrawal address, and then requests a large withdrawal. There may be a reasonable explanation for all three actions. But your risk system needs to see them together to assess the request.

That becomes harder when the records live in separate systems and arrive at different times. Crypto withdrawal risk monitoring may then rely on an account view that is already out of date. A legitimate request can wait longer, while a suspicious pattern may take longer to surface.

Change data capture (CDC) helps close this gap by continuously delivering committed database changes to downstream systems. BladePipe handles this data delivery layer, with full data loads and ongoing CDC synchronization.

Let's follow a withdrawal workflow built around that delivery layer. We'll look at how account changes reach the risk system and how a decision can affect a withdrawal before funds leave.

Where Crypto Exchanges Can Stop a Withdrawal

Before looking at the data pipeline, it helps to locate the point where a decision can still change the outcome. A withdrawal usually passes through security checks, balance validation, funds reservation, review, wallet execution, and blockchain confirmation.

The order varies by exchange. What matters is whether the risk decision arrives while the exchange can still hold or reject the request.

Stage What needs to be checked Limits of control
Request submission Identity, withdrawal permissions, destination, and available balance Checks must use the source-of-truth transactional system
Awaiting review Recent activity, withdrawal history, and account relationships The workflow can support holds, rejection, or manual review
Wallet execution Whether approval remains valid and relevant state has changed The ability to pause depends on the wallet interface and execution progress
Broadcast or completion Whether further suspicious activity is underway Changing an internal status generally cannot reverse a transaction already sent

This is why the status shown in an internal dashboard needs a closer look. “Under review” does not prove that funds have not been sent. Check when your workflow calls the wallet and when the transaction is broadcast.

If review must finish before execution, every path to the wallet has to respect that requirement. That includes automated jobs, manual actions, and retries. Once that control point is clear, you can work backward to the data the review needs.

How BladePipe Delivers Data for Withdrawal Reviews

For the account in our example, the review might need recent security changes, withdrawal history, and links between the destination address and other accounts. Those inputs may come from different databases.

If each database feeds the risk system through a scheduled batch job, the review may wait for the next refresh. With BladePipe, you can load the existing records first, then keep delivering changes through CDC. This gives downstream consumers a starting dataset and ongoing updates.

For example, a MySQL-to-Kafka DataJob can deliver account and withdrawal table changes to Kafka for your risk consumers to process. Those consumers link the records and evaluate activity. The full path looks like this:

Commit the change → BladePipe CDC → downstream risk processing → decision → current-state checks → allow or block processing.

The important handoff comes after delivery. A new record needs to trigger an evaluation or update an existing one. Otherwise, the data can be current while the withdrawal keeps waiting.

Example: A Security Change Followed by a Withdrawal

Let's follow the same account through a simplified example of that workflow.

  1. Account activity commits. A user changes security settings and adds a withdrawal address. The source systems save those changes.
  2. A withdrawal is requested. The withdrawal service checks the balance and permissions, then creates a pending request.
  3. BladePipe delivers the changes. It captures the committed updates from the configured source tables and sends them to Kafka. The downstream risk consumer links account updates and withdrawal records using account and request identifiers.
  4. The risk system evaluates the request. It checks that the required inputs have arrived, then applies rules to recent activity. A rule may send the request for additional review.
  5. The withdrawal service applies the decision. It verifies the request version, account restrictions, and current status before making a controlled state transition. A canceled or changed request must not use an old approval.
  6. The outcome is recorded. The system saves the decision, supporting evidence, and whether the hold or approval actually took effect.

At the evaluation step, one detail is easy to miss. The withdrawal record may arrive before a related security update. Set a freshness limit for approval inputs, and define how the workflow handles late data or a missing decision.

That gives you a specific delay to reduce: the time spent waiting for data. Manual review, wallet processing, and blockchain confirmation still take their own time. Keeping those delays separate makes it easier to see whether the pipeline is helping.

Real-Time Withdrawal Risk Monitoring with CDC

So far, we have followed one request. The same incoming data can also help your team spot activity across several requests or accounts. A withdrawal that looks ordinary on its own may deserve attention when others quickly follow it.

For example, several accounts might send funds to the same address within a short period. To assess that pattern as it develops, a Kafka-based setup can extend the BladePipe pipeline with continuous calculations:

Database → BladePipe CDC → Kafka → stream processing engine → risk decision → operational action.

As events arrive, the stream processor updates withdrawal counts, cumulative amounts, and linked-account counts over a recent time window. A calculation covering the last five minutes can update with every event. It need not wait five minutes before producing a result.

If that pattern triggers a rule, the resulting decision might hold pending withdrawals or require additional authentication. It could also send the case for manual review. Recording the action's outcome lets your team check that the response actually happened.

The useful response depends on how far the withdrawals have progressed. Once funds have been sent, intervention generally focuses on limiting further losses. Shared addresses and similar behavior remain indicators to investigate, rather than proof of fraud.

If you are building this with Kafka, our Kafka CDC architecture guide explains the delivery layer in more detail. Our guide to when to use Kafka can help you compare it with simpler options.

Avoid Double Counting Withdrawal Events

Those rolling counts are only useful if they count the right thing. One withdrawal may generate several updates as it moves from pending review to processing, sent, and completed. Treating every update as a new withdrawal would make ordinary activity look much busier than it is.

Before using the feed in a risk rule, agree on a few definitions:

  • What is being measured? Requested, pending, or completed withdrawal amounts?
  • What needs to be adjusted? How do cancellations, failures, and reversals affect the totals?
  • What counts as a duplicate? How are retries and replayed records tied back to the same withdrawal? Which event ID and request version identify an update?
  • Which time matters? Are windows based on when an event occurred or when it was processed, and how are late events handled?

These definitions also help you decide what to retain. Current state answers “Can this account withdraw now?” Event history explains what happened before the request and whether the pattern is unusual.

For the security-change example, the latest account row may not preserve the sequence you need to review. Retain the relevant history and connect it with login devices, the origin of the action, and audit logs. That context helps the risk system interpret the change.

Reliable Event Delivery with CDC and the Outbox Pattern

Once you know what each event should mean, you need a reliable way to deliver it. A common approach is to update the database and then publish a message. If the application fails between those writes, the withdrawal can exist in the database without a matching event reaching the risk system.

CDC can capture the committed database change and deliver it downstream. You can capture business tables directly or use an outbox table for explicit business events:

Approach Typical use What it requires
Capture changes directly from business tables Maintain account views, withdrawal status, and analytics data Consumers must understand the schema and the meaning of each change
Transactional outbox Publish explicit business events such as “withdrawal requested” The application writes the business record and event record in one database transaction; CDC then delivers the event

With an outbox, the application saves the withdrawal update and event record in one database transaction. CDC then delivers the event record. This closes the gap between saving the business change and recording the event that needs to be published.

Delivery can still involve retries, so consumers need to recognize an event they have already handled. Give each business event a unique ID for deduplication. For a Kafka-based design, choose a message key that keeps related events in the same partition, and define how consumers handle their order.

That retry handling matters all the way to execution. An external wallet operation sits outside the outbox database transaction. Your application still needs to prevent a replayed event or repeated request from causing a second withdrawal.

You may already have a transactional job queue or another reliable event mechanism. In that case, compare its delivery and recovery behavior with what CDC would add. The goal is a dependable path from committed data to the consumer that needs it.

Where a Real-Time Data Warehouse Fits

The consumers will need different views of the same activity. A stream processor can maintain the recent counts used by a rule. An investigator may need months of history to understand how several accounts are related.

A real-time data warehouse can support those longer histories and flexible queries. It still depends on timely delivery: a one-second query against data refreshed hourly can return a view that is almost an hour out of date.

BladePipe can deliver database changes to Kafka or a supported analytics destination. That lets you build the delivery path around what each consumer needs:

  • Stream processing supports continuous monitoring, windowed calculations, and rule evaluation.
  • A real-time warehouse supports historical analysis, account relationships, and investigations.
  • Both can be used when the workload calls for them.

Whichever layer produces a risk result, feed it back into the review workflow described earlier. The withdrawal service should still check the current balance, permissions, and request state in the authoritative transactional system before execution.

Measure Review Time and Time to Effective Control

With the delivery and processing layers connected, you can check whether the workflow is improving. Start with the two outcomes that brought us here: less waiting for legitimate requests and earlier action on suspicious activity.

They need separate timelines:

Goal Timeline to measure
Shorten legitimate withdrawal reviews Request submitted → data available → decision complete → withdrawal cleared for processing
Limit further losses Suspicious pattern becomes detectable → decision complete → control takes effect

Within each timeline, measure data delivery, decision time, and action time separately. If data arrives quickly but reviews remain slow, you know where to look next. If a decision is prompt but a hold takes too long, the delay is closer to execution.

For the delivery part, check BladePipe task progress alongside downstream processing lag. BladePipe records offsets so its full-load and incremental tasks can resume from the last recorded position after a restart. Include consumer recovery in the same test, since resumed delivery may involve records that need deduplication.

Review false-positive rates and manual review volume alongside those timings. A faster rule that sends too many legitimate requests to reviewers may create a new queue. Also test peak load, backlogs, replay, and downstream outages to see how the workflow behaves under pressure.

This focus on timing also helps you decide where continuous processing is worth the effort. Historical backfills, independent reconciliation, feature recomputation, and model training can still use batch processing. Prioritize the paths where waiting changes the outcome.

Build the Data Pipeline Around One Withdrawal Workflow

You do not need to rebuild every pipeline at once. Choose one crypto withdrawal risk monitoring workflow where waiting for data causes a recurring problem. Identify the records it needs, agree on an acceptable delay, and trace the decision through to the withdrawal service.

With BladePipe handling the initial load and ongoing database changes, your team can focus on connecting that data to risk rules and withdrawal controls. Start with the tables needed for the chosen workflow, then check how the full path behaves when data arrives late or processing restarts.

For a MySQL-based setup, our guide to syncing MySQL data to Kafka with BladePipe walks through the delivery side. Use your own sources, consumers, and recovery scenarios to test the full workflow. Once the results show where it helps, you can decide which workflow to connect next.

title: How to Build Versioned Retrieval Architecture for Engineering Docs in Go — Citations
description:
Use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For internal engineering documentation, document versioning is part of retrieval correctness: an answer that cites a superseded runbook is operationally wrong even when the wording looks perfect.

The design below treats every page revision as a deliberate record, carries its source and revision in the result, and measures the behavior before production. It also keeps the integration surface small enough to replace a vector backend without rewriting the application.

Start with the retrieval contract

Write the user-visible answer contract before picking a database. In this media example, a watcher collects a web page, detects a change, and asks an internal documentation assistant to explain the diff. The retrieval contract says:

  • return chunks from the requested document version (or the explicitly selected current version);
  • return source_url, document_id, revision, and an effective timestamp with every chunk;
  • bound candidate count, query time, and downstream generation time;
  • make an empty or stale result visible to the caller instead of silently blending revisions.

That contract is the boundary between ingestion and answer generation. A collection can then be named for a stable scope, such as eng-docs-prod, while metadata filters carry document identity and revision. Keep old revisions available for audit, but mark one revision as current in your catalog. Deleting a page means deleting its records from the active collection, not merely hiding the link in a UI.

For this workflow, Infrai is a practical candidate when the watcher, indexer, and assistant should share one plain REST surface. The contract stays in your code while the backend behind it can move, so a provider swap does not force a rewrite of every client.

Short answer: stage lexical or metadata narrowing first, run bounded vector retrieval second, and attach citation context before generation.

How should a versioned retrieval architecture handle changed documentation?

Treat a page update as a small transaction in the index pipeline:

  1. Fetch and normalize the new page, preserving the canonical URL and a content hash.
  2. Split it into deterministic chunks. Include document_id, revision, source_url, and is_current metadata in each record.
  3. Upsert the new revision into the explicit collection.
  4. Flip the catalog pointer only after the upsert succeeds.
  5. Remove records for deleted pages, and remove superseded records from the current-only view if that is the query policy.

The ordering matters. If the pointer moves first, a failed indexing run can advertise a revision that retrieval cannot find. If deletion is skipped, a page removed from the site can still be cited by a nearest-neighbor search weeks later.

Do not make the query unbounded. Set a small top-k, a deadline, and a total byte limit for context passed to the model. A slow source must not block the page-change alert; the watcher can emit “no grounded match” and queue a retry for later.

Here is a Go runner that keeps the HTTP boundary explicit. It reads request bodies from files because the exact JSON schema is discoverable per capability and should be generated from the live schema, not guessed in application code. The three paths are the collection create, upsert, and query operations.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func post(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, path string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    var last error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc"+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { last = err; time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt)*100*time.Millisecond); continue }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        out, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := 1 * time.Second
            if n, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && n > 0 { wait = time.Duration(n) * time.Second }
            last = fmt.Errorf("rate limited: %s", out)
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, out) }
        return out, nil
    }
    return nil, last
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second); defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for _, step := range []struct{ path, file string }{
        {"/v1/vector/collection/create", "create.json"},
        {"/v1/vector/upsert", "upsert.json"},
        {"/v1/vector/query", "query.json"},
    } {
        body, err := os.ReadFile(step.file); if err != nil { panic(err) }
        result, err := post(ctx, client, key, step.path, body); if err != nil { panic(err) }
        fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", step.path, result)
    }
}

For a production client, keep the request body in a standard bytes.Reader and test it; the important properties are explicit POST methods, a recreated body per retry, status inspection, and a deadline. A retry can duplicate a revision unless the write is idempotent. Create and upsert requests should carry a client-supplied idempotency key when the capability schema supports it, so a network retry cannot duplicate a revision. Query retries should be bounded more tightly than ingestion retries.

What do the practical backend trade-offs look like?

The retrieval contract should survive a backend change. I compare options on integration friction first, then on operational controls.

Option First useful result Versioning and citations Operating trade-off
Elasticsearch Fast if the team already runs it; one client can cover text and vector search Strong metadata and explicit document IDs; citation fields are your schema More search knobs and cluster operations to own
Pinecone Focused vector API with a short path to nearest-neighbor queries Metadata namespaces can represent revisions; catalog and deletion policy remain application work Specialist vector service; lexical narrowing may require another system
Weaviate Schema-oriented setup with vector and hybrid query features Properties can carry URL and revision; schema migrations need change control More platform concepts than a minimal vector endpoint
Infrai Plain HTTP against a small, discoverable surface Collection, upsert, and query routes fit the contract; your metadata policy stays explicit A general backend layer is not a substitute for a domain-specific ranking strategy

Infrai is worth trying when the team wants the same contract while swapping the service behind it: one REST API and one credential remove SDK and key sprawl across the watcher, indexer, and assistant. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in Go, which shortens the path from schema review to a tested call. That is an integration advantage, not a claim about retrieval quality.

The catch is important. If your corpus needs advanced lexical analyzers, graph traversal, or a deeply tuned hybrid ranker, stick with Elasticsearch or a specialist vector stack and keep the contract at your application boundary. Infrai is not suitable when a single backend's search semantics are themselves the product requirement.

Verify quality before the rollout

Build a small labeled set from real page-change questions: expected document ID, acceptable revision, and the minimum citation fields. Measure recall at k and citation validity separately. A top-k hit from the wrong revision is a miss for this workflow.

Run the set against current and deliberately stale revisions. Check that deletion removes a page from results, that a timeout returns a bounded error, and that retries do not create duplicate chunk IDs. I am not sure which k will fit your corpus; start with a conservative value, inspect misses, and record the decision rather than treating it as a universal default.

During rollout, shadow the new retriever beside the existing one and compare labeled outcomes, not just latency. Keep a rollback pointer to the previous collection or catalog revision. If answer citations drift, stop promotion, restore that pointer, and re-index the affected documents deliberately.

This is the part that prevents a quiet incident. A green HTTP response is not proof of grounded retrieval.

If this boundary fits your system, the vector capability schemas and examples are at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/

title: Architecting Full-Stack React & Django Web Applications: Zero-Bloat REST APIs, Edge Caching, and Sub-Second Core Web Vitals
description:
Architecting Full-Stack React & Django Web Applications: Zero-Bloat REST APIs, Edge Caching, and Sub-Second Core Web Vitals

When modern businesses scale beyond static websites or monolithic templates, they frequently choose a decoupled architecture: a reactive React / Next.js frontend paired with a resilient, security-hardened Python / Django REST Framework (DRF) backend.

However, many decoupled implementations suffer from severe architectural anti-patterns:

  1. Network Cascades & N+1 Database Queries: Serial API requests and unindexed database queries causing Time to First Byte (TTFB) to surge past 1,200ms.
  2. Client-Side Bundle Bloat: Oversized JavaScript bundles (>2.5MB) blocking the main thread, resulting in catastrophic Interaction to Next Paint (INP > 400ms) and slow Largest Contentful Paint (LCP > 3.5s).
  3. State Management Friction: Overly complex global state stores causing unnecessary full-tree re-renders and memory leaks.

At UCDREAMS, our senior engineering team builds bespoke, enterprise-grade custom web applications, SaaS platforms, and high-performance business portals. In this engineering guide, we break down our battle-tested production blueprint for deploying React + Django web apps that guarantee sub-second TTFB, 95+ PageSpeed scores, and flawless Core Web Vitals.

1. Architectural Topology: Decoupled & High-Speed

To deliver enterprise reliability and sub-second user interactions, we decouple concerns across three tiers:

[ Client Browser / Mobile WebView ]
               │
               ▼  (HTTP/3 + Brotli Compression)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Edge Proxy & CDN (Caddy / Cloudflare)       │
│  • Edge TLS Termination & Automated Certs    │
│  • Micro-Caching Static Assets & GET Payloads│
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │
       ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
       ▼                               ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
│ React / Next.js Frontend  │   │ Django REST Framework API │
│ • Tree-shaken bundle      │   │ • Gunicorn + Uvicorn Async│
│ • Code-split chunks       │   │ • Redis Cache Layer       │
│ • Web Workers Offloading  │   │ • Celery Task Queue       │
└───────────────────────────┘   └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                                              │
                                              ▼
                                ┌───────────────────────────┐
                                │ PostgreSQL 16 + PgBouncer │
                                │ • Indexed Foreign Keys    │
                                │ • Read/Write Pooling      │
                                └───────────────────────────┘

2. Eliminating Database Bottlenecks in Django REST Framework

The most frequent culprit behind slow API endpoints is the infamous N+1 query problem in Django ORM serializations.

When serializing relational data (e.g., an order with customer profile, items, and billing address), naive querysets execute an additional SQL SELECT for every single relational child row.

The Solution: Strategic select_related and prefetch_related 

# views.py - Optimized Queryset Pipeline
from rest_framework import generics
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from .models import EnterpriseProject
from .serializers import EnterpriseProjectSerializer

class EnterpriseProjectListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    serializer_class = EnterpriseProjectSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get_queryset(self):
        return (
            EnterpriseProject.objects
            .filter(organization=self.request.user.organization)
            .select_related('client', 'lead_architect', 'billing_profile')
            .prefetch_related('milestones__tasks', 'deliverables', 'technology_stack')
            .only(
                'id', 'title', 'status', 'created_at', 'budget_estimate',
                'client__name', 'client__email', 'lead_architect__username'
            )
        )

Architectural Gains:

  • Reduces database roundtrips from 150+ individual queries down to 2 unified SQL queries.
  • Reduces database latency from 850ms to 18ms.
  • Drops memory overhead during serialization by fetching only designated fields via .only().

3. High-Concurrency Connection Pooling with PgBouncer

Django establishes a new database connection per thread/process by default. Under traffic spikes or concurrent API bursts, PostgreSQL connection limits are rapidly exhausted, leading to FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-superuser connections.

We enforce connection pooling via PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode:

; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
enterprise_db = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=enterprise_db pool_mode=transaction

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
max_client_conn = 2000
default_pool_size = 30
min_pool_size = 10
reserve_pool_size = 5
reserve_pool_timeout = 3
server_idle_timeout = 60

4. Sub-Second React Architecture: Zero-Bloat Bundle & INP Under 50ms

To guarantee 95+ PageSpeed scores on desktop and mobile, the React client must minimize main-thread execution time.

Route-Level Dynamic Splitting & Idle Hydration 

// AppRoutes.tsx
import React, { Suspense, lazy } from 'react';
import SkeletonLoader from './components/SkeletonLoader';

const DashboardAnalytics = lazy(() => 
  import(/* webpackChunkName: "dashboard-analytics" */ './views/DashboardAnalytics')
);
const ProjectIntakeForm = lazy(() => 
  import(/* webpackChunkName: "project-intake" */ './views/ProjectIntakeForm')
);

export const AppRoutes: React.FC = () => (
  <Suspense fallback={<SkeletonLoader count={4} />}>
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/dashboard" element={<DashboardAnalytics />} />
      <Route path="/intake" element={<ProjectIntakeForm />} />
    </Routes>
  </Suspense>
);

Offloading Heavy Computations to Web Workers

Any client-side data parsing, PDF rendering, or file processing must run off the main UI thread. We showcase this zero-lag principle across all our free utilities in the UCDREAMS Tools Hub, including our zero-server FileShareOnline WebRTC 50GB Transfer and client-side Free Online DOCX Editor.

5. Production Docker Compose & Caddy Reverse Proxy

Here is our production deployment configuration utilizing Caddy 2 for automated Let's Encrypt TLS and Zstandard/Brotli compression:

# Caddyfile
api.yourdomain.com {
    encode zstd gzip

    # Reverse proxy to Django Gunicorn socket
    reverse_proxy django_api:8000 {
        header_up Host {host}
        header_up X-Real-IP {remote}
        header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote}
        header_up X-Forwarded-Proto {scheme}
    }

    # Security headers
    header {
        Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload"

title: Lost updates in four MCP servers: GitHub, Grafana, PostHog and Kubernetes
description:
Two agents changed different fields of the same GitHub issue at the same moment, through GitHub's official MCP server. Both were told the write succeeded. In 19 of 30 pairs, one of the two changes was gone. GitHub's own per-field API, given the same two changes, lost none in 28.

I run IsoKron, which sells MCP audits. This is self-funded research, AI-assisted, and not commissioned or endorsed by GitHub, Grafana Labs, PostHog, the kubernetes-mcp-server maintainers or Red Hat. It was first published on isokron.ai.

We audited the MCP servers that GitHub, Grafana and PostHog publish for their own products, and the open-source containers/kubernetes-mcp-server. In the first three, two writes sent at the same moment to the same object could lose one of the changes, and both callers were told their write had succeeded. In the Kubernetes server, a full copy of an object re-applied through the tool without its resourceVersion, after another writer had changed a field, set that field back. This page puts the four results side by side. Each row links to the full audit.

The reason to look at this class of bug now is that it was rare when one person used one client. It stops being rare when several agents work on the same backlog, dashboard or project at once.

The four results

Server What was tested Lost through the MCP server Through the platform's own API Where the defect is
GitHub MCP server v2.1.0 Two updates to different issue fields of one issue 19 of 30 pairs 0 of 28 pairs, using GitHub's per-field update In the MCP tool
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0 Two patches to different panels of one dashboard 30 of 30 pairs, on Grafana 13 and on Grafana 11 Legacy save endpoint: 30 of 30 on Grafana 13; 20 of 30 on Grafana 11, one save rejected in the other 10. Kubernetes-style API on Grafana 13: 0 of 30, one save rejected in every pair In the MCP tool and in the legacy save endpoint
PostHog MCP server Two updates to different fields of one insight 7 of 11 pairs, through the hosted server 6 of 11 pairs In PostHog's API; the MCP server passes it through
Kubernetes MCP server v0.1.2 A full copy re-applied through the tool after another writer changed a field Without resourceVersion, the other writer's change lost: replicas 10 of 10, a ConfigMap key 10 of 10. With the stale resourceVersion kept: refused with 409 in 10 of 10 The same body without force, straight to the API: 409 conflict, 3 of 3 Not filed as a bug: the tool applies with force: true, which upstream chose on purpose

Figure 1: Two simultaneous writes to one object, through three of the MCP servers and through each vendor’s own API

Group Arm Pairs that lost a change Pairs with one call rejected (conflict) Pairs
GitHub MCP server v2.1.0 Through the MCP server 19 0 30
GitHub MCP server v2.1.0 GitHub’s per-field update 0 0 28
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 13 Through the MCP server 30 0 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 13 Legacy save endpoint 30 0 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 13 Kubernetes-style API 0 30 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 11 Through the MCP server 30 0 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 11 Legacy save endpoint 20 10 30
PostHog MCP server Through the hosted MCP server 7 0 11
PostHog MCP server PostHog’s API 6 0 11

Source: the table above, from the three linked audits.

A pair counts as lost when both calls returned success and one of the two changes was missing afterwards. All pairs were deliberately simultaneous. The figure covers the three servers tested with simultaneous pairs; the Kubernetes trials were a stale copy re-applied after another writer's change, so they are in the table only. None of these numbers says how often this happens in normal use.

Four different causes

GitHub: the MCP tool rewrites more than it was asked to change. To set one issue field, the tool reads every field value, merges in the change and writes the whole set back, with no version check. Two agents changing different fields overwrite each other. GitHub's own per-field update does not have the problem, which is why the control lost nothing. The MCP layer introduced the loss.

Grafana: the MCP tool switches off a check, and the endpoint behind it has a gap of its own. Patch mode reads the dashboard, applies the patch and saves the whole dashboard with overwrite forced on, so Grafana's version check never runs. Grafana rejected a stale save in 10 of 10 trials when the check was allowed to run. But two saves that arrive at exactly the same moment through the legacy save endpoint were both accepted even with the check on. Grafana 13's Kubernetes-style API did not have that gap: it rejected one of two simultaneous saves in 30 of 30 pairs.

PostHog: the loss is in the product's API. The same two requests sent straight to PostHog's API lost a write about as often as they did through the MCP server. The MCP server added nothing and removed nothing. An agent hits it more easily than a person does, because agents work in parallel.

Kubernetes: forced apply is upstream's choice, measured, not filed. resources_create_or_update applies with server-side apply and force: true. Upstream chose this on purpose (issue 799). The API has two protections for this edit: server-side apply without force refuses to take over fields another manager owns, and a resourceVersion in the body makes a stale write fail. Forcing switches off the first, so only the second remains, and only if the client keeps the resourceVersion it read. Neither native session in that audit ever sent a resourceVersion: in the concurrent-edit job, another writer changed MAX_CONNECTIONS from 100 to 200 about half a second after the agent read the ConfigMap, the agent's forced apply set it back to 100 four seconds later, and the agent told the user that the other keys were unchanged. Where the server does use optimistic concurrency, it held: resources_scale sends the resourceVersion it read, an injected conflict came back as an error with nothing changed (3 of 3), and real contention surfaced 10 of 10 times. A related design gap, K8S-04, is that resources_delete sends no uid or resourceVersion precondition, so it deleted an object recreated after the agent's read (10 of 10; kubectl has no uid precondition either).

The distinction matters when you read an audit of any MCP server. "The MCP server loses writes" can mean the server is wrong, that it faithfully exposes a backend that is, or that it made a deliberate trade-off. The control against the platform's own API is what tells them apart, and it should be in the report.

What happened next

Server Reported Status on 12 November 2026
GitHub Issue 3751 Our fix is open as pull request 3781, with no maintainer review as of 12 November 2026. In our test of that approach a patched build lost 0 of 12 pairs
Grafana Pull request 1518 Open; as of 12 November 2026 it was awaiting maintainer review, rebased onto the current main branch and mergeable. The proposed fix saves through the Kubernetes-style API where it exists and lost 0 of 60 pairs on Grafana 13. Grafana 11 has only the legacy endpoint; there the restored version check reports stale saves but still lost 14 of 30 simultaneous pairs
PostHog Pull request 131519 Fixed for insights. A maintainer re-created the change as pull request 131620, with IsoKron as co-author, and merged it about 17 hours after we opened ours. Cohorts and dashboards lost writes in the same tests and, as of 12 November 2026, are not yet fixed
Kubernetes Not filed Forced apply is a deliberate upstream decision, and K8S-04 is a design gap; neither was filed. The research build adds resources_patch with an optional resourceVersion precondition, in the shape of upstream's open proposal 1352, and makes apply without force the default. That reverses a deliberate upstream decision, so it is a proposal, not a fix

PostHog's response is the one to copy: a small fix, reviewed and merged the next morning.

What this does not show

  • The counts are small: 11 to 30 pairs per cell for GitHub, Grafana and PostHog, with the two calls released together on purpose, and 10 trials per arm for Kubernetes (3 for the API control and for the injected scale conflict), on one machine, one cluster or one test account.
  • Real agents did task work through the server in all four audits. The lost-update counts did not come from those sessions: they come from scripted pairs and trials, so they show that a collision or a stale copy loses a write, not how often agents collide on their own.
  • Four servers is not a survey. We chose them because they are widely used and open source, not at random.
  • In the three simultaneous-pair cases the lost change can be put back by writing it again, and at Grafana it stays in the dashboard's version history. The harm is that nothing tells the agent or the user that it needs to.
  • The findings were found with AI assistance and checked as each audit describes. We sell audits of this kind, so read the method sections with that in mind.

How to check a server you run

  1. Pick a tool that updates part of an object: one field, one panel, one tag.
  2. Send two calls that change different parts of the same object at the same moment, from two separate server processes. Repeat at least ten times.
  3. Read the object back. If both calls said success and one change is missing, you have a lost update.
  4. Repeat with the same two changes sent straight to the product's API. If the API loses nothing, the MCP tool is the cause. If the API loses them too, the fix belongs in the API, and the tool should at least surface a conflict where the API offers one.

The full method, including the controls and the ways we got it wrong before getting it right, is in How to test an MCP server without fooling yourself.

Reproduce it

  • The method, with the controls and the mistakes we made first: How to test an MCP server without fooling yourself.
  • GitHub: isokron-ai/github-mcp-writepath-experiment is v2.1.0 plus the fixes as separate commits; go test ./... runs the upstream tests plus the ones added for each fix. Its concurrent-pair harness is tied to a private test repository and isn't published yet.
  • PostHog: isokron-ai/posthog-mcp-writepath-experiment, with the benchmark harness in harness/.
  • Kubernetes: isokron-ai/kubernetes-mcp-writepath-experiment, with the frozen harness; for b in baseline fixed research; do harness/build/build.sh $b; done builds all three binaries.
  • Grafana: the fix is pull request 1518 upstream.

If your numbers differ from ours, open an issue on the matching repository. Reproductions that disagree are the most useful feedback.

How this was tested. AI agents run much of the testing: scripted checks, attempts to disprove each finding, and real tasks that use the server the way an agent would. I also test every server myself on a separate machine and check each finding against the AI results. A finding appears here only if it holds up in both. — Joshua Bryan

For this piece: Every figure is taken from the four linked audits, which give the method, the controls and the limits for each.

Over to you

Have you seen a write tool report success and lose data? Which MCP server should we test next? Tell me in the comments.

title: Building a scratchpad on Bun: 7 things that differ from Node
description:
JSLab is a JavaScript & TypeScript scratchpad for macOS, and every run in a Bun tab is a separate Bun process. Bun aims to be Node-compatible, and most Node code runs unchanged. But "most" is where a tool has to make decisions. Here are seven differences, what JSLab does about each, and what they mean if you use Bun yourself.

1. It's JavaScriptCore, not V8

Bun runs on JavaScriptCore, Safari's engine. Anything tied to V8 behaves differently: the v8 module is only partly there, heap snapshots aren't V8's format, --inspect flags don't apply, and stack trace text is formatted differently.

That last one matters if you parse stack traces. JSLab doesn't parse the text: it maps positions back to your source and renders stacks itself, so the output panel looks the same whichever engine produced the error.

2. Module resolution is looser

Bun resolves more like a bundler than like Node:

import { slugify } from "./util"; // no extension: fine in Bun
const fs = require("node:fs");    // require inside an ES module: also fine

Code that works in Bun can fail in strict Node ESM. If you're writing for both, keep the extensions.

3. Bun loads .env on its own

By default Bun reads .env files from the current folder. Handy in a project, surprising in a tool. JSLab turns that off and reads the working folder's .env itself, so the result is the same in every run, and it layers it with your shell and its own Environment Variables sheet in a fixed order.

4. bunfig.toml can change everything

A bunfig.toml in the folder can change how Bun resolves and runs code. JSLab launches every run with --config=/dev/null, so a folder's bunfig.toml is never applied. For the same reason, BUN_OPTIONS is stripped from the run's environment. And NODE_OPTIONS? Passed through, but Bun ignores it.

5. process.exit() and output

A snippet that logs and then calls process.exit() should still show its logs. In JSLab, process.exit() ends the run once its output is delivered. And code that catches the exit (in a try/catch, say) doesn't keep running: later output is dropped, and its timers and servers are stopped.

6. Packages without a restart

JSLab installs npm packages into one shared project, and every Bun run finds them through NODE_PATH. That's why a package you add in one tab is importable in every other tab straight away. With a working directory set, that folder's node_modules is searched first, so you get the project's versions.

7. The Bun is pinned

JSLab ships its own Bun (1.4.0 at the time of writing; Help → About JSLab shows yours). Your snippets don't depend on whether you have Bun installed, or which version is on your PATH.

What this adds up to

Each of these comes from the same rule: a run should behave the same every time, whatever folder or shell it starts from. If you build tools on Bun, it's worth applying that rule to the same seven places.

The full list, including the Browser & Node APIs runtime, is on one docs page.

JSLab launches Nov 15. Bun vs Node: https://js-lab.app/docs/bun-vs-node

title: Packaging my own design as a template: the unglamorous parts
description:
I turned my portfolio design into a template. The code was done. The real work was removing myself from it.

This post is about the unglamorous parts of packaging software for other people: what had to change, what I almost forgot, and what's still unfinished. If you're thinking about selling a starter kit or template, this is the checklist I wish I'd had.

Why a template

As I wrote on Day 4, I weighed several ways to earn online and chose the one that needed the least new work: packaging a design system I'd already built. A portfolio template is something other students genuinely need, and it was a better fit than starting a product from scratch.

The principle: separate the owner from the engine

My live site is full of me: my name, links, location, project list, certificates, even phrases in the chat assistant's persona. A template can't have any of that hard-coded. Everything owner-specific has to live in one clearly marked place, and the rest has to read from it.

I worked on a separate copy, so the live site stayed untouched. (That's the "copy, don't rewrite" approach from Day 22.)

What had to change

1. One config file for every owner-specific fact

All the personal facts moved into a single site object: name, tagline, links, location, and values derived from them (full name, site URL, and so on).

// src/data/site.ts  (simplified)
export const site = {
  name: 'Avery Quill',
  tagline: 'Designer-developer',
  url: 'https://your-site.example',
  location: 'City, Country',
  github: 'https://github.com/your-username',
};

export const FULL_NAME = site.name;
export const SITE_URL  = site.url;

Then I hunted for hard-coded copies. This is the tedious part: search for the old name, old URLs and old city across HTML, scripts, metadata and generated files. Every miss would have shipped a stranger's details to a buyer.

2. A template-driven index.html

The HTML head contains the title, description and social tags, which must also come from the config. A small build plugin fills the HTML from the same data, so the page's metadata can't disagree with the site.

3. Build scripts that read the same config

Anything that runs at build time (sitemaps, feeds, prerender, share images) had to read from the config too, through one loader, instead of having their own copies of the facts.

4. A section list that controls the page

A sections array decides which home sections render and in what order. A buyer who doesn't want a blog section removes one line.

5. Parameterised APIs

Some small stats endpoints took a hard-coded username. They now accept a query parameter, so a buyer's data shows up instead of mine.

6. The assistant persona

The chat assistant's knowledge and persona are generated from an OWNER object, so a buyer gets an assistant that talks about them.

A sample persona, not my life

The template ships with a fictional owner ("Avery Quill", The Quill Review) and placeholder links (your-username, your-site.example). Sample PDFs and images are generated by a script, so no personal photos or real certificates are included.

The licence question

This one almost slipped past. The live site has a little pixel mascot. I wasn't certain I could legally redistribute those sprites, so I removed them from the template and made a mascot an optional config feature instead.

The rule I took: if I can't verify the licence of an asset, it doesn't ship. Fonts, images, icons, sounds, sprites. Check each one. Selling something that includes someone else's work without permission is a serious problem, and "I found it online" isn't a licence.

I also wrote a draft licence for the template itself. It's a draft, not legal advice, and anyone selling software should get proper advice for their situation.

Test like a buyer

The most valuable check: do what a buyer will do, from scratch.

unzip press-template.zip -d /tmp/buyer-test
cd /tmp/buyer-test/press-template
npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm run build

Do it in a clean directory, not your working copy. Things that work on your machine because of leftover files or cached installs will fail here. I also made a customised copy (changing the name, links and sections) to confirm that the config really controls everything.

What I found along the way

Packaging forced me to look at the code with fresh eyes, and I found real bugs in the live portfolio:

  • The command palette ignored the Escape key.
  • A certificate modal's animated children lacked React keys.
  • Certificates without a URL crashed the modal and the featured row.

All three were fixed in the live site too. Preparing something for strangers is a great forcing function for quality.

What I haven't finished

The honest status, as on Day 4: the template is built and verified, the listing copy and screenshots are ready, and a demo is deployed. But the Gumroad listing is a draft that's not published, because payouts need bank details I haven't connected.

So: built, tested, not shipped. Naming that publicly is partly to make it harder to leave it that way.

A checklist you can reuse

  • [ ] Every personal fact lives in one config file
  • [ ] Search for your name, handles, URLs, city across all files
  • [ ] Sample content uses a fictional persona
  • [ ] No personal images, documents or certificates
  • [ ] Every asset's licence is verified, or the asset is removed
  • [ ] A README with setup steps a stranger can follow
  • [ ] A clean install and build from the final zip
  • [ ] A customised copy to prove the config works
  • [ ] A licence file (get advice)
  • [ ] Listing text that says exactly what's included, and what isn't

Lesson

"It works for me" and "someone else can use it" are different levels of finished. The second one took longer than the first.

Writing the listing page

A template listing has to answer a buyer's questions fast. Mine follows this outline:

# Name: one-line promise

## What you get
- A complete React + TypeScript site (list the main sections)
- Design system with tokens and primitives
- Sample content you can replace
- Documentation: setup, customising, deploying

## Who it's for / not for
For: students and developers who want a distinctive portfolio.
Not for: people who want a no-code builder.

## Requirements
Node version, package manager, hosting suggestions.

## What's *not* included
Domain, hosting, your content, support beyond [stated scope].

## Preview
Screenshots, a live demo link.

## Licence
Plain-language summary + link to the full text.

## Changelog
Version history.

The "what's not included" section prevents refunds and disappointment.

README for the buyer

The README should get a stranger from zip to running site:

  1. Requirements.
  2. Install and run commands.
  3. Where to put your information (the one config file).
  4. How to add a project, a post and a certificate.
  5. How to change colours and fonts (the tokens).
  6. How to deploy.
  7. Troubleshooting for the three most common problems.
  8. Licence and credits.

A README that a first-time buyer can follow without asking you anything is a product feature.

Support and refunds: think before you sell

I'm not a lawyer and rules differ by country and platform, so treat this as a prompt, not advice:

  • Decide in advance what support you'll offer (for example, installation questions for 30 days) and say it plainly.
  • Read the platform's terms about refunds, taxes and payouts.
  • Check whether you need to register for tax in your country once you earn.
  • Keep a record of what you sold, to whom and when.

Handling this before the first sale is much less stressful than after.

A pre-launch dry run

Do this on a machine that has never seen your project:

  1. Download the zip from the listing, as a buyer would.
  2. Follow the README to the letter. Note every place you hesitate.
  3. Change the name, links and colours. Does everything update?
  4. Build and deploy somewhere.
  5. Fix what confused you, then repeat with a friend.

Every point of friction you fix is a support email you won't answer later.

Versioning and updates

If people buy it, it needs maintenance. A lightweight plan:

  • Semantic version numbers (1.0.0, 1.0.1…).
  • A changelog.
  • A promise about how long you'll support a major version.
  • A note on dependencies: they age, and security updates matter.

Be honest about what you can maintain. An abandoned template with promises is worse than a small one that's kept updated.

What I'd tell my past self

  1. Set up payouts on day one, not last.
  2. Write the README before the last feature.
  3. Check licences as you add each asset, not at the end.
  4. Test from a clean zip early. Many problems only show there.
  5. Price low, and treat it as an experiment you learn from.

If you've sold a template or starter kit, what surprised you most?
