title: SVG favicons: what browsers actually read in 2026 (and when you still need an ICO)
description:
SVG favicons are the dream: one crisp vector file, scales forever, tiny payload. And in 2026 most of that dream works — but "most" is doing a lot of heavy lifting. Depending on which browser, which platform, and which non-browser tool fetches your icon, the SVG you shipped may be read, ignored, or replaced by a request for /favicon.ico you never made. Here's what actually happens, and the link stack that keeps every consumer happy.

Who reads your SVG favicon

Chrome, Firefox, Edge — all read <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon.svg"> and prefer it over raster alternatives when declared correctly. Bonus you can't get from PNG: SVG favicons can embed CSS with media queries, which is exactly how the dark-mode Safari favicon trick swaps colors without JavaScript.

Safari on macOS — supports SVG favicons, with quirks: it historically ignored the type attribute and picked icons by sizes and order instead. Declaring both a PNG and an SVG without thinking about order leads to Safari grabbing the "wrong" one. If your icon looks right in Chrome and off in Safari, this is usually why.

iOS Safari — reads none of this. No ICO, no SVG. It only ever looks at apple-touch-icon (180×180, no transparency). If your fancy SVG "doesn't work on iPhone," it was never going to.

Not-a-browser consumers — feed readers, crawlers, chat-link previews, some enterprise tooling: a surprising number still ignore your HTML entirely and GET /favicon.ico by convention. Ship no ICO and those tools show a blank square or log 404 noise on every request.

The link stack that works everywhere 

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="32x32">
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">

ICO is the floor every consumer can fall back to, SVG is the upgrade modern browsers take, apple-touch-icon covers iOS. Two practical notes:

  • SVG with a bitmap floor beats SVG alone. The ICO costs a few KB and silences the direct /favicon.ico fetchers.
  • Keep the SVG small. Embedded fonts or giant path data blow up your document weight for a 16×16 render. Simplify paths before shipping — why favicons go blurry and how vector fixes it covers the sizing math.

Converting: the boring part everyone skips wrong

You have an SVG. You still need the ICO floor and the PNG ladder (16/32/192/512). Two wrong ways to do it: screenshot your icon and call it a day, or upscale a 32px export to 512px and ship mush. The right way is generating each raster size from the original vector:

  • SVG → multi-size ICO directly in the browser: svg-to-ico converter
  • PNG → ICO when your source is already raster: png-to-ico converter
  • No SVG yet, just text or an emoji idea: the SVG favicon generator and emoji-to-favicon build the vector from scratch — all client-side, nothing uploaded.

The full size-vs-format matrix (what each platform actually reads in 2026) is in the SVG vs PNG favicon breakdown — worth bookmarking next to your deploy checklist.

Verify before you blame the browser

The fastest way to lose an hour is arguing with Safari about an icon your page never actually declared. Run the deployed URL through a favicon checker — it fetches the live page, lists every declared icon, and shows what each one resolves to. If your SVG isn't in that list, the problem is your <link> tag, not the browser.

That's the whole game: vector for modern browsers, ICO floor for everything else, apple-touch for iOS, and a checker pass before you blame anyone. Ten minutes, once per project.

title: Optimizing Document Lookup: Making Atlas Search and Vector Search Up to 5x Faster
description:
Sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making core operations faster, but from eliminating unnecessary work surrounding them. That is exactly what we discovered while optimizing document lookup in MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search. By removing redundant query planning and execution overhead, we made search queries up to 5x faster without changing the underlying search algorithms.

When you run a $search or $vectorSearch query in MongoDB, two key stages work together to deliver the results. First, mongot, MongoDB's search process powered by Apache Lucene, executes the search query to identify and rank the most relevant documents. Then, mongod joins the search results with the corresponding BSON documents from the underlying collection using their _ids. The resulting documents can be further processed by additional aggregation pipeline stages before being returned to the application. Figure 1 illustrates this two-stage process:

Figure 1. Search execution in mongot and document materialization in mongod.

This second stage, known as document materialization, is handled by an internal aggregation stage called $_internalSearchIdLookup. While search execution has been extensively optimized, we discovered that document lookup had become a significant performance bottleneck. For every matching document, the stage repeatedly constructed a new query plan and acquired collection resources, introducing substantial overhead for queries returning hundreds or thousands of results. In our profiling, approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query planning and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents.

To address this, we redesigned the document lookup execution path to eliminate redundant query planning, reuse execution plans, and amortize resource acquisition across multiple lookups. The result: up to 4.9x faster $search queries, 5.5x faster $vectorSearch queries, and approximately 2.75x higher throughput under concurrency.

These optimizations shipped in MongoDB 9.0, are enabled by default, and require no application changes. In this post, we'll explore how we identified the bottleneck, redesigned the execution path, and achieved these performance improvements.

The hidden cost of repeated query planning

Looking up a document by its _id is typically a fast operation in MongoDB, thanks to its efficient _id index. However, the original $_internalSearchIdLookup implementation constructed and executed a new aggregation sub-pipeline for every document returned by mongot, even though only the _id value changed:

For each document, MongoDB parsed the query, optimized the pipeline, constructed an execution plan, acquired collection resources, attached a cursor, executed the lookup, and released resources.

The problem was not the indexed document retrieval, but the repeated preparation work surrounding it. Even though the query structure was identical across lookups, MongoDB rebuilt the execution plan and reacquired collection resources for every document instead of reusing them. This overhead accumulated linearly with the number of results. For example, a search query returning 1,000 documents could trigger 1,000 separate cycles of query planning, collection acquisition, and resource cleanup. As result sets grew, the repeated preparation work became a substantial contributor to end-to-end search latency. Figure 2 illustrates this repeated execution overhead.

Figure 2. Repeated query planning and resource acquisition for each document lookup.

To quantify this overhead, we profiled representative Vector Search workloads. The results revealed that approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query plan construction and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents. This confirmed that the bottleneck was not primarily the underlying document reads, but the redundant work surrounding them.

Redesigning the document lookup execution path

To eliminate redundant lookup overhead, we redesigned $_internalSearchIdLookup around two key optimizations: reusing parameterized execution plans and batching document lookups to minimize resource acquisition overhead. Together, these changes allow MongoDB to retrieve thousands of documents without repeatedly rebuilding query plans or acquiring collection resources.

1. Reusing a parameterized SBE execution plan

The first major optimization was introducing SbeSingleDocumentLookupExecutor, built on MongoDB's Slot-Based Execution (SBE) engine. The key observation was simple: every document lookup follows the same query structure, and only the _id value changes. Instead of constructing a new execution plan for each document, the optimized executor builds the lookup plan once, caches it, and reuses it by rebinding the _id parameter for subsequent lookups.

For example, when retrieving 1,000 documents, the original implementation could construct 1,000 separate query plans. With the optimized executor, all 1,000 lookups can reuse a single parameterized plan.

This eliminates redundant query parsing, optimization, and plan construction, significantly reducing per-document execution overhead.

2. Batching document lookups to reuse collection resources

While plan reuse eliminates repeated query planning, acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document can still introduce substantial overhead. To address this, we introduced a reusable BatchedEnrichmentStage that buffers incoming search results and processes them within a shared resource scope. Instead of independently acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document, the optimized execution path reuses collection resources across multiple lookups within a batch, amortizing the acquisition and cleanup costs. For example, with 1,000 documents and a batch size of 100, collection resources can be acquired just 10 times instead of 1,000 times, i.e., once per batch rather than once per document. Although the number of document lookups still grows linearly with the result set size, batching significantly reduces the repeated resource management overhead.

Combined with SBE plan caching, this allows thousands of document lookups to share both an execution plan and collection resources, substantially reducing CPU overhead. The result is a more efficient document lookup architecture: build the execution plan once, reuse it across documents, and minimize repeated resource acquisition.

Figure 3 illustrates how the optimized approach eliminates redundant work by reusing execution plans and collection resources across document lookups.

Figure 3. Original per-document lookup vs. optimized batched lookup with shared execution plans.

Performance results: End-to-end latency and throughput

As shown in Figure 4, both Atlas Search ($search) and Atlas Vector Search ($vectorSearch) achieved substantial reductions in end-to-end query latency across all evaluated result-set sizes (100, 1,000, and 10,000 documents). At 10,000 results, median latency dropped from approximately 2.6 seconds to 527 milliseconds for Atlas Search (4.9× faster) and from 3.1 seconds to 561 milliseconds for Atlas Vector Search (5.5× faster).

An important pattern emerges: the larger the result set, the greater the speedup. This is consistent with the underlying optimization. While search execution still incurs its own costs, eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition overhead becomes increasingly valuable as more documents are materialized.

Figure 4. End-to-end query latency improvements for Atlas Search and Atlas Vector Search in MongoDB 9.0.

Higher throughput under concurrency

Lower latency is only part of the story. We also evaluated performance under concurrent query execution. With 16 concurrent clients running a $search workload, the optimized implementation delivered:

  • Approximately 2.75x higher throughput

  • Approximately 3x lower median latency

These results demonstrate that the optimization does more than accelerate individual queries. By eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition, it reduces unnecessary CPU work per document lookup, allowing mongod to process more concurrent search requests with the same execution resources. The approximately 30% CPU overhead identified in our earlier profiling and the nearly 80% latency reduction observed in our benchmarks represent different measurements and workloads, rather than directly proportional improvements.

Real-world customer impact

To understand the potential impact on real-world workloads, we analyzed 163.8 million Atlas Vector Search executions across 610 customer clusters over 90 days. The analysis shows that larger result-set limits are used across a meaningful portion of the customer fleet. At least 40% of clusters execute queries with limits between 21 and 50, and at least 17% execute queries with limits above 100.

These workloads are particularly well-positioned to benefit from the document lookup optimizations, as eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition becomes increasingly valuable when more documents are retrieved.

Importantly, these improvements require no application changes. The optimized document lookup path is enabled by default in MongoDB 9.0.7. Applications do not need to rewrite queries, rebuild search indexes, or adopt new syntax. Existing $search and $vectorSearch pipelines can automatically benefit when running on supported configurations.

Faster search, without the extra work

This optimization began with a surprising observation: a simple _id lookup was spending a significant portion of its CPU budget preparing to execute rather than retrieving data. By replacing repeated aggregation planning with lightweight execution, introducing reusable batching infrastructure, and caching parameterized SBE plans, we removed a major source of overhead from Atlas Search and Vector Search. The result is up to 5.5× faster end-to-end queries in our benchmarks, along with substantial throughput improvements under concurrency.

More broadly, this work illustrates an important database engineering principle: sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making the core operation faster, but from eliminating the unnecessary work surrounding it. This effort was made possible through collaboration across MongoDB’s Atlas Search Query, Query Execution, Query Integration, Database Integration and Observability, and Server Triage & Release teams. Special thanks to Denis Grebennicov from the Database Integration and Observability team for his significant contributions to this optimization effort.

title: Reuse a Cached App Shell Without Blurring Query-Driven Responses
description:
A cached app shell may fail to load offline when a navigation adds a tracking or cosmetic query parameter. A request for /app and one for /app?utm_source=newsletter are different URLs under default cache matching, even when both should receive the same shell document.

The safe fix is route-scoped rather than global. First classify the request: allow only GET requests for a canonical shell path such as /app. For that one lane, use a cache lookup that ignores the URL search component. The cached shell can then satisfy navigations with campaign tags or other parameters that do not alter the shell response. The request still carries its full URL; only cache comparison changes.

Leave every other request on exact matching. API endpoints, searches, filtered results, user profiles, reports, and locale-specific content often use query parameters to select the response. In those cases, ignoring search could make one request receive a response intended for another query. Non-GET requests should bypass this shell-cache policy and continue to the network.

Expected behavior is intentionally limited. Two shell navigations with harmlessly different query strings can use one cached shell entry. If that entry is absent, the request falls back to the network. A query-sensitive request remains keyed by its complete URL and cannot select another query’s cached response.

Keep the decision function separate from service-worker event wiring. A controlled fixture can verify that application code selects the intended lookup option, preserves exact matching elsewhere, and bypasses non-GET requests. It cannot prove browser Cache API behavior, secure-context requirements, or the service-worker lifecycle; those require browser integration verification.

Ignoring search does not normalize different paths, reorder parameters, or establish a caching strategy for every route. Use it only where the path identifies a reusable shell and the search string does not change what that response means.

Working example 

// This module contains no service-worker side effects on import.
// Proof boundary: the route selection below is application code. A real browser
// service worker is still required to prove Cache.match()'s own cache semantics.

export const APP_SHELL_PATH = "/app";

export function isAppShellRequest(request) {
  const url = new URL(request.url);
  return request.method === "GET" && url.pathname === APP_SHELL_PATH;
}

/**
 * Handles an already-intercepted service-worker fetch request.
 *
 * Only GET requests are eligible for cache lookup. Within that set, only the
 * chosen app-shell route ignores its query string; API endpoints and other
 * query-driven routes use Cache.match()'s default exact matching.
 */
export async function handleAppShellFetch(request, { cache, networkFetch }) {
  // Cache.match() normally only matches GET and HEAD requests, but this policy
  // intentionally does not involve the cache for any non-GET operation.
  if (request.method !== "GET") {
    return networkFetch(request);
  }

  const cached = isAppShellRequest(request)
    ? await cache.match(request, { ignoreSearch: true })
    : await cache.match(request);

  return cached ?? networkFetch(request);
}

/**
 * Optional service-worker wiring. Call this from the service-worker script
 * after opening the intended Cache instance.
 */
export function registerAppShellFetchHandler(scope, dependencies) {
  scope.addEventListener("fetch", (event) => {
    event.respondWith(handleAppShellFetch(event.request, dependencies));
  });
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/cache-match-ignore-search-app-shell

title: CR80 card size in pixels, mm and inches: a developer's cheat sheet
description:
Sooner or later someone asks you to build a membership card preview, a gift card mockup or a "download your staff ID" feature. The first question is always the same: how big is a card, really? The answer is more precise than "about 86 by 54", and getting it slightly wrong is how you end up with artwork that gets cropped at the printer.

This is the reference I wish I'd had: the numbers, the pixel maths, and copy-paste snippets.

The numbers

A standard plastic card (bank card, loyalty card, ID badge) is the ID-1 format from ISO/IEC 7810. The printing industry calls it CR80.

Millimetres Inches
Width 85.60 mm 3.370 in
Height 53.98 mm 2.125 in
Corner radius ~3.18 mm 0.125 in (1/8")
Thickness (typical) 0.76 mm 0.030 in (30 mil)

Aspect ratio: 85.60 / 53.98 ≈ 1.586 : 1 (or 0.6306 the other way round). That's close to the golden ratio (1.618) but not equal to it, so don't reach for 1.618 as a shortcut.

You'll see 3.375 in quoted for the width in some printer drivers and US templates. That's 85.725 mm, a rounded imperial figure, not the ISO value. The difference is about 0.1 mm, which doesn't matter for a screen mockup, but use 85.60 mm when you're generating print files.

Bleed and safe area

Printed cards are cut from larger sheets, and the cut can drift slightly. Two margins handle that:

  • Bleed: background colour and images extend past the trim line, commonly 2–3 mm on each side, so a slightly off cut doesn't leave a white sliver.
  • Safe area: text and logos stay at least ~3 mm inside the trim line so a slightly off cut doesn't clip them.

With 3 mm bleed on every side, the artwork canvas is 91.60 × 59.98 mm (3.606 × 2.361 in). Always confirm which bleed the printer wants; 2 mm and 3 mm are both common.

Pixel sizes

Pixels = mm ÷ 25.4 × DPI. Rounded to whole pixels:

Canvas 300 DPI 600 DPI
Card only (85.60 × 53.98 mm) 1011 × 638 px 2022 × 1275 px
Card + 3 mm bleed (91.60 × 59.98 mm) 1082 × 708 px 2164 × 1417 px
Corner radius (3.18 mm) ~38 px ~75 px

On screen, CSS treats 1 in as 96 px, so a "true size" card is about 323.5 × 204 CSS px. That's only physically accurate if the display and zoom happen to cooperate, which they usually don't (more on that below).

Note the rounding: 637.56 px rounds up to 638. If you build a 1011 × 637 canvas, you've quietly changed the aspect ratio. Keep the mm values as your source of truth and derive the pixels from them.

CSS: a card that scales

Percentage border-radius is calculated separately against width and height, so border-radius: 3.7% gives you slightly elliptical corners on a non-square box. Drive everything from one width variable instead:

.card {
  --w: 340px;                       /* any width you like */
  width: var(--w);
  aspect-ratio: 85.6 / 53.98;
  border-radius: calc(var(--w) * 3.18 / 85.6);
  overflow: hidden;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #12355b, #1f8a8a);
  color: #fff;
  box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.2);
}

.card__safe {
  /* 3 mm safe margin, expressed relative to card width */
  position: absolute;
  inset: calc(var(--w) * 3 / 85.6);
}

Make .card position: relative if you use the safe-area box for layout. For a print stylesheet you can use real units:

@page { size: 85.6mm 53.98mm; margin: 0; }
.card--print { width: 85.6mm; height: 53.98mm; border-radius: 3.18mm; }

Chromium honours @page size; check your target browser before relying on it.

SVG: millimetres as user units

SVG is the most honest format for this, because you can make one user unit equal 1 mm:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     width="91.6mm" height="59.98mm" viewBox="-3 -3 91.6 59.98">
  <!-- bleed area: background runs to the outer edge -->
  <rect x="-3" y="-3" width="91.6" height="59.98" fill="#12355b"/>
  <!-- trim line (rounded corners) -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="85.6" height="53.98" rx="3.18"
        fill="none" stroke="#e33" stroke-width="0.2" stroke-dasharray="1 1"/>
  <!-- safe area -->
  <rect x="3" y="3" width="79.6" height="47.98"
        fill="none" stroke="#3c3" stroke-width="0.2"/>
</svg>

The negative viewBox origin puts (0, 0) on the trim corner, so all your layout coordinates are measured from the card edge, the same way a printer measures them. Remember to strip the guide rectangles before exporting the final file.

Canvas: export at print resolution

For a downloadable PNG, render at 300 DPI regardless of the user's screen:

const MM = 300 / 25.4;               // px per mm at 300 DPI
const W = 85.6, H = 53.98, BLEED = 3;

const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
canvas.width  = Math.round((W + BLEED * 2) * MM);   // 1082
canvas.height = Math.round((H + BLEED * 2) * MM);   // 708
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

ctx.scale(MM, MM);                   // now draw in millimetres
ctx.translate(BLEED, BLEED);         // (0,0) = trim corner

ctx.fillStyle = '#12355b';
ctx.fillRect(-BLEED, -BLEED, W + BLEED * 2, H + BLEED * 2);

ctx.fillStyle = '#fff';
ctx.font = '4px system-ui';          // 4 mm font size (units are mm now)
ctx.fillText('MEMBER NAME', 3, H - 6);   // inside the 3 mm safe area

canvas.toBlob(b => {/* download b */}, 'image/png');

For an on-screen preview, use ctx.roundRect(0, 0, W, H, 3.18) as a clip to show the rounded corners. Don't bake the rounding into a print file, though: the corners are die-cut, and the printer wants square artwork.

Common mistakes

  1. Using business card size. 3.5 × 2 in (88.9 × 50.8 mm) and the European 85 × 55 mm are paper business cards, not CR80. The aspect ratio is different, so artwork gets stretched or cropped.
  2. Rounding to 86 × 54. Fine for a quick UI sketch, but not for print files.
  3. No bleed. Backgrounds that stop exactly at the trim line give white edges.
  4. Text hugging the edge. Anything within ~3 mm of the trim is at risk.
  5. 72 DPI exports. A 324 × 204 px PNG looks fine on screen and prints soft. Export at 300 DPI minimum.
  6. Ignoring card features. Magnetic stripes, contact chips, signature panels and slot punches each cover part of the card. Keep important detail out of those zones.
  7. Trusting CSS mm on screen. 85.6mm in CSS is 323.5 px at the CSS reference of 96 px per inch, not a physical measurement. If "actual size" matters, add a calibration step (for example, ask users to hold a real card against the screen and drag a slider).
  8. Sending rounded corners or guide lines. Remove all guides before export.

Checking your output

If you're generating card artwork in an app, it helps to drop the exported file over a template with the trim, bleed and safe lines drawn in. A free CR80 artwork checker does exactly that in the browser (files aren't uploaded), and if you just need a quick starting design to test your pipeline with, there's a free online card designer as well.

TL;DR

  • CR80 = 85.60 × 53.98 mm = 3.370 × 2.125 in, corners ~3.18 mm, ratio 1.586.
  • 300 DPI: 1011 × 638 px (card), 1082 × 708 px (with 3 mm bleed).
  • 600 DPI: 2022 × 1275 px (card), 2164 × 1417 px (with 3 mm bleed).
  • Keep mm as the source of truth, keep text 3 mm inside, run backgrounds 3 mm outside.

title: Welvet: a Go AI engine that trains and runs on your hardware, from Raspberry Pi to CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, ROCm, MLX, and Qualcomm NPU
description:
Round 1 demos on Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android. These are working paths on real hardware, not a claim that anything is fastest or best.

I built Welvet because I wanted a Go engine that can actually train and run neural nets on my own machines, not just ship tensors off to somewhere else.

Source is at github.com/openfluke/welvet. There's a product page at openfluke.com/welvet and a feature book at openfluke.github.io/welvet.

This is a walkthrough of v1.7: backends, training modes, storage, and some of the messier runs (Macs, cheap VMs, ~1GB Raspberry Pi 3Bs).

What it does

Roughly four jobs:

  • Run: load weights, compute, get an answer
  • Train: update those weights from experience
  • Store: keep dtypes and quants as they are (no fake float32 master copy)
  • Measure: check what the chosen hardware actually did

Defaults are portable Go: CPU tiling, Plan 9 SIMD, and WebGPU. Extra accelerators are opt-in mounts. No silent "Prefer" path that pretends GPU/NPU work happened when it didn't.

Snapshot (v1.7)

Area What you get
Language Open-source Go AI / ML engine
Core Train + local inference
Numbers 34 storage dtypes, 20 quant formats, storage-truth (no QAT morph)
Training 29 named training modes, including cameral / multi-branch
Defaults Go CPU tiled, Plan 9 SIMD, WebGPU
Optional CPU NativeCPU via welvet.cpp C ABI
NVIDIA CUDA sessions (train + SyncToGo)
AMD ROCm sessions (library validated; GPU compute needs HSA)
Apple Metal train/run, MLX forward-only
Vulkan Linux x86_64 train + SyncToGo
Qualcomm Hexagon HTP on Windows ARM64 (Snapdragon X)
Other Layer packages, spatial grids, MoE / cameral parallelism
Platforms Linux, Windows, macOS (app also targets iOS and Android)
Docs Book chapters, examples, w2a validation

Paragon and Loom were earlier engines in the same project line. Welvet is the rewrite. They're history, not competing products.

Where it can run

Unsupported hosts soft-SKIP. Caps reject unsupported layer×dtype instead of lying.

Defaults

  1. Go CPU tiled (BackendCPUTiled): full layer set, 34 dtypes, 20 quants, train modes
  2. Plan 9 SIMD (BackendSIMD): Dense + Softmax/SiLU fused paths on amd64/arm64
  3. WebGPU (BackendWebGPU): Dense/MHA/CNN/norms and friends on compatible GPUs

NativeCPU

BackendNativeCPU + SyncToNative can push FormatNone forward, NormalBP, and TrainMode updates through sibling welvet.cpp on linux/amd64. Sync pending weights before writing .entity.

Optional accelerators

Backend Sibling Hosts Forward Train Notes
Apple Metal welvet.metal / nativemetal.Mount Apple silicon macOS Yes Yes Explicit SyncToGo. Not Apple Neural Engine. Book §82–88
Apple MLX welvet.mlx / nativemlx Apple silicon macOS Yes No Forward-only. Book §110–113
NVIDIA CUDA welvet.cuda / nativecuda.Mount Linux x86_64, Windows amd64 Yes Yes Two weight copies until SyncToGo(). Book §89–95
AMD ROCm welvet.rocm / nativerocm.Mount Linux x86_64, Windows amd64 Yes (API) Yes (API) Library validated; GPU compute untested until HSA. Book §96–102
Vulkan welvet.vulkan / nativevulkan.Mount Linux x86_64 Yes Yes No silent host fallback labeled as Vulkan. Book §103–109
Qualcomm Hexagon HTP welvet.qnn / BackendQNN Windows ARM64 (Snapdragon X) Yes n/a Explicit sync/prepare. Never Prefer default. Book §79–81

Mixed Go/C++/GPU JSON routing exists on the mount backends. Automatic routing is Linux amd64 today. You own sync and placement.

Dtypes and quants stay real in storage. Not a QAT morph that quietly becomes float32 underneath.

Some published timings

Same shapes, honest timers from the book / matrices. Not "peak marketing" numbers.

Metal, Mamba forwards (book §88):

dtype Go Metal Metal/Go
float64 89.3ms 29.0ms 3.1×
float32 69.0ms 29.0ms 2.4×
float16 190.5ms 28.9ms 6.6×
bfloat16 149.4ms 29.0ms 5.1×
fp8e4m3 265.9ms 29.2ms 9.1×

Qualcomm NPU, large shapes (go_v_qnn on Snapdragon X; DLL graphExecute vs Go f32 CPU):

Layer dtype Go f32 NPU DLL vs Go
Dense u8 3.05ms 164µs ~95% faster
Dense f32 3.05ms 201µs ~93% faster
CNN2 i8 12.56ms 763µs ~94% faster
MHA f16 4.51ms 372µs ~92% faster

Online layers still pay compose cost on the full Go→NPU call. The book calls that out on purpose.

Where it can train

Training lives in the Go runtime (forward, backward, step, TrainMode). You're not exporting to another framework to learn.

29 training modes

Not just SGD/backprop. See §67 TrainMode.

Modes include StepBP, Tween*, TweenSplit, HeadProxy, Linear, FastProxy, Sparse, Alt, cameral BranchModes, and more. On the big Tide boards, non-SGD modes beat matched SGD on Acc about 97–98% of the time. SGD still wins some individual boards. It's a baseline, not the religion.

Cameral

Cameral stacks sibling branches that share an input, merge, and can train under different rules. CamSync averages cam weights (and same-shape cross-layer pairs). Useful when you want learn / keep / share jobs running together under load.

Lucy

Lucy scores whether a net can keep serving while it learns:

Lucy Score ≈ Throughput × Availability × Acc (scaled)

That's what drove the Tide/Ocean runs: cameral×LR sweeps, Test53 mode farms, volatile cloud soaks, Pi 1GB layer farms.

Train support by backend

Path Train?
Go CPU / SIMD / WebGPU Yes
NativeCPU (welvet.cpp) Yes
Metal Yes (TrainMSE, then SyncToGo)
CUDA Yes (train on GPU, SyncToGo before save)
Vulkan Yes
ROCm API yes; GPU compute pending HSA
MLX No (forward-only)
QNN Forward / prepare-exec; see book caps

Layers and the Dense core

Most transformer/CNN FLOPs are weights × activations, so Welvet keeps one Dense stack as the shared MatVec kernel (FormatNone×34 + 20 quants × CPU/SIMD/WebGPU). Layers that are mostly GEMV reuse it.

Layers include Dense, MHA (RoPE / GQA), SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LayerNorm, Embedding, Softmax, Sequential, Residual, CNN1–3, RNN/LSTM, SeqMix, GDN, Mamba, ConvT 1–3, Soft K-Means, Parallel, Metacognition.

Also: volumetric grids, ENTITY save/reload, HF helpers, tokenizer/sampling, DNA/evolution/tween, telemetry.

Runs on ugly hardware

Catalogue: openfluke.com/welvet/experiments

Four experiment waves (cameral LR, Test53 modes, volatile Linode soak, Pi 3B ~1GB farm) finished 90,334 Tide model cells.

  1. Cameral × LR: does width and LR matter under Lucy live-fit?
  2. Test53: dense × all 29 modes × storage types × aggressive LRs; Ocean compares cam1 vs cam3
  3. Volatile online: cheap VMs, restarts, crowded dashboards. Checkpoint resume mattered. Cells stayed storage-truth (no silent float32 "rescue")
  4. Pi 3B / 1GB: 22 layer sprints. Dense/CNN/norms were fast; MHA/LSTM/Mamba still finished. One dense champ hit Lucy Score ~16344 on fp4 tween_chain with >100k outputs/sec. CNN1 hit ~94% hard Acc on a Lucy champ. Mode-vs-SGD Acc beat-rates ~97–98%

I'm not claiming SOTA. The point is live-fit on honest storage, from Macs to $5 VMs to 1GB Pis, with artefacts you can open.

Welvet app (separate, still early)

The library is the Go engine. The Welvet app (0.1.0+1) is a different thing: run and serve models on Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android.

  • openfluke.com/welvet/app
  • openfluke.com/welvet/models
  • Round 1 demos on CUDA/Metal/Vulkan-class stacks
  • 15 models in the public matrix right now
  • "Working" means it runs. Not that it's fast or best yet.

Not language-only. Detection, tracking, classification, depth, segmentation, pose, audio, etc. are in the mix.

Validation / family repos

Engine code stays in welvet/. Proof and wrappers live elsewhere, mainly w2a (Go↔native parity for cpp/cuda/metal/vulkan/rocm/mlx/qnn), plus C ABI, Python ctypes, and TypeScript/WASM.

Sibling engines: welvet.cpp, welvet.cuda, welvet.metal, welvet.vulkan, welvet.rocm, welvet.mlx, welvet.qnn.

Hard rules: no silent fallbacks, no hardcoded float32 tensors, storage-truth train, fail closed if a sibling binary is missing.

Links

Resource Link

Examples openfluke.com/examples

If you write Go and want train+infer in-process, or you care about dtype honesty and learn-while-serve on edge boxes, give it a look.

I'm Samuel Watson / OpenFluke, Australia. Forks and harsh readings of the scorecard are welcome. The docs try to keep implemented features, recorded measurements, and stubs clearly separated.

title: How modern-web-guidance-src Enhances Your Coding Agent's Skills

The Decision This Project Solves

Modern-web-guidance-src addresses the issue of coding agents often defaulting to legacy code patterns due to outdated training data. This results in bloated JavaScript and inefficient solutions when modern APIs and techniques are available. The repository provides expert-curated guidelines directly integrated into coding environments, promoting best practices in web development.

When the Project Is the Right Fit

This project is ideal for developers and teams using coding agents who want to ensure their applications leverage modern web capabilities. It specifically helps in utilizing modern browser APIs effectively, improving performance, and ensuring accessibility. If your team is focused on enhancing user experience, optimizing performance, or modernizing legacy code, this tool is a suitable fit.

Adoption Cost, Constraints & Exit Plan

To install, use the command:

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

This command initiates an interactive installation wizard. However, note that the project requires Node.js version 22.18.0 or higher. A potential limitation is that it may not cover every edge case in legacy code scanning, as it focuses on commonly used patterns and solutions. If the project does not meet your needs, it is easy to exit by simply uninstalling the package.

The Clear Recommendation

For teams looking to modernize their web development approach, adopting modern-web-guidance-src is highly recommended. It provides a direct pathway to integrating best practices into your coding agents, ensuring that they produce efficient, modern code. If your team is not ready for this shift or is working on projects where legacy code is heavily entrenched, it may be worth waiting until your strategies align with the capabilities of this tool.

title: Self-hosting a zero-trust network on one server with Lantern DSSE
description:
Lantern DSSE is an open-source (Apache-2.0), self-hosted zero-trust network: ZTNA and a secure web gateway that you run on your own servers. This post installs the 0.4.2 release on a single Linux server and connects a Windows PC to it.

Lantern DSSE is an experimental release. The single-server layout below is for trying it out: if that server stops, everything stops. Do not use it in production.

What Lantern DSSE does

It grew out of work on ransomware defense: if a device is compromised, which internal systems can it reach, and what can it send out?

  • Internal traffic. Observe which internal connections devices make, then limit each device to the applications it needs. Applications are reached through connectors that dial out to the Edge.
  • Out-of-band authentication with your IdP. For the internal destinations you mark, a connection such as SSH, RDP or SMB is held while the user signs in to your identity provider (OIDC) in a browser, and continues only after that.
  • Outbound traffic. Sites are allowed or denied by rule, and every decision is logged.
  • TLS inspection. For the traffic you choose, the Edge decrypts TLS with your organization's own certificate authority.

The same applies to AI agents. Prompts and guardrails shape what an agent tries to do, not what it can reach. We think the most dependable control is to decide access to each resource from an authenticated identity, outside the agent, and to log every decision.

What we are building

One server runs everything as containers.

What you need

  • One Linux x86-64 server with Docker Engine and Compose v2. I used a 4 vCPU, 16 GiB instance in AWS Tokyo with Ubuntu 24.04. You do not need Go or the source.
  • Port 443 open. Devices and administrators both come in through it.
  • The deployment's names resolving to the server, through DNS or hosts files. I used hosts files.
  • A Windows PC and the signed MSI from the release (DsseAgent-0.4.2-windows-x64.msi).

I did not limit port 443 by source address; the Console is protected by sign-in. Only SSH was limited to my own address.

1. Get the installer

Download the installer and the release manifest. The installer reads which container images to run from the manifest.

R=https://github.com/lantern-networks/dsse-core/releases/download/v0.4.2-experimental
curl -fLO $R/dsse-install-0.4.2-linux-amd64
curl -fLO $R/release-manifest.json
curl -fLO $R/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
sudo install -m 0755 dsse-install-0.4.2-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/dsse-install
sudo install -d -o "$USER" -g "$USER" -m 0755 /opt/dsse

2. Register the names

Choose a name for the deployment (one you control; example.test is a placeholder) and use the address the server actually has. The installer prints the line to add to the hosts file.

A='-up -deployment example.test -address 10.20.1.10 -admin-email admin@example.test
   -dir /opt/dsse/region-a -release-manifest release-manifest.json'
dsse-install $A -print-names | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

It prints one line: the address followed by eight names. On the administrator's PC and on the Windows PC, point the same names at the server's public address.

3. Install with one command 

dsse-install $A

The installer runs six steps in order. For me it took about four minutes, including pulling the images.

Step What it does
1 Creates the deployment's certificate authorities, certificates and configuration
2 Starts the containers
3 Creates the first administrator
4 Restarts the control plane and the Edge
5 Turns on the authentication features
6 Checks the whole deployment

The last step passes when nothing fails. I got 50 checks passed out of 51, with one not applicable because no customer organization existed yet. If a step fails, fix the cause and run the same command again: it skips the finished steps and continues.

Three of the files it creates in /opt/dsse/region-a are worth knowing:

File Contents
admin-credentials.txt The first administrator's password, the key for an authenticator app, and recovery codes. Readable only by its owner, and never printed to the screen
deployment-anchor.pem The certificate of this deployment's root authority. It holds no private key, so you can hand it out. Used on the administrator's PC in step 4
authority/ The private keys of the authorities. Guard this above everything else

admin-credentials.txt has this shape, with some notes around it:

  password        <the password>
  second factor   <the TOTP secret>
  recovery codes  <recovery codes, separated by spaces>
Line Use
password The password for signing in to the Console
second factor The key you register in an authenticator app (in step 4). At sign-in you enter the six digits the app shows
recovery codes Entered instead of the six digits when the app is unavailable. Each code works once

A layout with several servers is installed with the same -up and a plan file; see the deployment guide.

4. Create an organization in the Console

Copy /opt/dsse/region-a/deployment-anchor.pem from the server to the administrator's PC and trust it. On Windows, in an elevated PowerShell:

Get-FileHash .\deployment-anchor.pem   # must equal sha256sum on the server
Import-Certificate -FilePath .\deployment-anchor.pem -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\Root

Before signing in, register the second factor value in an authenticator app on your phone (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator and so on):

  1. Open the screen that adds an account by typing a key (in Google Authenticator, "Enter a setup key").
  2. Give the account a name you will recognize, for example the address you passed as -admin-email.
  3. Enter the second factor value as the key (32 capital letters and digits), with the key type "time based".

When the app shows six digits that change every 30 seconds, it is registered. Sign-in fails if the phone's clock is far off.

Open https://console.region-a.<your deployment>/console.html in a browser and sign in with the -admin-email address, the password from admin-credentials.txt, and the six digits from the app.

The tenant_default organization that already exists belongs to the operator. Create a customer organization (a tenant) for your devices:

  1. Under Tenants, press + Add tenant and give it a display name. Leave Who runs it at its default, We run it for them.
  2. Press Manage on that organization in the list. Inside it, under Certificates & PKI → Certificates, press Let this deployment issue them for device identity and Let this deployment make one for traffic inspection. In the dialog that appears first, press Ask for 20 minutes.
  3. Under Device configuration, press Make the configuration, then Download everything for one device to get the set for Windows.

The set contains the configuration (install_profile.json), the key that verifies its signature (profile_signing_key.txt) and a one-time enrolment token (enrolment_token.txt). It does not contain the MSI: download DsseAgent-0.4.2-windows-x64.msi from the release and put it in the same folder as DsseAgent.msi.

5. Install on Windows

Check the signatures of the MSI and the configuration first. dsse-profileverify.exe checks the configuration; build it on Windows from a clone of the repository with go build -o dsse-profileverify.exe ./cmd/dsse-profileverify.

Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\DsseAgent.msi | Format-List Status,SignerCertificate
.\dsse-profileverify.exe -profile install_profile.json -pin profile_signing_key.txt

The MSI must be Valid with the signer LANTERN NETWORKS, INC., and the configuration must report "signed by the pinned key" (it then prints the configuration itself, which holds certificates and public keys but no secret). In real use, the key reaches the device by a different route from the configuration.

Install from an elevated PowerShell:

$msi = (Resolve-Path .\DsseAgent.msi).Path
$config = (Resolve-Path .\install_profile.json).Path
$token = (Resolve-Path .\enrolment_token.txt).Path
$pin = (Resolve-Path .\profile_signing_key.txt).Path
$log = Join-Path $PWD 'install.log'
$p = Start-Process msiexec.exe -Wait -PassThru -ArgumentList "/i `"$msi`" /qn /l*v `"$log`" CONFIG=`"$config`" TOKEN=`"$token`" PIN=`"$pin`""
$p.ExitCode

When it prints 0, start the agent. On its first start the device enrols in the organization.

Get-Service DsseSteer,DsseWfp
Start-Service DsseSteer
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DsseSteer'" | Select-Object State,StartMode

It takes about half a minute before traffic goes through DSSE. It is ready when C:\Program Files\DSSE\dsse-steer.log shows steer_capture backend=wfp armed=true. The device also appears under Devices in the Console.

6. Check allow and deny

A new organization's Internet Access starts with one rule that allows and inspects everything. The idea is to make the traffic visible first and narrow it from there.

Add a rule that denies one site:

  1. Under Groups & Services, press + Add server and create the destination example.org.
  2. Under Internet Access, create a rule with example.org as the destination and Deny as the access. Give it a priority lower than the first rule's 100, for example 20 (the lower number wins).

In the PC's browser, an allowed site opens without a certificate warning, and the denied site shows a block page.

Logs & Audit records both the allowed and the denied requests, with the rule and the reason.

If you try it

If you try this in a lab, please tell us in an issue which version and operating system you used, what you tried, and where a step or the behaviour differed from what you expected. Do not include tokens, private keys or personal information. A star on GitHub is appreciated.

title: TechInventory: cómo modelar un inventario con documentos y revisiones de Apache CouchDB
description:
Autora: Victoria Lavarello Vidaurre

Cuando se registra un equipo en un laboratorio, no basta con guardar su nombre. También interesa conocer dónde está, quién es responsable y si puede utilizarse. TechInventory organiza esa información mediante una aplicación con React, una API en Express y documentos JSON en Apache CouchDB.

El proyecto tiene un alcance concreto: registrar, consultar, actualizar y eliminar equipos; buscar por sus datos principales; filtrar por estado y mostrar un resumen. La base elegida es CouchDB real. No se reemplaza por una colección en memoria para simplificar el alojamiento.

Por qué un documento por equipo

Un equipo reúne datos que suelen consultarse juntos. Por eso el documento incluye código, nombre, categoría, ubicación, responsable, estado y notas. El identificador se obtiene del código: un equipo LT-001 utiliza asset:LT-001. Las cuentas de acceso se distinguen con type: user y no aparecen en el listado del inventario.

Esta decisión tiene una consecuencia útil: dos altas concurrentes con el mismo código compiten por el mismo identificador. CouchDB acepta una y rechaza la otra. Una validación previa en la interfaz, por sí sola, no garantizaría esa unicidad.

El código queda fijo después del registro. De lo contrario, cambiarlo implicaría decidir cómo trasladar el documento y tratar referencias anteriores. Esa complejidad no forma parte del alcance de este trabajo.

Una revisión evita sobrescribir cambios ajenos

CouchDB devuelve _rev al guardar un documento. La API conserva esa revisión y la exige para editar o eliminar. Si dos usuarios abren el mismo equipo y uno guarda primero, el segundo debe actualizar la información antes de volver a intentarlo.

En TechInventory el conflicto se convierte en HTTP 409 y en un mensaje que pide actualizar. No se reintenta de manera ciega con la revisión más reciente: hacerlo podría ocultar la pérdida de un cambio. La revisión es un mecanismo de concurrencia, no un historial de auditoría ni una copia de seguridad.

El navegador no necesita conocer la base

React llama únicamente a rutas /api. Express valida cada entrada y construye el documento permitido. Las propiedades desconocidas se rechazan; un cliente no puede agregar su propio rol o cambiar el tipo de documento mediante el formulario de equipos.

La comunicación con CouchDB ocurre dentro de la red de Docker. El puerto 5984 no se publica al exterior. Las contraseñas de la base permanecen en variables del servidor y los usuarios de la aplicación tienen contraseñas derivadas con scrypt y una sal aleatoria.

Se diferencian dos roles: administración y consulta. Ocultar un botón en React facilita el uso, pero la autorización que protege los datos está en Express. Una cuenta de consulta recibe 403 si intenta escribir directamente contra la API.

Cómo verificarlo sin confundir evidencias

El repositorio incluye dos niveles de prueba. npm test comprueba rutas, validación, sesión, protección CSRF, roles y conflictos usando un doble de la base. Estas pruebas son rápidas, pero no demuestran persistencia en CouchDB.

Para probar la integración se inicia Docker Compose y se ejecuta npm run test:integration. Esa prueba crea un código aleatorio, registra un documento, actualiza su estado, intenta una escritura con una revisión antigua, consulta el resultado y elimina el documento de prueba.

La comprobación de persistencia exige un paso adicional: registrar un equipo, reiniciar los contenedores y volver a consultar el mismo documento. El volumen couchdata conserva los archivos. Eliminar ese volumen eliminaría también la evidencia que se intenta comprobar.

El 12 de noviembre de 2026, la ejecución CI #3 terminó correctamente: seis pruebas de API y una integración con CouchDB real. La evidencia está en evidence/ci-couchdb-real.txt y evidence/03-ci-exitoso.jpg. La prueba de reinicio se documenta por separado: leer tras escribir no demuestra por sí solo persistencia entre reinicios.

Lo que mejoraría al crecer

El listado actual recorre los documentos del inventario y filtra en el servidor. Es suficiente para una demostración pequeña, pero un inventario grande necesitaría índices Mango, paginación y límites explícitos. También agregaría historial de movimientos, recuperación de acceso y revocación central de sesiones.

CouchDB aporta documentos y control de concurrencia; no resuelve por sí mismo el diseño de permisos, las copias de seguridad o la experiencia de uso. La parte más valiosa del proyecto es poder explicar esas responsabilidades y comprobarlas por separado.

Código y referencias

  • Repositorio TechInventory
  • Ejecuciones de validación
  • API de documentos de CouchDB
  • Control de conflictos
  • Instalación oficial con Docker

Resultado verificado de la demostración

El 12/11/2026 se publicó TechInventory con HTTPS en una VM Ubuntu de Azure for Students. El despliegue automático #4 terminó correctamente. También se ejecutó CRUD real desde la URL HTTPS y se comprobó que asset:LT-DEMO conservaba su identificador y revisión después de reiniciar Express y CouchDB. Los registros y capturas están en evidence.

La URL utilizada fue https://techinventory-codexvex-20261112.eastus.cloudapp.azure.com. El alojamiento es temporal: se retira después de recopilar las evidencias para evitar consumo continuo de créditos. Esa dirección no debe considerarse un servicio permanente. El repositorio y los registros de Actions permiten revisar la construcción y el despliegue aunque el servidor se haya retirado.

Video público: construcción y despliegue

Ver la demostración de TechInventory en YouTube. Duración inferior a cinco minutos (aproximadamente 3:54). Explica la construcción Docker, los documentos de CouchDB, la integración, el workflow CI/CD y el despliegue real en Azure mediante capturas y texto en español, sin audio.

La VM de la demostración ya fue eliminada para ahorrar créditos; el video y las evidencias documentan el resultado obtenido.

title: How to run a 5-person usability test on your app for about $30
description:
You built the onboarding, so you can't really see it anymore. You know which button matters, what the icon means, and why step three asks for a phone number. Someone opening the app for the first time knows none of that. Most of them won't tell you where they got lost, either. They just close it.

A small usability test gets that view back. It doesn't take a research team or a sales call. It takes five strangers and an afternoon of watching. This is how I'd run one. I run a testing marketplace, so there's a disclosure near the end, but every step before it works the same however you find your five people.

Why five people

Jakob Nielsen's well-known argument is that five users find about 85% of the usability problems in a design, and each extra user mostly repeats problems you've already seen. His advice is to split the budget into several small rounds: test with five, fix, test with five more.

The same article has two caveats. The math assumes your users are roughly one group. If you have two very different audiences, say teachers and students, test three or four from each. And five people find problems; they don't measure anything. If you want a conversion rate, that's analytics.

Step 1: pick one flow

Not "the app". Pick one path with a clear end that every new user has to get through:

  • Sign-up to the first useful screen
  • Creating the first thing your app makes (a habit, a budget, a playlist)
  • The paywall, from the moment it appears to a decision
  • Checkout

If you can't choose, take the flow right after install. Every user sees it, and you've looked at it so often you no longer notice it.

Step 2: write tasks as goals, not instructions

Most first tests go wrong here. If the task says "Tap the + button and add a habit", you've told the tester where the button is, which is the exact thing you wanted to find out.

Write what the person wants to get done, in their words, and leave the how to them:

Leads the user Lets you learn something
Tap "Create budget" and set a monthly limit You want to spend less than $400 on food this month. Set that up.
Go to Settings > Notifications and turn on reminders You keep forgetting to log your workouts. See if the app can help.
Use the search bar to find a vegetarian recipe Find something you could cook tonight without meat.

Three to five tasks fill 10 to 15 minutes. Put them in the order a real user would meet them.

Step 3: the script

This is the whole thing I'd send. Copy it and swap in your tasks.

Thanks for doing this. Please record your screen and talk out loud the whole time: what you're looking at, what you expect to happen, anything that confuses you. There are no wrong answers. We're testing the app, not you.

  1. Install the app from [link] and open it. Before you tap anything, tell us what you think it does.
  2. [Goal task 1]
  3. [Goal task 2]
  4. [Goal task 3]
  5. If you could change one thing about what you just used, what would it be?
  6. Would you keep this app after today? Why or why not?

The first task does more work than it looks like. "What do you think this does?" tells you whether your first screen explains the app. If three of five people guess wrong, that's your first finding, and nobody has reached the flow yet.

Don't tell them how long anything should take, and don't explain the app beforehand. Your real users won't get a briefing.

Step 4: find five people who have never seen it

They need to be new to the app and reasonably close to your audience. Roughly from cheapest to most expensive:

  • Friends of friends, not friends. Friends are polite, and they already know what you were going for. Someone one step removed is a better stand-in for a stranger.
  • Communities your users already spend time in: a subreddit, a Discord, a Facebook group. Read the rules first. Many don't allow test requests, and the ones that do usually expect something back.
  • Your waitlist. People who signed up but haven't opened the app yet are close to your audience by definition. Offer a small thank-you.
  • A paid testing service. You pay per person and skip the scheduling. Prices vary a lot: some of the big platforms sell by quote or annual contract, and smaller marketplaces charge per tester.

Whichever route you take, ask for a screen recording with their voice, not a written summary. People describe what they think they did, and it often isn't what they did. A recording shows the four seconds of hesitation before they tap the wrong tab.

Step 5: watch with a sheet open

Watch each recording once all the way through, then again with a sheet:

Tester Time What happened Task Severity
2 01:40 Tapped the logo, expecting to go home 1 Low
2 03:15 Looked for "save" for 20 seconds, gave up 2 High

What I write down:

  • Hesitation. A pause of several seconds before a tap usually means the screen didn't make the next step obvious.
  • Backtracking: into a screen, back out, back in again.
  • Saying one thing and doing another, like "OK, that's easy" followed by the wrong tap.
  • Workarounds: finishing the task by a route you didn't design, like closing the app to get "back".
  • Their words. If everyone calls it "my list" and your tab says "Collections", the tab is wrong.

Severity doesn't need to be scientific. High means the task failed or nearly did. Medium means they got there but struggled. Low is a moment of friction.

Step 6: fix three things, then test again

After five recordings you'll usually see the same two or three problems again and again. Fix those first. It's tempting to redesign everything after one round, and I'd resist it. The point of small tests is that the next round tells you whether the fix worked.

Then run five new people through the same tasks. They have to be new, because the first five have learned your app by now.

What it costs and how long it takes

Recruiting yourself is free, and you pay in time. Expect a day or two of messages before five people actually send a recording.

On the marketplace I run, a screen recording costs $5.99 per tester, so five people come to $29.95. Some numbers from our side: 54 recorded campaigns went live after 1 June and got at least five recordings. For half of them, the fifth recording arrived within 15.4 hours, and 44 of the 54 had it within three days. Across all 825 recordings since March, the median session lasted just under 14 minutes.

Disclosure

I run TestFi. Testers there record their screen and talk through your tasks on their own phones, and each recording comes with a transcript and timestamps for the moments they got stuck. If you'd rather not recruit, it's here. Everything above works the same with five people you found yourself.

If you try the first-screen question ("what do you think this does?"), I'd like to hear in the comments what people guessed.

title: Taming Rust Compile Times in 2026: A Practical Playbook with cargo --timings, Cranelift, mold and sccache
description:
Rust 1.100 vừa ra, cộng đồng lại bàn về một dự án JIT compiler cho Rust với mục tiêu giảm build time. Điều này cho thấy compile time vẫn là nỗi đau lớn nhất của Rust, dù ngôn ngữ đã trưởng thành nhiều. Team mình có một service khoảng 80k dòng Rust, chia thành 14 crate trong workspace. Có thời điểm một lần cargo build incremental sau khi sửa đúng một dòng mất 40 giây. Khi AI agent tự sửa code rồi tự chạy test liên tục thì 40 giây đó bị nhân lên hàng trăm lần mỗi ngày. Bài này tổng hợp những gì mình đã làm để đưa con số đó xuống khoảng 6 giây. Không có phép màu nào cả, chỉ là đo đúng chỗ rồi sửa đúng chỗ.

1. Đo trước, tối ưu sau

Lỗi phổ biến nhất mình thấy là đổi linker hoặc thêm cache theo cảm tính mà không biết thời gian thực sự bị tiêu vào đâu. Cargo có sẵn công cụ đo khá tốt:

# Báo cáo HTML: crate nào build lâu, crate nào chặn song song
cargo build --timings
open target/cargo-timings/cargo-timing.html

# Xem generic nào sinh ra nhiều LLVM IR nhất
cargo install cargo-llvm-lines
cargo llvm-lines -p my-core --lib | head -20

# Thời gian từng pass của rustc (cần nightly)
cargo +nightly rustc -p my-core -- -Z time-passes

Trong báo cáo cargo-timing.html, hãy chú ý hai thứ. Thứ nhất là các thanh dài nằm trên critical path, thường là crate trung tâm mà mọi crate khác phụ thuộc vào. Thứ hai là phần màu tím (codegen) so với phần màu xanh (frontend). Nếu codegen chiếm phần lớn, vấn đề nằm ở LLVM và monomorphization. Nếu frontend chiếm phần lớn, nguyên nhân thường là macro (serde, sqlx, tokio) hoặc trait resolution phức tạp.

Để chọn đúng công cụ, cần biết mỗi giai đoạn build tương ứng với công cụ nào:

flowchart LR
    A[Source .rs] --> B[Frontend: parse, macro, typeck]
    B --> C[MIR + monomorphization]
    C --> D[Codegen: LLVM / Cranelift]
    D --> E[Linker: ld / lld / mold]
    E --> F[Binary]
    S[sccache] -.cache toàn crate.-> D
    W[Tách crate / bớt generic] -.giảm.-> C
    CL[Cranelift] -.thay LLVM.-> D
    M[mold / lld] -.tăng tốc.-> E

2. Linker và codegen backend: thắng nhanh nhất

Với incremental build, phần link thường chiếm tỷ lệ lớn đến bất ngờ, vì mỗi lần sửa một dòng là phải link lại toàn bộ binary. Từ Rust 1.90, target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu đã dùng lld làm linker mặc định, nên nếu bạn đang dùng toolchain mới trên Linux thì đã được hưởng phần lớn lợi ích này. Trên các target khác, hoặc khi muốn nhanh hơn nữa, mold (bản 2.x) vẫn là lựa chọn rất đáng thử.

Bước tiếp theo là Cranelift. Đây là codegen backend viết bằng Rust, sinh code chạy chậm hơn LLVM nhưng compile nhanh hơn đáng kể. Cranelift hợp với dev build và test, không nên dùng cho release. Hiện tại nó vẫn cần nightly:

rustup toolchain install nightly
rustup component add rustc-codegen-cranelift-preview --toolchain nightly

Sau đó cấu hình trong .cargo/config.toml và Cargo.toml:

# .cargo/config.toml
[target.x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu]
linker = "clang"
rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold"]

[unstable]
codegen-backend = true

# Cargo.toml (workspace root)
[profile.dev]
codegen-backend = "cranelift"
debug = "line-tables-only"   # đủ cho backtrace, nhẹ hơn debug=2 rất nhiều

# Dependency ít thay đổi: tối ưu một lần, cache mãi
[profile.dev.package."*"]
codegen-backend = "llvm"
opt-level = 2

Có một mẹo ở đây: dependency bên ngoài vẫn dùng LLVM với opt-level = 2, vì chúng chỉ build một lần rồi được cache. Còn code của mình, phần thay đổi liên tục, thì dùng Cranelift. Kết quả là test vẫn chạy đủ nhanh mà vòng sửa-build lại ngắn. Với project của mình, riêng bước này đã giảm incremental build từ 40 giây xuống khoảng 14 giây.

Lưu ý: một số crate dùng SIMD intrinsics hoặc inline asm có thể chưa tương thích với Cranelift. Nếu gặp lỗi, hãy chuyển riêng crate đó về llvm qua [profile.dev.package.ten-crate].

3. Cấu trúc workspace: tối ưu bền vững nhất

Linker và backend chỉ giúp bạn đi nhanh hơn trên con đường sẵn có. Cấu trúc crate mới quyết định con đường đó dài bao nhiêu. Có ba nguyên tắc mình áp dụng:

  • Tách crate theo tần suất thay đổi. Domain types ít thay đổi thì để vào crate riêng ở đáy dependency graph. Business logic thay đổi liên tục thì để ở các crate lá. Sửa crate lá thì chỉ crate đó cùng binary phải build lại.
  • Không để mọi thứ phụ thuộc vào một crate common khổng lồ. Mỗi lần sửa common là cả workspace phải build lại. Đây là nguyên nhân chính khiến build của team mình chậm.
  • Giảm monomorphization. Dựa vào kết quả cargo llvm-lines, với các hàm generic lớn, hãy tách phần thân thành một hàm non-generic bên trong: 
// Trước: toàn bộ thân hàm bị nhân bản cho mỗi kiểu P
pub fn load_config<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Result<Config> {
    // ... 80 dòng parse ...
}

// Sau: chỉ wrapper mỏng là generic
pub fn load_config<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Result<Config> {
    fn inner(path: &Path) -> Result<Config> {
        // ... 80 dòng parse, chỉ compile một lần ...
    }
    inner(path.as_ref())
}

Thư viện chuẩn cũng dùng đúng pattern này, ví dụ std::fs::read. Ngoài ra, hãy chạy cargo machete hoặc cargo udeps để loại bỏ dependency không dùng, và rà soát feature flags. Bật tokio với features = ["full"] trong một crate chỉ cần sync là lãng phí.

4. Cache trên CI và giữa các máy

Ở local, incremental compilation đã làm khá tốt. Trên CI, mỗi job bắt đầu từ trạng thái trống, nên cache là bắt buộc. Mình kết hợp hai lớp:

sequenceDiagram
    participant CI as CI Job
    participant RC as rust-cache (target/)
    participant SC as sccache (S3/GCS)
    participant R as rustc
    CI->>RC: Restore target/ theo hash Cargo.lock
    CI->>R: cargo build
    R->>SC: Hash input của crate
    SC-->>R: Hit: trả artifact
    SC-->>R: Miss: compile rồi upload
    CI->>RC: Save target/ (chỉ trên main)

File workflow GitHub Actions rút gọn:

- uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
- uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
  with:
    save-if: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
- uses: mozilla-actions/sccache-action@v0.0.9
- run: cargo nextest run --workspace
  env:
    RUSTC_WRAPPER: sccache
    SCCACHE_GHA_ENABLED: "true"
    CARGO_INCREMENTAL: "0"

Ba chi tiết dễ bị bỏ qua:

  1. CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 trên CI: incremental artifact rất lớn và gần như không có ích khi đã có sccache.
  2. save-if chỉ lưu cache trên main: nếu mọi PR đều ghi cache, giới hạn 10GB của GitHub sẽ bị dùng hết rất nhanh.
  3. cargo-nextest (0.9.x) chạy mỗi test trong một process riêng và song song tốt hơn cargo test. Với test suite lớn, nó thường nhanh hơn 30-50%.

Kết luận

Build time của Rust không phải là thứ bắt buộc phải chịu đựng. Nếu chỉ có một buổi chiều, mình gợi ý làm theo thứ tự sau:

  1. Chạy cargo build --timings để xác định critical path trước khi thay đổi bất cứ thứ gì.
  2. Kiểm tra linker: trên Linux x86_64 với Rust từ 1.90 trở lên, bạn đã có lld. Trên target khác, hãy thử mold.
  3. Thử Cranelift cho profile.dev, đồng thời giữ LLVM với opt-level = 2 cho dependency.
  4. Đặt debug = "line-tables-only": thay đổi một dòng nhưng giảm kích thước target/ rõ rệt.
  5. Rà soát dependency graph: tách crate common, xử lý các hàm generic lớn, cắt feature flags thừa.
  6. Trên CI, dùng rust-cache + sccache + nextest và chỉ lưu cache trên main.

Trong thời đại AI agent tự build và tự test hàng trăm lần mỗi ngày, mỗi giây tiết kiệm được ở vòng lặp build sẽ được nhân lên rất nhiều lần. Đầu tư vài giờ cho build time thường là khoản đầu tư có lợi nhất cho team Rust.

title: Node.js Image Processing Recovery With 3 Moderation Checkpoints and Tagged Metrics
description:
TL;DR: For a Node.js Express photo intake service, start with three application-owned checkpoints: transformation completed, OCR completed, and moderation decided. Report processed counts, original and delivery byte sizes, failures, and observed processing cost with transformation tags; keep a photo held until its required checks finish. Retry attempts need their own accounting. A successful compression count cannot tell a property manager whether a maintenance photo is safe to release or whether its text was extracted.

Consider this proposed page: property photo releases are stalled while the processing dashboard is green. The responder sees completed delivery copies, a growing set of photos awaiting decisions, and no clear distinction between a check that rejected content and a check that never completed. This is a design exercise, not an account of a production incident. The least complex fix is a durable record of each checkpoint and its outcome, with metrics derived from those records.

What page fired?

That question comes before the vendor comparison, because a dashboard displaying healthy throughput can be completely accurate and still conceal the condition keeping the property manager from reading a photographed notice.

What should have fired before the release queue stalled?

Work backward from the blocked release. For a property management intake workflow, treat the original photo as evidence, the compressed copy as a delivery artifact, and OCR text as a separate output that needs its own review decision. A smaller file proves none of the latter conditions. The moderation policy must say whether it covers the photograph, extracted text, or both, and what happens while a required decision is missing.

The earlier signal is the age of the oldest photo missing a required checkpoint, broken down by the checkpoint that is holding it. Pair that with attempt failures and a count of terminally rejected photos. Otherwise, a deliberately held photo and an operationally stuck photo become the same red number, and the responder has to reconstruct policy from logs while the queue grows.

Keep them separate.

Property management teams should try Infrai for image processing and metrics reporting when one key and one bill would reduce the backend credentials and accounts they must reconcile during recovery. The shared REST API also avoids requiring a separate SDK for each operation, while its public, self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas and runnable examples for checking the worker's contract. These are operational reasons to evaluate it; the moderation policy still needs a deliberate provider choice.

Compression success, OCR success, and a policy decision are different claims, even if one provider appears in several boxes on an architecture diagram.

Choose moderation coverage before consolidating the plumbing

A useful comparison asks which inputs receive a decision and which decisions your application must combine. These are integration choices, not a measured accuracy ranking. Evaluate them against the same consented property-photo test set, including readable notices, blurred text, and otherwise acceptable photos that contain sensitive text.

Option Relevant coverage to evaluate Recovery boundary to own
Google Cloud Vision Text detection and SafeSearch image annotations. Track OCR and image screening separately; a SafeSearch result does not establish a review of extracted text.
Amazon Rekognition Text detection and image moderation. Persist each result and decide what happens if only one check finishes.
Azure AI Vision with Azure AI Content Safety OCR and content safety have separate documented service surfaces. Make the handoff from extracted text to the required safety check explicit.
Cloudinary A media management and transformation option to evaluate for the delivery artifact. Establish the OCR and moderation contracts separately from delivery success.
imgix An image processing and delivery option to evaluate for transformed copies. Keep evidence retention and release decisions outside the delivery measurement.
ImageKit An image optimization and media management option to evaluate for delivery copies. Verify the required review coverage rather than inferring it from image optimization.
Infrai A common backend interface for image processing and reporting, with contracts exposed through discovery. Keep the application checkpoint ledger and moderation acceptance criteria explicit.

A direct specialist is the better choice when its documented moderation categories and results on your test set fit the property manager's release policy more closely. Infrai's unified interface is not a substitute for that evaluation. Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit belong on a shortlist when delivery transformation is the problem; the OCR and moderation candidates address a different acceptance decision, so counting all of them as interchangeable would obscure the actual trade-off.

Consolidating credentials cannot establish moderation coverage. Nor does a text detector establish that it can reliably interpret every photographed notice: the release criteria must account for an unreadable result, rather than treating an empty extraction as evidence that the photo contains no text.

Test the decision you need.

How should Express measure image processing cost and byte savings during retries?

For the Express service, carry a stable photo revision identifier from intake into the worker and record an attempt for each checkpoint. Keep the original byte size, delivery byte size, transformation recipe, outcome, and any observed per-call cost associated with that attempt. These are application record names, not a provider request schema. A retry can consume another attempt while producing no new accepted artifact, so an attempt counter and a completed-photo counter answer different operational questions.

Use low-cardinality tags such as transformation recipe and checkpoint for metrics. Keep photo identifiers in the durable ledger and diagnostic logs, where the responder can inspect a particular item without creating a metric series for every tenant upload. Before publishing a completion measurement, commit the accepted result against its photo revision and checkpoint. Deduplicate that completion identity; retain separate records for attempts and their costs.

Here is a synthetic counting example. A failed attempt a1 is followed by successful attempt a2, whose completion observation is delivered twice; a later attempt a3 also succeeds for the same photo revision and recipe. The correct totals are 3 distinct attempts, 1 failure, and 1 completed photo. If the original is 800,000 bytes and the accepted delivery copy is 320,000 bytes, count 480,000 fewer delivery bytes once. Those numbers demonstrate arithmetic, not measured savings.

The duplicate observation disappears. The extra attempt doesn't.

Record observed cost and record missing cost metadata separately; never silently substitute zero. Infrai specifies native response metadata including cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, cache_hit, and request_id, which can support attribution without inventing a second cost estimate. For other providers, establish the corresponding accounting source before comparing totals. Add attempt costs even when their output is discarded, and attribute them to the transformation and checkpoint that incurred them.

Production deduplication belongs in a durable transaction or equivalent atomic operation, so a worker restart cannot erase the record of an accepted result. Include checkpoint identity when applying the rule to OCR and moderation, and do not sum their output sizes into delivery-byte savings. Bytes belong to the artifact being delivered, not to every operation that touched it.

Before wiring provider calls into that accounting, inspect their contracts. This runnable Go example calls Infrai's public discovery surface, which requires no key, and prints its response rather than guessing compression or metrics payload fields. It is a contract inspection step for the Node.js service's integration owner, not the OCR worker itself. Save it as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It sets an explicit GET method, checks response status, and bounds rate-limit retries by both attempt count and a context deadline.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry delay exceeds local budget: %s", value)
                }
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(when); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The sample stops rather than retrying earlier than a Retry-After interval that exceeds its local delay budget. It never submits a processing job. Keep the production request schemas and runnable examples from discovery beside the worker implementation; a schema lookup should precede a request change, not become another network dependency on every photo.

Recover the missing checkpoint without replaying the whole photo

Start recovery from the ledger entry that lacks a required decision. If the delivery copy exists and its transformation revision matches, a moderation retry should not cause the worker to create another delivery copy or count another processed photo. Preserve the hold until the required review has a terminal outcome. Keep policy rejection distinct from transport failure: retrying a rejection until it disappears is a change in policy disguised as recovery.

For rate limiting, honor Retry-After when present and use bounded exponential backoff rather than immediately resubmitting work. Keep a retry budget and send exhausted work to an operator-visible review state. For a write, use an idempotent request contract where the chosen operation supports it; Infrai documents the Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window, but the application still needs its durable completion identity for recovery beyond that window.

No blind replay.

An incident review should ask whether the page named the missing checkpoint, whether duplicate attempts inflated costs or completions, and whether the accepted image revision matched the OCR and moderation results. Those questions expose a recovery defect that aggregate throughput can conceal, without assuming that a provider outage explains every held photo.

Page on stalled decisions without paging on every hold

A hold is expected work while review is in progress. Set the alert against the release deadline your property workflow can tolerate, with a minimum affected-photo count and separate visibility for sparse traffic; a percentage by itself is unstable when the denominator is tiny. Keep the oldest pending age visible even when traffic falls to zero, since the absence of new uploads does not resolve yesterday's blocked photo.

Choose the actual threshold from observed review duration and the operational deadline, then examine historical held items before enabling paging. No latency distribution or safe universal timeout is established here. A threshold that is too generous misses a growing backlog; one that is too tight pages on legitimate review work, interrupts the responder, and teaches the team to discount the next alert. That false-positive cost belongs in the postmortem alongside byte savings and processing cost.

References

These sources document the format and coverage boundaries discussed above.

  • MDN image file type and format guide
  • Google Cloud Vision text detection
  • Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch
  • Amazon Rekognition text detection
  • Amazon Rekognition moderation
  • Azure AI Vision OCR
  • Azure AI Content Safety overview
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • imgix documentation
  • ImageKit documentation

Further reading

If the shared backend boundary fits your recovery plan, start with the request contracts and conventions in the Infrai documentation.
