title: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange
description:
Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693). Amazon Cognito helps you add sign-up, sign-in, and access control to your web applications, mobile applications, and AI agents. With token exchange, a service or AI agent acting on a user's behalf can exchange the user's token for a new token scoped to a specific downstream service. Previously, a service that called another service on a user's behalf had to forward the user's original token or build and maintain its own token minting logic.

With token exchange, you can issue a new token that has a narrower scope than the original token, is bound to a single audience, and comes without a refresh token. When you include an actor token, Cognito adds an act claim that identifies the intermediary, so downstream services can tell a request that an agent made on a user's behalf from one the user made directly. For example, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server can exchange a user's token for a narrowly scoped token to call a backend API, with the act claim recording the MCP server as the actor.

You can exchange tokens through the token endpoint or with the new GetDerivedToken API. Token exchange is available on the Essentials and Plus feature plans in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see exchanging tokens for downstream services in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

title: One library, several languages, held to one set of test vectors
description:
genever generates TypeScript types from JSON Schema and OpenAPI documents. Since November 8 it also has a Go version, released as v0.1.0:

go get -tool github.com/JacobLey/leyman/apps/genever/go/cmd/genever@v0.1.0

It reads the same schemas, has the same strict mode, and rejects the same bad schemas with the same kind of error at the same JSON Pointer. It writes Go structs instead of TypeScript types. Two of genever's dependencies came along, because the Go command has to sign its output and keep a manifest the way the TypeScript one does: populate-files and generated-signature are Go modules now too, released at the same version.

This continues a pattern in my adoption of Go, which forces language-agnostic support for common functionality (in this case, type-ifying JSON Schema + OpenAPI).

None of the Go code is tested against the TypeScript code. Both are tested against a set of test vectors: inputs and expected outputs, as JSON, that the TypeScript implementation computed once and that are committed to the repository.

One directory per package, one per language

Each of these packages is a directory named after the package, with one project per language beside the vectors they share:

apps/genever/
├── README.md what every implementation promises
├── ts/ published to npm as genever
├── go/ the Go module github.com/JacobLey/leyman/apps/genever/go
└── test-vectors/ schemas, sample values and error cases, as JSON

populate-files and generated-signature have the same shape. constant-consistent-hash, the oldest of the four, has ts/, go/, rust/, and a wasm/ package that calls the Rust implementation from TypeScript.

Until the release, the TypeScript package was the root and the Go code lived in a go-impl/ folder next to it. Moving each language into its own directory means neither is the package. The group README describes what holds in every language (the format a file is signed in, which schemas are rejected and where), and a third language has an obvious place to go.

Where the expected values come from

genever's vectors are a TypeScript package that writes JSON files under out/ on every build:

  • 45 schema fixtures, each with sample values it accepts. The schemas are Juniper definitions and the samples come from juniper-arbitrary with a fixed seed, so a file only changes when a fixture does.
  • Two OpenAPI documents, 3.0.3 and 3.1.0, with samples of each component.
  • errors.json: 74 schemas genever rejects, each with the kind of error and the JSON Pointer it must name.

The files are committed, and CI fails if one is stale. The TypeScript genever runs the vectors from the package; the Go one reads the JSON by relative path:

func testVectors() fs.FS {
    return os.DirFS(filepath.Join("..", "test-vectors"))
}

Reading by path was a late change. The vectors started as a Go module that embedded the JSON, which works until you release: a published Go module can't require one that isn't published, and the vectors are only for tests. So the Go tests read the working copy, and the Go project lists the vectors in its Nx implicitDependencies so its tests rerun when they change (commit).

generated-signature has 187 cases in one file (signing, verifying, manual sections, manifests), and populate-files has 71 scenarios: files written, hand edits made, then one call with the results, error and files it must leave behind.

No implementation regenerates the values it is tested against: if the Go port could rewrite them, a change in Go would update the vectors and pass.

The same error, at the same pointer

genever's error cases are vectors too. One per kind, from errors.json:

{
    "invalid": {
        "type is unknown": { "schema": { "type": "date" }, "pointer": "#/type" }
    },
    "strict": {
        "unknown keyword": { "schema": { "type": "string", "foo": 1 }, "pointer": "#/foo" }
    },
    "unsupported": {
        "$dynamicRef": { "options": { "strict": false }, "schema": { "$dynamicRef": "#node" }, "pointer": "#/$dynamicRef" }
    }
}

The Go test checks the error's kind with errors.Is and its pointer, and that each strict mode case is accepted once strict mode is off:

var geneverErr *genever.Error
if !errors.Is(err, kind) || !errors.As(err, &geneverErr) || geneverErr.Pointer != item.Pointer {
    t.Fatalf("got %v, expected %s at %s", err, kind, item.Pointer)
}

Moving the cases out of the TypeScript tests made those tests stricter too. They had checked the error's class but not the pointer. And the whole suite had run as OpenAPI 3.0, which hid that one check (exclusiveMaximum) behaved differently outside it; now only the two cases that need OpenAPI 3.0 run as it (commit).

What the vectors caught

generated-signature's vectors cover the places where Go and JavaScript disagree by default: what JavaScript's \s and trim() count as whitespace, Node.js's extname, lowercase İ, the byte order mark TextDecoder drops, and JSON.stringify's escaping. One case lists five manifest keys, Z, a, é, 😀 and , in that order. JavaScript compares strings by UTF-16 code unit, so the emoji (a surrogate pair starting at `0xD83D`) sorts before. Go compares UTF-8 bytes, where `comes first. A manifest written by one would look edited to the other, so the Go code sorts byutf16.Encode`.

In populate-files, the TypeScript package was the one that changed. The Go port decided every file before writing any, so a refused write left everything as it was. The TypeScript package wrote files in parallel as it decided them, so a refusal could come after other files were written. The scenarios couldn't pin the files a failed call leaves while the two disagreed, so the TypeScript package changed to match the port in populate-files 1.2.3 (commit), and the scenarios now pin those files.

A third turned up the day before release. The released modules declare go 1.24, the oldest Go they support, and CI now runs each released module's tests on Go 1.24 as well as the current Go. That run failed: Go 1.24's JSON decoder reports an unclosed { or [ only when asked for the closing delimiter, which genever-go's order-keeping JSON parser had been discarding, so truncated JSON was accepted. It now fails with ErrSyntax (commit).

Where vectors stop

The vectors say which schemas are accepted and which values every generated type must hold. They can't say how narrow a Go type is, since Go has no union or literal types and a json.RawMessage field would hold every sample. So the Go tests also read each fixture's generated declarations back with go/types and compare them with what's expected: struct fields and their types, union variants, enum constants. A fixture without expectations fails, so a new one can't go unchecked. Neither implementation's tests compare generated text, so formatting can change freely.

For how genever-go compares with other Go generators, the Go comparison runs it, go-jsonschema and oapi-codegen through the same probes every night: 18 values decoded into the type generated from a JSON Schema, and 7 into the type for an OpenAPI request body. I wrote genever-go, and only its results are tested.

In the run of November 11, 2026:

Tool Version JSON Schema probes OpenAPI probes
genever-go 0.1.0 18 / 18 7 / 7
go-jsonschema 0.24.1 13 / 18
oapi-codegen 2.8.2 (kin-openapi 0.152.0) 5 / 7

go-jsonschema's type doesn't keep null apart from an absent property, can't hold null as a member of a mixed enum, and decodes three values it should reject: a tuple with a string member, a oneOf branch with a property of the wrong type, and a patternProperties value of the wrong type. oapi-codegen's type decodes the tuple with a string member and doesn't keep null apart from absent in a mixed enum. Before kin-openapi 0.152.0, oapi-codegen's loader rejected the 3.1 document, so it scored 0 / 7.

Try it

`go
go get -tool github.com/JacobLey/leyman/apps/genever/go/cmd/genever@v0.1.0

//go:generate go tool genever openapi.yaml --package api --signed
package api
`

It needs Go 1.24 or later, as does the code it writes. The released modules keep replace directives pointing at each other's workspace copies, so a change to populate-files is tested against genever before either is tagged. go install refuses a module with replace directives, which is why the install line uses go get -tool: it ignores a dependency's replaces and pins the version in your go.mod.

The Go guide covers the options and how Go types differ from the TypeScript ones. If a schema is accepted by one implementation and rejected by the other, that's a bug in one of them, and the test vectors are where the fix starts.

title: velo: your music, in the terminal
description:
To listen to music while I work I used the browser, with a tab for each thing: one for lofi, one for a particular artist and one for the radio. Every switch pulled me out of the terminal, which is where I spend my day.

What bothered me most was something else, though: none of it felt like mine. It did not have my colours and it was not set up the way I like. I wanted to open it and feel at home with what I saw.

The closest thing I knew was gentle-stream, by Gentleman Programming. I liked its interface, but it generates music and I was looking for a player. The other piece was cliamp: I liked its interface too, and I was already listening to its radio.

That is how velo started: a player for the terminal that owes a lot to those two projects.

What it does

velo is a music player for the terminal. You point it at your folder, it indexes the library from your files' own tags, and you browse it by artist, album, track or genre.

This is a video in the original post.

  • Local library. The index lives in SQLite, refreshes in the background on every launch, and has fuzzy search across all of it.
  • Gapless playback. MP3, FLAC, M4A/AAC, OGG Vorbis, Opus and WAV, with no silence between one track and the next.
  • An editable queue. Append, reorder, remove and shuffle without stopping the music.
  • Internet radio. The Radio Browser directory, the cliamp channels, or any stream URL.
  • Subsonic servers. Navidrome, Airsonic or Gonic sync into the same index. Still in early access.
  • What you expect from a serious player. ReplayGain with clipping protection, bit-perfect mode, output device selection and the system's media keys.
  • Cover art, nine visualizers and thirteen themes. Or your terminal's own colours.

The keys are Vim's: j and k to move, / to search, enter to play. ? lists all of them.

Turn on the transparent background and velo lets your terminal's own show through. This is it on my desktop, with a lofi channel playing:

This is a video in the original post.

Favourites, playlists and history are kept in TOML files you can open and edit. And there is no telemetry: velo only contacts what you point it at, plus one request a day to GitHub to learn whether a newer version exists, which one line of configuration turns off.

What already existed

There are many terminal players and several are very good. The truth is I did not try most of them in depth. I looked at them as references while I designed velo, to see what each one solved and how.

One decision came out of that. Some of the best known, like ncmpcpp and rmpc, are MPD clients: before you hear a song you have to install, configure and keep a separate server running.

I wanted the opposite: one binary. You install it, tell it where your music is, and it plays. No daemon, no server and no account.

How it works inside

The audio callback only copies memory. The operating system asks velo for samples every few milliseconds, and if they arrive late you hear a click. So the expensive work (decoding, resampling, applying ReplayGain) happens on another thread, one buffer ahead. The two threads talk through a lock-free ring buffer. The callback measures how many samples are ready, copies them and fills the rest with silence. It does not allocate, take a lock or write a log.

Gapless means gapless. The next track is decoded before the current one ends and joined to it with no silence inserted. Lossy encoders add padding at the start and end of every file, and velo trims it at the seam. On a live album or a concept album, you can hear the difference.

One binary, for real. Every dependency had to pass that rule. SQLite is compiled in. Symphonia, the library that decodes the other formats, has no Opus decoder, so libopus is built statically. For media keys on Linux I chose a pure Rust D-Bus implementation, because the default one required a system library to be installed.

Remote servers go through a cache. A Subsonic track is downloaded once, untranscoded, and played from disk. That way seeking, gapless playback and ReplayGain work exactly as they do for a local file.

How I built it

The repository does not hide it, so I will say it myself: velo went from its first commit to version 1.0.0 in six days, with 479 commits and 75 published versions. I did not write those 70 thousand lines of Rust by hand. AI agents wrote them, with the same system I described in my AI dev stack.

What I did was direct. Every feature started as a document with numbered requirements that quote my own words, and every task was closed against those requirements. There are 21 of those documents in the repository's odd/tasks folder, in plain sight.

The code is not accepted on faith either. There are more than 1,200 tests, and a single script runs the formatter, the linter with warnings treated as errors, and every test. It is the same one continuous integration runs.

Not everything went to plan. velo was my first time with many of these technologies and with nearly every audio concept. Gapless, ReplayGain and bit-perfect were the most technical terms for me, and I did not fully understand what they implied. So when the agent proposed a scope I accepted it, and on top of that I asked for Subsonic servers, which I hardly use. It is in the project's first document, in my own words. Later there were moments when I did not know enough to question it, and I simply let it continue.

velo ended up bigger than I needed. That was not a bad thing: those features left the application more complete. But it made one thing clear to me: when you do not understand the subject, you stop directing and start approving.

Try it

velo runs on macOS and Linux. With Homebrew:

brew install alvaldes/tap/velo

Or with the install script, which verifies the checksum and does not ask for sudo:

curl -fsSL https://alvaldes.github.io/velo/install.sh | sh

Then run velo, press o and type the path to your music folder. On the site there is a player you can press play on before installing anything.

To see cover art you need a terminal that speaks the kitty, sixel or iTerm2 protocol. Windows is untested.

It is open source, under the MIT license. If something does not work or you have an idea for an improvement, open an issue in the repository.

title: Architecting Offline-First Invoicing Without a Backend Black Box
description:
Every freelancer has experienced the 'airplane mode panic.' You’re sitting in a coffee shop with spotty Wi-Fi, the client is ready to sign, and your SaaS-based invoicing tool is stuck on a spinning loading wheel, failing to authenticate against a remote server. It’s a failure of architectural philosophy: why should your ability to generate a PDF depend on a server halfway across the world?

When we started building Vanza Invoices, we decided to stop treating the browser and mobile device as thin clients. We inverted the model. The device is the source of truth; the cloud is optional, or completely irrelevant.

The Death of the 'Sync-Everything' Middleware

Most modern apps rely on a 'sync-everything' middleware that pipes data to a central database before reflecting it back to the UI. This introduces latency, subscription overhead, and catastrophic failure points when the connection drops.

We moved to a local-first storage architecture utilizing IndexedDB, wrapped in a reactive persistence layer. By treating the local storage as the primary database, the app achieves sub-10ms read/write operations. When a user creates an invoice, the data lives exactly where it was typed—on the device.

Here is the stack logic we implemented:

  • Persistence Layer: We leverage Dexie.js for a robust IndexedDB wrapper, allowing for complex queries without hitting a network request.
  • State Synchronization: Instead of REST/GraphQL calls, the UI binds directly to the local database change listeners. If an invoice is updated, the view refreshes automatically.
  • Asset Generation: PDFs are generated on-device using a worker thread to ensure the main UI thread remains buttery smooth during signature rendering and complex document assembly.

Solving the 'Zero-Middleman' PDF Problem

Generating a professional invoice typically happens on the server. You send JSON to an API, a server-side process (like Puppeteer or a specialized library) renders the PDF, and it’s piped back to you.

At Vanza, we stripped the middleman. By bringing the document engine to the client, we eliminated the need for a monthly SaaS subscription. There is no server cost to pass on to the user. We utilized specialized PDF generation primitives that execute natively in the browser/Capacitor environment. This allows for:

  • Privacy by Default: Your financial data never leaves your device unless you explicitly export it.
  • Instant Previews: Since we aren't waiting for a server round-trip, the document updates in real-time as you type.
  • Offline Signature Capture: Using a canvas-based touch handler, we capture high-fidelity vector signatures that are embedded directly into the final PDF buffer via the browser’s internal file system API.

The Capacitor Advantage

We chose React and Capacitor to bridge the gap between web speed and native reliability. By shipping the application as a bundled binary, we bypass the browser's aggressive cache-clearing policies. Your invoices are stored in the app’s private container on your OS, effectively making them as durable as any native file.

For developers considering this route, the biggest hurdle isn't writing the code—it's managing the data schema migrations locally. Since you don't have a backend to migrate, your local database schema must be versioned within the app binary itself. We rely on a strict migration strategy triggered on initial app startup, ensuring that as we add new invoice fields, older data structures are upgraded seamlessly without loss.

Why We Built This

We built Vanza Invoices because the freelance economy is tired of paying rent for the privilege of creating a simple invoice. By leveraging local-first storage and offloading the computation to the hardware you already own, we’ve created a tool that lasts as long as your phone does, with zero dependency on our servers.

If you are a developer or a freelancer looking for a tool that respects your privacy and works without a signal, check out our implementation on the Google Play Store. It is a testament to what is possible when you stop building for the cloud and start building for the machine in your pocket.

title: Designing a 2-Tap UX for Gyms: Why Speed Beats Social Feeds
description:
Sweat dripping onto a smartphone screen under flickering gym fluorescent lights is the ultimate usability stress test. When you are between heavy sets, exhausted, and running on a strict rest timer, you do not want to scroll through a social feed, dismiss notification badges, or wait three seconds for a cloud round-trip to log your workout. Yet, modern fitness applications have increasingly bloated into social media clones packed with algorithmic feeds, leaderboards, and heavy animations.

At VanzaLabs, we asked a fundamental engineering question: what if a workout app behaved more like a calculator and less like Instagram? That core thesis led us to design a radical 2-tap interaction model for SPOT, our minimalist fitness tracking tool engineered specifically for high-intensity environments.

The Problem: Latency and Friction in the Iron Zone

Most mobile developers optimize for engagement loops—metrics like session length, daily active time, and ad impressions. In a gym, those metrics are actively toxic to the user experience. High-intensity training requires high cognitive focus. Every millisecond of UI latency or unnecessary tap introduces friction that breaks flow state.

Traditional fitness apps suffer from three architectural bottlenecks:

  1. Cloud Dependency: Requiring an active API round-trip to persist set weights and reps.
  2. UI Bloat: Navigation hierarchies buried three layers deep behind tabs for social sharing, messaging, and community challenges.
  3. Battery & Thermal Throttling: Complex UI frameworks rendering heavy lists and animations, causing devices to heat up in pockets.

When we prototyped our initial iterations, we measured time-to-log. Traditional apps averaged 7 to 12 taps and roughly 4.2 seconds of cognitive overhead per set. For a workout with 30 sets, that translates to over two minutes wasted purely on fighting user interfaces.

The Engineering Solution: Local-First and Zero Middleman

To achieve a frictionless 2-tap UX, we had to rethink the client architecture from the storage layer up. We adopted a strict local-first paradigm.

1. Zero Middleman Servers with Local SQLite

Instead of routing every set logged through an API gateway, session data is written directly to an embedded local database using optimized SQLite queries. We use lightweight abstractions to ensure write operations resolve in under 5 milliseconds. There are no middleman servers blocking the main thread waiting for network acknowledgments.

// Simplified local-first persistence layer
class WorkoutRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val localDatabase: SpotDatabase
) {
    suspend fun logSetQuickly(exerciseId: String, weight: Float, reps: Int) {
        val setEntity = SetEntity(
            timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis(),
            exerciseId = exerciseId,
            weight = weight,
            reps = reps
        )
        // Direct disk write with immediate UI state emission
        localDatabase.setDao().insert(setEntity)
    }
}

2. Optimistic UI and State Reductions

In SPOT, the UI state updates instantaneously. The user taps the weight, taps the reps, and the database write happens asynchronously in the background. If the app is closed abruptly, the local SQLite transaction log guarantees durability without needing complex conflict resolution algorithms.

3. Battery and Privacy Benefits

By minimizing network calls, we drastically reduced radio wake-ups, preserving battery life during long training sessions. Furthermore, because workout data stays local by default, user privacy is inherently protected. There is no telemetry profiling your squat PRs to serve targeted fitness supplements.

Practical Takeaways for Builders

If you are building tools for high-stakes, real-world environments—whether it is fitness trackers, inventory scanners, or point-of-sale systems—consider these architectural rules:

  • Measure the Thumb Zone: Design for single-handed use under physical fatigue. Vital actions must sit comfortably within the natural thumb arc.
  • Local-First is King: Never block user input on network availability. Gym basements famously have terrible cellular reception.
  • Kill the Feed: Strip away any feature that does not directly serve the core utility of the product. Speed is a feature.

Experience the Speed

Building tools that respect user time and cognitive load remains a core engineering philosophy for our team. If you want to experience an interface built entirely around raw utility and ultra-fast interactions, try out SPOT available now on the Google Play Store.

To explore more developer-focused tools and open experiments from our team, check out VanzaLabs.

title: Rust: Day 3, Arithmatic
description:
Hello there developer community. This is my second day learning rust so I decided to try something simple. How do I add 20 and 30 together. So this is me trying to figure that out. I encounted some issues with the "Unique" variable types, Like what the hell is i32. But anyway. This is my first attempt.

fn main() {
    let a i32: 20;
    let b i32: 30;

    println!("{}", a + b);
}

This is an example of apparently the wrong thing. Because to assign types you need to use let a: i32 = 20; but I didn't know this by the time I was learning this. The correct method of doing this is below.

fn main() {
    let a: i32 = 20;
    let b: i32 = 30;

    println!("{}", a + b);
}

And this program outputs:

50

Next post I am going to attempt conditional logic and function calling so well yeah, stay tuned. And lastly, I hope my suffering brings comfort to those who as well are learning rust that I may help you in your journey.

title: Responsive Design and Mobile Performance Fixes That Make a Real Difference
description:
Most "mobile problems" on websites come from a small set of repeat offenders: oversized images, layout jumps, unreadable text, tiny tap targets and too much JavaScript. The good news is that none of them need a full rewrite. You can fix most of them on an existing site, one change at a time.

This guide walks through twelve fixes, each with code you can adapt. It is ordered roughly from the easiest wins to fix issues to the more involved ones, and ends with how to measure the results so you know the work paid off.

Why mobile deserves its own attention

A phone is not just a small desktop. It usually has a slower CPU, a less stable network, a touch screen instead of a mouse, and a user who is often distracted or in a hurry. A page that feels fine on your development laptop over fast Wi-Fi can feel sluggish on a mid-range phone over a mobile connection.

Google's Core Web Vitals give us three useful measures of that experience:

LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): how quickly the main content appears.
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): how much the layout jumps around while loading.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint): how quickly the page responds when someone taps or types.

Every fix below maps to at least one of these, or to plain usability.

  1. Start with the viewport tag

Without it, mobile browsers render your page at a desktop-width canvas and then shrink it down, which makes everything tiny.

html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Avoid adding maximum-scale=1 or user-scalable=no. They block pinch-zoom, which is an accessibility problem for people with low vision.

  1. Serve the right image size to each device

A 2400px-wide image on a 390px-wide phone wastes bandwidth and slows down LCP. Use srcset and sizes so the browser can pick the best file for the screen.

How it works: srcset lists the available files and their real widths. sizes tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed at different viewport sizes. The browser combines that with the device's pixel density and chooses a file.

Where your build pipeline allows it, also offer modern formats such as WebP or AVIF using the element:

Browsers that don't support a format simply fall back to the next option.

  1. Always set image dimensions to prevent layout shift

The width and height attributes in the examples above let the browser reserve the correct amount of space before the file downloads. Without them, text jumps down when the image finally appears, which is exactly what CLS measures.

Pair the attributes with this CSS so images remain fluid:

css
img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

The browser uses the attributes to work out the aspect ratio, and the CSS lets the image shrink to fit its container. The same idea applies to embedded videos and iframes. The aspect-ratio property is a clean way to reserve space for them:

css
.video-embed {
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  width: 100%;
}
  1. Lazy-load below the fold, prioritize above it

A common mistake is lazy-loading everything, including the largest image at the top of the page. That delays LCP. Treat the hero or main product image as a priority and lazy-load the rest.

  1. Use fluid typography instead of a pile of breakpoints

clamp() lets text scale smoothly between a minimum and a maximum size, so you don't need a font-size rule at every breakpoint.

css
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.15;
}

body {
  font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.125rem);
  line-height: 1.6;
}

Keep body text at around 16px or larger on phones so nobody has to zoom to read it. Using rem units rather than px also respects the user's browser font-size settings.

  1. Build layouts that adapt without media queries

CSS Grid's auto-fit creates a card layout that reflows on its own as the container changes size:

css
.cards {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 260px), 1fr));
}

The min(100%, 260px) part is important. Without it, a column with a 260px minimum can overflow a very narrow screen and cause accidental horizontal scrolling, one of the most common mobile bugs.

For simple one-dimensional layouts, Flexbox with wrapping does a similar job:

css
.row {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.row > * {
  flex: 1 1 240px;
}
  1. Use container queries for reusable components

Media queries respond to the viewport. But a card component might sit in a wide main column on one page and a narrow sidebar on another. Container queries let the component respond to the space it actually has.

css
.card-wrapper {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: 0.75rem;
}

@container (min-width: 480px) {
  .card {
    grid-template-columns: 160px 1fr;
  }
}

This makes components more portable and reduces the number of one-off overrides in your stylesheet. Container queries are supported in all current major browsers.

  1. Make tap targets big enough

Small links and buttons are frustrating on touchscreens, and they cause mis-taps. A good rule is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels. WCAG 2.2 sets 24px as a minimum for a pass, and Apple's and Google's guidelines suggest larger.

css
button,
.nav a {
  min-height: 44px;
  min-width: 44px;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
}

Leave some space between neighbouring targets too. A row of tightly packed text links in a footer is a classic problem. Padding the links, instead of only increasing the gap, enlarges the tappable area.

  1. Tame fonts

Web fonts are a frequent cause of slow first paint and of text that flashes or jumps.

css
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-var.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 100 900;
  font-display: swap;
}
html
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

Use font-display: swap so text appears right away in a fallback font.
Preload only the one or two font files used above the fold.
Serve WOFF2 and limit the weights and character sets to what you actually use.
Consider a variable font if you use several weights, since one file can replace many.

  1. Control third-party scripts and JavaScript weight

On mobile, JavaScript is often the biggest cost, because it has to be downloaded, parsed and executed on a slower CPU. It is also the main driver of poor INP.

html
<script src="/analytics.js" defer></script>
<script src="/chat-widget.js" async></script>

Practical steps:

Use defer for scripts that need the DOM and async for independent ones.
Audit your tags. Old tracking pixels, unused chat widgets and duplicate analytics are very common.
Split large bundles so each page loads only what it needs.
Break up long tasks. If a click handler does heavy work, yield back to the browser so the interface can update:

js
button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  showSpinner();
  // Let the browser paint before heavy work
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
  doHeavyWork();
});
  1. Respect user preferences

Responsive design is also about the person using the device, not only the screen size. Two media queries cost almost nothing and help a lot:

css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --bg: #0f1115;
    --text: #e8eaed;
  }
}

Heavy animations can be uncomfortable for some users and drain battery. A dark theme also helps people who use their phone at night.

  1. Prevent horizontal scrolling and fix the usual suspects

Sideways scrolling on a phone makes a site feel broken. Common causes and quick fixes:

css
/* Long words or URLs breaking the layout */
p, li {
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

/* Wide tables */
.table-wrap {
  overflow-x: auto;
}

/* Elements wider than the screen */
*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

To find the culprit, open DevTools in responsive mode at 320px width and look for the element that extends past the edge. Avoid hiding the problem with overflow-x: hidden on body as a first resort, since that can mask real layout bugs and break sticky positioning.

Measure before and after

Fixes only matter if you can see their effect. Use a mix of lab and real-world tools:

Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools, with mobile throttling turned on, for a quick lab test.
PageSpeed Insights to see real-user field data (Core Web Vitals) when your site has enough traffic.
Chrome DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling to find long tasks.
A real mid-range phone on a mobile connection. Emulators hide a lot.

Change one thing at a time and re-test, so you know what helped. Lab scores fluctuate between runs, so compare trends rather than single numbers.

Common mistakes to avoid
Lazy-loading the main hero image.
Using fixed pixel widths on containers.
Hiding content on mobile instead of designing it properly for small screens.
Disabling zoom.
Loading every font weight "just in case".
Testing only at your own device's screen size.
Quick checklist
Viewport meta tag present
Responsive images with srcset, plus width and height
Hero image prioritized, others lazy-loaded
Fluid type with clamp()
Flexible grids with no horizontal scrolling at 320px
Tap targets at least 44px
Fonts preloaded, with font-display: swap
Scripts deferred and audited
Reduced-motion and dark-mode preferences respected
Tested on a real phone
Final thoughts

Good mobile performance rarely comes from one big trick. It comes from many small, sensible decisions: send fewer bytes, reserve space for what's coming, keep the main thread free, and make everything easy to read and tap. Start with the quick wins at the top of this list, measure, and work down.

Which of these has made the biggest difference on your projects? Let me know in the comments.
